aq-108articul-105.blurb: A reply to the master general of the Dominican order, who had forwarded a list of one hundred and eight propositions excerpted from another friar's teaching and asked whether each could be held. Thomas answers them in order, marking what is true, what is false, what is merely badly worded, and what he would not himself say. A record of how he judged other men's formulations when he had no room to argue.

aq-1cor-56.blurb: Lectures on the first letter to Corinth, given as part of Thomas's course on the whole Pauline corpus. He follows Paul through the factions at Corinth, the case of the incestuous man, marriage and virginity, food offered to idols, the conduct of the assembly, the institution of the Supper, the gifts and the primacy of charity, and the argument for the resurrection of the body in chapter fifteen. The eucharistic and resurrection sections are the fullest.

aq-1thess-62.blurb: A short exposition of the first letter to the Thessalonians, read as instruction to a young church under pressure. The commentary turns on the fourth chapter, where Paul answers the community's anxiety about those who have already died, and on the coming of the Lord like a thief in the night. Brief throughout, with Thomas's divisions of the text carrying much of the weight.

aq-1tim-64.blurb: An exposition of the first pastoral letter, taken as Paul's instruction to a bishop about the ordering of a church: the correction of false teachers, public prayer, the qualities required in bishops and deacons, the treatment of widows and elders, and the warning about the love of money. Thomas reads the letter as legislation for the clergy, and much of the commentary is practical rather than speculative.

aq-2cor-57.blurb: Lectures on the second Corinthian letter, the most personal of Paul's, in which the apostle defends his ministry against rivals. Thomas follows the argument on the letter that kills and the Spirit that gives life, the treasure held in earthen vessels, the collection for the saints at Jerusalem, and the account of the thorn in the flesh and the rapture to the third heaven, which he treats at length.

aq-2thess-63.blurb: A brief exposition of the second letter to Thessalonica, most of it spent on the second chapter, where Paul describes the falling away and the man of sin who must come before the day of the Lord. Thomas sets out the readings available to him for the restraining force and declines to date what Paul left undated. The closing rule that the idle should not eat receives a short treatment.

aq-2tim-65.blurb: An exposition of the letter presented as Paul's last, written to Timothy from prison. Thomas takes up the charge to guard the deposit of teaching, the images of the soldier and the athlete, the description of the last days, the statement that all Scripture is inspired and useful for teaching, and the final commission to preach in season and out.

aq-30articuli-106.blurb: Three pages answering a list of thirty propositions sent by a Dominican lector at Lodi. The questions are of the kind a working teacher runs into, and Thomas replies to each in a sentence or two, conceding some, correcting others, and occasionally noting that a question has been put in a way that cannot be answered as it stands.

aq-36articuli-108.blurb: A second and longer set of replies to the same Dominican lector at Lodi, this time on thirty-six articles. The form is the one Thomas used for all such requests, question followed by short determination, but the answers here run further than in the shorter list, and several touch on matters he treats at length elsewhere.

aq-43articuli-107.blurb: Answers to forty-three questions put by the master general of the order, a shorter companion to the reply on one hundred and eight articles sent to the same correspondent. Each article gets a determination of a few lines. Read together, the two sets show what a Dominican superior thought worth referring to Thomas and how quickly Thomas was willing to settle it.

aq-6articulis-109.blurb: A page of replies to six questions sent by a Dominican of Besancon. The shortest of the several lists of articles Thomas was asked to adjudicate, and the least systematic, but of a piece with the rest: a question stated flatly, a determination given in a line or two, and no argument beyond what the answer requires.

aq-abiciamus-126.blurb: A university sermon on the words of Romans thirteen, let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light. Like the rest of Thomas's surviving preaching it comes down as a report taken by a hearer, and it is short. The text is the sermon's whole frame; Thomas divides the verse and preaches the divisions.

aq-adbernardu-114.blurb: A single page written to the abbot of Monte Cassino, who had sent Thomas a passage from Gregory the Great that seemed to make divine foreknowledge destroy the freedom of the man foreknown. Thomas answers with a distinction about how God's knowledge stands to what is future for us, and returns the passage read in a way that leaves free choice intact.

aq-attendite-137.blurb: A sermon on the warning of Matthew seven, beware of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing. Three pages, surviving as a hearer's record of what was preached. Thomas takes the marks by which a true teacher may be told from a deceiver, but this is preaching rather than the sort of polemic he conducts in his disputed and controversial writings.

aq-avemaria-150.blurb: Short conferences on the angelic salutation, taken down from Thomas's preaching and belonging with his series on the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the commandments. He goes through the greeting clause by clause, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, blessed art thou among women, treating each as a statement about what God has done in Mary rather than as devotional praise.

aq-beata-143.blurb: A sermon on the psalm verse, happy the nation whose God is the Lord. Two or three pages, preserved as a report of preaching rather than as a text Thomas wrote out. The verse supplies the divisions and the sermon keeps to them, which is most of what can be said of it.

aq-beati-142.blurb: Preaching on the psalm verse, happy those who dwell in your house, they will praise you for ever. Like the other surviving sermons it is short and comes down secondhand, taken from the mouth of the preacher rather than composed on the page. The house of the verse gives the sermon its structure.

aq-beatus-144.blurb: A sermon on the psalm verse, happy the man whose help is from you, who has set ascents in his heart. Two pages, recorded by a hearer. Thomas takes the ascent of the verse as his frame and preaches on it, and there is little here beyond the sermon itself.

aq-cajohn-72.blurb: The John volume of the chain of patristic comment Thomas assembled on the four gospels. The method is the same throughout: the gospel is taken a few verses at a time and glossed with passages from the fathers, each named, so that the running commentary is made entirely of other men's words. The John volume leans heavily on Augustine and Chrysostom, with Greek authors Thomas had obtained in new translations.

aq-caluke-71.blurb: Luke's volume in the gospel chain, the longest of the four. Thomas quotes Greek and Latin fathers verse by verse, giving each an attribution, and arranges the excerpts so that they answer one another and carry the exposition forward. The infancy chapters and the parables peculiar to Luke draw the fullest gatherings of patristic material.

aq-camark-70.blurb: Mark's volume in the gospel chain, and the shortest, since the gospel is short and much of what the fathers said about it they said while commenting on Matthew. Thomas still supplies a running commentary of named patristic excerpts for every passage, and the volume is worth having for the Greek writers on Mark whom Latin readers had not previously seen.

aq-camatt-69.blurb: Matthew's volume, the first of the four to be compiled and the one undertaken at the request of Urban the Fourth. The gospel is broken into short lemmas, each followed by excerpts from the fathers with the source named, so that the exposition is a chain of authorities rather than Thomas's own comment. The Sermon on the Mount attracts the densest gathering.

aq-coelum-129.blurb: A single page of preaching on the saying that heaven and earth will pass away but my words will not pass away. Recorded by a hearer rather than written out by Thomas. Too brief to do more than divide the text and press it home.

aq-col-61.blurb: An exposition of the letter to Colossae, given with the rest of the Pauline course. The commentary is organised around the first chapter's account of Christ as image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation, and head of the body, which Thomas takes as the letter's doctrinal core and reads against any account that would make Christ one among the heavenly powers. The later chapters on observances and household duties go briskly.

aq-contradoct-97.blurb: A defence of the right of young men to enter religious life without delay, written against those who argued that they should be held back until older or better tested. Thomas answers the objections one by one, including the charge that a vow taken young is rash, and argues that counselling delay in a good is itself a harm. One of the pieces belonging to the Paris quarrel over the mendicant orders.

aq-contraimpu-95.blurb: Thomas's answer to the secular masters at Paris who attacked the mendicant orders, William of Saint-Amour above all. The questions are the ones the quarrel turned on: whether religious may teach, whether they may live by begging, whether manual labour is commanded, whether an order may be founded for study or preaching. He argues from law and Scripture rather than speculation, and the polemical edge is unusually visible.

aq-corpuschri-121.blurb: The office for the feast of Corpus Christi in the version beginning Sacerdos in aeternum, with its antiphons, responsories, lessons, and the hymns sung at the hours. Thomas is traditionally named as its compiler at Urban the Fourth's request. A second office, opening Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum, also circulates under his name, and the relation between the two is disputed.

aq-credo-147.blurb: Conferences on the Apostles' Creed, taken down from Thomas's preaching to ordinary hearers and preserved in Latin. He goes through the twelve articles in order, from belief in one God to life everlasting, giving under each a plain account of what is held, the reasons that support it, and the errors it excludes. Catechesis rather than disputation, and the simplest sustained statement of his theology.

aq-ct-90.blurb: An unfinished summary of Christian teaching addressed to Reginald of Piperno and organised on the three theological virtues. The treatise on faith is complete and runs from the Trinity through creation, the fall, the incarnation, and the last things; the treatise on hope breaks off early in the exposition of the Lord's Prayer, and the part on charity was never written. Shorter and more continuous than the Summa, with no objections and replies.

aq-deaeternit-99.blurb: A single page arguing that a world both created and without beginning involves no contradiction, written against theologians who held that the eternity of the world could be refuted by reason. Thomas holds that the world did begin, on the authority of faith, but denies that the beginning can be demonstrated, and shows that being caused and being everlasting are compatible. Aimed at fellow Christians rather than at Aristotelians.

aq-dean-79.blurb: A line by line exposition of Aristotle's three books on the soul, and not to be confused with the disputed questions on the same subject. Thomas follows the text through the opinions of earlier thinkers, the definition of soul as the act of an organic body, the nutritive and sensitive powers, the account of sensation, and the difficult chapters on intellect in the third book, where his case against the Averroist reading is made from within the commentary.

aq-dearticuli-102.blurb: A brief handbook written for an archbishop who had asked for something usable: first the articles of faith, listed as they concern the divinity and then the humanity of Christ, each paired with the errors that deny it, then the seven sacraments with their matter, form, minister, and the defects that can occur in them. Practical instruction for clergy rather than argument.

aq-decael-76.blurb: An exposition of Aristotle's books on the heavens, treating the perfection of the universe, the nature of the fifth body of which the heavens are made, the claim that the world is one and complete, weight and lightness, and the elements. The commentary is unfinished and breaks off partway through the third book. Read for Thomas handling a cosmology he took seriously without treating it as a matter of faith.

aq-decemprae-149.blurb: Conferences on the ten commandments, from the same course of preaching as the series on the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. Thomas takes the precepts in order, explains what each forbids and what it requires, and works through cases: what honouring parents obliges, how far killing and stealing extend, how the sabbath precept stands in the new law. Moral instruction pitched at ordinary hearers.

aq-decretalem-101.blurb: A short exposition of two decretals of the Fourth Lateran Council, undertaken at the request of an archdeacon. The first is a creedal text and gives Thomas occasion to gloss its clauses on the Trinity, creation, and the sacrament of the altar; the second condemns the trinitarian teaching of Joachim of Fiore. A rare instance of Thomas commenting on canon law.

aq-dedivnom-88.blurb: A commentary on the Dionysian treatise about the names given to God, which Thomas read as a serious authority and took chapter by chapter: the good, being, life, wisdom, the one, and the question whether evil has any nature at all. Much of the labour goes into rendering a Neoplatonic text in terms he could use, and it is here that his account of participation and of the analogy of names is worked out at length.

aq-deemp-110.blurb: A single page answering a question from a lector about merchants who sell goods on credit at one price and for cash at another. Thomas distinguishes charging for time, which is usury, from a price that reflects a genuine difference in the thing sold or a real risk borne, and gives a rule the questioner could actually apply.

aq-deente-92.blurb: Six pages on what essence is and how it is found in different kinds of being: in composite substances, where it takes in matter and form; in the separate substances and the soul, where Thomas argues that essence and existence remain distinct and that this distinction is what keeps them creatures; and in accidents, which have essence only in a qualified sense. Generally placed among his early writings, and the shortest statement of the metaphysics underlying the rest.

aq-deforma-104.blurb: On the words used in sacramental absolution, written to settle whether the priest should say I absolve you or should instead pray that God absolve. Thomas defends the indicative form, arguing from what a sacrament is and from the way the other sacraments are administered, and answers the objection that the older prayers of petition show the indicative to be an innovation.

aq-degen-77.blurb: An exposition of Aristotle on coming to be and passing away, distinguishing substantial change from alteration, growth, and mere mixture, and taking up the action of one body on another and the combination of the elements. The commentary is unfinished and stops within the first book. Of interest chiefly for Thomas's treatment of matter and of what does and does not survive a substantial change.

aq-deheb-87.blurb: A commentary on the short Boethian treatise asking how substances can be good in what they are without being the good itself. Thomas takes the axioms one at a time and uses the question to set out the difference between what a thing is and the act by which it is, and the sense in which creatures are good by participation while God is good by essence. Five pages, and dense.

aq-deiudiciis-113.blurb: A page-long reply on whether a Christian may make use of astrology. Thomas allows that the heavenly bodies act on bodies, and so on the dispositions that incline men, and permits judgments about weather, health, and the like; he denies that they determine choices, and so rejects predictions of human acts and any consultation that amounts to seeking hidden knowledge from another source.

aq-demem-81.blurb: A commentary on Aristotle's short treatise on memory and recollection, one of the pieces of the Parva naturalia that Thomas expounded. It treats what memory is, its dependence on the image and on the sense of time, the difference between simply remembering and deliberately hunting for what has been forgotten, and the order among images that makes recollection possible.

aq-demix-116.blurb: A single page on an old problem: when elements combine into a compound, do they remain in it or not? Thomas rejects both the view that they persist unchanged, which would leave the compound a heap, and the view that they are destroyed, which would leave it without their qualities, and argues that their powers remain in the compound while their forms do not.

aq-demotu-117.blurb: A short piece on the movement of the heart, asking what kind of motion it is, given that it is neither voluntary nor obviously forced, and how a motion continuous through the whole of life can be natural to the organ. Thomas answers within an Aristotelian physics and refers the motion to the soul as the principle of the living body.

aq-deoccultis-118.blurb: A reply about the powers in natural things that produce effects with no evident cause, the magnet being the standing example. Thomas argues that such powers belong to the forms of the bodies themselves and are given with the influence of the heavens, and that there is no need to explain them by hidden agreements with spirits, which is what the question was really asking.

aq-deperfect-96.blurb: A treatise on where the perfection of the Christian life lies, written in the course of the Paris quarrel about the religious orders. Thomas argues that perfection consists essentially in charity, that the counsels are instruments of charity rather than its substance, and that bishops and religious stand in a state of perfection in different ways. The later part answers the charge that voluntary poverty and the religious state are novelties.

aq-deprinnat-91.blurb: Six pages introducing the vocabulary of Aristotelian natural philosophy for a beginner: matter, form, and privation as the principles of change; the difference between coming to be simply and coming to be in a certain respect; and the four causes, with an account of how causes may be prior to one another and how the same thing can be cause and effect in different orders. Written plainly, with no objections and replies.

aq-deratio-100.blurb: Written for a correspondent in Antioch who had to argue with Muslims, Greeks, and Armenians and asked how to proceed with people who would not grant the same authorities. Thomas answers that the articles of faith cannot be demonstrated and should not be defended as though they could, then treats the Trinity, the incarnation, the Eucharist, predestination, and purgatory in a way meant to show that they involve no absurdity.

aq-deregimine-115.blurb: A reply to a noblewoman who had put a series of practical questions of government to Thomas: whether she might tax the Jews of her lands and on what terms, what to do with money got by usury, whether taxes may be levied on subjects and when, and how officials should be appointed and punished. The answers are cast as rulings rather than arguments, and the treatment of the Jewish communities is severe.

aq-deregno-94.blurb: A treatise on kingship addressed to a king of Cyprus, arguing that rule by one man is best, distinguishing the king from the tyrant, and asking what reward could be adequate to a good king. The second part turns to the founding of a city, the goods a ruler must provide, and the relation between temporal rule and the priesthood. The work is unfinished, and the continuation printed with it is another hand's.

aq-desecreto-111.blurb: A determination on the obligation of secrecy, produced together with others in the course of the order's business: whether a superior may command a brother to disclose what he learned in confidence, and whether the brother is bound to answer. The distinctions concern what can be commanded by obedience and where the bond of secrecy stands against it.

aq-desen-80.blurb: An exposition of Aristotle on sensation and the objects of sense, the longer of the two Parva naturalia commentaries Thomas produced. It covers the sense organs and their relation to the elements, colour, sound, odour, flavour, and touch, the question whether sensible qualities and bodies are divisible without limit, and how several senses can be at work at once.

aq-desortibus-112.blurb: On the drawing of lots, written for a correspondent who wanted to know when the practice is legitimate. Thomas sorts the cases: lots cast to divide property, lots cast to settle who shall hold an office, and lots cast to learn what is hidden or what is to come. The first two he allows within limits; the last he treats as an attempt to force an answer from a cause that owes none.

aq-desubstant-93.blurb: An unfinished treatise on the angels, beginning with what the philosophers held about separate substances, Plato and Aristotle first, then Avicebron and the later Platonists, correcting each in turn. Thomas then sets out what is to be held on the authority of Scripture: the number and orders of the angels, their knowledge and will, their creation, and the fall of some of them. It stops before the treatment is complete.

aq-detrin-86.blurb: An exposition of the opening of Boethius on the Trinity that turns into something larger. Thomas asks how the mind knows God at all, whether the divine can be the object of a human science, and, in the fifth and sixth questions, how the speculative sciences divide into natural philosophy, mathematics, and divine science, and by what degree of abstraction each proceeds. Incomplete, and the questions on method are the part most often read.

aq-deunitate-98.blurb: Five pages against the position that all men share a single separate intellect, held at Paris by masters reading Aristotle through Averroes. Thomas argues first that the position is not Aristotle's, going through the text of the De anima, then that it is false in itself, and finally that it destroys any ground for saying that this particular man understands. The tone is sharper than anywhere else in his writing.

aq-ecceego-130.blurb: A page of preaching on the prophecy quoted in the gospels, behold I send my messenger before your face. A hearer's record of a sermon rather than a composed text. The verse supplies the divisions and the sermon keeps to them, in the manner of the rest of the surviving preaching.

aq-eccerex-128.blurb: Preaching on the words behold your king comes to you, three pages long and preserved as a report taken down by someone who heard it. Thomas divides the text and draws out the manner of the king's coming. Short, occasional, and of a piece with the other sermons that survive under his name.

aq-emitte-134.blurb: A single page on the psalm verse, send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth. Recorded from Thomas's preaching rather than written by him. Brief enough that the divisions of the verse are most of what has come down.

aq-eph-59.blurb: An exposition of the letter to Ephesus, read as Paul's fullest statement about the church. Thomas takes the opening chapters on election, on the reconciliation of Jew and gentile into one body, and on the gifts given for the building up of that body, then the moral chapters on the new man, the household, and the armour of God. The treatment of Christ as head of the church is the doctrinal centre.

aq-eth-83.blurb: A commentary on the whole of the Nicomachean Ethics, following Aristotle's text closely and without the theological additions a reader might expect. It covers happiness as the end of human life, virtue as a mean, the particular virtues, voluntariness and choice, justice, the intellectual virtues, incontinence, pleasure, friendship at length, and the return to contemplation at the end. Thomas expounds Aristotle here as Aristotle, leaving the corrections to be made elsewhere.

aq-exiit-132.blurb: A sermon on the parable's opening, a sower went out to sow his seed, running to a few pages and surviving as a hearer's record. Thomas works from the parable and the explanation given with it, taking the kinds of ground as the kinds of hearer. Preaching, not exegesis of the sort found in his gospel commentaries.

aq-gal-58.blurb: An exposition of Galatians, the letter in which Paul defends his gospel against those requiring circumcision. Thomas follows the autobiographical opening, the confrontation with Peter at Antioch, which he treats carefully because Augustine and Jerome had read it differently, the argument that the law cannot justify, the allegory of the two covenants, and the closing contrast between the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit.

aq-germinet-141.blurb: Preaching on the words let the earth bring forth. Four pages, taken down by a hearer rather than composed by Thomas on the page. He divides the verse and preaches from it in the manner of the other surviving sermons; the occasion on which it was given is not evident from the text alone.

aq-graecorum-103.blurb: Written at the pope's request on a dossier of Greek patristic texts assembled for the negotiations with the Eastern church. Thomas takes the passages that had been urged as evidence against Latin teaching and argues that the fathers, read with attention to how Greek and Latin usage differ, do not say what they were being made to say. The topics are the procession of the Spirit, the primacy of the Roman see, purgatory, and unleavened bread.

aq-heb-68.blurb: An exposition of Hebrews, which Thomas read as Pauline and as the letter that treats Christ's priesthood most fully. The commentary follows the argument for Christ's superiority to the angels and to Moses, the priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, the comparison of the old covenant's sacrifices with the one offering, and the chapter on faith and its examples. The christology is the reason to come to it.

aq-hicest-45.blurb: An inaugural lecture given on taking up a chair, built on the words this is the book of the commandments of God. Thomas uses the text to commend Scripture and to lay out the division of the sacred books, Old Testament and New, with an account of what each part contains and why the order stands as it does. A short piece, and formal in the way its occasion required.

aq-homo-fecit-136.blurb: A sermon on the parable of the man who made a great supper and invited many. Three pages, preserved as a report of preaching. Thomas takes the invitation, the excuses, and the gathering of the poor from the highways in turn, and does not stray far from the text he is expounding.

aq-homoerat-138.blurb: Preaching on the gospel opening, there was a certain rich man, over four pages and recorded by a hearer rather than written out. Thomas divides the text and presses it in the ordinary way of his sermons. It is preaching for a particular day whose identity the text alone does not fix.

aq-hymns-120.blurb: The eucharistic hymns written for the office of Corpus Christi and traditionally given to Thomas: Pange lingua with the Tantum ergo that closes it, Verbum supernum with O salutaris hostia, Sacris solemniis, and the sequence Lauda Sion. Adoro te devote is printed with them and has long been ascribed to him, though that ascription is not secure. Three pages of verse.

aq-immensa-123.blurb: The sermon read within the office of Corpus Christi, opening with the boundless benefits of divine generosity, on the institution of the sacrament and what the feast was established to commemorate. A single page, belonging with the other office material that comes down under Thomas's name.

aq-inveni-139.blurb: A short sermon on the psalm verse, I have found David my servant, with my holy oil I have anointed him. Two pages, surviving as a hearer's record. The verse is divided and preached, and the sermon does not extend beyond its text.

aq-ioan-53.blurb: The first half of Thomas's lectures on John, covering chapters one through eight. The exposition of the prologue is the longest continuous treatment of the Word in his writings and answers a long list of misreadings of in the beginning was the Word. The lectures then run through Cana, Nicodemus, the woman at the well, the discourse on the bread of life, and the disputes in the temple. Taken down from his teaching by a hearer.

aq-ioan-54.blurb: The second half of the John lectures, chapters nine to twenty-one. It covers the man born blind, the good shepherd, the raising of Lazarus, then the long farewell discourse and the prayer of chapter seventeen, which occupies a large part of the volume, before the passion and resurrection narratives. The christology and the treatment of the Spirit's mission are what a reader comes here for.

aq-isaiah-49.blurb: A literal exposition of Isaiah, working through the prophecy verse by verse with attention to the historical sense before the spiritual. Some manuscripts carry short marginal collations gathering scriptural texts on the themes as they arise. It is generally counted among the earliest of Thomas's scriptural works and reads as a young lecturer's course rather than as a mature commentary.

aq-jerem-47.blurb: A running exposition of Jeremiah, brief on each verse and concerned first with the letter: the call of the prophet, the oracles against Judah, the confrontations with the false prophets, and the material on the new covenant. Like the exposition of Isaiah it belongs with Thomas's early lecturing on the Old Testament, and it does not linger.

aq-job-50.blurb: An exposition of Job read strictly according to the letter, on the ground that the spiritual sense had already been supplied by Gregory the Great. Thomas takes the book as an argument about divine providence: whether God governs human affairs, and how the suffering of the just is compatible with that government. The speeches of the friends are treated as positions to be examined, and the answer from the whirlwind as the resolution.

aq-lam-48.blurb: A short exposition of Lamentations, taken verse by verse and mostly literal, following the sequence of the alphabetic poems on the destruction of Jerusalem. It belongs with the expositions of Isaiah and Jeremiah among Thomas's early Old Testament lecturing, and it keeps close to the text throughout.

aq-lauda-125.blurb: Preaching on a prophetic call to praise and rejoice. Two pages, recorded from a sermon rather than composed as a text. The verse gives the divisions and the sermon holds to them, as with the rest of the preaching that survives under Thomas's name.

aq-libcaus-89.blurb: A commentary on the anonymous Book of Causes, a set of propositions on the first cause and the separate intelligences that had circulated as Aristotle's. Thomas, having Moerbeke's translation of Proclus in hand, identified the work as an Arabic reworking of the Elements of Theology and says so, then expounds it proposition by proposition, marking where the Neoplatonic doctrine of emanating intelligences must be corrected.

aq-lux-140.blurb: A sermon on the psalm verse, a light has risen for the just. Three pages, surviving as a hearer's report of preaching. Thomas divides the verse and preaches the divisions; the piece is occasional and short, and does not develop beyond its text.

aq-matt-51.blurb: The first half of Thomas's lectures on Matthew, chapters one through twelve, taken down by hearers. It includes the genealogy and infancy narratives, the baptism and temptation, and a long treatment of the Sermon on the Mount, which Thomas reads as the law of the new covenant. The transmission of these lectures is uneven, and in some copies part of the text comes from a second reporter.

aq-matt-52.blurb: The second half of the Matthew lectures, chapters thirteen to twenty-eight: the parables of the kingdom, the confession at Caesarea Philippi and the promise to Peter, the transfiguration, the discourses on the church and on the last things, and the passion. Reported from Thomas's teaching rather than written by him, and briefer verse by verse than his lectures on John.

aq-metaph-82.blurb: A commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics covering the first twelve books, the last two being left aside. Thomas expounds the search for wisdom as knowledge of first causes, the survey of earlier philosophers, the aporiae, the account of being as being and of substance, act and potency, and finally the argument to the first unmoved mover in the twelfth book. His prologue on the subject of the science, and his reading of substance, draw the most readers.

aq-meteor-78.blurb: An exposition of Aristotle's Meteorology, on the region below the heavens and above the earth: comets and the milky way as they were then explained, rain, wind, thunder, the sea and its saltness, rivers, and the halo and the rainbow. The commentary is unfinished and breaks off in the second book. The natural science is obsolete; the interest lies in watching Thomas work through it.

aq-officesas-122.blurb: The office for Corpus Christi in the version beginning Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum, distinct from the office opening Sacerdos in aeternum and shorter than it. Both come down under Thomas's name, and the relation between them, including whether one is a first draft superseded by the other, is a question the manuscripts have not settled.

aq-orationes-119.blurb: The prayers that circulate under Thomas's name, among them the prayer before study, the prayers before and after communion, and a prayer for the ordering of a life. Eight pages of devotional matter, some of it securely his and some attached to his name by long use. They are prayers rather than arguments, printed as the tradition transmitted them.

aq-osanna-127.blurb: A sermon on the acclamation, hosanna to the son of David, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Three pages, preserved as a record of what was preached rather than as a text Thomas composed. The verse is divided and expounded in the ordinary way of his surviving sermons.

aq-paternoste-148.blurb: Conferences on the Lord's Prayer, from the same preaching as the series on the Creed and the commandments. Thomas takes the address and the seven petitions one by one, explaining what is asked in each, why the order stands as it does, and how the prayer answers the whole range of human need. He treats it as the model of all prayer and keeps the exposition within reach of an unlearned hearer.

aq-peri-73.blurb: A commentary on Aristotle's On Interpretation, treating the noun and the verb, the proposition as the kind of speech that can be true or false, affirmation and negation, contradictories and contraries, and the argument of the ninth chapter about statements concerning future contingents, which Thomas uses to distinguish what is necessary given God's knowledge from what is necessary in itself. The commentary is incomplete and was finished by a later hand.

aq-petite-133.blurb: Two pages of preaching on the words ask and you will receive, that your joy may be full. A hearer's record rather than a composed text. The sermon divides the promise and presses it, and does not run beyond the occasion for which it was given.

aq-philemon-67.blurb: Two pages on the shortest of Paul's letters, the note asking Philemon to receive back the runaway slave Onesimus. Thomas treats it as an example of how a request may be made with authority and yet left free, and draws from it what can be drawn about the standing of slaves and the obligations of a Christian master.

aq-philip-60.blurb: An exposition of the letter to Philippi, given with the rest of the Pauline course. The weight falls on the second chapter, where Paul says that Christ, being in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant; Thomas reads the passage against any account that would make the emptying a loss of divinity, and treats the exaltation that follows. The rest of the letter is handled briefly.

aq-phys-75.blurb: A complete commentary on the eight books of the Physics. It runs from the principles of natural things and the definition of nature through the four causes and chance, then motion, the infinite, place, the void, and time, and ends with the books arguing that motion has no beginning and that it requires a first unmoved mover. Thomas stays close to the text, and where he thinks a conclusion cannot be held he says so without rewriting Aristotle.

aq-polit-85.blurb: An exposition of Aristotle's Politics covering the household, slavery, property, the criticism of Plato's Republic, the definition of the citizen, and the classification of constitutions. Thomas's own work breaks off in the third book, and what circulates beyond that point is a continuation by another Dominican. This is where his treatment of political community as natural rather than merely remedial is set out at length.

aq-post-74.blurb: A commentary on the Posterior Analytics, Aristotle's account of what makes a body of knowledge a science: demonstration from premises that are true, prior, and causes of the conclusion; the difference between knowing that and knowing why; definition and its relation to demonstration; and the final chapter on how the mind arrives at first principles that cannot themselves be demonstrated. The theory of science Thomas relies on everywhere else is explained here.

aq-psalm-46.blurb: An exposition of the psalms that breaks off partway through the psalter, covering the first fifty-odd psalms in the Latin numbering. Thomas prefaces it with an account of how the psalms are to be read, taking David as a prophet and the literal sense as often referring to Christ. The comment on each verse is short, and much of it is occupied with the christological reading of the psalms of suffering.

aq-puer-131.blurb: A sermon on the boy Jesus remaining behind in Jerusalem without his parents' knowledge. Four pages, recorded from preaching rather than written out. Thomas divides the gospel text and preaches its parts; the sermon is occasional and does not develop the material as his commentaries do.

aq-qdean-27.blurb: Disputed questions on the soul, and not the commentary on Aristotle's treatise of the same name. The form is the scholastic question: objections, a determination, replies to the objections. The matter is whether the soul can be both a subsistent thing and the form of a body, whether all men share one intellect, how soul and body are united, what the soul's powers are, and how a separated soul knows anything at all.

goodwin-apologeticall-narration-humbly-s.blurb: The manifesto of the five Dissenting Brethren of the Westminster Assembly, subscribed by Goodwin together with Philip Nye, Sidrach Simpson, Jeremiah Burroughs and William Bridge. Addressed to Parliament rather than to the Assembly itself, it sets out the Congregational way as a path between Presbyterian classes on one side and separatism on the other, appeals to the authors' years in the exiled English churches of the Netherlands, and asks for forbearance toward brethren who agree in doctrine but not in discipline.

goodwin-childe-light-vvalking-darknesse-.blurb: A treatise on spiritual desertion: why God withdraws the sense of his favour from those who are truly his, and how a believer is to walk when assurance fails. Goodwin distinguishes desertion from unbelief and from bodily melancholy, traces the ends God has in withdrawing, and gives directions for waiting in the dark without concluding against oneself. Written for consciences in trouble rather than for the schools.

goodwin-christ-universall-peace-maker-re.blurb: An argument that the reconciliation Christ effects holds together all who are truly God's people, whatever the differences of judgment and practice standing between them. Composed amid the divisions among the English godly, it presses peace on parties agreed in the foundation, without conceding that the points at issue are matters of indifference. Short, occasional, and of a piece with Goodwin's Independent commitments.

goodwin-demeanour-good-subject-order-acq.blurb: A short discourse on the obedience a Christian owes the civil power, and on how the quiet carriage of subjects serves the peace of a kingdom. Thomas Goodwin the Independent died in 1680, so a piece issued under the name in 1681 is either posthumous or another man's, and nothing in the title settles which. Best read simply as a brief treatment of subjection and public order.

goodwin-fair-prospect-shewing-clearly-di.blurb: A discourse on the contrast between things seen and things not seen, the visible being temporal and the invisible eternal, after the manner of Paul's argument to the Corinthians. That comparison governs the whole: what a Christian may expect of present things and what is laid up for him out of sight. Beyond the title, little can be said with confidence about the text preached or the occasion.

goodwin-happiness-princes-led-divine-cou.blurb: A funeral sermon for a prince, taking as its theme the good that comes to rulers who are guided by divine counsel. Thomas Goodwin the Independent died in 1680, so a sermon printed under the name in 1695 belongs to a later hand, most probably his son and namesake. The occasion given in the title is the only firm evidence of its subject.

goodwin-happinesse-saints-glory-treatise.blurb: A treatise of heaven built on Romans 8:18, that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. Goodwin weighs both sides of the apostle's comparison, the affliction the saints carry now and the happiness prepared for them, and turns the disproportion between them into practical use for those under trial.

goodwin-moses-aaron-ciuil-ecclesiastical.blurb: Not by Thomas Goodwin the Independent divine but by Thomas Godwin, the Abingdon schoolmaster, whose name catalogues regularly confuse with his. A handbook of Hebrew antiquities describing the civil and religious institutions of Israel: tribes and magistrates, the sanctuary and its furniture, priesthood and sacrifices, feasts, oaths, and the sects of the later Jews. Compiled for students reading the Old Testament, and long used as a school and university reference.

goodwin-most-holy-profitable-sayings-tha.blurb: A single printed sheet gathering the dying sayings of Goodwin, who died in February 1680, issued for readers who wanted a record of how he spoke at the end. Two pages only, and of interest as a deathbed relic of the Independent divine rather than as a specimen of his divinity.

goodwin-roman-histori-anthologia-english.blurb: The work of Thomas Godwin, schoolmaster of Abingdon, and not of Thomas Goodwin the Independent divine; the two names are persistently conflated. An English handbook of Roman antiquities compiled for schoolboys, laying out the offices and government of Rome, its calendar and religion, its military and domestic customs, with English usages set alongside for comparison. A classroom reference book, not a work of theology.

goodwin-sermon-on-occasion-death-reveren.blurb: A funeral sermon for Stephen Lobb, a London Independent minister and controversialist who died in June 1699. Since the elder Thomas Goodwin died in 1680, the preacher here is a later Goodwin, most probably his son. The substance of the sermon cannot be recovered from the title, though the occasion places it among the Congregational circles of the 1690s.

goodwin-vanity-thovghts-discovered-their.blurb: An anatomy of the sinful thought, taking its text from Jeremiah's complaint that vain thoughts lodge within us. Goodwin sorts the kinds of vanity the mind falls into, argues that thoughts are sins in their own right and not merely the seed of sins, weighs the danger of a heart left to wander, and prescribes the discipline by which thoughts are to be governed.

goodwin-vvorld-come-kingdome-christ-asse.blurb: Two expository lectures on Ephesians 1:21 and 22, where Paul sets Christ above every name that is named, in this world and in that which is to come. Goodwin reads the world to come as the kingdom given to Christ, and argues from the text for the reach of his dominion over all things and his headship to the church.

preston-christ-s-revvard-christians-watc.blurb: A funeral sermon at the burial of John Berry, printed among the many pieces issued under Preston's name after his death in 1628. The governing figure is the soldier's watch and ward: the Christian keeps the post assigned him, and Christ pays the reward when the watch is done. Nothing further about the text preached or the circumstances can be established from the title.

preston-deformed-forme-formall-professio.blurb: A short discourse setting the true Christian against the merely formal one, the profession that keeps the shape of religion while wanting its life. Preston's standing concern, the difference between a real work of grace and its counterfeit, governs the whole. Sixteen pages, one of the brief sermons printed from his papers after his death in 1628.

preston-fulnesse-christ-vs-sermon-preach.blurb: A sermon preached at court before James I, from the years when Preston held a chaplain's place there. Its doctrine is that the whole fullness a sinner needs is laid up in Christ and drawn from him by faith, not supplemented from any store of the hearer's own. Printed after Preston's death, as almost all his preaching was.

preston-great-sea-fight-which-was-fought.blurb: An eight page news pamphlet reporting a naval action off the Dunkirk coast, dressed in the language of Babylon and its adversaries. John Preston the Emmanuel divine died in 1628, so this cannot be his; the name attached is either a different John Preston or a stationer's convenience. Civil war newsbook material rather than sermon divinity.

preston-lavv-out-lavved-charter-gospell-.blurb: A short discourse on the believer's freedom from the law as a covenant of works, with the gospel produced as a charter securing the saint's privileges against the law's claim upon him. The imagery is legal throughout: the law outlawed, the charter shown, the prerogative pleaded. Twelve pages, taken from Preston's sermon notes and printed after his death.

A fuller printing of the same short discourse on the saint's freedom from the law as a covenant, the gospel standing as the charter of his privilege and prerogative. Preston's remains were issued in small pieces of this kind through the years after 1628, and the printings vary in length; this one runs to twenty pages against the twelve of the earlier.

preston-mysticall-match-between-christ-c.blurb: Sermons on the marriage between Christ and his church, the union Scripture figures as espousal: the contract, what each side brings to it, and the duties that follow for the bride. Preston works the metaphor closely, as the divines of his circle habitually did from the Song of Songs and the prophets. Printed from his remains after his death.

preston-nevv-covenant-saints-portion-tre.blurb: Preston's largest and best known work, a long course of sermons on God's word to Abraham, walk before me and be thou perfect. The all-sufficiency of God is expounded as his side of the covenant and uprightness as ours, the covenant of grace being handled as a real transaction with terms, promises and conditions. The sermons return constantly to how a man may know himself to stand within it.

preston-position-john-preston-doctor-div.blurb: A brief posthumous statement of Preston's judgment on converting grace and whether it may be resisted, printed in 1654 while English divines were still arguing over the will's freedom. It gives the substance of his teaching on efficacious grace in compressed form, stripped of the sermon frame in which he ordinarily delivered it.

preston-remaines-that-reverend-learned-d.blurb: A posthumous gathering of sermons and short treatises left at Preston's death in 1628, edited by the friends who took charge of his papers. Nearly all of Preston reached print in this way, from auditors' notes rather than from copy he prepared, and the several collections overlap. Substantial in bulk, but a volume of remains and not a book he wrote.

preston-sermon-preached-at-funerall-mr-i.blurb: A funeral sermon for Josiah Reynell, esquire, preached at East Ogwell in Devon in August 1614 and printed the year following. It stands apart from the preaching on which Preston's reputation rests, in date and in setting alike, and the title does not settle whether the preacher is the Emmanuel divine, then a young man, or another of the name.

preston-sermon-spirituall-life-death-pre.blurb: A sermon on spiritual life and death preached at Whitehall before the king in November 1616, printed after Preston's death. The division is the familiar one between the man dead in trespasses and the man quickened by grace, with the marks by which each condition may be discerned.

preston-three-sermons-sacrament-lords-su.blurb: Three sermons on the Lord's Supper, preached in the ordinary course of Preston's ministry and printed from his remains. They treat the sacrament as a seal of the covenant of grace, with the attention his tradition gave to preparation, to worthy receiving, and to what a communicant should carry away from the table.

hill-an-olive-branch-of-peace-and-accomm.blurb: A sermon at Basingshaw church pressing peace and accommodation among the contending parties of the godly, preached in 1648, when the differences between Presbyterian and Independent had hardened into settled camps. Hill's plea is for an agreement that gives up none of the truth yet refuses to force every difference to a breach.

hill-god-s-eternal-preparations-for-his-.blurb: A sermon at Paul's in May 1648 on what God has prepared from eternity for saints who come to die. The doctrine is that a believer's end is no accident but the term of an eternal purpose, and the use is preparation for dying. Hill was among the Westminster divines most often called on for public occasions of this kind.

hill-natvrall-and-artificiall-conclvsion.blurb: Not by Thomas Hill the Westminster divine but by Thomas Hill, or Hyll, the Elizabethan compiler of popular science, whose books on gardening, physiognomy and natural curiosities went on being reprinted long after his death. A gathering of experiments, sleights and household secrets taken out of Latin authors: small marvels of nature and art, set down for use and amusement.

hill-the-best-and-worst-of-paul-and-his-.blurb: A sermon taking Paul at his best and at his worst, the apostle serving as a case of the two conditions a Christian may be found in, with his character drawn in each. Twenty-five pages, one of the occasional sermons Hill printed in 1648. The text preached is not named in the title.

hill-the-declaration-and-resolution-of-c.blurb: An eight page pamphlet of civil war news carrying Colonel John Poyer's declaration against Cromwell, from the Welsh rising of 1648 that ended in the siege of Pembroke. It is political ephemera and has no connection with Thomas Hill the Westminster divine, under whose name it has come to be filed.

hill-the-good-old-vvay-gods-vvay-to-sovl.blurb: A sermon on returning to the old paths, taking up Jeremiah's charge to stand in the ways and ask for the good old way wherein is rest for souls. Preached before a parliamentary audience in 1644, it argues that reformation means the recovery of what was first delivered rather than the invention of anything new, and that rest for the soul is found nowhere else.

hill-the-militant-chvrch-trivmphant-over.blurb: A fast sermon preached to both Houses of Parliament in 1643 on the war of Revelation 12 between the woman's seed and the dragon with his angels, applied without much disguise to England's present quarrel. The church militant is shown already sharing in the victory of her head, and the hearers are pressed to conduct themselves as men on the winning side of a settled conflict.

hill-the-right-separation-incouraged-in-.blurb: A sermon to the House of Lords distinguishing the separation God requires, from sin and from the world, from the separation of those who withdrew from the church itself. Hill turns the distinction into an argument for pursuing reformation within the national church rather than out of it, at a moment when both courses had advocates in his audience.

hill-the-season-for-englands-selfe-refle.blurb: A fast sermon calling England to examine herself and to press on with the building of the temple, the standing figure in assembly preaching for the work of reformation. Delivered in 1644, while the settlement of religion was under debate and the temple language of Haggai and Zechariah was in constant use from parliamentary pulpits.

hill-the-spring-of-strengthning-grace-in.blurb: A plain discourse on where a Christian's strength comes from, namely Christ the Rock of Ages, treated as the spring out of which strengthening grace flows. The title advertises plainness and brevity, and the piece keeps to both. Its text and occasion are not given.

hill-the-strength-of-the-saints-to-make-.blurb: A short sermon on the saints' skill in making Christ their strength, the heavenly art of drawing on him rather than on any resource of their own. Twenty-eight pages, described on the title page as briefly commended to its hearers, with nothing further said of the occasion.

hill-the-trade-of-truth-advanced-in-a-se.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons in 1642, working Solomon's charge to buy the truth and sell it not. Truth is handled throughout as a commodity, to be traded for at any price and parted with at none, and the members are pressed to advance that trade in the settlement they were undertaking. From the early years of the parliamentary monthly fasts.

hill-truth-and-love-happily-married-in-t.blurb: A sermon on the joining of truth and love in the saints and in the churches of Christ, drawn up in the form of a marriage contract between the two. The concern is the one running through Hill's preaching in these years: that zeal for right doctrine and charity toward brethren are to be held together, not traded one against the other.

bonaventure-collationes-de-decem-praecep.blurb: A course of conferences delivered before the masters and students of Paris by the Franciscan minister general, working through the commandments one by one. Bonaventure treats each as a precept of the natural law confirmed and sharpened by revelation, and uses the series to press moral reform on an academic audience he judged slack in it. Preached theology rather than disputed theology, and plainer in manner than his commentaries.

bonaventure-collationes-de-septem-donis-.blurb: University conferences on the seven gifts named in Isaiah 11, fear and piety, knowledge and fortitude, counsel, understanding and wisdom. Bonaventure treats them as the ordinary furniture of a Christian life rather than as extraordinary graces, and arranges them as an ascent that terminates in wisdom. They belong with the conferences on the Decalogue and the Hexaemeron as part of his late Paris preaching to the schools.

bonaventure-collationes-in-evangelium-s-.blurb: Collations on the Fourth Gospel, shorter and more occasional than his full commentary on the same text, gathering points of doctrine and moral application rather than expounding the Gospel continuously. The themes Bonaventure returns to everywhere, the Word, light, and the mind's ascent to God, govern what he stops over and what he passes by.

bonaventure-collationes-in-hexameron-siv.blurb: The last of the Paris conferences, broken off unfinished when Bonaventure was called away, expounding the six days of creation as a series of illuminations by which the mind and the church are carried toward wisdom. The lectures double as a sustained attack on errors he saw spreading in the arts faculty, the eternity of the world and the unicity of the intellect among them, and on the pursuit of philosophy as an end in itself.

bonaventure-commentarius-in-ecclesiasten.blurb: An exposition of Ecclesiastes from Bonaventure's years lecturing on Scripture at Paris, ordered by the vanity Solomon exposes and the wisdom he commends. It proceeds by division of the text with questions raised where the letter invites them, and reads the book's contempt of the world as instruction in right use rather than as despair of created things.

bonaventure-commentarius-in-evangelium-s.blurb: A full running commentary on John from his time as bachelor of Scripture at Paris, proceeding through the text by division and exposition, with disputed questions taken up at the points that provoke them. Christological and Trinitarian matter dominates, as the Gospel requires, and the moral application is never far from the doctrine.

The largest of Bonaventure's scriptural works, expounding Luke at length with divisions of the text, patristic authorities, and questions raised where the narrative provokes them. It carries more moral and pastoral matter than his other commentaries, and generations of preachers used it as a quarry for sermon material on the Gospel narratives.

bonaventure-quaestiones-disputatae-de-sc.blurb: Three sets of disputed questions from Bonaventure's Paris regency. On the knowledge of Christ takes up the divine ideas, the eternal exemplary reasons and the illumination of the human mind, along with what Christ knew in his created soul. On the mystery of the Trinity treats the certitude of God's existence and the plurality of persons in one simple essence. On evangelical perfection defends the mendicant life, poverty above all, against the secular masters attacking it.

bonaventure-in-primum-librum-sententiaru.blurb: The doctrine of God, treated distinction by distinction in the order Peter Lombard set: the divine unity and attributes, the eternal processions, the persons and their properties, appropriation and mission. Bonaventure keeps the Lombard's sequence but answers by question, article and response, and the exemplarism that governs all his later writing is worked out here. The Quaracchi text, with the editors' scholia and critical apparatus.

bonaventure-in-secundum-librum-sententia.blurb: Creation and the creature: the production of things from nothing, the angels and their fall, the work of the six days, the constitution of man in soul and body, original righteousness, and the sin transmitted from Adam. Bonaventure's positions on matter and form, on seminal reasons, and on the impossibility of a created world without a beginning all stand in this book. Quaracchi text with scholia.

bonaventure-in-tertium-librum-sententiar.blurb: The Incarnation and the Christian life: how the Word assumed human nature, the grace, knowledge and merit of Christ, his passion, and then faith, hope and charity, the gifts of the Spirit, and the commandments as they bear on the believer. The Lombard's distinctions supply the order; the questions and the answers are Bonaventure's own. Quaracchi text with editorial apparatus.

bonaventure-in-quartum-librum-sententiar.blurb: The sacraments and the last things, and the longest of the four books: what a sacrament is and how it causes, then baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, extreme unction, orders and marriage taken in turn, followed by the resurrection, the judgment, and the final condition of the blessed and the damned. The Quaracchi editors' text, with their scholia and apparatus.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-1.blurb: The opening tome of the Oratorian's year by year history of the church, undertaken as the Catholic answer to the Lutheran Magdeburg Centuries and built out of the manuscripts of the Vatican and the Roman archives. The annalistic form is itself the argument: every year is entered with the documents bearing on it, so that continuity with the apostolic church may be shown rather than asserted. This volume opens at the Nativity and carries the record through the apostolic age and the first century.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-2.blurb: The record continues into the second and third centuries, the age of the apologists and of the persecutions under the pagan emperors. Martyr acts, episcopal successions, heresies and the earliest synodical documents are entered under their years as Baronius found them in Roman collections, with his own notes on the credit due each source.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-3.blurb: The annals reach the fourth century, the age of Constantine and of the Arian controversy, where Baronius has conciliar acts and imperial legislation in quantity to work from. His concern with the standing of the Roman see against Eastern claims, present throughout the work, becomes plainest in the years handled here.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-4.blurb: The record runs through the later fourth century and into the fifth, the generation of Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom and Augustine, with the Nicene settlement consolidating in the West and the Pelagian and Christological quarrels beginning. Letters, canons and imperial constitutions are entered year by year in the usual manner of the annals.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-5.blurb: The fifth century and its Christological controversies, the councils held over them, the Roman bishops of the period, and the barbarian settlement of the western provinces. Baronius enters the letters and conciliar acts under their years and argues his case against the Protestant historians in the notes rather than in continuous narrative.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-6.blurb: The sixth century: Justinian's reign and his ecclesiastical legislation, the long dispute over the Three Chapters, the monastic foundations taking root in the West, and the missions to the peoples settled on the old imperial frontiers. Documentary throughout, with the sources set out under each year.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-7.blurb: The annals move through the late sixth and seventh centuries: Gregory the Great and his correspondence, the conversion of western peoples, the monothelite controversy and the council called to settle it, and the arrival of Islam on the eastern frontier. Gregory's letters give Baronius unusually full documentation for these years.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-8.blurb: The eighth century and after: the iconoclast quarrel and the council of Nicaea called against it, the shifting relations of Rome with Constantinople, and the rise of the Frankish kings, with Charlemagne's coronation among the events the volume must account for. Baronius handles the Roman see's western alignment as a matter of documented right.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-9.blurb: The ninth century, its Carolingian councils and its disputes over doctrine and discipline, and above all the Photian quarrel at Constantinople. Baronius treats that controversy at length, since the Roman claims his whole work was written to establish were directly in question there.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-10.blurb: The tenth century, the stretch Baronius himself describes in the darkest terms, when the Roman see fell under the control of local families and the surviving record grows thin. He does not conceal the scandals of those years, and his willingness to enter them under their dates is part of the work's claim to be an honest annal rather than an apology.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-11.blurb: The eleventh century: the reforming popes and the discipline they imposed, the beginnings of the quarrel over lay investiture, and the breach with Constantinople in 1054, whose documents are entered under their year. The materials here are fuller than for the century preceding, and Baronius uses them heavily.

baronius-annales-ecclesiastici-vol-12.blurb: The twelfth century, and the last tome of the annals as Baronius left them at his death. Papal elections and schisms, the growth of canon law, the crusading enterprise and the new orders occupy the record; the continuation of the work beyond the point he reached was undertaken by later hands.

bullinger-confessio-tigurina.blurb: The confession and defence of the church of Zurich, issued over the names of its ministers after Luther's last attack on the sacramentarians. Bullinger sets out what Zurich holds on Scripture, the church, the ministry and above all the Lord's Supper, defends Zwingli's memory against the charge of heresy, and declines to answer abuse in kind. The plainest statement of the Zurich position in the years before agreement was reached with Geneva.

bullinger-de-origine-erroris.blurb: Two books on where religious error comes from: the first tracing the growth of the invocation of saints and the veneration of images out of pagan practice, the second the corruption of the Supper into the sacrifice of the mass. The method is historical throughout. Bullinger argues that the disputed usages can be dated, that they entered the church late, and that antiquity therefore stands with the reformers rather than against them.

bullinger-de-scripturae-authoritate.blurb: On the authority, certainty and sufficiency of Holy Scripture, joined with a treatment of the institution and office of bishops. Bullinger's contention is that the church is constituted by the word rather than the word authenticated by the church, and that the bishop's office is nothing other than the ministry of that word. Written with an English readership in view and addressed to Henry VIII.

bullinger-decades.blurb: Fifty sermons arranged in five sets of ten, amounting to a full body of divinity in preached form: the word of God and faith, the Decalogue at length, sin, grace and justification, then God and the Trinity, Christ, the church and its ministry, the sacraments, prayer and the office of the magistrate. Written for pastors and for ordinary Christians, and long used as a working manual by English clergy, who were at one point required to read it.

bullinger-in-acta-apostolorum.blurb: A commentary on Acts, following the narrative from the ascension to Paul's arrival at Rome. Bullinger writes plainly and pastorally, with a steady eye on what the apostolic churches show about ministry, order, and the handling of the word, and on the reformers' claim to be restoring that pattern rather than inventing a new one.

bullinger-in-apocalypsim.blurb: A course of sermons on Revelation, reading the visions as a prophetic history of the church from the apostles to the end, with the persecuting powers of the past and the papacy of the present identified in the imagery. Prepared in the years when Protestant refugees from Marian England were sheltering in Zurich, and shaped throughout by the problem of how a suffering church is to read its own circumstances.

bullinger-in-danielem.blurb: A sermon commentary on Daniel, taken as both history and prophecy: the four monarchies read as a succession of empires running down to Bullinger's own day, and the court narratives read as instruction for believers who must live under hostile powers. The homiletic form is the one he used for most of his later expositions.

bullinger-in-ioannem.blurb: A continuous exposition of the Fourth Gospel, with attention to the Word made flesh, to faith and eternal life, and to the discourses of the upper room. The manner is that of the Zurich prophezei: philology kept short, doctrine drawn out plainly for preachers, controversy admitted only where the text forces it forward.

bullinger-in-luculentum-evangelium.blurb: The wording here is the standard formula from the title pages of Bullinger's Gospel commentaries, and as given it does not say which evangelist the volume expounds. What holds of the series holds of this volume: continuous exposition in the Zurich manner, brief philological notes, doctrine and use drawn plainly from the text. A reader should establish the evangelist from the volume itself before relying on it.

bullinger-in-matthaeum.blurb: An exposition of Matthew, the fullest of Bullinger's Gospel commentaries, working through narrative and discourse alike. The Sermon on the Mount is treated at length, as is Matthew's material on the church and its discipline, a question on which Zurich's settlement and Geneva's did not agree and on which Bullinger had reason to be careful.

bullinger-in-pauli-epistolas.blurb: The Pauline commentaries gathered into a single volume, running from Romans to Philemon. Bullinger expounds continuously and draws doctrine and use from the text rather than arguing at length with other interpreters, giving sustained attention to justification, to the use of the law, and to the church order the epistles take for granted. A collected edition of work first issued piece by piece.

bullinger-in-priorem-corinthios.blurb: A commentary on First Corinthians, from Bullinger's early years as Zwingli's successor at Zurich. The epistle gave him occasion for much of what a newly reformed city needed said: the ministry and the divisions that gather round it, discipline in the congregation, the ordering of public worship and of gifts, the Lord's Supper, and the resurrection of the body.

gerhard-commentarius-in-1-petri.blurb: A full commentary on the first epistle of Peter from the Jena professor, expounding verse by verse with the whole apparatus of Lutheran orthodox exegesis: the Greek weighed, the fathers cited, doctrinal questions opened where the text raises them, and practical use appended. Peter's matter on suffering, on baptism, on the priesthood of believers and on the ordering of the household receives the fullest handling.

gerhard-commentarius-in-2-petri.blurb: An exposition of the second epistle of Peter on the same plan as his commentary on the first: continuous verse by verse treatment, philological notes, patristic testimony, doctrinal questions taken up as they arise, and application drawn at the close of each section. The epistle's warnings against false teachers and its account of the dissolution of the elements at the last day occupy much of the volume.

gerhard-confessio-catholica-liber-1-as.blurb: The first and general book of Gerhard's long demonstration that the doctrine confessed at Augsburg is the catholic doctrine, argued out of Roman Catholic authors themselves. The method is to establish each article from the concessions of approved doctors, councils and canonists on the other side, so that the Lutherans stand as the party keeping the church's own teaching. This opening book sets out the principles and rules of proof before the particular articles are taken up.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-1.blurb: The opening volume of the standard dogmatic system of Lutheran orthodoxy, issued over more than a decade from Jena. It begins where the method requires, with the nature of theology and with Scripture, its inspiration, canon, perspicuity, sufficiency and authority, and then treats the being and attributes of God and the doctrine of the Trinity. Scholastic in form and polemical in aim, with the Roman, Reformed and Socinian positions answered under each head.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-2.blurb: Creation and the works of the six days, the angels, the government of providence, election and predestination, and then the fall, original sin and actual sin. Gerhard's doctrine of election is the Lutheran one, taken in view of faith in Christ and refusing any decree of reprobation, and the argument with Reformed authors is heavier in this volume than in most of the others.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-3.blurb: The law and its uses, the gospel and its promises, repentance, and then justification by faith, the article on which the whole system turns for Gerhard as for his tradition. Faith is defined and distinguished from its counterfeits, imputed righteousness is defended against the Roman doctrine of infusion, and the place of good works with respect to justification is fixed.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-4.blurb: Good works and their necessity, then the sacraments in general, their number, their efficacy and what they are said to confer, followed by baptism at length: its institution, its necessity, the baptism of infants and its defence, and the effects Lutherans ascribe to it against those who would make it a bare sign of a grace received elsewhere.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-5.blurb: The Lord's Supper, treated at the length the quarrel with the Reformed demanded: the words of institution and how they are to be read, the presence of Christ's body and the manner of it, the communication of attributes as it bears on the question, and the eating by the unworthy. The volume then turns to the church, its marks, its unity, and the authority it may claim.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-6.blurb: The ministry of the church, its institution, call, offices and power, including the keys and the exercise of discipline, and then the civil magistrate: the origin of political authority, its limits, the obedience owed it, and the relation between the two governments. Both estates are handled in the Lutheran manner as distinct in kind and each of divine ordinance.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-7.blurb: Marriage as an estate ordained by God and not a sacrament: its institution and ends, impediments, the degrees of kindred, divorce and remarriage, with the canonical tradition examined at every point. Set against it is the long argument over celibacy and vows, and over the Roman requirement of an unmarried clergy, which Gerhard answers from Scripture, the fathers and the canonists in turn.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-8.blurb: The last things as far as the resurrection: death and what it is, the condition of the soul between death and the end, the consolations proper to the dying, and then the raising of the body, its identity with the body laid in the grave, and the qualities ascribed to it when raised.

gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-9.blurb: The closing volume of the system: the last judgment, its time, its judge and its manner, the end of the world, and then the two final states, the punishment of the damned and the eternal life of the blessed, with what may be said of the vision of God and the fellowship of the saints. The order ends where the older dogmatic tradition required it to end.

caryl-exposition-practical-observations-.blurb: The first instalment of Caryl's exposition of Job, covering the opening three chapters in twenty-one lectures: Job's estate and integrity, the accusation and the two trials, the loss of goods and children, the affliction of his body, the coming of the friends, and Job's cursing of his day. The method is set out here and holds for the whole: the text opened phrase by phrase, then practical observations drawn from it, which is why three chapters fill a volume and the book fills twelve.

The exposition enters the debate, taking Eliphaz's first speech with its night vision and its counsel to commit the cause to God, Job's reply, and the complaint of chapters 6 and 7 that his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and his life a wind. Text opened clause by clause in Caryl's usual manner, with practical observations appended throughout.

caryl-exposition-practicall-observations.blurb: Bildad's first speech, with its appeal to the verdict of former ages, followed by Job's answer in chapters 9 and 10: how should a man be just with God, and the plea for a daysman who might lay his hand upon them both. Opened word by word, with practical observations drawn from each clause.

Eliphaz's second speech and Job's reply, covering the charge that Job's own mouth condemns him, his answer to miserable comforters, his appeal to a witness in heaven, and the failing of his hope in chapter 17. The exposition proceeds in the settled manner, the words opened in detail and observations drawn for use.

The last round of the debate: Eliphaz's final charge with its catalogue of alleged oppressions, Job's longing to find the seat of God and his account of the wicked who go unpunished, and Bildad's short closing speech on how man can be righteous before God. Expounded clause by clause with practical observations at every stage.

The entrance of Elihu, the young man who has waited on his elders and now answers Job and the three friends alike, through his opening speeches on the ways God speaks to men, on the discipline of the pit, and on the justice of the Almighty. Text opened word by word, with observations drawn for practice.

caryl-exposition-practical-observations-.blurb: Elihu's closing speeches: whether a man's righteousness profits God, the use God makes of affliction to instruct, and the long account of his works in cloud, storm, thunder and snow that leads directly into the voice from the whirlwind. One of the late instalments, from the closing stretch of an exposition Caryl preached over some two decades.

The voice out of the whirlwind: God's questioning of Job from the foundations of the earth through the ordering of the heavens, the beasts and the birds, and then the long descriptions of behemoth and leviathan. Caryl opens the interrogatories one by one and draws his observations from each, the answer to Job's case being given in questions rather than in explanations.

caryl-ioy-out-joyed-joy-overcoming-evil.blurb: A sermon on the joy that overcomes joy, evidently from Christ's word to the returning seventy that they should rejoice less in the subjection of spirits than in their names written in heaven. Triumph over enemies, whether evil spirits or evil men, is set below the better ground of rejoicing, a distinction worth preaching in 1646, when English victories were supplying plenty of the lesser kind.

caryl-renuntiation-declaration-ministers.blurb: A short declaration by ministers and preachers of the Congregational churches disowning the Fifth Monarchy rising in London and the principles that produced it, published to separate their congregations from the insurrection at a moment when every gathered church stood under suspicion. Eleven pages, subscribed by Caryl among others, and a document of self-defence rather than of divinity.

caryl-saints-thankfull-acclamation-at-ch.blurb: A sermon on the thanksgiving of the saints when Christ takes to himself his great power and begins to reign, the acclamation of the Apocalypse applied to what Caryl and his hearers took for the first stirrings of that kingdom in England. Preached in 1644 and printed with its occasion noted, as such sermons were.

caryl-sermon-pressing-directing-that-gre.blurb: A sermon to the Parliament at Westminster on the duty of praising God, pressing the obligation first and then directing how it is to be discharged. Preached in the later years of the Protectorate, when days of public thanksgiving had as fixed a place in the parliamentary calendar as days of humiliation, and preachers were expected to furnish both.

jeremy-taylor-answer-letter-written-r-r-.blurb: A reply to John Warner, Bishop of Rochester, who had written to object to the chapter on original sin in Taylor's Unum Necessarium.
