Taylor answers the charge of Pelagianism, distinguishing the corruption of nature that Adam transmitted from a guilt personally imputed to his posterity, and argues that the fathers before Augustine do not teach what the schools took from them. The most exposed position Taylor ever defended in print.

jeremy-taylor-bishop-taylor-s-judgment-c.blurb: A single leaf, printed decades after Taylor's death, lifting out of the Ductor Dubitantium his ruling on how far the authority of parents extends over their children. The Ductor was Taylor's large handbook of cases of conscience; this is one case extracted and sold on its own, in the manner of printers who found a use for a particular answer.

jeremy-taylor-copie-tvvo-letters-vvritte.blurb: Two letters between friends about a disputation that one of them says never happened as reported, printed at the height of the pamphlet war of the early 1640s. The form is familiar in that literature: private correspondence published to correct a public account. The attribution to Taylor is the catalogue's, and the piece is slight.

jeremy-taylor-discovrse-baptisme-its-ins.blurb: Taylor on the institution of baptism, what it effects in those who receive it, and whether the church rightly administers it to infants. He had earlier stated the Anabaptist case against infant baptism with such force in The Liberty of Prophesying that he was thought to hold it; here he answers those arguments and defends the practice of the church, though on grounds of ecclesiastical tradition more than of scriptural command.

jeremy-taylor-dissvvasive-from-popery-pe.blurb: Written for the people of his Irish dioceses and addressed to a population largely Roman Catholic, this argues that the Church of Rome has departed from the doctrine of the primitive church and that its practice is unsafe for souls: invocation of saints, indulgences, communion in one kind, prayers in an unknown tongue, the papal claim itself. Polemical throughout, and the most sustained anti-Roman work by a writer usually read for his devotional books.

jeremy-taylor-funerall-sermon-preached-a.blurb: Preached at the burial of Frances, Countess of Carbery, wife of Taylor's patron at Golden Grove, where he had taken refuge after the collapse of the royalist cause. It belongs with Holy Dying, written in the same household and in the same season of loss: a meditation on mortality and on a particular Christian death, given in the presence of the family that had sheltered him.

jeremy-taylor-last-speech-confession-who.blurb: A Gunpowder Treason squib cast as a scaffold speech, with the Church of Rome personified as the Whore of Babylon making her last confession before execution on the fifth of November. This is pope-burning literature rather than divinity. It is dated some years after Taylor's death, and the attribution carried in this catalogue should be treated with caution.

jeremy-taylor-real-presence-spirituall-c.blurb: Taylor's principal sacramental treatise, affirming that Christ is really present in the Eucharist to the faith of the receiver while denying that the elements are changed in substance. He works through the words of institution, the sixth chapter of John, the testimony of the fathers, and the scholastic account of accidents without a subject, arguing that transubstantiation is a late doctrine that offends against sense, reason and antiquity alike.

jeremy-taylor-sermon-preached-at-funeral.blurb: A funeral sermon for Sir George Dalston of Dalston in Cumberland. Beyond the occasion named on the title page there is little to report: it belongs to the large body of Taylor's preaching at burials, where doctrine on death and judgment is joined to the character of the person buried.

jeremy-taylor-treatises-liberty-prophesy.blurb: Three of Taylor's controversial works gathered in one volume. The Liberty of Prophesying argues that the articles necessary to salvation are few and plain, that scripture, councils, fathers and popes are each fallible guides in the rest, and that the magistrate should therefore not punish error; the discourse on ex tempore prayer defends set forms and the liturgy against extemporary praying; Episcopacy Asserted defends bishops as an apostolic institution.

jeremy-taylor-two-discourses-baptisme-it.blurb: The short tract on baptism paired with the discourse on prayer by set form against prayer ex tempore, printed together in a small volume. Both arguments appear at greater length elsewhere in Taylor; this is the compact form in which they first circulated.

jeremy-taylor-vnum-necessarium-doctrine-.blurb: A long treatise on repentance, arguing that the gospel requires not sorrow alone but an entire change of life, and setting the measures by which a penitent may judge himself. Taylor writes against what he took to be the easy deathbed absolutions of both Rome and the Protestant casuists. The chapter on original sin, in which he denied that Adam's guilt is imputed to his children, drew objections from his fellow episcopal clergy and occasioned several defences.

sibbes-bovvels-opened-discovery-neere-de.blurb: Sermons on the Song of Songs, taking the bride and the bridegroom as the church and Christ and drawing from the poem an account of communion between them: how Christ woos, how the soul withdraws, how he returns. The title comes from the beloved's words in the fifth chapter. Published from Sibbes's papers after his death, and the fullest statement of the affectionate divinity he was known for at Gray's Inn.

sibbes-christians-portion-is-unfolded-un.blurb: On what belongs to the believer by his interest in Christ, argued as an inventory of riches already possessed rather than a promise of future reward. Sibbes preaches assurance by way of enumeration, setting out what the Christian may reckon his own. A short volume in his usual manner, warm rather than polemical.

sibbes-evangelicall-sacrifices-xix-sermo.blurb: Nineteen sermons gathered after Sibbes's death, opening with thanksgivings for national deliverance and continuing through occasional and doctrinal preaching. The sacrifices of the title are the evangelical ones of praise and of a broken heart. A posthumous collection of the kind his editors assembled from notes and from sermons already in print.

sibbes-excellencie-gospell-above-law-lib.blurb: An exposition of the close of the third chapter of Second Corinthians, where the ministry of the letter is set against the ministry of the Spirit. Sibbes takes from it the liberty of the sons of God, the veil taken away, and the soul changed from glory to glory as it beholds Christ in the glass of the gospel. His characteristic subject: sanctification worked by sight rather than by threat.

sibbes-learned-commentary-exposition-fir.blurb: A verse by verse exposition of the first chapter of Second Corinthians, taken down from Sibbes's preaching and printed some years after his death. The chapter gives him the God of all comfort, affliction as the ground of comfort for others, and the sealing and earnest of the Spirit, which is the doctrine of assurance he returned to throughout his ministry.

sibbes-riches-mercie-two-treatises-lydia.blurb: Two treatises printed together. The first takes the conversion of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened as she listened by the riverside, as a case study in how grace works quietly and without violence on the affections; the second, A Rescue from Death, is a discourse of deliverance. Both are short, and both are addressed to the doubting rather than the secure.

sibbes-saints-priuiledge-christians-cons.blurb: A short treatise on Christ as the believer's advocate, pleading his cause continually before the Father. Sibbes uses the legal figure for pastoral ends, against the fear that sin after conversion cancels standing. Brief, direct, and aimed at troubled consciences.

sibbes-saints-safetie-evill-times-delive.blurb: The lead sermon was preached at Great St Mary's in Cambridge on the fifth of November, the anniversary of the Gunpowder deliverance, on the safety of God's people in dangerous times; further sermons fill out the volume. The occasion was a fixed one in the university calendar, and the preaching is national in reference as well as personal.

sibbes-spirituall-favorite-at-throne-gra.blurb: A short work on access to God in prayer and on the favour the believer finds at the throne of grace. The figure in the title is the courtier admitted to a prince's presence and heard there, turned to the use of a doubting Christian who suspects he has no such standing. Printed among the Sibbes materials issued in the years after his death.

sibbes-spirituall-mans-aime-guiding-chri.blurb: On the governing purpose of a Christian life, and how the affections and actions are to be directed by it through the ordinary passages of this world. Sibbes habitually treats the affections as the seat of religion, so the counsel here is less about rules than about what the soul is set upon.

sibbes-tvvo-sermons-first-words-christs-.blurb: Two sermons on the opening words of the fourteenth chapter of John, let not your heart be troubled, which the title page notes were also the last Sibbes preached. Christ's farewell discourse to disciples about to lose him, expounded by a dying man to a congregation about to lose him. The subject is trouble of heart and the grounds on which it may be quieted.

sibbes-two-sermons-preached-that-faithfu.blurb: Two sermons issued under Sibbes's name after his death, with the title page identifying him by his preachership rather than by the texts he preached on. One of the many small volumes his executors and printers drew from the surviving notes.

bond-a-doore-of-hope-also-holy-and-loyal.blurb: Two treatises worked up from sermons preached at Exeter, where Bond was then ministering, on hope held out to a troubled nation and on the activity that loyalty requires of subjects. Preached in the first year of the Long Parliament, before the fighting began, and already reading the public situation through prophetic texts.

bond-englands-reioycing-for-the-parliame.blurb: A short news pamphlet of 1641 celebrating the return of Parliament and the good expected from its counsels. Seven pages of occasional print rather than divinity; the ascription to Bond is the catalogue's, and ephemera of this kind circulated under common names without much security of authorship.

bond-eshcol-or-grapes-among-thorns-as-th.blurb: A thanksgiving sermon before Parliament, taking its title from the cluster of Eshcol carried back by the spies from Canaan: grapes gathered among thorns, mercies found in a season of trouble. Preached in 1648, when the second war and its aftermath made the mixture the obvious figure for the moment.

bond-exon-aprill-8-1643-having-lately-se.blurb: A single leaf printed at Exeter in which Bond disowns a pamphlet that had been published as a sermon of his. Notices of this kind were the only remedy a preacher had against printers who took down or invented sermons and sold them under a known name.

bond-king-charles-his-welcome-home-or-a-.blurb: A congratulatory pamphlet of 1641 on the King's return, thanking God on behalf of his subjects. Occasional verse and prose of the sort produced in quantity that year; it is not a sermon, and the attribution should be held loosely.

bond-occasus-occidentalis-or-job-in-the-.blurb: Two sermons preached at public occasions in the west country, the Latin title announcing a sunset in the west and the English one casting the region as Job. The west was then the theatre of royalist success and parliamentarian collapse, and Bond takes his hearers' losses as the sufferings of a man stripped and still under God's hand.

bond-oriens-ab-occidente-or-a-dawning-in.blurb: A sermon before Parliament reporting a dawn in the west, the counterpart to Bond's Occasus Occidentalis of the same period. The turn of the war in the western counties supplies both the occasion and the figure: light rising where the sun had set.

bond-salvation-in-a-mystery-or-a-prospec.blurb: A fast sermon setting out England's case in a perspective glass, arguing that salvation comes in a mystery, by ways that look at the time like ruin. Preached in 1644 to hearers who needed the argument. One of the parliamentary fast sermons that make up most of Bond's printed work.

bond-the-downfal-of-old-common-counsel-m.blurb: Five pages reporting the defeat of the old common council men at Guildhall the previous Friday, a City election squib from 1642, when control of London's government was worth contesting in print. News reporting rather than preaching, and attributed here on the strength of a name shared with the Exeter minister.

bond-the-parliaments-and-londons-prepara.blurb: A short 1641 pamphlet describing the preparations made by Parliament and the City for the King's return, with an account of who was to ride out and in what order. A piece of civic reporting; nothing in it is theological.

bond-the-poets-recantation-having-suffer.blurb: A verse recantation and penitent submission written after a sentence in the pillory in April 1642. It belongs to the literature of public punishment rather than to divinity, and its presence under this author's name reflects a shared name rather than an established attribution.

bond-the-states-stability-a-sermon-preac.blurb: Preached at Exeter before the deputy lieutenants and captains of the county in 1643, on what makes a state stand. Bond addresses men then responsible for holding the west for Parliament, and argues the stability of a commonwealth from religion and justice rather than from arms.

cheynell-a-plot-for-the-good-of-posterit.blurb: A sermon to the House of Commons proposing what Cheynell calls a plot laid for the benefit of those who come after, the settlement of religion and learning being the legacy in view. Preached in 1646, while the Westminster Assembly was still sitting and the shape of the national church was the open question.

cheynell-an-account-given-to-the-parliam.blurb: The report of the ministers Parliament sent to Oxford to preach and to reduce the university to obedience, Cheynell among them. It records what they found, how their preaching was received in a town still royalist in sympathy, and what they judged necessary. A primary document of the parliamentary visitation of Oxford.

cheynell-aulicus-his-dream-of-the-kings-.blurb: Eight pages of satire against Mercurius Aulicus, the royalist newsbook printed at Oxford, imagining its author dreaming of the King's sudden arrival in London. Newsbook warfare rather than divinity, and typical of the pamphlet skirmishing Cheynell took part in during the war.

cheynell-aulicus-his-hue-and-cry-sent-fo.blurb: Another episode in the running quarrel between the royalist Mercurius Aulicus, printed at Oxford, and the parliamentarian Mercurius Britanicus, cast here as a hue and cry raised after a man generally reported lost. Short, topical, and written for readers who followed the weekly newsbooks and knew the personalities behind them.

cheynell-chillingworthi-novissima-or-the.blurb: Cheynell's account of the last illness and death of William Chillingworth, taken prisoner at Arundel and attended by Cheynell in his final weeks. It reproduces their arguments, presses the charge that the author of The Religion of Protestants had abandoned the Trinity, and describes the burial, at which Cheynell threw Chillingworth's book into the grave. Read since as evidence against its author as much as its subject.

cheynell-sions-memento-and-gods-alarum-i.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons at Westminster in 1643, warning the nation and calling it to remembrance. Preached in the year the Solemn League and Covenant was taken and the Westminster Assembly convened, and belonging to the regular series of fast sermons by which Parliament had itself admonished.

cheynell-the-beacon-flameing-with-a-non-.blurb: A contribution to the pamphlet quarrel of 1652 over the printing and sale of popish and heretical books, defending those who had raised the alarm against their opponents' answer. Cheynell's standing concern, that error circulates freely while the orthodox are told to be quiet, is the argument throughout.

cheynell-the-divine-trinunity-of-the-fat.blurb: Cheynell's substantial dogmatic work on the Trinity, defending the three coessential and coeternal persons in one God against the Socinians and their English readers. He argues from scripture and from the fathers and councils, and treats the doctrine as the article on which the gospel stands or falls. The positive counterpart to his controversial writing against Socinianism.

cheynell-the-man-of-honour-described-in-.blurb: Preached before the House of Lords in the Abbey Church at Westminster in 1645, on what true honour consists in. The audience is the point: Cheynell tells peers that honour is a moral and religious quality rather than an inherited one, and describes the man who deserves the name.

cheynell-the-rise-growth-and-danger-of-s.blurb: The tract for which Cheynell is chiefly remembered, tracing anti-Trinitarian doctrine from its continental origins into England and alleging a design among certain divines to unsettle the received articles under cover of moderation and reason. Chillingworth and the circle around Lord Falkland are the immediate targets. Polemical, suspicious, and an important record of how the Socinian danger looked to a Westminster divine in 1643.

cheynell-the-svvorne-confederacy-between.blurb: A short pamphlet from the years of the Oxford visitation, alleging a sworn confederacy between the university's convocation and prisoners in the Tower. Thirteen pages of controversy tied closely to its moment, and difficult to follow without the local quarrel it belongs to.

cheynell-truth-triumphing-over-errour-an.blurb: A brief relation of a public disputation held in St Mary's church at Oxford, written by one of the disputants and claiming the victory for the orthodox side. Seven pages, printed quickly, and to be read as a partisan report of an occasion the other party described differently.

lightfoot-a-commentary-upon-the-acts-of-.blurb: A commentary on Acts concerned with chronology and with textual difficulty rather than with edification: when each event fell, how the narrative squares with the epistles, and what Jewish custom and place names lie behind the text. Lightfoot brings rabbinic learning to bear throughout, which is what distinguishes his commentaries from those of his contemporaries.

lightfoot-a-few-and-new-observations-vpo.blurb: Twenty-eight pages of notes on difficulties in Genesis, offered with Lightfoot's usual grading of his own results as certain or merely probable. Chronology, Hebrew usage and the reconciling of apparently discordant places are his subjects. A small early piece from a scholar who worked in such observations before he worked in large volumes.

lightfoot-a-letter-to-a-member-of-parlia.blurb: Two pages addressed to a member of Parliament about business then in hand, with nothing in the title to indicate the subject beyond present transactions. The date given is well after Lightfoot's death, so the attribution carried here should be treated with caution; short political letters were often printed under a borrowed name of weight.

lightfoot-a-sermon-preached-before-the-h.blurb: One of the sermons Lightfoot preached to the House of Commons at St Margaret's Westminster during his years in the Westminster Assembly. The parliamentary fast and thanksgiving sermons were an obligation laid on Assembly divines, and this is his discharge of it.

Preached at the public fast before the Commons at St Margaret's Westminster in 1647. Like Lightfoot's other parliamentary sermons it draws its matter from close handling of a scriptural text rather than from the week's news, though the occasion was a political one.

lightfoot-an-handfull-of-gleanings-out-o.blurb: Notes on the harder places in Exodus, proposing solutions to the scruples Lightfoot thought most pressing: chronology, the ordering of events, and the Hebrew of particular verses. A companion to his observations on Genesis, and written in the same modest form of gleanings rather than commentary.

lightfoot-elias-redivivus-a-sermon-preac.blurb: A sermon to the House of Commons in 1643 on Elijah revived, the prophet of reformation taken as the figure for what the preacher hoped the assembled Parliament would accomplish. Preached in the year the Westminster Assembly began its work, of which Lightfoot was among the most learned members.

lightfoot-erubhin-or-miscellanies-christ.blurb: Lightfoot's first book, a miscellany named for the rabbinic tractate on mixtures, gathering observations Christian and Jewish written, as he says, for recreation at spare hours. Short essays on Hebrew words, Jewish custom, scriptural cruxes and points of learning. The beginning of the rabbinic study that produced the Horae Hebraicae thirty years later.

lightfoot-the-harmony-chronicle-and-orde.blurb: The New Testament arranged as one narrative in the order Lightfoot judged the events to have happened: the four gospels methodized into a single account, then the history of Acts with the epistles set into the years they belong to. His concern is the frame rather than the exposition, giving a reader the sequence and dating of the whole.

lightfoot-the-harmony-of-the-foure-evang.blurb: The first part of Lightfoot's gospel harmony, reconciling the evangelists with each other and with the Old Testament and supplying an exposition as it goes. Where the accounts differ he argues from Jewish custom and from chronology rather than smoothing the difficulty away.

lightfoot-the-temple-especially-as-it-st.blurb: A description of the Jerusalem temple as it stood in the first century: courts, chambers, gates, vessels, and the priestly service carried on in them, reconstructed chiefly from the Talmud and the Mishnah. Lightfoot wrote it so that readers of the gospels would know what building the narratives are set in, and it remains the use to which it is put.

lightfoot-the-works-of-the-reverend-and-.blurb: The collected works of the Cambridge Hebraist, gathered after his death into a folio of some two and a half thousand pages. It brings together the harmonies and chronologies, the commentaries, the temple and the miscellanies, and the Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae, in which the gospels are illustrated line by line from rabbinic sources. The single volume in which the whole of Lightfoot's scholarship can be consulted.

vines-a-treatise-of-the-institution-righ.blurb: Vines on the Lord's Supper: what Christ instituted, how a church should administer it, and what is required of those who come. The presbyterian concern with admission and exclusion runs through it, since the question of who might be kept back from the table was the practical dispute of the 1640s and 1650s. His fullest theological work, and the one his contemporaries valued most.

vines-calebs-integrity-in-following-the-.blurb: A sermon at St Margaret's Westminster before the House of Commons, taking Caleb, who followed the Lord fully while the other spies drew back, as the pattern for men then deciding how far to go. Preached in 1642, on the edge of the war.

vines-gods-drawing-and-mans-coming-to-ch.blurb: Thirty-two sermons on a single verse, no man can come to me except the Father draw him, printed after Vines's death. The series works through the divine drawing and the human coming as two things that must both be accounted for, which is the standard reformed problem of grace and will handled at a preacher's pace rather than a schoolman's.

vines-his-maiesties-concessions-to-the-b.blurb: Nine pages stating and weighing what the King had conceded on the bill abolishing archbishops and bishops. Vines was among the divines who attended Charles in the treaty negotiations, and the piece was printed in 1660, when what had been conceded then mattered again for the settlement of the church.

vines-peitharchia-obedience-to-magistrat.blurb: Three sermons on obedience to magistrates supreme and subordinate, published under a Greek title taken from the word for submission to rule. Preached under the Protectorate by a minister who had lost his mastership at Cambridge for refusing the Engagement, which gives the subject some weight.

vines-sermons-preached-upon-several-publ.blurb: Vines's occasional preaching collected into one volume: fast sermons before the Commons, sermons before the Lords and the City, and funeral sermons for public men. Since almost all his printed work took the form of such occasions, this is the body of his preaching in one place, and a record of what a leading presbyterian said to those in power between the war and the Protectorate.

vines-the-authours-nature-and-danger-of-.blurb: A sermon before the House of Commons on where heresy comes from, what it is, and what it does to a church, preached in 1647 when the growth of the sects and the question of toleration divided Parliament from the army. The presbyterian case for restraint, argued from the pulpit to the men who would have to legislate it.

vines-the-corruption-of-minde-described-.blurb: A sermon at Paul's in June 1655 on corruption of the mind, understood as a disorder of the understanding and the judgment rather than only of the appetites. The distinction matters for Vines, since a mind corrupted cannot be reformed by restraining the body. Twenty-four pages, from the last year of his life.

vines-the-hearse-of-the-renowned-the-rig.blurb: The funeral sermon for Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, the first lord general of Parliament's army, who died in 1646 with the war won and his own command already surrendered. Vines preaches before a nation that had honoured Essex and then set him aside, and the sermon has to do the work of public commemoration as well as of divinity.

vines-the-impostures-of-seducing-teacher.blurb: Preached before the Lord Mayor in 1644 on teachers who lead their hearers astray, and on the marks by which a congregation may know them. The sects were then multiplying in London, and the sermon is an early instance of the presbyterian alarm that would grow louder over the next three years.

vines-the-purifying-of-vnclean-hearts-an.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons in 1646 on the cleansing of hands and hearts, applying to public men the demand that reformation of the nation begin with the reformation of those who undertake it. One of the regular monthly fast sermons by which Parliament kept itself under preaching.

vines-the-saints-nearness-to-god-being-a.blurb: A discourse on part of the hundred and forty-eighth Psalm, which ends by calling Israel a people near unto God, written at request and printed after Vines's death. The subject is what nearness to God consists in and what it does not guarantee, treated at the length of a small book rather than a sermon.

beza-ad-brentii-argumenta.blurb: A point by point answer to the arguments of Johannes Brenz and the theses of Jacob Andreae, the two chief Lutheran defenders of the ubiquity of Christ's body. Beza argues that a human nature everywhere present is no longer a human nature, and that the presence promised in the Supper is given to faith by the Spirit rather than by an extension of the flesh. The Genevan side of the sacramental quarrel that divided the two Protestant confessions.

beza-apologia-pro-iustificatione.blurb: A defence of justification by faith in Christ alone, written late in Beza's life against Roman controversialists who charged the doctrine with destroying good works. He argues the forensic sense of the term, the imputation of Christ's righteousness, and the place of works as fruit rather than ground.

beza-confessio-christianae-fidei.blurb: Beza's confession of faith, set out article by article through the persons of the Trinity, the church, the sacraments and the last things, and followed by a comparison of each head with the doctrine of Rome. Written in the first instance for a private reader and then published, it became one of the most widely translated summaries of reformed belief in the sixteenth century.

beza-de-haereticis-puniendis.blurb: Written in the aftermath of the burning of Servetus, this defends the right and duty of the civil magistrate to punish heretics, answering the argument for toleration that Castellio had published under a borrowed name. Beza reasons from the Mosaic law, from the magistrate's care for the first table, and from the harm he takes heresy to do to souls. The classic statement of the position, and the document to read against any account of Geneva that avoids it.

beza-de-polygamia-et-divortiis.blurb: A treatise on plurality of wives and on the grounds of divorce, arguing from scripture, the early church and the civil law. Beza writes as a pastor of a church that had to decide actual cases, so the work is casuistical as well as doctrinal: what constitutes a marriage, what dissolves one, and what a magistrate may allow.

beza-defensio-sacramentalis-coniunctioni.blurb: A defence of the sacramental union of the body and blood of Christ with the bread and wine, maintaining a real communication to the believer while denying that the elements contain the body corporally. Directed at Lutheran opponents, and one of the several works in which Beza held the Genevan line on the Supper after Calvin's death.

beza-du-droit-des-magistrats.blurb: The resistance tract, written in French and published anonymously after the massacre of St Bartholomew's Day. Beza argues that political authority is held on conditions, that subjects owe obedience to a tyrant only within them, and that the lesser magistrates, the estates and officers of a realm, may lawfully take arms to defend the commonwealth and true religion. One of the founding texts of Huguenot constitutional theory.

beza-epistolarum-theologicarum.blurb: A single book of theological letters, gathered from Beza's correspondence with ministers, magistrates and scholars across reformed Europe. The letters answer questions of doctrine, discipline and pastoral practice as they were put to Geneva, which makes the volume a record of how the reformed churches consulted one another as much as a statement of Beza's own views.

beza-lex-dei-moralis-ceremonialis-politi.blurb: The law of God set out under the three heads of moral, ceremonial and political, with the Mosaic material sorted into each and the question pressed of what binds Christians and what does not. A short work, useful chiefly for seeing how a reformed theologian handled the abiding authority of the Old Testament law.

beza-sermons-resurrection.blurb: A long series of sermons in French on the resurrection narratives, preached in Geneva and printed near the end of Beza's life. He works through the gospel accounts as history, harmonising the evangelists where they differ and drawing consolation from each stage of the story. The preaching Beza, rather than the controversialist or the textual critic.

beza-theses-theologicae-genevenses.blurb: Theses disputed in the Genevan Academy, covering the standard heads of doctrine in the compressed propositional form that academic exercises required. They show what students at Geneva were trained to defend and how the reformed system was ordered for teaching in the generation after Calvin.

doronzo-de-sacramentis-in-genere.blurb: The general treatise that opens Doronzo's Latin series on the sacraments: what a sacrament is, how the sign causes what it signifies, institution by Christ, the sevenfold number, matter and form, the intention required of the minister, the disposition required of the recipient, and the character imprinted by three of them. Neo-scholastic in method throughout, each question stated, the adversaries listed, the thesis proved from scripture, the fathers, the magisterium and reason.

doronzo-de-ordine-1.blurb: The first volume of Doronzo's three on holy orders, given to the institution of the sacrament: whether Christ instituted an order of priests distinct from the faithful, the evidence of the New Testament and the fathers, and the answers to the Protestant and modernist accounts of how a Christian ministry arose. A thousand pages on a question that earlier manuals settled in a chapter.

doronzo-de-ordine-2.blurb: The second volume on holy orders, completing the question of institution and then treating the matter and form of the sacrament: whether the essential rite is the imposition of hands or the handing over of the instruments, and what words constitute the form in each grade. The historical dossier is large, since the Latin and Eastern rites differ and the tradition had argued the point for centuries.

doronzo-de-ordine-3.blurb: The third volume on holy orders, on the extrinsic causes: the minister who confers the sacrament and the subject who may receive it. Questions of the validity of orders conferred by a bishop outside the church, the requirements laid on candidates, and the grades of the ministry belong here. The last of the three, and the one closest to practical canonical concerns.

doronzo-de-baptismo-et-confirmatione.blurb: The two sacraments of initiation after the general treatise, handled in a single volume: the necessity of baptism, its matter and form, the minister and subject, the effects and the character, and then confirmation, its sacramental status, its rite and its proper minister. The scholastic apparatus is the same as in the rest of the series, though the compass is smaller than Doronzo gave to orders or the Eucharist.

doronzo-de-eucharistia-1.blurb: The first of two volumes on the Eucharist, on the sacrament rather than the sacrifice: the real presence, transubstantiation and the accidents that remain, the moment of consecration, the manner of Christ's presence under each species, the effects of communion and the dispositions required of the communicant. The controversies with the reformers are stated in their own terms and then answered.

doronzo-de-eucharistia-2.blurb: The second Eucharistic volume, on the Mass as sacrifice: whether it is a true and proper sacrifice, what the sacrificial action consists in, how it relates to the one offering of the cross, and for whom and to what effect it is offered. The theories of the schools on the essence of the sacrifice are laid out and weighed against each other.

doronzo-de-poenitentia-2.blurb: The second volume on penance, on the first two acts of the penitent: contrition, with the distinction between perfect sorrow and attrition and the long dispute over what suffices for the sacrament, and confession, its necessity, integrity, and the obligations it lays on both penitent and priest. The largest single volume in the series.

doronzo-de-poenitentia-3.blurb: The third volume on penance, on satisfaction and absolution: the works imposed on the penitent and their relation to the temporal punishment due to sin, then the judicial form of the sacrament, the power of the keys, the effect of the priest's sentence, and the conditions under which absolution is valid or is to be withheld.

doronzo-de-extrema-unctione-1.blurb: The first of two volumes on the anointing of the sick, on the intrinsic causes: the institution of the sacrament, the evidence of the epistle of James and of the fathers, and the matter and form, the oil and the words of the anointing. Doronzo gives the historical development of the rite at length before drawing the doctrinal conclusions.

doronzo-de-extrema-unctione-2.blurb: The second volume on the anointing of the sick, on the extrinsic causes: the priest who administers it, the sick person who may receive it, and the conditions of danger of death that govern its use. The effects of the sacrament and the question of its repetition belong to this part of the treatise.

wilkinson-jr-a-sermon-against-lukwarmene.blurb: A university sermon preached at St Mary's in Oxford on the sixth of September and printed in 1641, against the middling, unoffending religion that will neither freeze nor burn. The complaint is a standing one in Puritan preaching, and the setting gives it its edge: a scholarly congregation, addressed from the chief pulpit of the university, in the year the quarrel between king and Parliament became open.

wilkinson-jr-babylons-ruine-jerusalems-r.blurb: A sermon preached before the House of Commons and printed in 1643, reading the wars of the three kingdoms through the fall of Babylon and the raising of Jerusalem. Sermons of this kind were preached to Parliament on its appointed fast days and printed at its order, and they carry the political theology of the period in its rawest and least guarded form.

wilkinson-jr-characters-of-a-sincere-hea.blurb: Practical divinity on the marks by which a Christian may know his own sincerity, gathered, as the title page says, out of the Word of God, and on the comfort that follows such knowledge. It belongs to the large body of seventeenth-century English writing on assurance, addressed to readers who doubted whether their own hearts were honest. Printed 1674.

wilkinson-jr-counsels-and-comforts-for-t.blurb: A letter written to a friend, printed in 1679 and grown to book length, addressed to a conscience under trouble. The genre is pastoral casuistry rather than consolation: the doubting or despairing Christian brings his case, and the minister resolves it by argument from Scripture before he offers any comfort.

wilkinson-jr-doctrine-of-contentment-bri.blurb: A treatise on 1 Timothy 6:8, having food and raiment, let us be therewith content. The text is explained briefly and then applied at length, in the ordinary proportion of Puritan practical divinity. Contentment is handled as a duty to be learned under providence, not as a temperament some men happen to possess. Printed 1671.

wilkinson-jr-miranda-stupenda-or-the-won.blurb: A thanksgiving sermon printed in 1646, recounting the mercies the preacher took God to have lately wrought for England. It is the counterpart of the parliamentary fast sermon turned to the opposite occasion, public gratitude for deliverance rather than public humiliation for sin, and it reads the recent course of the war as an argument.

wilkinson-jr-the-debt-book-or-a-treatise.blurb: A treatise on Romans 13:8, owe no man any thing but to love one another, taking the verse in both of its senses: the civil debt of money, with the duties of lender and borrower, and the debt of love that is never discharged. Printed in 1625, well before the other pieces filed here under this name, and the attribution is worth checking against the several divines called Henry Wilkinson.

wilkinson-jr-the-gainefull-cost-as-it-wa.blurb: A sermon delivered before the House of Lords and printed in 1644, on cost that returns more than it takes. It was preached while Parliament was pressing its supporters for money and men, and the argument that what is spent on God's cause is not lost had an obvious application at that moment.

wilkinson-jr-the-information-of-capt-hen.blurb: Not a work of divinity but a short printed information of eleven pages, in which a Captain Henry Wilkinson sets out what had passed between himself and certain other persons. Depositions of this kind were printed in numbers in 1681, in the years of the Popish Plot and the trials that followed it. The catalogue has filed it with the sermons of the divine of the same name.

wilkinson-jr-three-decads-of-sermons-lat.blurb: Thirty sermons preached to the university at St Mary's Church in Oxford and printed together in 1660, the year the monarchy returned and the Puritan settlement of Oxford began to be undone. Nearly seven hundred pages of university preaching, learned and close to the text, addressed to an audience of scholars rather than a parish.

wilkinson-jr-two-treatises-concerning-i-.blurb: Two treatises, the first on the all-sufficiency of God for the soul that has him and the second on the preciousness of Christ to those who believe, described on the title page as the substance of what had been preached. Both subjects are staples of Puritan practical divinity. Nearly five hundred pages, printed 1681.

howe-ansvver-dr-stillingfleet-s-mischief.blurb: Howe's contribution to the controversy set off by Edward Stillingfleet's 1680 sermon The Mischief of Separation, which charged the Dissenters with the sin of schism. It is cast, as the title page has it, as a letter written out of the country to a person of quality in the city. Baxter, Owen and Alsop answered Stillingfleet as well, and the exchange is the fullest airing of the conformity question between the ejection and the Toleration Act.

howe-blessednesse-righteous-discoursed-f.blurb: An extended discourse from Psalm 17:15, I shall be satisfied when I awake with thy likeness, running to nearly five hundred pages. Howe takes the verse as a statement of what the blessedness of the righteous consists in, the vision and the likeness of God, and works out what that end implies for the soul that is still on the way to it. The manner is contemplative and Platonizing, slower than most practical divinity of the period.

howe-charity-reference-other-mens-sins-j.blurb: A short discourse, printed in 1681, on how a Christian is to think and speak of the faults of other men: the limits of censure, the duty of charitable construction, and the difference between judging an action and judging the person who did it. Howe produced a number of such single-subject discourses in the years after his ejection.

howe-funeral-sermon-on-death-that-pious.blurb: A funeral sermon for Judith Hamond, wife of the dissenting minister George Hamond, printed in 1696. Sermons of this kind do two things at once, a doctrinal discourse on a text and then a character of the deceased, and the character is often the only surviving account of a dissenting household from the inside.

howe-funeral-sermon-on-decease-that-wort.blurb: A funeral sermon for Margaret Baxter, wife of Richard Baxter, who died in June 1681. Baxter published his own Breviate of her life in the same year. Howe's sermon is the pulpit counterpart to it, a discourse on a text with a character appended, spoken of a woman whom the dissenting ministers of London knew well.

howe-funeral-sermon-that-very-reverend-m.blurb: A funeral sermon for a fellow minister, printed in 1699. The name of the deceased is cut off in the title as this catalogue carries it. By that date Howe was among the last of the ministers ejected in 1662 still preaching in London, and much of his late printed work is of this kind.

howe-heads-agreement-assented-united-min.blurb: The text of the Happy Union of 1691, in which the Presbyterian and Congregational ministers in and about London agreed a set of common principles of church order rather than a common confession. Howe was among the leading Presbyterians in the negotiation. The union broke apart within a few years over the reprinting of Tobias Crisp's sermons and the antinomian dispute that followed.

A second and more compactly printed issue of the same 1691 Heads of Agreement between the united Presbyterian and Congregational ministers of London, eleven pages here against twenty-three in the other copy held in this collection. The articles on church order are the same text.

howe-letter-friend-concerning-postscript.blurb: A pamphlet from the Trinitarian controversy of the 1690s, which began when William Sherlock defended the doctrine in terms his critics judged tritheistic and Robert South answered him in kind. Howe had entered the argument with A Calm and Sober Enquiry earlier in 1694; this letter takes up a postscript attached to one of the defenses made on Sherlock's side.

howe-thoughtfulnes-morrow-appendix-conce.blurb: A short discourse on the gospel command against taking thought for the morrow, with an appendix on the immoderate desire of foreknowing things to come, which Howe treats as the same anxiety in a speculative key. Thirty-four pages, printed 1681.

sanderson-ad-clerum-sermon-preached-at-v.blurb: A visitation sermon preached to the clergy at Grantham in the county and diocese of Lincoln on the eighth of October, printed in 1670, some years after Sanderson's death. Ad clerum was the standing designation for a sermon addressed to ministers rather than to magistrates or to the people, and Sanderson sorted his preaching by that rule. The business of such a sermon is the duties and the temptations of the ministry itself.

sanderson-de-juramento-seven-lectures-co.blurb: Seven lectures on the obligation of promissory oaths, read publicly in the divinity school at Oxford and here rendered in English. Sanderson works as a casuist: what makes an oath binding, what defeats the obligation, how far an oath extorted by force, or sworn in error, or sworn against a prior duty, holds the swearer. The question was not academic when these were delivered, since the Covenant and the Engagement had put it to every English conscience.

sanderson-episcopacy-as-established-law-.blurb: A treatise arguing that episcopal government, as the law of England establishes it, takes nothing away from the power of the crown. The title page says it was written in the time of the troubles; it was printed in 1661, when the bishops were being restored along with the king. The charge it answers, pressed from both the Presbyterian and the Erastian side, is that prelacy erects a rival jurisdiction within the realm.

sanderson-sermon-preached-at-nevvport-is.blurb: Preached at Newport in the Isle of Wight in October 1648, during the last negotiation between Charles I and the parliamentary commissioners, which the title calls the treaty. Sanderson was among the divines attending the king there. The sermon was not printed until 1653, by which time the treaty, the king and the church settlement it was meant to save were all gone.

sanderson-ten-sermons-preached-i-ad-cler.blurb: Ten sermons arranged by the hearers they were preached to: three ad clerum to the clergy, three ad magistratum to men in office, four ad populum to the people. The division runs through all of Sanderson's printed preaching and is not merely tidy, since he pitches the argument differently for each. Printed in 1627, the earliest of his gathered collections.

sanderson-tvvo-sermons-former-concerning.blurb: Two sermons, the first preached at Paul's Cross in London on the right use of Christian liberty. The question at issue is where liberty ends and how far things indifferent, the ceremonies and observances that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, may lawfully be imposed by authority and lawfully obeyed by a scrupulous conscience. Sanderson worked that ground more exactly than most of his contemporaries. Printed 1635.

sanderson-tvvo-sermons-preached-at-tvvo-.blurb: Two visitation sermons preached at Boston in the diocese and county of Lincoln, printed in 1622 and the earliest of Sanderson's preaching held in this collection. A visitation sermon is delivered to the assembled clergy at the bishop's or archdeacon's formal inspection, and its ordinary subject is the conduct of their office.

sanderson-twenty-sermons-formerly-preach.blurb: Twenty sermons first gathered in 1656, sixteen of them ad aulam, preached at court, with three to magistrates and one to the people. The court sermons are what distinguishes the volume from the other sets. Sanderson had preached before Charles I as one of his chaplains, and these went to press in the middle of the Interregnum, when there was no court left to preach to.

sanderson-two-cases-conscience-resolved-.blurb: Two cases put to Sanderson and resolved by him, printed in 1668 under his title as late Bishop of Lincoln. He was the most exact of the English casuists, and the form here is the strict one: the case stated, the question distinguished, the authorities weighed on either side, the resolution given with its limits marked.

sanderson-xxxvi-sermons-viz-xvi-ad-aulam.blurb: The collected preaching in one volume of nearly eight hundred pages, thirty-six sermons sorted as Sanderson always sorted them: sixteen ad aulam, six ad clerum, six ad magistratum, eight ad populum, with a large preface. It gathers what had appeared in smaller sets during his lifetime and is the form in which later readers usually met him. Printed 1686.

jackson-a-sober-word-to-a-serious-people.blurb: A moderate discourse concerning the Seekers, those who held that the true church, its ministry and its ordinances had been lost, and that nothing could be relied on until God should send a fresh commission. Printed in 1651. Accounts of the Seekers written without heat are rare, and this one has generally been read as sympathetic to them.

jackson-a-treatise-concerning-mans-futur.blurb: A treatise on what the title calls the great doctrine of the eternity of all mankind, the endless existence of every soul, and on what follows from it for the state of the lost as well as the blessed. Printed 1661, in a period when both the natural immortality of the soul and the everlastingness of punishment were being disputed in English.

jackson-ecclesiastes-the-worthy-church-m.blurb: A portrait of the faithful minister of Christ, described, as the title page has it, by the polishing of the preacher. Ecclesiastes here is not the Old Testament book but the preacher as such, the sense Erasmus had given the word in his treatise on the art of preaching. Printed 1628.

jackson-hosannah-to-the-son-of-david-or-.blurb: A testimony to the Lord's Christ, offered by its own title indifferently rather than to any one party. It was printed in 1657, when the English sects had multiplied and each was pressing its particular warrant, and the address to all of them at once is the point of the thing.

jackson-index-biblicus-or-an-exact-conco.blurb: A concordance to the Holy Bible in what the title page calls the last translation, meaning the Authorized Version of 1611. Printed 1668. What is held here runs to only eight pages, so this copy gives the opening of the book, its title and preliminaries, rather than the concordance itself.

jackson-strength-in-weakness-or-the-burn.blurb: An answer, republished under this title, taking the bush that burned without being consumed as the figure of a church that suffers and is not destroyed. Forty-two pages, printed 1655. The writing it answers is not named in the title as this catalogue carries it.

jackson-the-booke-of-conscience-opened-a.blurb: A sermon preached at the Spital on Easter Tuesday, one of the fixed occasions of the London preaching year, taking conscience as a book written within a man and read out at the judgment. The printed text runs to a hundred and fifty pages, a good deal more than an hour in the pulpit would hold. Printed 1642.

jackson-the-key-of-knowledge-which-is-a-.blurb: A little book of elementary instruction, offered on its title page as useful to Christians of every degree. Printed 1640. Writing of this kind carried the rudiments of the faith into English households, and its measure is the plain reader rather than the scholar.

jackson-the-pedigree-and-perigrination-o.blurb: An abridgement of sacred history, beginning at the creation of Adam and following the line of Israel through its descent and its wanderings. Compendia of this sort set the biblical narrative in order for readers who knew the texts in pieces and the chronology not at all. Nearly four hundred pages, printed 1649.

jackson-the-true-euangelical-temper-wher.blurb: A treatise on the temper proper to a Christian, argued, as the title page says, by interweaving divinity with the history of the church, so that the disposition commended is shown from the record of how Christians have actually behaved toward one another. Printed 1641.

musculus-in-corinthios.blurb: A commentary on both epistles to the Corinthians from the Bern professor whose expositions were among the standard Reformed helps of the middle sixteenth century. The Corinthian letters force questions of church order, discipline, marriage, the Lord's Supper and the use of gifts, and Musculus handles them with an eye to the ordering of the reformed congregations of his own day as well as to the text in front of him.

musculus-in-esaiam.blurb: A commentary on Isaiah printed at Basel in 1557, running past eight hundred pages. Musculus proceeds as he does everywhere, a careful construction of the words followed by the doctrinal questions the passage raises and the observations he draws from it. Isaiah gave a Reformed expositor of this generation his fullest occasion for treating prophecy, the fate of nations, and the promises the church reads as fulfilled in Christ.

musculus-in-galatas-ephesios.blurb: A commentary on Galatians and Ephesians in one volume. The pairing sets the sharpest of Paul's arguments against the works of the law beside the fullest of his statements about the church and its head. Musculus is writing in the decades when justification was the disputed article of the age, and the Galatians half of the book is shaped accordingly.

musculus-in-genesim.blurb: A commentary on Genesis of nearly nine hundred pages, covering the creation and the fall, the flood, and the histories of the patriarchs. Reformed exposition of this book carried a great deal of doctrinal weight in the sixteenth century, since creation and providence, the image of God, the entry of sin, and the covenant made with Abraham were all settled from these chapters.

musculus-in-matthaeum.blurb: A commentary on Matthew printed at Basel in 1548, the year the Interim unsettled the reformed cities of the empire and Musculus's own ministry at Augsburg with them. Matthew carries the Sermon on the Mount, and with it the matters the Reformation had made contentious: law and gospel, the lawfulness of oaths, and how much of Christ's teaching binds an ordinary Christian in an ordinary calling.

musculus-in-philippenses-colossenses.blurb: One volume on the shorter Pauline letters, Philippians, Colossians, the two to the Thessalonians and Timothy. Colossians supplies the doctrine of Christ's person and pre-eminence, the Thessalonian letters the last things and the man of sin, and Timothy the ordering of the ministry and the qualifications of those who hold it.

musculus-in-romanos.blurb: A commentary on Romans, the shortest of Musculus's Pauline volumes at some three hundred pages. Every Reformed expositor of the century had to give his account of this letter, and the weight falls in the same places: the righteousness of God received by faith, the standing and use of the law, and the chapters on election and the future of Israel.

musculus-loci-communes.blurb: Musculus's body of divinity, arranged as commonplaces after the pattern Melanchthon had established, printed at Basel in 1560. It is one of the substantial Reformed dogmatics of the generation before scholastic orthodoxy set, and it treats the magistrate, oaths and the covenant at greater length than most books of its kind. Englished in 1563 as the Common Places of Christian Religion, in which form it was read in England for decades.

musculus-in-psalterium-commentarii.blurb: A commentary on the whole Psalter and the largest of Musculus's works, close to twelve hundred pages. Reformed exposition of the Psalms was written for congregations that sang them, so the pressure of the commentary is practical as well as doctrinal: what a Christian is to make of the psalmist's complaints, his imprecations against enemies, and his confidence before God.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-1.blurb: The first volume of the course of theology Perrone taught at the Collegio Romano, on true religion: whether God has revealed, by what marks a revelation may be known, and the case for the Christian revelation against deists, rationalists and the indifferentism that held one religion as good as another. This is fundamental theology in the nineteenth-century Roman manner, laid out in numbered theses with the adversaries named and the proofs taken from Scripture, tradition and reason. Louvain, 1838.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-2.blurb: The second volume, on the one God and on the Trinity. The first tract treats the divine existence, unity and attributes; the second the processions, persons and relations, established from Scripture, the fathers and the conciliar definitions before the scholastic questions are taken up. The opponents Perrone has chiefly in mind here are the rationalist critics and the German philosophical theology of his own century. Louvain, 1838.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-3.blurb: The third volume, on God as creator: creation in time and out of nothing, the angels, the constitution of man, and the state in which man was made and from which he fell. The form is the manual's throughout, a sequence of theses each with its proofs, its authorities and its objections answered in order. Louvain, 1839.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-4.blurb: The fourth volume, joining the tract on the incarnation to the tract on the veneration of the saints. The first treats the person of Christ, the hypostatic union and the work of redemption; the second defends invocation of the saints, the honour given to relics and images, and the Marian devotion then gathering strength in Rome. Perrone would publish separately on the Immaculate Conception in the following decade. Louvain, 1839.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-5.blurb: The fifth volume, on grace and on the sacraments in general. The tract on grace covers actual and habitual grace, justification, merit and predestination, with the Jansenist and Baianist controversies still in view a century and a half after their condemnation. The sacramental tract treats institution, number, matter and form, and the manner in which a sacrament effects what it signifies. Louvain, 1840.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-6.blurb: The sixth volume takes the sacraments singly: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist and penance. The eucharistic tract is the long business of the volume, covering the real presence and transubstantiation, communion under one kind, and the sacrifice of the Mass, argued outward from the decrees of Trent. The tract on penance treats contrition, confession, satisfaction and the power of the keys. Louvain, 1841.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-7.blurb: The seventh volume gathers what remains of the sacramental course, extreme unction, orders and matrimony, together with the treatise on indulgences. Marriage in a Roman manual of this date carries a heavy canonical load, since the impediments, the form required by Trent, and the relation of the sacrament to the marriage law of the new civil codes all have to be settled together. Louvain, 1842.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-8.blurb: The eighth volume opens the treatise on the theological loci, the sources from which doctrine is drawn, and begins with the church and the Roman pontiff: the constitution of the church, her marks and authority, the primacy of Peter and of his successors, and the infallibility of the pope, defended here a generation before the definition of 1870. Gallican and Febronian claims for national churches and for the superiority of councils are the adversaries in view. Louvain, 1843.

perrone-praelectiones-theologicae-9.blurb: The ninth and last volume continues the treatise on the theological loci past the church and the papacy, taking up the remaining sources of doctrine, Scripture and tradition among them, and the weight each carries in establishing a theological conclusion. At nearly six hundred pages it is the largest volume of the set. Louvain, 1843.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-1.blurb: The introductory volume of Pesch's dogmatic course, the propaedeutic to sacred theology: religion and revelation, the credibility of the Christian revelation and its marks, the church as the authority that proposes it, and the sources and method of theology as a science. This is fundamental theology of the neo-scholastic revival, set out in theses with proofs, scholia and objections answered. Freiburg, 1924, a late printing of a course by then long in use.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-2.blurb: The tract on the one and triune God: the existence of God and how far he can be known, the divine attributes, then the processions, the persons, and the missions. Pesch writes within the Thomist recovery that followed Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris, so the questions are put in the older scholastic terms while the opponents answered are modern ones. Freiburg, 1906.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-3.blurb: Creation and elevation, with the tract on God as man's last end. Creation out of nothing, the angels, the constitution of man, the supernatural order and the gifts of original justice, their loss, and beatitude as the end for which man exists. Pairing De Deo creante with De Deo elevante is standard in manuals of this school, since the whole question of nature and grace is settled at that seam. Freiburg, 1925.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-4.blurb: The incarnate Word, the Blessed Virgin, and the veneration of the saints in one volume. The Christological tract takes the hypostatic union, the knowledge, will and grace of Christ, and the work of redemption. The Marian tract is written half a century after the definition of the Immaculate Conception and handles it as settled doctrine rather than as a disputed question. Freiburg, 1922.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-5.blurb: Grace and the divine positive law: actual grace and the long dispute over how it is efficacious, habitual grace, justification, merit, predestination, and then the law God has positively imposed and the obligation it carries. A Jesuit manual of this date has the Molinist controversy in its bones, and Pesch sets out the Thomist and the Molinist accounts before he decides between them. Freiburg, 1916.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-7.blurb: Penance, extreme unction, order and matrimony. The penitential tract covers contrition, confession and satisfaction, the power of the keys, and the conditions of absolution. The tract on marriage was printed three years after the Code of Canon Law of 1917 had recast the church's marriage discipline, and it has the civil marriage law of the European states to reckon with as well. Freiburg, 1920.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-8.blurb: Virtue in general, then the theological virtues: what faith, hope and charity are, what each has for its object and its acts, how each is lost and recovered. The tract on faith carries the weight of the volume, since the nature of the act of faith was the point most pressed in the years around the modernist crisis. Freiburg, 1910.

pesch-praelectiones-dogmaticae-9.blurb: The moral virtues, sin, and the last things. Prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance are handled in the scholastic manner as habits with their proper objects and opposed vices; the tract on sin treats its nature, its kinds, and the distinction of mortal from venial; the closing tract takes death, judgment, purgatory, hell and heaven. Freiburg, 1902.

pesch-de-inspiratione-sacrae-scripturae.blurb: A monograph of some six hundred pages on the inspiration of Scripture: what inspiration is, how far it reaches, and what follows from it for the inerrancy of the sacred books. It was printed in 1906, between Leo XIII's Providentissimus Deus and the decrees of the Biblical Commission, at the moment when Catholic scholarship was under most pressure from historical criticism and from proposals to confine inerrancy to matters of faith and morals.

owen-animadversions-on-treatise-intitule.blurb: Owen's reply to Fiat Lux, a widely read and deliberately irenic tract by the Franciscan John Vincent Canes, which argued from the multiplying divisions of English Protestantism that peace could be had only under Rome. Owen answers at length and anonymously, denying both that Protestant differences are what Canes takes them for and that Rome supplies the unity she advertises. Canes replied, and Owen answered him again two years later. Printed 1662.

owen-declaration-faith-order-owned-pract.blurb: The Savoy Declaration, the confession of faith and platform of order agreed by the Congregational churches of England at their meeting in the Savoy and printed in 1659. Owen was among its principal framers, with Thomas Goodwin, Philip Nye and William Bridge. The doctrinal chapters follow the Westminster Confession closely, with the alterations falling mainly on the church, and the appended platform states the Congregational account of a gathered church, its officers and its liberties.

owen-divine-originall-authority-self-evi.blurb: Owen's argument that Scripture carries its own evidence of divinity, and does not hold its authority on the testimony of the church or on proofs supplied from outside itself. Printed in 1659 with his defence of the purity and integrity of the Hebrew and Greek texts, written against the apparatus of variant readings in Brian Walton's London Polyglot, which Owen judged to unsettle the ground of faith. Walton answered him sharply.

owen-eben-ezer-memoriall-deliverance-ess.blurb: A memorial of the deliverance of Essex, its county and its committee, framed as an exposition of the first ten verses of a text that the title, as this catalogue carries it, leaves incomplete. Printed 1648. Owen was then minister at Coggeshall in Essex, and the fighting of the second civil war in that county ended with the surrender of Colchester in August of that year. The method throughout is providential reading of recent events.

owen-enquiry-into-original-nature-instit.blurb: Owen's late ecclesiology: where a Christian church comes from, what constitutes it, what power it holds and by whose institution, how its officers are set and how its congregations hold communion with one another. This is the first part only, printed in 1681 near the end of his life, and it argues the Congregational case at the length of a treatise against the parochial establishment on one side and the presbyterian classis on the other.

owen-exercitations-concerning-name-origi.blurb: Owen on the Sabbath: the name, origin, nature, use and continuance of a day of sacred rest, and how far the fourth commandment binds Christians, as a moral precept, as a positive institution, or not at all. The exercitation is the form he used alongside his work on Hebrews, a long free-standing dissertation on a question raised by the text. Printed separately in 1671.

owen-review-annotations-hugo-grotius-ref.blurb: A short review of Grotius's Annotations on the Bible with respect to the deity and the satisfaction of Christ. Grotius had written against Socinus on the satisfaction, but many Reformed divines read his later exegesis as conceding in the notes what he had defended in the treatise, and Owen presses that charge here. Twenty-five pages, printed in 1656 with his further writing on the death of Christ.

owen-temptation-nature-povver-it-danger-.blurb: An exposition of Christ's warning to watch and pray lest ye enter into temptation: what temptation is, where it gets its power, what it is to enter into it as distinct from merely being tempted, and the means of prevention. It belongs with Owen's treatises on mortification and on indwelling sin, and it is the plainest of the three, written for a Christian examining his own case rather than for controversy. Printed 1658.

owen-vision-vnchangeable-free-mercy-send.blurb: A sermon preached before Parliament in 1646 on the sending of the means of grace to sinners who have no claim on them, God's freedom in the disposal of the gospel being the whole of its argument. It was printed with a short appendix on church government, toleration and the petitions then being pressed about both, from the years in which Owen was moving toward the Congregational way.

ashe-a-letter-of-many-ministers-in-old-e.blurb: A letter from ministers in England putting nine positions of church order to their brethren in New England and asking for their judgement, printed in 1643 with the answers returned. The questions concern the gathering of churches, the power that rests in a congregation, and who may be admitted to the sacraments. The exchange belongs to the argument between the presbyterian and congregational ways that was running while the Westminster Assembly sat.

ashe-a-svpport-for-the-sinking-heart-in-.blurb: A sermon preached in London and printed in 1642, to uphold hope in a time of public distress. Its business is the ordinary pastoral one of keeping a congregation from despair when the news is bad, and it was preached in the year the kingdom went to war with itself.

ashe-a-true-relation-of-the-most-chiefe-.blurb: Not a sermon but a piece of war reporting, fifteen pages, relating the chief occurrences at and since the late battle at Newbury. Ashe served as chaplain to the Earl of Manchester and sent accounts of the army back to London, where they were printed as news. Printed 1644.

ashe-christ-the-riches-of-the-gospel-and.blurb: A funeral sermon printed in 1654, on Christ as the wealth of the gospel and the ground of a Christian's hope. The form is the usual one for the occasion, a doctrine raised out of the text and applied to the hearers, with a character of the deceased at the close.

ashe-good-courage-discovered-and-encoura.blurb: A sermon preached before the commanders of the military company and printed in 1642, on courage and on what can properly warrant it. Preaching to the officers of the London trained bands was a standing occasion in the city calendar, and in that year it had stopped being ceremonial.

ashe-gray-hayres-crowned-with-grace-a-se.blurb: A funeral sermon preached at Redriff on the first of August 1654, its title echoing the proverb that the hoary head is a crown of glory when it is found in the way of righteousness. Old age honoured by grace is the subject, and the sermon runs to eighty-five pages in print.

ashe-living-loves-betwixt-christ-and-dyi.blurb: A funeral sermon preached at St Mary Magdalene, Bermondsey, in Southwark, on the love that holds between Christ and his people at their death. Ninety-two pages, printed 1654, one of several funeral sermons Ashe put into print in that year.

ashe-reall-thankfulnesse-or-a-sermon-pre.blurb: A sermon preached in Paul's church, London, on the second of November 1645, on the day appointed for public thanksgiving. The point the title presses is that thankfulness which stops at words is not real. Days of thanksgiving were set by Parliament for particular deliverances, and the sermons preached on them went into print as a matter of course.

ashe-religious-covenanting-directed-and-.blurb: A sermon on the swearing of covenants and the keeping of them, printed in 1646, three years after the Solemn League and Covenant had been imposed on England and while the question of what exactly it bound men to was still open. The preacher's concern is that a covenant publicly taken is not discharged by the taking.

newcomen-a-sermon-preached-at-the-funera.blurb: A funeral sermon for a fellow minister, printed in 1658. The name of the deceased is cut off in the title as this catalogue carries it. Sermons at the burial of ministers were the occasion on which the surviving clergy took stock of their own work, and the character appended to them is often the fullest account of the man that survives.

newcomen-a-sermon-tending-to-set-forth-t.blurb: A fast sermon preached before Parliament and printed in 1644, on what is to be made of the defeats that befall one's own armies. Providential reading of the war cut both ways, and preachers had the harder task in weeks like these, explaining reverses to men who took their cause to be God's. Newcomen was among the ministers Parliament called on regularly.

newcomen-irenicum-or-an-essay-towards-a-.blurb: An essay toward peace and union between those of the congregational and the presbyterian way, printed in 1659, when the collapse of the Protectorate had made the divisions among the godly a political danger as well as a scandal. Newcomen was a Presbyterian, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and one of the five authors who wrote as Smectymnuus.

newcomen-jerusalems-vvatch-men-the-lords.blurb: A fast sermon preached at the Abbey at Westminster before the House of Commons and printed in 1643. The watchmen of Jerusalem who are the Lord's remembrancers, and who are charged not to keep silence, stand for the preaching ministry pressing God for the deliverance of the nation and pressing the nation about its sins. Newcomen preached before Parliament often in these years.

newcomen-the-all-seeing-vnseen-eye-of-go.blurb: A sermon preached before the House of Commons and printed in 1647, on the God who sees everything and is himself unseen, and on what it means to conduct public business under that eye. The application to men holding power in a season of political bargaining is the point of the choice of subject.

newcomen-the-best-acquaintance-and-highe.blurb: A discourse on acquaintance with God, printed in 1668, after Newcomen had been put out of his living by the Act of Uniformity and had gone to the Netherlands. This is practical divinity rather than controversy: what it is to know God as one knows a friend, and what such knowledge does to a life.

newcomen-the-craft-and-cruelty-of-the-ch.blurb: A sermon preached at St Margaret's Westminster and printed in 1643, on the cunning and the violence by which the enemies of the church work against her. St Margaret's was the parish church of the House of Commons, and the sermons preached there on the appointed fast days were ordered into print by the House itself.

newcomen-the-duty-of-such-as-would-walke.blurb: A sermon arguing that those who would walk worthy of the gospel must labour for union, and neither divide nor settle for toleration, which the title treats as a third thing no better than the second. Printed in 1646, in the middle of the argument over whether the new church settlement would grant liberty to the gathered congregations. Newcomen takes the Presbyterian side of it.

newcomen-ultimum-vale-or-the-last-farewe.blurb: A minister's last farewell to a beloved people, printed in 1663. The farewell sermons of the ministers put out by the Act of Uniformity in August 1662 were gathered and printed in numbers, and dissenting families kept them long afterward as the record of what the ejection had cost. Newcomen had served at Dedham in Essex, and he left England not long after.

palmer-a-full-ansvver-to-a-printed-paper.blurb: An answer to an anonymous printed sheet putting four questions about excommunication and the barring of the ignorant and scandalous from the Lord's Supper. Palmer defends the church's own power to exclude, against the Erastian argument that discipline belongs finally to the magistrate. Thirty-two pages, written out of the Westminster Assembly's quarrel with Parliament over who holds the keys.

palmer-an-endeavovr-of-making-the-princi.blurb: A catechism, built on the standard heads of Reformation instruction and naming the Creed and the Ten Commandments on its title page, arranged so that a household head or a plain reader could carry the substance of doctrine in short question and answer. Palmer sat in the Westminster Assembly and was known there for catechising; this is that side of his work rather than his controversial writing.

palmer-memorials-of-godliness-christiani.blurb: Palmer's book of practical divinity in three parts, issued after his death with a short account of his life prefixed. Not controversy but the ordering of a Christian's day: rules for self-examination, brief meditations, and directions for keeping the heart. It is the work by which readers outside the Assembly knew him.

palmer-scripture-and-reason-pleaded-for-.blurb: The parliamentary case for taking up arms against the king, argued first from Scripture and then from reason, and framed as a direct reply to the royalist position that subjects may never resist. Palmer is usually named as the leading hand, though the book was the work of several divines together. One of the fullest English statements of the resistance argument made in the first year of the war.

palmer-the-duty-honour-of-church-restore.blurb: A sermon to the House of Commons on what is owed to a church one undertakes to rebuild, preached while the Assembly's settlement was still before Parliament. The occasion governs the argument throughout: the duty is laid on the men in the pews, who were then deciding how far the reformation of the English church would actually go.

palmer-the-glasse-of-gods-providence-tow.blurb: A fast sermon before both Houses on providence toward the faithful, printed at their order. It is chiefly remembered now for a passing complaint against a book lately published in defence of liberty of divorce, an allusion readers have long taken to be aimed at Milton's tract. The rest is ordinary fast-day divinity, read backward from the war's providences.

palmer-the-necessity-and-encouragement-o.blurb: A fast sermon urging that everything be ventured for the church's help, with the sin of those who hold back set alongside it as the title indicates. Preached to hearers who were being asked for men and money in the first year of the war. Sermons of this kind commonly turned on the curse pronounced on Meroz for not coming to the help of the Lord.

palmer-the-soule-of-fasting.blurb: Nine pages on what a day of solemn fasting and humiliation requires inwardly, the affections without which the outward observance is empty. Written for the monthly fasts kept by order of Parliament during the war, and addressed to the ordinary person keeping one rather than to the man in the pulpit.

palmer-the-upright-protestant-as-he-was-.blurb: Nine pages describing the Protestant as the Reformation left him, purged of what the title calls the superstitious errors of popery, and dated by reference to an earlier reign. A short polemical portrait of true religion against false, printed in the first year of the civil war. Nothing beyond the title indicates more of its argument.

ames-bellarminus-enervatus-1628-as.blurb: Two tomes of Ames's point by point answer to Bellarmine, whose Disputationes were the standard Roman controversial handbook of the age. Ames follows his opponent's own order and replies article by article in the compressed, distinction-driven Latin of his Franeker lectures. These later books carry the controversies that stand last in Bellarmine's arrangement, among them the sacraments, grace and justification.

ames-bellarminus-enervatus-1628-quatuor-.blurb: The whole of Ames's answer to Bellarmine in four tomes, printed at Franeker, where he held the chair of theology. The method is Ramist throughout: every question dichotomised, defined and answered in the fewest words that will carry the distinction, so that a student could hold the shape of a controversy in his head. Bellarmine's text supplies the order; Ames supplies the refutation.

ames-analyticall-exposition-both-epistle.blurb: A commentary on the two epistles of Peter in the analytic manner Ames preferred, resolving each passage into its logical parts, then drawing a doctrine out of every text with its uses appended. Printed from his lectures some years after his death. The best place to watch the method of the Marrow of Theology applied to a continuous stretch of Scripture.

ames-declaration-witness-god-manifested-.blurb: A short spiritual testimony tracing the witness of God in the writer from his youth. The date places it well after the death of the Ames who taught at Franeker, and both the idiom and the form belong to the other William Ames, the Quaker preacher who worked in the Low Countries. Catalogues frequently file the two men under one name. Nine pages of testimony rather than argument.
