ames-good-counsell-advice-all-friends-tr.blurb: An epistle of counsel to Friends, to be read aloud in their families. Friends of truth is Quaker usage, and the date falls long after the death of the Franeker theologian, so this is the William Ames who preached for the early Quakers rather than the author of the Marrow. Sixteen pages of pastoral direction for households in a young movement.

ames-light-candlestick-serving-observati.blurb: Twelve pages on the inward light, issued in English under Ames's name and generally traced back to a Dutch original from the Collegiant circle around the Amsterdam Friends. It answers a book named on its own title page, and states about as plainly as any short piece of the period the claim that the light within a man is the ground of religious certainty. Again the Quaker Ames, not the theologian.

ames-saints-security-against-seducing-sp.blurb: Sermon material on the anointing from the Holy One that teaches all things, the promise in the first epistle of John, applied against the teachers the title calls seducing spirits. Which William Ames stands behind it cannot be settled from what is given here: the date falls after the death of the Franeker divine, and the argument does not read like the Quaker of the same name.

ames-sound-out-sion-from-holy-mountain.blurb: Sixteen pages in the prophetic voice the title announces, a sound out of Zion declaring what the Lord is said to be establishing above all the mountains. The idiom and the date belong to the Quaker William Ames rather than to the Franeker theologian. Written to be read aloud; the title carries nearly the whole of what can be said about it here.

rutherford-de-divina-providentia.blurb: A scholastic disputation in Latin on divine providence, and the most technical thing Rutherford wrote. The chief target is middle knowledge: he argues at length that the scientia media of the Jesuits and the Arminians cannot secure God's knowledge of free acts without making the divine will wait on the creature. Along the way he treats God's concurrence with second causes, the permission of sin, and the physical predetermination the Dominicans defended.

rutherford-exercitationes-apologeticae.blurb: A Latin defence of the Reformed doctrine of grace against Arminius and the Jesuit theologians, published in the Netherlands because it could not be published at home. Predestination, the efficacy of grace, and the bondage of the will are argued in the language of the schools. The book brought Rutherford before the High Commission and into the confinement at Aberdeen from which his letters were written.

rutherford-examen-arminianismi.blurb: An examination of Arminianism in Latin, taken from Rutherford's divinity lectures and published after his death. It works through the disputed heads in order, election and reprobation, the extent of the atonement, grace and the will, perseverance, stating the Remonstrant position and answering it at each point. The length and the pace are those of a lecture course rather than a treatise.

rutherford-lex-rex-law-prince-dispute-ju.blurb: Forty-four questions on the origin and the limits of royal power, written against the royalist case that John Maxwell had put for the king. Rutherford derives the office of king from a covenant with the people, makes the law rather than the prince supreme, and defends resistance by inferior magistrates and, in extremity, by the people themselves. The book was called in and burnt at the Restoration.

rutherford-peaceable-temperate-plea-paul.blurb: Rutherford's first large defence of presbyterian government, arguing that the discipline of the Scottish kirk is the polity of the apostolic church, and answering the episcopal and the independent objections in turn. Written as the Westminster Assembly was being called and shortly before he was sent south to sit in it. Much of the argument here returns in the Assembly's debates on ordination and the power of presbyteries.

rutherford-sermon-preached-before-right-.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Lords in the Abbey Church at Westminster, printed at their order, by one of the Scottish commissioners sent to the Assembly. The Scots preached these occasions with an eye to the covenanted uniformity they had come to secure. The printed text runs to some seventy pages, well past what an hour in the pulpit would hold.

rutherford-survey-spirituall-antichrist-.blurb: A long attack on antinomianism, tracing what Rutherford takes to be one continuous error from the Familists of the previous century down to the antinomian preachers of his own decade. Saltmarsh, Tobias Crisp and the sectaries around the army are handled by name and at length. The questions that carry the argument are assurance, the place of the law in a believer's life, and the claim to immediate revelation.

rutherford-survey-survey-that-summe-chur.blurb: An answer to Thomas Hooker's Survey of the Summe of Church-Discipline, and so the presbyterian side of the argument with New England congregationalism. Rutherford presses where church power resides, whether a single congregation is complete in itself, and what a synod may bind upon a particular church. It appeared after Hooker's death, and after Rutherford's own hopes for a uniform settlement across the three kingdoms had failed.

urraburu-institutiones-logica.blurb: The first volume of an eight-volume Latin course in philosophy by a Spanish Jesuit who taught at the Gregorian in Rome. Logic here covers both the formal apparatus, term, proposition and syllogism, and the material logic of certitude, evidence and the criterion of truth, with the modern objections stated before they are answered. The scale sets the pattern for the whole course.

urraburu-institutiones-ontologia.blurb: The second volume, on being as such: essence and existence, substance and accident, act and potency, the transcendentals, and the kinds of cause. Urraburu writes in the neo-scholastic revival that followed Leo XIII's call for a return to Thomas, though as a Jesuit he often follows Suarez where the two schools divide, and he reports the opinions of both at length before deciding between them.

urraburu-institutiones-cosmologia.blurb: The third volume, on the material world: the constitution of bodies, matter and form set against the atomism and dynamism of nineteenth-century physics, space, time, motion, and the order of nature. This is the point at which a scholastic course of the period meets contemporary natural science head on, and Urraburu takes up the mechanical theories by name rather than passing them over.

urraburu-institutiones-psychologia-1.blurb: The first of three volumes on the soul, which is the longest single division of the course. Psychology in this vocabulary means the philosophy of living things rather than the empirical discipline: the principle of life, the vegetative and sensitive orders, the internal and external senses, and the question of what kind of thing a soul is. How the topics are divided across the three volumes is not stated in this record.

urraburu-institutiones-psychologia-2.blurb: The second of the three volumes on the soul, continuing what volume four begins. In a course of this shape the rational soul falls here or in the volume following: the origin of ideas, the intellect's abstraction of the universal, and the freedom of the will argued against determinism. The exact division of matter between the three psychology volumes is not indicated in this record.

urraburu-institutiones-psychologia-3.blurb: The third and last volume on the soul, closing the longest section of the course. A treatment of this length would ordinarily end with the soul's spirituality and immortality and its union with the body, arguing both against the materialist psychology then in the ascendant. What this particular volume contains is not stated in the record here.

urraburu-institutiones-theodicea-1.blurb: The first of two volumes on God as reason can know him: his existence, argued through the classical proofs and against the atheism, pantheism and agnosticism the nineteenth century had put in their way. Theodicy in this vocabulary means natural theology entire, not merely the problem of evil, and Urraburu treats the modern objections as seriously as the scholastic ones.

urraburu-institutiones-theodicea-2.blurb: The eighth and final volume, carrying natural theology on into the divine attributes and God's relation to the world: simplicity and infinity, knowledge and will, creation, conservation and providence, and the difficulty of evil under a first cause both good and omnipotent. It closes a Latin philosophy course written for seminary teaching and running to eight volumes.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-1.blurb: The opening volume of the modern collected edition of Georgios Scholarios, later Gennadios II, who went to the council at Ferrara and Florence as a layman and imperial adviser, turned against the union afterward, and was made the first patriarch of Constantinople under Ottoman rule when the city fell. The edition prints him in Greek. What this particular volume contains is not indicated in the record here.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-2.blurb: A volume of the collected works of Gennadios Scholarios. Much of his surviving output is polemical: against the Latin addition to the creed, against the union agreed at Florence, and against the Jewish and Muslim objections he had to meet as patriarch of a subject church. The contents of this volume are not specified beyond its number.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-3.blurb: A volume of the collected Scholarios. He is the most thoroughgoing Thomist the Greek church produced, translating and abridging Aquinas into Greek and defending him by name while rejecting the filioque and the Latin claims that Aquinas defended. That combination is what makes him difficult to place and worth reading. This volume's specific contents are not given here.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-4.blurb: A volume of the collected works. Among the pieces gathered in this edition is the confession of faith that Scholarios drew up for Mehmed II, a short statement of Christian doctrine composed for a Muslim sovereign, which is one of the few documents of its kind from the century of the conquest. Which volume holds it is not indicated in the record here.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-5.blurb: The fifth volume of the collected works of Gennadios Scholarios. Besides theology he wrote extensively on Aristotle, and he stood against Plethon's attempt to set Plato above him, a quarrel that runs through the last generation of Byzantine learning. The record here gives the volume number but not its contents.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-6.blurb: The sixth volume of the collected works. Scholarios left letters, homilies, treatises, translations from the Latin and occasional pieces written from the patriarchal throne and from the monasteries he twice retired to, and the edition gathers them all. What falls in this volume is not stated in the record here.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-7.blurb: The seventh volume of the collected works. Scholarios held the patriarchate under Mehmed II and resigned it more than once, and a good deal of what he wrote was written for a church learning how to exist without an emperor. The contents of this volume are not indicated beyond its number.

gennadius-scholarios-works-vol-8.blurb: The eighth and last volume of the collected Scholarios, an edition assembled in the twentieth century from manuscripts scattered across Europe and the East and the first to put his works together in one place. A final volume in such a set commonly carries the shorter and the doubtful pieces along with the apparatus. What this one holds is not specified here.

jewel-apologie-aunswer-defence-church-en.blurb: The Apology in its first form, defending the religion of the Church of England against the charge of novelty and schism at the moment the Council of Trent was closing without English attendance. Jewel argues from Scripture, the ancient councils and the fathers, and puts it to Rome to produce equal authority from the first six hundred years. It set the terms of the long controversy with Thomas Harding.

jewel-apologie-answere-defence-churche-e.blurb: The Apology of the Church of England in English, in the translation made by Ann Bacon and published with the archbishop's approval, which gave the Elizabethan settlement its official self-defence in the vernacular. The case is that the English church has departed not from the catholic faith but from Rome's later additions to it, and that the appeal lies to Scripture and the first six centuries.

jewel-defence-apologie-churche-englande-.blurb: Jewel's reply to Harding's confutation of the Apology, and the largest of his controversial works. The Apology is printed in sections with Harding's objection and Jewel's answer following each, so that the dispute can be followed clause by clause. Eight hundred pages of patristic citation, assembled by the method with which Jewel meant to settle the question of antiquity in the English church's favour.

jewel-replie-vnto-m-hardinges-ansvveare-.blurb: The answer to Harding's reply to the Challenge Sermon, arranged under the articles Jewel had dared his opponents to prove from the first six hundred years: private mass, communion in one kind, service in an unknown tongue, the papal supremacy and the rest. Each is argued out of the fathers and the councils. The whole Jewel and Harding exchange is here in its most concentrated form.

jewel-second-tome-homilees-such-matters-.blurb: The second Book of Homilies, the appointed sermons ordered to be read in parish churches where the incumbent could not preach. Jewel is generally credited with a substantial hand in the collection and with the editing of it. Doctrine, worship and civil obedience as the Elizabethan church wanted them stated to ordinary congregations, including the long homily against wilful rebellion added after the northern rising.

jewel-expositio-two-epistles-apostle-s-p.blurb: Lectures on the two epistles to the Thessalonians, taken down and printed after Jewel's death, and the fullest surviving specimen of his ordinary teaching rather than his controversy. He works through the text in order, and the eschatology of the second epistle, the man of sin and the power that restrains him, is handled at length in the sense Reformation exegetes gave it.

jewel-seuen-godly-learned-sermons-preach.blurb: Seven sermons gathered and printed a generation after the bishop's death. The texts and the occasions are not indicated in the record here, and the title is nearly all there is to go on.

jewel-true-copies-letters-betwene-reuere.blurb: The correspondence that followed the Challenge Sermon at Paul's Cross, printed with the letters given in full on both sides. Dr Cole took up Jewel's dare to prove the disputed Roman practices from the first six hundred years, and the exchange is where Jewel first laid out the appeal to antiquity that governs everything he wrote afterward.

hooker-lavves-ecclesiasticall-politie-ei.blurb: The defence of the English church's constitution against the presbyterian discipline, arguing from law in the largest sense, eternal, natural, divine and human, that not every particular of church order is fixed by Scripture and that the church may determine things indifferent for itself. The title announces eight books, but only the first five appeared in Hooker's lifetime; the last three came out long afterward and in texts whose authority has been disputed ever since.

hooker-ansvvere-mr-richard-hooker-suppli.blurb: Hooker's reply to Walter Travers, who had been silenced for preaching against him at the Temple and had petitioned the Privy Council over it. The quarrel was over predestination, the standing of the Church of Rome, and whether Hooker's teaching on the salvation of forefathers who died in Roman error could be borne. Short, personal, and the nearest thing to autobiography he left.

hooker-learned-discourse-iustification-w.blurb: The sermon that provoked Travers and set off the Temple controversy. Hooker holds justification by an imputed righteousness, and holds also that many who died in the Church of Rome, keeping the foundation while building error upon it, may yet be saved. The distinction between overthrowing the foundation of faith and merely obscuring it carries the argument, and it is the part of his teaching his critics found least tolerable.

hooker-learned-comfortable-sermon-certai.blurb: A sermon distinguishing the certainty of evidence from the certainty of adherence, and arguing that faith may be weak in feeling without being lost. Hooker's answer to the anxious conscience: the elect are not undone by their doubts, since the perpetuity of faith does not rest on the constancy of assurance. Twenty pages, and among the most quoted of his shorter pieces.

hooker-learned-sermon-nature-pride-richa.blurb: A sermon on pride, printed with the other short pieces gathered after Hooker's death. He treats pride as a disorder in the will's estimate of itself rather than as one vice standing among others, which is the same anatomy of law, reason and appetite that runs through the Laws, here brought to bear on a single sin.

hooker-remedie-against-sorrow-feare-deli.blurb: A funeral sermon, eighteen pages, on the sorrow and the fear that attend death and what reason and faith can set against them. One of the short works gathered and printed some years after Hooker's death.

hooker-tvvo-sermons-part-s-judes-epistle.blurb: Two sermons on part of the epistle of Jude, from Hooker's Oxford years and printed long afterward. Jude's warning against those who creep in unawares gave him his occasion to speak about contention and corruption within the church, and readers have generally heard the later Temple controversies anticipated in them.

ford-aytokatakritos-or-the-sinner-condem.blurb: Titled with the Greek for self-condemned, a plea for God against the ungodly which argues that the sinner's own judgment convicts him, so that no man will stand at the last with a case to make. Ford was a presbyterian minister at Exeter, put out of his place in 1662, and this belongs to the practical divinity he wrote after losing the pulpit.

ford-felo-de-se-or-the-bishops-condemned.blurb: Forty-four pages against the bishops, arguing from their own printed words that they have condemned themselves, with the legal term for a suicide serving as the title's conceit. Written by a minister ejected from Exeter after the Restoration settlement, and polemical from the first page to the last.

ford-grace-and-mercy-to-a-sinner-in-a-ti.blurb: Meditations written under affliction and printed as such, closer to a spiritual diary than to a treatise. Grace and mercy are handled as a sinner meets them in trouble rather than as heads of doctrine to be defined.

ford-logos-autopistos-or-scriptures-self.blurb: On the self-authenticating authority of Scripture, the Greek of the title meaning self-credible. Ford argues that the existence, authority and certainty of the Bible are established by its own evidence rather than by the testimony of the church, which is the Reformed answer to the Roman argument from tradition and, by this date, to the sceptical challenge as well.

ford-reformation-sure-and-stedfast-or-a-.blurb: A sermon for the reforming moment of 1641, on what makes a reformation hold rather than collapse. Twenty-eight pages, preached and printed as the Long Parliament was beginning to remake the English church and while it was still an open question how far that would go.

ford-singing-the-psalmes-the-duty-of-chr.blurb: A defence of congregational psalm singing as a duty binding under the New Testament, against those who held that set forms and the singing of another man's words quench the Spirit. The question divided Independents, Baptists and Quakers from the presbyterians through the 1650s, and Ford argues the presbyterian side at length from Scripture.

ford-the-times-anatomiz-d-in-severall-ch.blurb: A book of Theophrastan characters on the types thrown up by the civil war, short satirical prose portraits signed only with initials. The attribution to Thomas Ford is not secure, and the genre sits oddly beside the divinity otherwise filed under his name.

taylor-an-exposition-with-practicall-obs.blurb: A commentary on the first three chapters of Proverbs, grammatical, logical and theological in turn as the title promises, with practical observations drawn from each portion. Taylor sat in the Westminster Assembly and was a Hebraist, and the philological work here is more than ornament. The longest of his works.

taylor-gods-covenant-the-churches-plea-o.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons, printed at their order, taking God's covenant as the plea a church may make in a time of war. Thirty-three pages, one among the many parliamentary fast sermons preached by members of the Westminster Assembly during these years.

taylor-gods-glory-in-mans-happiness-with.blurb: On election and the freeness of grace, with the Arminian objections stated and answered as the title indicates. Taylor argues the Reformed position that God's glory and man's happiness are not competing ends but one end rightly ordered, with election as the means by which both are reached.

taylor-grapes-from-canaan-or-the-believe.blurb: A divine poem on the believer's present taste of future glory, taking the grapes the spies carried back from Canaan as its figure for what is enjoyed before the inheritance is entered. Verse rather than sermon or treatise. The title supplies nearly everything the record gives, and the attribution is worth checking.

taylor-selfe-satisfaction-occasionally-t.blurb: Sermons from the weekday lecture at St Magnus near London Bridge, on contentment with one's own condition, addressed to a city congregation. Sixty pages, printed from the lecture as it was delivered.

taylor-the-danger-of-vowes-neglected-and.blurb: A sermon on the peril of vows left unkept and the reformation still owed, preached at a public fast before one of the Houses. The vow in view by this date was the Solemn League and Covenant, which every English adult had been required to swear, and the sermon presses the obligation it laid on the men who took it.

taylor-the-faith-of-the-chvrch-of-englan.blurb: On the English church's doctrine of God's work upon the human will, argued from the subscriptions the clergy were required to make, which is to say from the Articles and formularies as the received standard. Written against the Arminian reading of those Articles that the Laudian party had advanced, at the moment when Parliament was in a position to overturn it.

amyraut-brief-traitte-predestination.blurb: The short treatise on predestination and its principal dependencies that gave the Saumur school its controversy. Amyraut argues a conditional decree of salvation for all, made effectual only by the absolute decree of election, so that the satisfaction of Christ is universal in its provision while its application stays particular. The scheme was examined at three national synods of the French Reformed churches and not condemned.

amyraut-de-mysterio-trinitatis.blurb: A Latin treatise on the mystery of the Trinity, arguing the doctrine from Scripture and defending it against the Socinian denial, which was the live threat to it in this century. Amyraut is known chiefly for his account of the decrees; this is the same man on the central dogma, working in the ordinary scholastic form.

amyraut-elevation-de-la-foy.blurb: On the raising of faith and the lowering of reason, a French treatise on how far reason may go in matters of religion and where it has to give way. Amyraut neither surrenders reason nor lets it sit as judge over revelation, and the argument is pitched at educated lay readers rather than at the divinity faculty.

amyraut-exercitatio-symbolum-apostolorum.blurb: An exposition of the Apostles' Creed in Latin, article by article, cast as an academic exercise rather than as a catechism. The Creed serves as the frame for a full statement of Christian doctrine, which is the older way of ordering a body of divinity.

amyraut-morale-chrestienne-2.blurb: The second part of Amyraut's Christian ethics, addressed to Monsieur de Villarnoul and published at Saumur. The whole work runs to several volumes and treats the moral life in French for educated lay readers, taking in the passions, the virtues and the duties of a Christian in society. What this volume covers within that scheme is not indicated in the record here.

amyraut-traitte-des-religions.blurb: Against those who hold all religions to be equally indifferent. Amyraut argues first that religion as such is not a thing a man may be indifferent about, and then that the Christian religion alone carries the marks of truth. The opponent here is the sceptic and the libertine rather than a rival confession, which makes this apologetics rather than controversy between churches.

laymann-theologia-moralis-1.blurb: The first book of a moral theology that became one of the standard Jesuit manuals of the seventeenth century, covering the general principles: human acts, conscience, law, sin, and the rules for resolving a doubtful case. Laymann taught at Ingolstadt and Dillingen and wrote for confessors, so the treatment stays practical, but the doctrine of probable opinion that later controversy fastened on is set out here.

laymann-theologia-moralis-2.blurb: The second book, on the theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, with the sins opposed to each and the obligations they lay on a Christian, treated throughout for the confessor's use. The shortest of the five books.

laymann-theologia-moralis-3.blurb: The third book, on justice and right, and the longest of the five. Property, contract, restitution, usury, wages and the questions thrown up by commercial life belong here, which is what made moral theology of this period as much a body of practical jurisprudence as of divinity.

laymann-theologia-moralis-4.blurb: The fourth book, on the religious state: vows and their obligation, obedience, poverty and chastity as professed, the government of the orders, and the standing of clerics. Written by a Jesuit for a church whose orders were the chief instrument of the Catholic reform, and concerned throughout with what a rule actually binds a man to do.

laymann-theologia-moralis-5.blurb: The fifth book, on the sacraments, with penance necessarily at its centre since the whole work is written for confessors: matter and form, the conditions of valid and of worthy reception, marriage and its impediments, and the cases that arise in the confessional.

laymann-theologia-moralis-repertorium.blurb: The index volume to the five books, an alphabetical repertory of cases and terms. Manuals of this kind were consulted rather than read through, and the repertory is the instrument that made the rest of the work usable at speed by a confessor with a penitent waiting.

hardt-constantiense-concilium-1.blurb: The first tome of a six-volume documentary collection on the Council of Constance, assembled by a Lutheran orientalist at Helmstedt from manuscripts gathered across Germany. A good deal of what it prints had not been in print before. The council's business was the ending of the schism, the reform of the church, and the trial of Hus, and a Protestant editor had reasons of his own for putting the whole record in the open.

hardt-constantiense-concilium-2.blurb: The second tome, continuing the documents of the council under the same general heading as the first. Von der Hardt gathered treatises, letters and memorials from the men who attended, Gerson and d'Ailly among the most substantial, and printed them alongside the official record. The particular contents of this volume are not specified beyond that heading.

hardt-constantiense-concilium-3.blurb: The third tome, headed as concerning matters of religion and faith, and so carrying the doctrinal business of the council: the condemnation of Wyclif's articles, the trial and burning of Hus, and the case of Jerome of Prague. For a Lutheran editor working in the 1690s this was the part of the record that mattered most.

hardt-constantiense-concilium-4.blurb: The fourth tome, the acts of the sessions, which is to say the official record of the council itself: the decrees, among them the assertions of a general council's authority over the pope and the provision for councils at fixed intervals thereafter, the removal of the rival claimants, and the election of Martin V.

hardt-constantiense-concilium-5.blurb: The fifth tome, on the display and ceremonial of the council, the entries and processions and the crowd that Constance carried for four years. The material here is chronicle and description rather than act or treatise, and it is the volume to go to for the council as an event in a city rather than as a set of decrees.

hardt-constantiense-concilium-6.blurb: The sixth and last tome, the index and the miscellaneous matter for the set. Two hundred pages of apparatus for five volumes of documents, which is what makes a collection on this scale navigable at all.

mansi-sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-27.blurb: The years 1409 to 1418 in the great conciliar collection begun in the eighteenth century by the archbishop of Lucca, which enlarged the earlier collections of Labbe, Hardouin and Coleti and remains the standard reference for conciliar texts. This tome carries the Council of Pisa, which tried to end the schism and produced a third claimant instead, and then the Council of Constance. Acts, decrees and associated documents in Latin, chronologically arranged.

mansi-sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-28.blurb: The years 1414 to 1431: the remainder of Constance, including the sessions on Wyclif and Hus and the decrees asserting the authority of a general council, then the provincial synods of the following decade and the summoning of the council to Basel.

mansi-sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-29.blurb: The years 1431 to 1434, which is the Council of Basel in its first and most assertive phase: the refusal to dissolve when Eugenius IV ordered it, the negotiations with the Hussites that produced the Compacts, and the reform decrees the council pressed on a pope who had tried to close it.

mansi-sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-30.blurb: The years 1434 to 1439, the period in which Basel and the papacy broke apart: the later Basel sessions, the transfer of the council to Ferrara and then to Florence, and the opening of the negotiations with the Greeks over reunion.

mansi-sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-31.blurb: The years 1439 to 1449: the decree of union with the Greeks at Florence and the further unions with the Armenians and other eastern churches, set against the continuing acts of the rump remaining at Basel, its deposition of Eugenius IV, and the election and eventual submission of the last antipope.

mansi-sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-32.blurb: A long span, from 1438 to 1549, carrying the collection out of the conciliar age, through the Fifth Lateran Council, and up to the eve of Trent. Provincial and national synods make up much of the volume, and the material is thinner and more scattered than in the tomes on either side of it.

brooks-apples-gold-young-men-vvomen-crow.blurb: Directions to the young on early piety, with a second address to the old, from a London preacher whose books were among the most read of the puritan practical writers. Brooks works in short numbered heads packed with Scripture and homely similitude, so that the argument can be followed by a reader with no learning at all.

brooks-cabinet-choice-jevvels-box-precio.blurb: On the marks by which a man may know his own spiritual condition, arranged as a series of trials or evidences of grace, with the conceit of jewels and ointment sustained through the whole. Assurance is Brooks's constant subject, and this is his longest treatment of the question of how a true work of grace is told from a counterfeit.

brooks-crovvn-glory-christianity-holines.blurb: Fifty-eight sermons on holiness from a single text in Hebrews, arguing that holiness is the way to happiness rather than the price of it. Preached in London and printed in the year of the ejection, which put Brooks out of his living. The length and the repetition are those of a long sermon course rather than a treatise.

brooks-privie-key-heaven-twenty-argument.blurb: Twenty arguments for closet prayer, the private prayer commanded in the sixth chapter of Matthew, with objections answered and directions given for the practice. Brooks argues by multiplying reasons, instances and Scripture rather than by pressing a tight case, and the book is long for its single subject.

brooks-heavenly-cordial-all-those-servan.blurb: Written for those who had lived through the plague, thirteen maxims put to the reader who was spared, on what such a deliverance obliges him to. Brooks was one of the London ministers who stayed in the city through the visitation, and the book is addressed to people who had watched their neighbours die.

brooks-ton-anexichniaston-plouton-tou-ch.blurb: On the unsearchable riches of Christ, the phrase from Ephesians that supplies the Greek of the title. The subtitle describes the method exactly: meat for strong men and milk for babes, doctrine and plain application mixed together on the same page, which is how Brooks wrote everything.

burroughs-eighth-book-mr-jeremiah-burrou.blurb: Printed from Burroughs's papers as the eighth in the numbered series of his posthumous works, this is a long treatise on sin considered in itself: what makes it worse than any affliction, why the least sin carries an infinite offence, and how a Christian should reason when suffering seems the greater evil. The argument runs through scores of short chapters, each pressing one aggravation of sin. Practical divinity in the Puritan casuistic manner.

burroughs-exposition-prophesie-hosea-beg.blurb: Lectures on the first three chapters of Hosea, delivered at Michael's, Cornhill, and printed some years after Burroughs's death. The prophet's marriage to Gomer occupies him at length, read as a figure of God's dealing with an apostate people, and the sermons turn steadily from Israel's case to England's. Further installments carried the exposition deeper into the prophecy; this volume is where the series begins.

burroughs-four-usefull-discourses-viz-je.blurb: A posthumous gathering of four discourses printed nearly thirty years after Burroughs died. The shortened title as given here does not name them, so their subjects cannot be reported. Readers who know his other work will expect practical divinity of the usual kind, sermon material worked up for the press by the men who held his manuscripts.

burroughs-irenicum-lovers-truth-peace-he.blurb: An anatomy of division among Christians, written in the middle of the English civil wars and addressed, as the title says, to lovers of truth and peace. Burroughs traces heart-divisions to their causes in pride, self-interest, misjudged zeal, and the mistaking of opinions for fundamentals, then sets out cautions and remedies. The voice is that of an Independent arguing for forbearance among the godly, not for indifference about doctrine.

burroughs-rare-jevvel-christian-contentm.blurb: Sermons on Paul's saying that he had learned, in whatsoever state he is, therewith to be content. Burroughs defines contentment as an inward, quiet, gracious frame of spirit, then works through the mystery of it, the lessons Christ teaches in it, the excellence of it, the evils of a murmuring heart, and the aggravations of discontent. The best known of his practical works.

burroughs-sermon-preached-before-right-h.blurb: A fast sermon preached to the Lords in Westminster Abbey and printed by order, as such sermons were. Burroughs was an Independent and one of the Dissenting Brethren at the Westminster Assembly, and the fast before Parliament was the occasion on which preachers of his party addressed the nation's rulers to their faces. Neither the text nor the argument is given in the title as it stands.

manton-englands-spirituall-languishing-c.blurb: A fast sermon preached before the Commons and printed by their order, diagnosing the nation's spiritual decay and prescribing its cure. Manton was still early in his London ministry. The parliamentary fast sermon was a fixed institution of the 1640s and this is a specimen of it: national sin identified, judgement threatened, reformation pressed on the men who had the power to enact it.

manton-one-hundred-ninety-sermons-on-hun.blurb: An exposition of the whole of Psalm 119, preached in course and printed after Manton's death. Every verse receives at least one sermon, and the psalm's revolving vocabulary of law, testimonies, statutes and judgements is turned over again and again without the treatment going slack. It is the work by which Manton is usually known, and a full specimen of consecutive Puritan preaching on a single text.

manton-practical-commentary-exposition-n.blurb: A verse by verse exposition of Jude, delivered for the most part as sermons and afterwards worked up for print. Manton takes the epistle's warning against teachers who creep in unawares as a standing description of the church's danger, and the short letter yields a full treatise on apostasy, on contending for the faith once delivered, and on the preservation of the saints. Application follows each doctrine in the usual order.

manton-second-volume-sermons-preached-la.blurb: The second of the posthumous collections of Manton's preaching, issued in two parts and running to well over a thousand pages. The title as given does not identify the texts or the occasions. What can be said is generic: consecutive expository sermons in the plain method, doctrine stated, proved from scripture, then applied.

manton-sermon-preached-at-funerall-m-chr.blurb: A funeral sermon for Christopher Love, the London Presbyterian minister executed that August for his part in a plot to bring in Charles II. The occasion was dangerous as well as mournful, since the preacher had to bury a man the government had killed and say something true about him. Sixteen pages, preached at St Laurence church three days after the execution.

manton-sermons-preached-late-reverend-le.blurb: A gathering of Manton's sermons printed in 1678, drawn from a much larger body of preaching. The title as given identifies neither the texts nor the occasions, and the volume is a selection rather than a series. Expect the plain method throughout: a text opened, a doctrine raised from it, reasons, then uses.

stillingfleet-answer-some-papers-lately-.blurb: A reply to papers in defence of the Roman church published under James II, two of them attributed to the late Charles II and one to Anne Hyde, the king's first wife, dead some years before. Stillingfleet answers the claim that the authority of the Catholic Church settles matters of faith, and his answer drew further replies. Controversial writing from the years when a Roman Catholic king was pressing the case in print.

stillingfleet-defence-discourse-concerni.blurb: A large defence of Stillingfleet's earlier discourse charging the Church of Rome with idolatry in the worship of images, saints and the host, written against the answers that discourse provoked. The method is historical as much as dogmatic, with the fathers and the councils brought in on the definition of idolatry itself, since the quarrel turns on how far the word can be made to reach.

stillingfleet-ecclesiastical-cases-relat.blurb: Cases of conscience and of law touching the parish clergy, stated and resolved: residence, tithes, the rights attached to a cure of souls, and the duties an incumbent owes. Stillingfleet wrote as bishop of Worcester and as a man at home in canon and civil law. The volume belongs with the practical and jurisdictional side of his work rather than with the controversial writings against Rome.

stillingfleet-second-discourse-vindicati.blurb: A continuation of Stillingfleet's defence of the Protestant rule of faith against the Roman claim that certainty in religion requires an infallible living judge. He argues that the grounds on which Protestants believe are sufficient for a rational and a saving assent, and that the demand for infallibility either proves too much or ends in a circle. One instalment of a long paper war.

stillingfleet-sermon-preached-at-publick.blurb: A sermon preached at a public ordination at St Peter's Cornhill in March 1685, printed at the customary length. Ordination sermons in this period take up the ministry itself: the warrant for it, the qualifications of the men admitted to it, and the account they will have to give. The title supplies the occasion and nothing further.

stillingfleet-six-sermons-discourse-anne.blurb: Six sermons, with a discourse annexed on the true reason of Christ's sufferings. The discourse is the substantial part: a defence of the satisfaction made by Christ's death against the Socinian account, and against Crellius in particular, who had answered Grotius on the same question. Stillingfleet argues that the sufferings were properly penal and vicarious, not merely exemplary or a declaration of God's hatred of sin.

seaman-a-glasse-for-the-times-wherein-is.blurb: A sermon on the malady and the remedy of divisions, printed in the years when the godly party in England was breaking into parties of its own. Seaman sat in the Westminster Assembly and was a London Presbyterian, which makes it likely that the divisions in view are those among Protestants rather than those between Protestants and Rome. Thirty-five pages; the text and occasion are not given here.

seaman-reverend-and-beloved-it-hath-plea.blurb: A single printed leaf, apparently a circular letter to ministers concerning something set in motion by the Lord Mayor of London. Its opening words serve as its title, which is the usual way of cataloguing such a sheet. One page survives and nothing further about its business can be reported from it.

seaman-solomons-choice-or-a-president-fo.blurb: A sermon on Solomon at Gibeon, where the young king asked for an understanding heart rather than riches or long life, held up as a pattern for kings, princes and all in authority. It was printed in 1644, when what those in authority ought to ask for was a live question in England. Seaman sat in the Westminster Assembly and was among the ministers Parliament called on to preach.

seaman-the-diatrib-proved-to-be-paradiat.blurb: A controversial reply in which Seaman turns an opponent's Diatribe back on him and vindicates the judgement of the Reformed churches against it. The title as given is cut short before it names the point in dispute. The genre is plain enough: an academic answer taken point by point, in the manner of the mid-century English exchanges over church government and ordination.

seaman-the-head-of-the-church-the-iudge-.blurb: A short treatise on the day of judgement, with Christ set out under two titles, head of the church and judge of the world. Forty-six pages, printed in 1647. The doctrine is briefly opened, which in the usage of the time means stated, proved from scripture, and applied to the hearer, in that order.

seaman-the-second-and-last-collection-of.blurb: The second gathering of the sermons London ministers preached in August 1662 as they were put out of their livings by the Act of Uniformity, Seaman among them. The farewell sermons were printed and reprinted despite official displeasure. They are the nearest thing to a public record of what the ejected men said to their congregations at the parting.

chemnitz-de-duabus-naturis-in-christo.blurb: The Lutheran treatise on the person of Christ: the two natures, the personal union, and above all the communication of properties, which Chemnitz sorts into kinds and defends from scripture and the Greek fathers. Behind it stands the quarrel with the Reformed over whether the humanity of Christ can receive divine majesty and be present wherever the Supper is celebrated. Its argument shaped the eighth article of the Formula of Concord.

chemnitz-examen-concilii-tridentini.blurb: A point by point examination of the Council of Trent, taking the decrees and canons in order and answering each from scripture and the fathers. Chemnitz grants what can be granted, shows where Trent's language is deliberately ambiguous, then presses the historical question of whether the doctrine defined is in fact what the ancient church taught. Composed over several years and issued in parts.

chemnitz-loci-theologici-pars-1.blurb: The first of three parts of the dogmatics assembled after Chemnitz's death from his lectures on Melanchthon's Loci Communes, which he had given to ministerial candidates at Brunswick. The order of topics follows Melanchthon; the treatment is much fuller, with patristic testimony and the controversies of the day worked in at each head. Which loci fall in this part is not indicated by the volume label.

chemnitz-loci-theologici-pars-2.blurb: The second of the three parts into which this dogmatics is divided. The parts break up a single continuous work, so a reader after a particular locus should consult the table rather than guess from the numbering. Chemnitz's manner throughout is fixed: the article stated, the scriptural grounds set down, then the testimony of the fathers, then the objections of opponents answered.

chemnitz-loci-theologici-pars-3.blurb: The third and last part of the posthumous dogmatics drawn from Chemnitz's lectures on Melanchthon. In Melanchthon's order the closing heads run toward the church, the ministry, the sacraments and the last things, though the volume label does not confirm what is here. The whole was edited and seen through the press by later Lutheran hands, not by the author.

oecolampadius-in-1-ioannis.blurb: Twenty-one homilies on the first epistle of John, from the reformer of Basel, printed while that city's evangelical settlement was still being fought over. The Greek word in the title, demegoriae, signals popular addresses rather than academic lectures. Oecolampadius was a Greek and Hebrew scholar and an editor of the fathers, and his exposition keeps close to the text rather than running to commonplaces.

oecolampadius-in-danielem.blurb: Two books of commentary on Daniel, printed in 1530. The historical chapters and the visions both receive treatment. A Reformed reader of that century came to Daniel for the succession of the four monarchies and for the identity of the little horn, questions that ran straight into the polemics of the day, and Oecolampadius reads the prophet with the philological care he brought to the fathers.

oecolampadius-in-hebraeos.blurb: Expositions of the epistle to the Hebrews, printed in 1534, three years after the author's death, and so presumably taken from lecture or sermon notes. Hebrews on the priesthood and on the once for all sacrifice of Christ was ground the Basel reformer had already worked in the eucharistic controversy, and the epistle's argument about shadow and substance suited his reading of the Old Testament.

oecolampadius-in-iob.blurb: Expository notes on the book of Job, printed in 1532, the year after Oecolampadius died. The Latin exegemata promises exposition rather than a continuous running commentary. Job's speeches, the arguments of the friends, and the question of why the righteous suffer are the matter, and a sixteenth century Reformed reader would have come here for the doctrine of providence as much as for the text.

oecolampadius-sermo-de-eucharistia.blurb: A short piece on the Lord's Supper from the Basel reformer who, with Zwingli, denied that the words this is my body require a bodily presence. Oecolampadius had already argued the case at length out of the fathers, and at Marburg in 1529 he stood with Zwingli against Luther on it. Twenty-nine pages, printed in 1531, the year he died.

petavius-dogmata-tomus-1.blurb: The first volume of the dogmatics that set out to establish Catholic doctrine historically rather than by scholastic demonstration, tracing each article through the fathers and the councils in order. This tome treats the one God: his existence, the divine names, and the attributes. Petau was a Jesuit of great learning in patristics and chronology, and the positive method he uses here changed how dogmatic theology was written.

petavius-dogmata-tomus-2.blurb: The second tome, on the Trinity, and the most argued over part of the whole work. Petau assembles the ante-Nicene testimony at length and admits that some of it falls short of the language later fixed at Nicaea, a candour that Anglican and Reformed writers were glad to quote and that some of his own side found awkward. The treatment runs from the scriptural grounds through the Arian crisis to the settled doctrine of persons and processions.

petavius-dogmata-tomus-3.blurb: The third tome, on the angels and the created world: the nature and orders of the angelic host, their knowledge and will, the fall of the wicked angels, and the six days of creation. The method is the same as elsewhere in the series, a historical assembly of patristic and conciliar testimony first, with the questions of the schoolmen taken up afterwards rather than before.

petavius-dogmata-tomus-4.blurb: The fourth tome, on the incarnation: the person of Christ, the hypostatic union, the two natures and two wills, and the christological councils from Ephesus onward. Petau's habit of quoting the Greek fathers at length is at its most useful here, since this doctrine was hammered out in Greek and the Latin summaries of it repay checking against the originals he prints.

petavius-dogmata-tomus-4-pars-altera.blurb: The second half of the fourth tome, continuing the treatise on the incarnation. The division is a matter of bulk rather than of subject, and the label says nothing about which questions fall on this side of the break. A reader should treat the two halves as one book and consult the table.

zanchi-de-natura-dei.blurb: Five books on the nature of God and the divine attributes, from the Italian Protestant who taught at Strasbourg, Heidelberg and finally Neustadt. Zanchi treats the essence, simplicity, immensity, eternity, knowledge, will and power of God with the full apparatus of the schools, Aristotle and Aquinas used without embarrassment, and the whole tied back to exegesis. It belongs to the larger summa on the works of God he was assembling.

zanchi-de-religione-christiana-fides.blurb: Zanchi's confession of the Christian religion, drawn up in his own name and running through the articles of faith in order, with the points at issue between the confessions noted as they arise. It was written as a personal profession rather than as a church symbol, and it was later put into English. Plainer and shorter than his disputational works.

zanchi-de-tribus-elohim.blurb: Thirteen books on the Trinity, argued from the Hebrew scriptures as much as from the New Testament, with the plural Elohim joined to singular verbs taken as one of the traces of the three persons in the Old Testament. The immediate opponents are the antitrinitarians of the sixteenth century, Servetus and those who followed him, and Zanchi meets them on their own exegetical ground before turning to the fathers.

zanchi-miscellaneorum-libri-tres.blurb: Three books of miscellaneous pieces: shorter treatises, letters and occasional writings gathered up outside the main dogmatic works. The title says nothing of the contents and they cannot be listed from it. A volume of this kind is usually opened for one particular item that the reader already knows is inside it.

zanchi-de-operibus-dei.blurb: On the works God created in the space of six days, divided into three parts. Zanchi uses the hexaemeron as the frame for a full doctrine of creation: the angels, the heavens, the elements, the living creatures, and then man in body and soul, with the state of innocence and the fall following. The natural philosophy of his own century is worked in throughout and is part of what a reader will find here.

gazzaniga-praelectiones-1.blurb: The first of five volumes of a printed course of dogmatic theology by an eighteenth century Dominican who taught at Vienna. Courses of this kind proceed treatise by treatise, commonly opening with the grounds of belief before turning to God and the rest, though the volume label does not confirm what stands here. Gazzaniga writes as a Thomist and answers the objections of his own century rather than the sixteenth's.

gazzaniga-praelectiones-2.blurb: The second of five volumes of the same course of Vienna lectures. Textbooks of this sort were re-edited and reissued for seminary use for decades after their authors died, so volume numbering and arrangement vary between editions and the copy in hand should be checked rather than the series description. The treatises contained here are not named in the label.

gazzaniga-praelectiones-3.blurb: The third of five volumes. Scholastic dogmatics of this period keeps a fixed shape: the thesis stated, the adversaries named, proof from scripture, from tradition and from reason, then objections resolved in order. The subject matter of this particular volume is not given in the label and cannot be inferred from the series title alone.

gazzaniga-praelectiones-4.blurb: The fourth of five volumes of the Vienna lectures, with no subject supplied by the label. In courses of comparable shape the later volumes carry the sacraments and the last things, but that is an expectation drawn from the genre and not a report of what is here. The method throughout the series is Thomist and disputational.

gazzaniga-praelectiones-5.blurb: The fifth and last volume of the course. Nothing in the label identifies the treatises it contains. Gazzaniga's lectures belong to the Thomist school teaching of the later eighteenth century, and the set was still being reissued for seminary use long after his death, which is why so many differing printings survive.

dedeken-thesaurus-consiliorum-vol-2.blurb: The second volume of a Lutheran collection of consilia, gathering the political cases: magistracy, oaths, war, and the dealings of the church with the civil power, each answered by named theologians or by a university faculty. Consilia of this kind are the nearest Lutheran equivalent to case divinity, and they show what the doctrine looked like when it had to be applied to one man in one difficulty.

dedeken-praxis-conscientiarum.blurb: A work of case divinity from the compiler of the great Lutheran collection of consilia. The title promises the practice of consciences, which is to say the handling of particular cases, the same business as the consilia but set out as instruction rather than as a file of answers already given. The contents cannot be described further from the title alone.

dedeken-thesaurus-consiliorum-vol-3.blurb: The third volume, on mixed cases and above all on marriage: degrees of kindred, betrothal and the breaking of it, desertion, divorce, remarriage, and the tangle where church and civil jurisdiction overlap. Marriage generated more consultation than any other subject, which is why it has most of a volume to itself. The entries are opinions given on particular cases, not a continuous treatise.

dedeken-thesaurus-consiliorum-vol-1.blurb: The first and largest volume of a collection of Lutheran consilia, written opinions and judgements returned by theologians and by theological faculties on questions put to them. This volume holds the ecclesiastical cases: doctrine, ministry, discipline and worship. Dedeken was a Hamburg minister, and the work was assembled as a reference book for pastors and church officials who needed to know what had been ruled before.

dedeken-thesaurus-appendix-nova.blurb: A later supplement to the Thesaurus, adding further opinions and decisions to those in the three volumes of the original collection. Supplements of this kind accumulate as new cases are put and new faculty judgements are returned. The arrangement follows the parent work, which means a reader hunting one subject has to look in both places.

chillingworth-mr-chillingworth-s-book-ca.blurb: A later edition of Chillingworth's answer to the Jesuit who wrote as Edward Knott, issued under James II with additional matter bound in to make it, as the title has it, more generally useful. The book argues that the Bible alone is the religion of Protestants and that a man who follows scripture with an honest and diligent mind cannot be damned for the errors he falls into. Its reappearance in 1687 was not an accident of the trade.

chillingworth-petition-most-substantiall.blurb: A printed petition from London inhabitants to the Lords, from the crisis of 1642, catalogued here among Chillingworth's works. Petitions of this kind were instruments of politics rather than records of opinion, gathered and printed to display weight of numbers. The attribution comes with the volume, and the title by itself will not settle whether he had any hand in it.

chillingworth-religion-protestants-safe-.blurb: The answer to Mercy and Truth, the Jesuit Edward Knott's book charging that Protestants cannot be saved. Chillingworth concedes far more than his own side liked: that no church is infallible, that councils have erred, that a man may be mistaken in much and still be saved, and that the Bible alone is the religion of Protestants. It came out of the circle around Lucius Cary at Great Tew and remains the fullest English case for a minimal, rationally held Christianity.

chillingworth-sermon-preached-at-publike.blurb: A fast sermon preached before Charles I at Christ Church while Oxford was the royalist capital, printed in 1644. Chillingworth had attached himself to the king's party and followed the army, and he died that January in parliamentary hands after the fall of Arundel, which makes this a posthumous printing. The text of the sermon is not named in the title.

chillingworth-sermon-preached-preached-b.blurb: A court sermon preached before Charles I at Reading, printed in 1644, the year Chillingworth died in parliamentary custody. Sermons before the king in the war years carried political weight whatever their text, since the court congregation was also a war council. The title supplies neither the text nor the date of delivery.

downing-a-discoursive-coniecture-vpon-th.blurb: A speculative political essay on the causes at work in the troubles of Great Britain and on what might bring them to the end its author wanted. Downing was a parliamentarian clergyman who had already argued in print that arms could lawfully be taken up against the king's evil counsellors. Written in 1641, when the outcome was still open and conjecture was the honest form for such a piece.

downing-a-discoverie-of-the-false-ground.blurb: An attack on the grounds claimed by what the author calls the Bavarian party, meaning the Catholic and imperial interest that had prevailed in the German wars, and on the design attributed to it in Britain. Downing wrote in 1641, when continental popery and domestic prelacy were routinely treated as one conspiracy. The rest of the argument is not recoverable from the shortened title.

downing-a-sermon-preached-to-the-renowne.blurb: The sermon to the Artillery Company of 1 September 1640 that made Downing notorious, printed the following year. He argued that arms might lawfully be taken up against the king's evil counsellors, and against the bishops in particular, for the defence of religion and the kingdom. The doctrine was dangerous enough that he withdrew from London for a time. Preached before the Scottish war had finished its work on English opinion.

downing-considerations-toward-a-peaceabl.blurb: Nine pages of proposals for reforming the church without tearing the country apart, submitted, as the title says, to judicious consideration. It appeared in 1641, when the fate of episcopacy was before Parliament and schemes for a limited or reduced episcopacy were being floated from several directions. What Downing proposed in detail cannot be told from the title.

downing-the-cleere-antithesis-or-diametr.blurb: A short piece setting presbytery and prelacy against each other as opposites, printed in 1644, when the Westminster Assembly's work had made the question practical rather than theoretical. Downing had by then thrown in with Parliament. The title promises a demonstration of the opposition, not an even handed comparison, and the reader should expect the case to be made in one direction.

heyrick-a-sermon-preached-at-the-collegi.blurb: A sermon at the collegiate church in Manchester on 23 April 1661, the day of Charles II's coronation. Heyrick was warden there, a Presbyterian who had opposed the Independents and the regicide and had been implicated in Christopher Love's plot to bring in the king. Preaching the coronation was in that light a consistent act rather than a turn, and he kept his place after the Restoration.

heyrick-queen-esthers-resolves-or-a-prin.blurb: A sermon on Esther's resolve to go in to the king though it was against the law, held up as a pattern of resolution for those who love God and their country. Printed in 1646. Heyrick was warden of the collegiate church in Manchester and a leading Lancashire Presbyterian, and sermons of this kind were preached to stiffen a party as much as to open a text.

heyrick-the-harmonious-consent-of-the-mi.blurb: The Lancashire ministers' subscription to the testimony their London brethren had published against the errors, heresies and blasphemies of the time and against a general toleration. Heyrick, warden at Manchester, stood at the head of the province's clergy. It is a corporate declaration rather than a treatise, and one of the plainest statements of what provincial Presbyterians thought they were defending in 1648.

heyrick-the-paper-called-the-agreement-o.blurb: A ministers' answer to the Agreement of the People, the army's constitutional proposal, weighing whether subscription to it was lawful. It was printed in 1649, in the months around the king's trial and execution, when Presbyterians who had fought the king refused the settlement the army was imposing. The title is cut short before it says which way it decides, though the Lancashire papers of these months leave little doubt.

heyrick-three-sermons-preached-at-the-co.blurb: Three sermons preached at the collegiate church in Manchester and printed together in 1641, running to two hundred pages. The texts and the occasions are not named in the title. Heyrick was warden there and would shortly be among the leading Presbyterian ministers of Lancashire, but nothing in the title fixes these sermons to that later career.

strickland-a-discovery-of-peace-or-the-t.blurb: A sermon on God's purposes of peace toward a people under judgement, preached in 1644 during the war. Strickland was a Wiltshire minister who sat in the Westminster Assembly and preached repeatedly before the Houses, and sermons of this kind were ordered into print by whichever House had heard them. The text is not identified in the title as given.

strickland-gods-vvork-of-mercy-in-sions-.blurb: A fast sermon before the Commons in 1644, on mercy shown in the midst of Zion's misery. The monthly fast sermon ran through the war years and was printed by order of the House. The standard shape is a national application: this is what God is doing with us, and this is what he requires of the men who sit here and can act on it.

strickland-immanuel-or-the-church-triump.blurb: A sermon before the Lords, taking the name Immanuel, God with us, as the ground of the church's triumph, and printed by order as parliamentary sermons were. The year is that of Marston Moor, when the war had begun to turn, though nothing in the title ties the sermon to any particular event. Forty-six pages.

strickland-mercy-rejoycing-against-judge.blurb: A sermon on God waiting to be gracious to a sinful nation, printed in 1645. The first half of the title echoes James on mercy rejoicing against judgement and the second echoes Isaiah on the Lord who waits that he may be gracious. Strickland preached before Parliament more than once in these years and this belongs to that series; the occasion is cut from the title as given.

strickland-the-kings-entertainment-at-yo.blurb: A single leaf of news reporting how Charles I was received at York in March 1642, as related by one John Strickland who had come from there. It is a newsbook item rather than a sermon, and whether the reporter is the minister of the same name is not something the title can settle. One page.

ward-an-encovragement-to-warre-or-bellvm.blurb: A short piece of 1642 arguing that a parliamentary war is lawful where the recent bishops' war against the Scots was not, the two set against each other in the Latin tags of the title. It was printed as the fighting began. The argument turns on the ends of the war and the authority under which arms are taken up, which is where the whole English debate over resistance sat.

ward-god-iudging-among-the-gods-opened-i.blurb: A sermon before the Commons in 1645, opening the words of the eighty-second psalm, where God stands in the congregation of the mighty and judges among the gods. That psalm was the standing text for preaching to magistrates: you are called gods, and you will be judged as men. Printed by order of the House, and at sixty-eight pages one of the longer specimens of the form.

ward-the-christians-incouragement-earnes.blurb: A call to contend earnestly for the gospel and for Christian liberties, printed in 1643 with the war a year old. The phrasing joins Jude's contending for the faith once delivered to the political vocabulary of liberties, which is what preachers on the parliamentary side were doing throughout the decade. Nothing further about the occasion appears in the title.

ward-the-good-vvill-of-him-that-dwelt-in.blurb: A sermon taking a phrase from Moses's blessing on Joseph, the good will of him that dwelt in the bush, and applying it to the happiness of living under an extraordinary providence. Printed in 1645. The bush that burned and was not consumed was a favourite figure for the church in trouble among the preachers of this decade.

ward-the-taking-of-vvinchester-by-the-pa.blurb: Twelve pages of war news reporting the capture of Winchester by parliamentary forces and the surrender of the castle, printed in 1642 among the flood of such accounts that followed every action. It is a newsbook rather than a sermon, and its attachment here to a preacher of the same name should be treated with care.

franciscus-sylvius-opera-omnia-tom-1.blurb: The first of four volumes of the collected works of the Douai theologian François du Bois, who wrote as Franciscus Sylvius. His main labour was a commentary on the whole Summa Theologiae of Aquinas, taken article by article, and the collected edition carries that along with shorter treatises and controversial pieces. The label gives no subject, so which part of the Summa falls here must be checked in the book itself.

franciscus-sylvius-opera-omnia-tom-2.blurb: The second of four volumes of the collected works. Sylvius reads Aquinas closely and plainly, without the vast length of the Spanish commentators, which is part of why his commentary stayed in seminary use and was reprinted long after his death. The volume label does not say which questions or treatises are gathered here.

franciscus-sylvius-opera-omnia-tom-3.blurb: The third and largest of the four volumes, running past a thousand pages. A collected edition of a working commentator gathers three things: the commentary on Aquinas itself, disputations hung on particular questions, and occasional or controversial writings. Which of them, and which part of the Summa, this volume holds is not stated in the label.

franciscus-sylvius-opera-omnia-tom-4.blurb: The fourth volume of the collected works of Sylvius, the Douai commentator on Aquinas. He taught and wrote in the first half of the seventeenth century, when Douai was a chief centre of Catholic theology in the north and a training ground for the English mission. The contents of this particular volume are not identified by the label.

gwalther-ad-galatas.blurb: Homilies on Galatians from the pastor who succeeded Bullinger at the head of the Zurich church, printed in 1576. The epistle's argument about law and gospel and its account of Paul's quarrel with Peter at Antioch were both live matters in that century, the second in disputes over church authority. Preached to a congregation first and printed in Latin afterwards for readers abroad.

gwalther-ad-romanos.blurb: Homilies on Romans, printed in 1566, from a Zurich minister of Bullinger's circle who preached through books of scripture in course and then published the series in Latin. That practice carried Zurich exposition across Protestant Europe and particularly into England, where Gwalther was read and cited. The homily form means continuous exposition with application rather than disputation, though the Reformed reading of justification and election is plain throughout.

gwalther-posteriorem-corinthios.blurb: Homilies on the second epistle to the Corinthians, printed alongside its companion series in 1572. The matter of that epistle is the ministry itself, its afflictions, its authority, and its defence against rivals, which is why it was preached and read as a manual for pastors. Gwalther composed these for delivery in Zurich and printed them in Latin for readers elsewhere.

gwalther-priorem-corinthios.blurb: Homilies on the first epistle to the Corinthians, the longer of Gwalther's two Corinthian series, printed in 1572. Divisions in the church, discipline, marriage, the Lord's Supper and the resurrection all gave a Zurich preacher a great deal to say to his own city. Gwalther was Zwingli's son in law and spent his whole working life in the service of that church.

suarez-de-legibus.blurb: Ten books on law and on God as lawgiver: what a law is, the eternal law, the natural law, the law of nations, human and civil law, penal law, custom, privilege, and the divine positive law of the old and the new covenants. Suárez's account of political authority as given by God to the community and conveyed by it to rulers is the part later readers went to, and it stands behind much of the argument over the origin of civil power.

suarez-de-triplici-virtute.blurb: Disputations on the three theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, following the order of the questions in the Secunda Secundae. The treatise on charity carries the discussion of war, where Suárez sets out the conditions of just cause, right authority and right conduct, and that section has had a life of its own apart from the rest. Jesuit school disputation at its fullest.

suarez-defensio-fidei.blurb: Written at Rome's request against James I and the English oath of allegiance, and against the king's own printed defence of it. Suárez argues that the Church of England is a sect rather than a church, that the pope holds an indirect power over temporal rulers in matters touching religion, and, in the sixth book on the oath, presses the question of what subjects owe a heretical prince. The book was burned publicly in London.

suarez-in-primam-partem-commentarii.blurb: Commentary on the first part of the Summa, printed at Venice in 1608, on God one and triune. Suárez does not paraphrase Aquinas so much as reopen his questions and settle them by disputation, which is why a commentary of this kind runs many times the length of the text it follows. Readers of the Metaphysical Disputations will recognise the same method turned on theological matter.

mazzella-de-deo-creante.blurb: Lectures on creation from a Jesuit who taught at Woodstock in Maryland and then at the Gregorian in Rome before he was made a cardinal, printed as part of a course of scholastic and dogmatic theology. The treatise covers creation out of nothing, the six days, the angels, and the constitution and elevation of man. Nineteenth century Roman manuals also had to answer materialist and evolutionary accounts, and the length here suggests they are answered at leisure.

mazzella-de-gratia-christi.blurb: The volume of Mazzella's course dealing with grace: its necessity, actual and habitual grace, the relation of grace to free will, predestination, and the quarrel between the schools over efficacious grace that Rome had left formally open. Scholastic and dogmatic lecturing in the Roman manner, thesis by thesis, with adversaries named and proofs marshalled from scripture, the fathers and the councils.

mazzella-de-religione-et-ecclesia.blurb: Lectures on religion and the church, which in a Roman course of this period means two things joined: first the rational grounds for revealed religion against unbelief, then the constitution of the church, its marks, its authority, and the papal primacy defined not long before at the Vatican Council. Mazzella taught this material in the United States and afterwards in Rome, and the manual form reflects the classroom.

mazzella-de-virtutibus-infusis.blurb: The volume on the infused virtues: faith, hope and charity, the infused moral virtues, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, handled in the scholastic manner as habits given with grace rather than acquired by practice. Part of the same course of lectures as the other volumes in the series, with the thesis stated, proved, and defended against objections at each step.

finke-acta-concilii-constanciensis-1.blurb: The first volume of a critical edition of documents bearing on the Council of Constance, edited by a German historian and published at Münster. This band gathers the material of the prehistory: negotiations, memoranda and correspondence from the years before the council met, when the schism had produced three claimants to the papacy and pressure for a council had become irresistible. Sources in Latin with German editorial apparatus.

finke-acta-concilii-constanciensis-2.blurb: The second band, printing the diaries kept by men who were at Constance, sermons preached there, and the acts touching reform and the constitution of the council. Diaries of this kind are what make Constance legible as an event rather than a set of finished decrees, since they record how the nations voted and what the daily business was like. Latin and German texts with editorial apparatus.

finke-acta-concilii-constanciensis-3.blurb: The third band, on the three popes and the council, with the writings concerning the papal election. Constance had to unmake Gregory XII, John XXIII and Benedict XIII before it could make Martin V, and the documents gathered here are the working papers of that operation, including the arguments over whether a council may sit in judgement on a pope.

finke-acta-concilii-constanciensis-4.blurb: The closing band of the edition, published thirty-two years after the first. The label calls it simply the final volume and does not specify what it contains. Long running documentary editions of this kind usually end by printing what surfaced too late for the earlier volumes, together with the indexes, but that is an expectation from the genre rather than a report.

davenant-treatise-on-justification-vol-1.blurb: The first of two volumes of the English translation of the Disputatio de Justitia Habituali et Actuali, which grew out of Davenant's divinity lectures at Cambridge. The question throughout is which righteousness God accepts in a sinner: the righteousness infused and inherent, the righteousness of works, or the righteousness of Christ imputed to faith. Davenant argues the last, and argues it against Bellarmine and the other Roman controversialists point by point. This volume carries the earlier part of the disputation.

davenant-treatise-on-justification-vol-2.blurb: The second and concluding volume of the disputation on justification. Davenant's method is to state a Roman position in its own authors' words and then answer it, so the argument runs as a sustained engagement with Bellarmine rather than a treatise built from first principles. Readers who know Davenant only as a moderate at Dort will find him conceding more to inherent renewal than many of his contemporaries would, and conceding nothing at all where the ground of acceptance is concerned.

davenant-dissertation-on-the-death-of-ch.blurb: Davenant sat for Britain at the Synod of Dort, and this dissertation states the position he defended there and afterward. Christ's death is of infinite value and was ordained as a remedy applicable to every man, which is what makes the general gospel offer a sincere one, while its effectual application belongs to the elect by a special intention of God. It is the classic English statement of what later writers call hypothetical universalism, and it travels with the dissertation on predestination and reprobation.

davenant-on-predestination-and-reprobati.blurb: The companion dissertation to that on the death of Christ, taking up the decree itself. Davenant defends election as free and unconditional while refusing to make reprobation its exact mirror, and he is careful to keep the decree from swallowing the general promise, so that the offer of Christ to all remains an offer God means. The argument is that of a bishop who had sat at Dort and wanted the Reformed doctrine stated in terms that answered the Arminian charge rather than dismissed it.

flavel-divine-conduct-mysterie-providenc.blurb: An exposition of the psalmist's words about the God who performeth all things for me, turned into a whole practical divinity of providence. Flavel traces God's dealing with a believer through the stages of a life: birth and upbringing, conversion, calling and employment, family, and preservation in trouble. The second half is directions for the work he thinks Christians most neglect, the deliberate recollection and recording of God's dealings with them, so that yesterday's mercies are available to tomorrow's fear.

flavel-planelogia-succinct-seasonable-di.blurb: A discourse on the sources and the cure of error in religion, published in the year of Flavel's death. He follows the sequence the title sets out, the occasions that give an error its opening, the causes that produce it, its nature and rise, the way it grows once entertained, and the remedies. He is at least as interested in the temper of mind that receives an error as in the proposition itself.

flavel-two-treatises-first-fear-from-isa.blurb: Two treatises printed together in the years when Flavel was preaching to Dissenters under the penal laws. The first works from Isaiah's command not to fear what the people fear but to sanctify the Lord of hosts, distinguishing the fear that is sin from the fear that is duty. The second turns from the anatomy of fear to its remedy, setting the righteous man's refuge in God against a season of public trouble.

flavel-tydings-from-rome-england-s-alarm.blurb: A short alarm against the growth of Roman Catholic influence in England, setting out grounds for suspecting that the popish interest was gaining and calling Protestants to take the warning seriously. Thirty-two pages, occasional, and written in the temper of the anti-popish pamphlet rather than of Flavel's practical works.

gillespie-sermon-preached-before-honoura.blurb: Preached at one of the monthly fasts Parliament kept through the war, by one of the Scottish commissioners then sitting in the Westminster Assembly.
