Gillespie was the youngest of them and the most formidable in debate, and his business before the Commons was the same as his business in the Assembly, to press for a settled church government along presbyterian lines as the Solemn League and Covenant had bound both kingdoms to seek.

gillespie-sermon-preached-before-right-h.blurb: A fast sermon preached before the House of Lords in the Abbey Church at Westminster and printed in 1646. Gillespie was in London as a commissioner from the Church of Scotland to the Westminster Assembly, and appearances before the two Houses were part of how the Scottish party pressed its case while the Assembly's work on church government lay before Parliament.

gillespie-usefull-case-conscience-discus.blurb: A case of conscience on whether a covenanted people may enter associations and confederacies with idolaters, printed after Gillespie's death and bearing directly on the Scottish quarrel over treating with the king and his party. He argues in the manner of the casuists, taking the Old Testament kings who allied with idolatrous neighbours and were rebuked for it, and concluding that such confederacies are forbidden whatever advantage they promise.

gillespie-vvholesome-severity-reconciled.blurb: An argument against liberty of conscience as the sectaries and some Independents were then pleading for it. Gillespie's case is that the magistrate's duty to suppress heresy and blasphemy can be reconciled with a Christian liberty rightly defined, so that the severity he defends is wholesome rather than tyrannical, and the liberty he grants is real but does not extend to error. It belongs to the pamphlet war over toleration that ran alongside the Assembly's debates.

poole-advertisement-concerning-fourth-la.blurb: Two pages of notice concerning the fourth and final part of the Synopsis Criticorum, the digest of biblical commentators that occupied Poole for the better part of a decade. It is publishing ephemera rather than divinity, and its interest lies in what it shows of how a subscription folio on that scale was financed and brought out.

poole-evangelical-worship-is-spiritual-v.blurb: A single sermon on the spiritual character of gospel worship, preached before a civic audience and printed in 1660. Poole is remembered now for the Synopsis Criticorum and the English Annotations, and this is a specimen of the ordinary preaching that filled his years in a London parish.

poole-mr-matthew-pool-author-that-elabor.blurb: A single leaf printed in the year of Poole's death, reporting words he spoke shortly before it. Sheets of this kind were a common memorial for a well-known minister, and the interest of this one is biographical rather than doctrinal.

Another setting of the same single leaf reporting Poole's dying sayings, from the same year. Broadsides were reprinted quickly and by more than one press when the subject was a minister as well known as the author of the Synopsis Criticorum.

arrowsmith-a-great-wonder-in-heaven-or-a.blurb: A sermon on the woman clothed with the sun in Revelation 12, preached to Parliament and printed in 1647. Arrowsmith takes the vision as a picture of the church militant, reading her adornment, her travail, and the dragon's pursuit of her as the standing condition of the church rather than as a prophecy of one moment. Sermons of this kind were the ordinary way the Westminster divines addressed the two Houses.

arrowsmith-armilla-catechetica-a-chain-o.blurb: Arrowsmith's catechetical divinity, drawn from his teaching as Regius Professor at Cambridge and printed after his death. It is built as a chain: a series of theological aphorisms, each stated in a sentence or two and then unfolded in an exercitation that argues, illustrates and applies it. The aphorisms run from the being and attributes of God through Scripture, the fall, and the person and work of Christ to the last things, and the exercitations carry most of the substance.

arrowsmith-englands-eben-ezer-or-stone-o.blurb: A thanksgiving sermon of 1645, set up as a stone of help in acknowledgment of what Arrowsmith and Parliament took to be God's assistance in the war. The genre is fixed: recount the deliverance, warn against ascribing it to arms or to men, and press the duties of a nation that has been helped.

arrowsmith-theanthr-pos-or-god-man-being.blurb: An exposition of the first eighteen verses of John, published after Arrowsmith's death. The title names the subject, God and man in one person, and the prologue is handled as the ground of that doctrine: the eternity of the Word, his part in creation, the light the darkness did not overcome, and the Word made flesh. This is an academic divine's commentary, close to the text and heavy with distinctions rather than devotional in the usual puritan manner.

chambers-a-motive-to-peace-and-love-deli.blurb: A sermon preached at Paul's in June 1649, urging peace and love on a church and a nation that had just executed a king and were dividing further. Chambers sat in the Westminster Assembly and held a Wiltshire living, and the sermon belongs with the appeals for unity that multiplied in the first months of the Commonwealth.

chambers-an-answer-of-humphrey-chambers-.blurb: A printed defence against charges brought by a named accuser, issued in 1660 as the Restoration reopened the conduct of ministers who had served under the Commonwealth. Chambers, rector of Pewsey, had acted for the parliamentary commissions in Wiltshire, and the tract is his account of what he did and on what authority.

chambers-an-apology-for-the-ministers-of.blurb: A defence of the Wiltshire ministers who took a hand in the election of members to the parliament of 1654, answering the objection that clergy had no business in it. Local in occasion and thirty-one pages long, it is useful chiefly as evidence of how far parish ministers were drawn into the politics of the Protectorate.

chambers-animadversions-on-mr-william-de.blurb: Notes in reply to William Dell's book The Crucified and Quickened Christian. Dell was among the radicals who held that the Spirit's inward work made the settled ministry, the universities and much received divinity dispensable, and Chambers answers him as a parish minister and Westminster divine, taking the book passage by passage.

price-a-sermon-preached-at-st-maries-spi.blurb: One of the Spital sermons, preached in Easter week before the Lord Mayor, the aldermen and the governors of the London hospitals, a civic occasion of long standing. The date, April 1642, places it in the months between the king's departure from London and the outbreak of fighting.

price-gods-working-and-brittains-wonder-.blurb: A thanksgiving sermon for the return of Charles II, preached in 1660 and taking the Restoration as a work of God rather than of men or armies. Sermons of this kind were preached in great number that summer, and the common note in them is the bloodlessness of the change, read as evidence of a divine hand.

price-ianitor-anim-the-soules-porter-to-.blurb: A long treatise on the fear of God, figured in the title as the soul's porter, whose office is to put sin out of the house and keep it from returning. Price works the image out at length in the manner of the earlier seventeenth-century practical writers, dividing the kinds of fear and distinguishing the fear that drives a man from God from the fear that keeps him near.

price-mans-delinquencie-attended-by-divi.blurb: A sermon on human guilt and the justice that follows it, with mercy mixed in, preached in 1646 and printed at sixty pages. The title gives the whole structure: delinquency, the justice it draws upon itself, and the mercy that tempers the sentence.

simpson-diatrib-vvherein-the-iudgement-o.blurb: A short tract in which Simpson, one of the five Dissenting Brethren who argued the Independent case at the Westminster Assembly, gathers the judgment of the reformed churches and Protestant divines on a point then in dispute. It runs to fifteen pages, and it uses the method both parties relied on in 1647, which was to settle an English question by citing what the churches abroad had already resolved.

simpson-diatrib-vvherein-the-judgement-o.blurb: Another setting of the same tract from 1647, running to seventeen pages. Simpson was among the Dissenting Brethren at Westminster, and the argument proceeds by collecting the verdict of the reformed churches and their divines rather than by reasoning from Scripture directly.

simpson-reformations-preservation-opened.blurb: A fast sermon preached before the House of Commons at Westminster in 1643, on how a reformation once begun is to be kept. Simpson had returned from exile among the English churches in the Netherlands and would shortly be one of the Dissenting Brethren, arguing the Independent case against the Assembly's presbyterian majority.

simpson-two-books-of-mr-sydrach-simpson-.blurb: Two treatises by Simpson gathered and printed after his death, the title page identifying him as master of Pembroke Hall in Cambridge and a preacher in London. Those were the offices he ended with; the work he is better remembered for was done as one of the Independent minority at the Westminster Assembly.

bellarmine-disputationes-de-controversii.blurb: The first tome of the controversies Bellarmine lectured on at the Roman College and then published as a systematic reply to the whole Protestant case. It carries the disputations on the Word of God, where canon, versions and the right of interpretation are argued out; on Christ; on the supreme pontiff, the four books that drew answers from every Protestant university; and on councils and the church with its members. Protestant divines answered him article by article for the next century.

The second tome, taking up the church beyond this life and then the sacraments. Bellarmine argues for purgatory and the state of the souls there, the beatitude of the saints, their invocation, and the veneration of relics and images, which was the ground the Reformed contested most hotly. The sacramental disputations begin here, with the sacraments in general, baptism and confirmation, and the Eucharist, where the defence of the real presence and transubstantiation is at its fullest.

The third tome, running from the remaining sacraments, penance and extreme unction, orders and matrimony, into the disputations on grace and free will, on justification, and on good works. These last are the ones a reader of the Reformed controversialists meets most often in citation, since it is here that Bellarmine states the doctrine of inherent righteousness and of merit that Davenant, Chamier and their successors set out to answer.

burgersdijck-idea-philosophiae-as.blurb: A pair of compact epitomes by the Leiden professor whose textbooks taught philosophy to a generation in the Dutch and English universities and in the colonial colleges. The natural philosophy is Aristotelian and arranged by the usual heads, matter and form, motion and place, the heavens, the elements and mixed bodies, and the soul; the moral philosophy runs the questions of the highest good, happiness and the virtues. Both are written for the classroom, in short numbered theses.

burgersdijck-logica-as.blurb: The logic textbook that carried Burgersdijk's name into English and American classrooms, in two books. The first treats terms, the predicables and the categories; the second moves to propositions, the syllogism and its figures, demonstration and method. He is an Aristotelian who has taken from Ramus a concern for arrangement, and the whole is set out as numbered theses with commentary, for teaching rather than for reading through.

burgersdijck-metaphysica-as.blurb: Metaphysics in two books, on the same classroom plan as his logic. The first treats being as being and its properties, unity, truth and goodness; the second the divisions of being, substance and accident, finite and infinite, and what natural reason can reach concerning God and separated substances. This is the kind of textbook the Reformed theologians of the period assumed when they used metaphysical vocabulary, which is what makes it useful for reading their systems.

coccejus-epistolae-ad-hebraeos.blurb: Cocceius on the epistle nearest to his own theology, since its subject is the passing of one covenant and the establishment of a better. The exposition follows the argument about priesthood, sacrifice and the heavenly sanctuary, and the second half of the title promises a demonstration of the epistle's truth, which is to say a defence of its reasoning against Jewish objection. Cocceius read the rabbinic literature closely and draws on it throughout.

coccejus-iudaicarum-responsionum.blurb: A consideration of Jewish answers and questions, that is, of the objections and counter-readings that Jewish interpreters brought against the Christian use of the Old Testament. Cocceius was among the most capable Hebraists of his generation and had worked through the Talmud himself, so the replies are made from the sources rather than from the Christian handbooks of anti-Jewish argument then in circulation.

coccejus-summa-theologiae.blurb: The second edition of Cocceius's system, and the fullest statement of the covenant theology that divided the Dutch faculties for the rest of the century. Doctrine is arranged as the history of God's dealings rather than as a set of standing loci, the governing scheme being the covenant of works, broken, and the covenant of grace unfolding through successive periods. The account of the abrogations of the covenant of works, and of what remains of the law under grace, is the part his opponents fastened on.

daille-exposition-philippiens.blurb: Twenty-nine sermons on Philippians preached at Charenton, the church that served Protestant Paris, and printed in French as they were delivered. Daillé is remembered now for his book on the use of the fathers, but the greater part of his working life went into expository preaching of this kind, taking an epistle a few verses at a time across a season.

jean-daille-adversus-latinorum-tradition.blurb: A disputation against the Latin church's tradition concerning the object of religious worship, which is to say against the honour paid to saints, relics and images as distinct from the worship due to God alone. Daillé's method is the one he used everywhere, to show from the fathers themselves that a practice defended as apostolic cannot be found in the early centuries.

jean-daille-de-imaginibus.blurb: Four books on images, arguing that their veneration was unknown to the early church and grew by stages that can be traced and dated. Daillé works through the patristic testimonies, the councils and the iconoclast controversy, and the weight of his case rests on the silence and the contrary evidence of the first centuries rather than on the second commandment alone.

daneau-christianae-isagoges.blurb: Two books of an introduction to the commonplaces of Christian theology, from a minister who had worked at Beza's side in Geneva. Daneau's habit is to state a locus, set out its scriptural grounds, and then bring in the fathers, whom he had edited and knew at first hand. The result is a compend of ordinary Reformed doctrine with an unusual weight of patristic citation for its date.

daneau-physice-christiana.blurb: An attempt at a natural philosophy drawn from Scripture rather than from Aristotle, treating the origin of created things and the use a Christian is to make of them. Daneau begins from Genesis and the six days, on the argument that an account of nature should start where revelation starts. It stands near the head of the Mosaic physics that Protestant writers went on producing for the next century.

daneau-physices-christianae-pars-altera.blurb: The second part of the Christian physics, on the nature of created things, and considerably longer than the first. Where the opening volume set out the origin of the creation and its use, this one turns to the created orders themselves, in the manner of a natural history put to theological work.

estius-annotationes.blurb: Notes on the chief and more difficult places of Scripture, ranging across both testaments, by the chancellor of Douai whose commentaries were read and cited by Protestants as well as Catholics. Estius is a literal exegete with little appetite for allegory, and his sympathies on grace are Augustinian, which is part of why Reformed writers used him as freely as they did.

estius-in-pauli-epistolas-1.blurb: The first tome of the commentary on all the epistles of Paul, the work Estius is remembered for. He keeps to the literal sense, weighs the Greek, and settles the argument of a passage before drawing any doctrine from it, with Augustine quoted at every turn. Protestant divines cited him with a freedom they extended to very few Roman commentators.

estius-in-pauli-epistolas-2.blurb: The second tome of the Pauline commentary, carrying the later epistles and adding the Catholic Epistles, as the title notes. The method is unchanged from the first volume, close attention to the literal sense with Augustine at his elbow.

gomarus-disputationes-theologicae.blurb: Disputations held under Gomarus in the several universities he served, gathered into one volume. Each takes a locus, states it in numbered theses, and appends the corollaries the respondent was to defend, so that the collection amounts to a compressed system by the man whose quarrel with Arminius at Leiden gave the contra-Remonstrant party its name.

gomarus-evangelii-iohannis.blurb: An exposition of selected passages from John, printed among Gomarus's collected theological works. He was a considerable philologist as well as a controversialist, and this kind of selective commentary takes up the places where the text is difficult or the doctrine contested rather than working through the gospel verse by verse.

gomarus-evangelii-matthaei.blurb: The companion volume of selected places from Matthew, on the same plan, with attention to the Greek and to the Old Testament citations that the first gospel presses hardest. It belongs with his illustration of selected passages in John, printed at the same time.

hoornbeek-orationes.blurb: Academic orations delivered at Utrecht, a short volume of the formal Latin addresses a professor of theology gave at an inauguration, a funeral, or the close of a rectorate. Their interest is for the life of the university and for Hoornbeeck's own concerns rather than for doctrine.

hoornbeek-summa-controversiarum.blurb: A survey of every controversy the Reformed church then had, arranged by opponent: first those outside the faith, pagans, Jews and Muslims; then the ancient heresies; then Socinians, Anabaptists, Roman Catholics, Lutherans and Remonstrants. Each position is stated from its own sources and the state of the question fixed before the argument begins. Hoornbeeck taught at Utrecht and Leiden and belonged to the Voetian party, and the book served afterward as a working handbook of polemical theology.

hoornbeek-theologiae-practicae.blurb: Practical theology in two parts and at great length, from one of the chief writers of the Dutch Further Reformation. The subject is the Christian life treated as a matter for teaching and for cases of conscience: faith, hope and love, the commandments, prayer, and the duties belonging to particular callings and conditions. It stands nearer to the English puritan casuistry than to the Dutch systematic tradition, though Hoornbeeck was at home in both.

jansenius-augustinus.blurb: Twenty years of reading Augustine, set out in three books and published after Jansen's death. The first is a history of the Pelagian and semi-Pelagian disputes; the second treats the state of innocence, fallen nature, and the limits of what philosophy can know of either; the third expounds the grace of Christ the healer, with the doctrine that a delight in the good, given by grace, is what actually moves a fallen will. Five propositions drawn from it were condemned at Rome, and the quarrel over whether they were in the book ran for a century.

jansenius-pentateuchus.blurb: A commentary on the five books of Moses, printed long after Jansen's death and quite unlike the Augustinus in character. It is a plain literal exposition of the kind Louvain produced, concerned with the sense of the Hebrew and the coherence of the narrative rather than with the doctrine of grace.

jansenius-tetrateuchus.blurb: A commentary on the four gospels, published after Jansen's death and just before the Augustinus. It is brief, literal, and built on the agreement of the four accounts, and it shows the exegete rather than the controversialist. A reader who knows Jansen only through the five condemned propositions will find nothing of that quarrel here.

lavater-ezras-liber-primus-ezrae.blurb: Thirty-eight homilies on Ezra, preached in Zurich and printed in Latin for the use of other ministers. Lavater was Bullinger's son-in-law and his successor in the Zurich pulpit, and this belongs to the long Zurich practice of expounding whole books of the Old Testament in course, with the returned exiles taken as instruction for a reformed city.

lavater-liber-ruth.blurb: Twenty-eight homilies on Ruth, which is a great many for four chapters. Lavater takes the story slowly, and the Zurich manner shows in his attention to the ordinary duties of household and kinship and to the providence that governs an unremarkable family.

lavater-nehemias-liber-nehemiae.blurb: Fifty-eight homilies on Nehemiah, which Latin usage called the second book of Ezra, published in the same year as his homilies on the first. The rebuilding of the walls and the reform of the returned community gave a Zurich preacher a great deal to say to his own city, and the sermons are expository first and applied second.

lefevre-commentarii-in-epistolas-catholi.blurb: A commentary on the seven Catholic Epistles by the French humanist whose biblical work went before the Reformation and in some measure prepared the way it read Paul. Lefevre attends to the Greek and to the plain sense, and writes for readers he expects to have the text open in front of them.

lefevre-commentarii-in-quatuor-evangelia.blurb: Introductory commentaries on the four gospels, meant to open the text to ordinary readers rather than to settle the questions of the schools. Lefevre prefaces the whole with an argument that Scripture is the proper food of the Christian people, and the exposition keeps to the literal and spiritual sense without the apparatus of the medieval commentators. The Paris faculty of theology censured him for it.

lefevre-epistolae-pauli-commentarii.blurb: Paul's epistles with commentary, in the arrangement that gave the book its influence: the Vulgate text and Lefevre's own corrected Latin version printed together, so that a reader could see where the received translation had gone astray, with the exposition following. Luther had it at hand when he lectured. Lefevre reads Paul on faith and works in terms a Roman censor could find alarming, though he remained in the church he was born into.

leydekker-de-historia-jansenismi.blurb: Six books on the history of Jansenism, by a Utrecht professor of the Voetian party who watched the Augustinian revival inside the Roman church with a mixture of sympathy and suspicion. The narrative runs from Baius through Jansen's book and the condemnation of the five propositions to the quarrels of Port-Royal, and it is written as Reformed history, which is to say that the doctrine of grace is the thread throughout.

leydekker-de-veritate-religionis-reforma.blurb: A defence at length of the truth of the Reformed religion, against Rome on one side and against the parties that had unsettled the Dutch church on the other. Leydekker was a Voetian and a controversialist by temperament, and the argument is conducted in the polemical mode of the Utrecht faculty of his day.

leydekker-medulla-theologica.blurb: A compend of theology, the marrow of the subject reduced to a volume a student could carry, from the Utrecht professor better known for his controversial writing. The title places it in the line of Ames, and the genre is the same, a short ordered summary of the loci for use in teaching.

meisner-philosophia-sobria-1.blurb: The first of three parts of a work on the sober use of philosophy in theology, by a Wittenberg Lutheran writing while the schools were arguing over how far reason may be trusted in controversies of faith. Meisner's rule is that philosophical principles hold within their own order and cannot overrule an article of faith, and the work proceeds by testing that rule against the disputed questions one at a time.

meisner-philosophia-sobria-2.blurb: The second of the three parts. The project throughout is to fix the standing of philosophy in theological dispute, granting reason its rights within its own order and denying it jurisdiction over what is revealed, then carrying that principle through the places where Lutheran divines found themselves pressed by philosophical objection.

meisner-philosophia-sobria-3.blurb: The third and last part, carrying the same method into the remaining questions. Meisner's book was read in the Lutheran faculties long after his death, and it belongs beside the Reformed treatments of the same problem, the use and abuse of reason in divinity, rather than to the polemical literature of either side.

pallavicino-istoria-concilio-trento-1.blurb: The Roman answer to Paolo Sarpi, written by a Jesuit with the acts of the council and the Vatican archive open to him and intended to replace Sarpi's history rather than merely correct it. This first part covers the long prehistory of the council, the negotiations and delays that kept it from meeting, and its opening sessions under Paul III. Pallavicino corrects Sarpi by the hundred, so a reader gets the documentary record and the partisanship together.

pallavicino-istoria-concilio-trento-2.blurb: The second part, following the council through its middle years, the quarrels over precedence and procedure, the doctrinal decrees, and the interruption that suspended it. The running correction of Sarpi continues throughout, so the volume reads as history and as rebuttal at once.

pallavicino-istoria-concilio-trento-3.blurb: The third and last part, carrying the council through its reconvening under Pius IV to the final sessions of 1563 and the confirmation of its decrees. The reform legislation is thickest here, and here too Pallavicino is most concerned to show that the council deliberated freely rather than at Rome's direction.

piscator-analysis-logica-ad-romanos.blurb: Romans taken apart by the Ramist method, which is what the title means: the epistle divided and subdivided by dichotomy until the structure of each argument is visible, with scholia and observations of doctrine attached. Piscator taught at Herborn, the most thoroughly Ramist of the Reformed academies, and he gave most of the New Testament the same treatment. A reader wanting paraphrase will find something drier and more useful, a diagram of Paul's reasoning.

piscator-analysis-logica-secundum-marcum.blurb: Mark under the same logical analysis Piscator applied across the New Testament, the text divided by dichotomy with scholia and doctrinal observations appended. A narrative gospel resists the method more than an epistle does, which makes this volume a fair test of what the Herborn analysis could and could not do.

piscator-analysis-logica-septem-epistola.blurb: The seven Catholic Epistles under the same analysis, from James through Jude. Their short compass suits the method well, and the volume gives the argument of each letter in outline before the observations of doctrine Piscator draws from it.

schmid-articulorum-formulae-concordiae.blurb: A repetition, meaning a restatement and defence, of the articles of the Formula of Concord taken one at a time, by the Strasbourg professor better known for his commentaries and his strictly literal Latin version of the Bible. It appeared in the year of his death, more than a century after the Formula was subscribed, so the objections it answers are those the intervening century had raised.

schmid-disputatio-de-christo.blurb: A single academic disputation on Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, twenty-three pages, held at Strasbourg. The form is the usual one, numbered theses defended by a respondent, and the verse serves as the ground for the doctrine of Christ's person.

schmid-fasciculus-disputationum.blurb: A bundle of theological disputations from Schmid's teaching at Strasbourg, gathered and printed together. Each is a set of numbered theses on one question, defended in the schools, and the collection is a record of what a Lutheran faculty was arguing about at the end of the seventeenth century.

viret-de-la-vraye-et-fausse-religion.blurb: A long French work on true and false religion, turning on vows and oaths, which Viret takes to be the point at which a false religion binds a conscience most tightly. Monastic vows, the oaths of the church courts, and the swearing of ordinary life are all in view. Viret wrote for readers without Latin and in a style meant to hold them, and he was the most widely read of the French-speaking reformers in his own lifetime.

viret-de-vero-verbi-dei-ministerio.blurb: On the true ministry of the Word, of the sacraments and of the church, written in Latin against the Roman account of all three. Viret had rebuilt the church at Lausanne alongside Farel and Calvin, and the questions here are the practical ones of that work: who may preach, what a sacrament does, and what makes a church a church.

viret-instruction-chrestienne.blurb: Christian instruction in the doctrine of the law and the gospel, cast as dialogue and running to great length. Viret expounds the commandments and then the gospel in the catechetical order the Reformed churches used, but the conversational form lets him raise and answer objections as an ordinary reader would put them. It is the fullest thing he wrote, and the best place to see why he was read so widely in French.

bouix-tractatus-de-papa-1.blurb: The first of three volumes on the papacy and the ecumenical council, by a French canonist who wrote a shelf of tracts on the law of the church. Bouix argues the case for papal primacy and for the pope's authority in relation to a council, against the Gallican positions still defended in France when he wrote. The treatment is canonical rather than dogmatic, with the sources set out at length.

bouix-tractatus-de-papa-2.blurb: The second volume of the treatise on the pope and the council, continuing the canonical argument. Bouix works through the historical objections, among them the councils commonly cited against papal supremacy, in the years when the question was moving toward decision at Rome.

bouix-tractatus-de-papa-3.blurb: The third and last volume, closing the treatise on the pope and the council. Bouix's series of canonical tracts served French clergy as a working reference, and this treatise is the one that put his canon law at the service of the ultramontane case.

passaglia-de-immaculato-conceptu-1.blurb: The first part of a vast commentary on the Immaculate Conception, published in the year the doctrine was defined by Pius IX. Passaglia taught at the Roman College and had a hand in preparing the definition, and the work is an assembly of evidence rather than an argument from principle, beginning with the scriptural grounds and the earliest testimony, set out at a scale nobody had attempted before.

passaglia-de-immaculato-conceptu-2.blurb: The second part, continuing the documentation through the fathers, Greek and Latin, and the testimony of the Eastern churches. Passaglia's habit is to print the texts at length and then argue from them, which makes the volume useful as a collection even to a reader who rejects the conclusion.

passaglia-de-immaculato-conceptu-3.blurb: The third and longest part, published the year after the definition. It carries the evidence through the liturgies, the medieval schools where Dominicans and Franciscans divided over the question, and the acts of the papacy, and where the earlier parts mostly collect, this one presses the argument toward the definition itself.

bossuet-defensio-declarationis-1.blurb: The first of three volumes, in the Versailles edition of Bossuet's works, of his Latin defence of the Declaration of the French Clergy of 1682. The Four Articles held that kings are independent of the pope in temporal things, that a general council stands above the pope, that the ancient liberties of the Gallican church are inviolable, and that a papal judgment in matters of faith is not irreformable apart from the consent of the church. Bossuet had drafted the declaration and spent much of his later life defending it.

bossuet-defensio-declarationis-2.blurb: The second volume of the defence of the Gallican Declaration. Bossuet's case rests on history: the practice of the ancient church, the councils of Constance and Basel, and the received teaching of the Sorbonne, all marshalled to show that the Four Articles state nothing new. He writes as a bishop who believed he was defending Catholic tradition against an innovation, not the crown against Rome.

bossuet-defensio-declarationis-3.blurb: The third and last volume of the defence, in the Versailles collected works. Written under Louis XIV and printed only after Bossuet's death, it remained the most substantial statement of the Gallican position until the First Vatican Council settled the question the other way.

franzelin-de-ss-eucharistiae-sacramento-.blurb: A dogmatic treatise on the Eucharist as sacrament and as sacrifice, set out in theses with the patristic and conciliar documentation that gave Franzelin's lectures at the Gregorian their reputation. The real presence, transubstantiation, the manner of Christ's presence and the nature of the sacrifice of the mass are each argued from Scripture, the fathers and the definitions of Trent. Franzelin was a principal draftsman at the First Vatican Council, and the method here is the one he brought to it.

franzelin-de-sacramentis-in-genere.blurb: The general treatise that stands before any treatment of the individual sacraments: what a sacrament is, how it was instituted, its matter and form, the causality by which it confers grace, the character it impresses, and what is required of minister and recipient. Franzelin proceeds by thesis and proof, with the patristic evidence printed out in full rather than cited.

franzelin-de-divina-traditione-et-script.blurb: The book Franzelin is remembered for, and the standard Roman treatment of its subject in the nineteenth century. It sets out what tradition is, how it is transmitted and recognised, how the teaching office of the church stands to it, and how Scripture and tradition are related as sources of revealed doctrine. Much of the vocabulary later used in Roman discussions of the two sources comes from here, and the argument runs directly into the constitution Dei Filius, which Franzelin helped to draft.

selden-de-jure-naturali-et-gentium.blurb: Seven books deriving natural law from Jewish sources, on the argument that the law binding all men is the one the rabbis taught under the seven precepts given to the sons of Noah. Selden was the most learned Hebraist among English lawyers, and he handles the Talmud and its commentators as a jurist handles authorities. The book stands against the attempt to ground natural law in reason alone, since Selden held that a law requires a lawgiver and an obligation requires promulgation.

selden-opera-omnia-vol-1.blurb: The first volume of the collected works of the English jurist, antiquary and orientalist, printed and previously unprinted together. Selden's range ran from the law of tithes and the titles of honour to the Syrian gods, Jewish marriage and the Sanhedrin, and a collection of this kind preserves the smaller pieces alongside the books he is known for.

selden-opera-omnia-vol-2.blurb: The second volume of the collected works. Selden wrote in Latin and in English, on English legal antiquities and on rabbinic law with equal command, and a gathered set of this sort is the only way most of that output can be read together.

charnock-sayings-that-reverend-great-pre.blurb: A single printed sheet of sayings gathered from Stephen Charnock and issued at his death in 1680. It is a memorial broadside rather than anything Charnock composed for the press, and a reader will find in it only what an admirer thought worth preserving of his talk.

charnock-sermon-preached-late-eminent-mr.blurb: A single sermon on 2 Corinthians 5:19, God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself, printed after Charnock's death. Thirty-eight pages on the reconciling work named in that verse, handled in the doctrine-and-use manner of the Nonconformist pulpit rather than in the extended discursive form of his better known remains.

charnock-supplement-several-discourses-v.blurb: Further discourses gathered to fill out the posthumous collection of Charnock's Several Discourses upon Various Divine Subjects, the volumes better known for what they contain on the existence and attributes of God. Some hundred and thirty pages of the same practical and doctrinal kind, printed with the rest of his papers after his death.

byfield-a-brief-view-of-mr-coleman-his-n.blurb: Adoniram Byfield, scribe to the Westminster Assembly, answering Thomas Coleman's model of church government, which Coleman had delivered in a sermon and then printed. Thirty-six pages from the Assembly's side of the Erastian dispute over whether the power of censure belongs to the eldership or to the civil magistrate.

byfield-a-letter-sent-from-a-worthy-divi.blurb: An eight-page letter addressed to the Lord Mayor of the city of London, printed in 1642 and presented as coming from an unnamed worthy divine. The title breaks off before saying what it concerns, so nothing beyond the address, the date and the length can be stated with any confidence.

byfield-the-principle-of-all-principles-.blurb: Sermons reduced to a summary, arguing what the title calls the principle of all principles concerning religion. Sixty-nine pages printed in 1624; the title is cut short before naming what the sermons set out to prove, so the subject can only be given here as the title itself gives it.

carter-israels-peace-with-god-beniamines.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons, its two halves set against each other in the title: Israel at peace with God, and Benjamin overthrown. The pairing points to the war among the tribes in Judges 20, and the occasion is the opening of England's own civil war. Forty-eight pages.

carter-light-in-darknesse-discovered-in-.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons, preached in November and printed in 1648. Thirty-six pages promising light discovered in darkness, one of the many sermons delivered to the House on its monthly days of humiliation and then printed at the members' request.

carter-the-covenant-of-god-with-abraham-.blurb: A treatise on the covenant with Abraham written to establish infant baptism, the first of its parts clearing that duty and the rest answering what is urged against it. Nearly two hundred pages from 1654, when the Baptist challenge was at its height and the argument had settled on whether the covenant made with Abraham still stands.

carter-the-nail-the-wheel-the-nail-fastn.blurb: Two discourses under emblematic titles, the nail fastened by a hand from heaven and the wheel turned by a voice from the throne. A hundred and nine pages printed in 1647; the title is all the record gives of what either discourse contains, and the figures are left to explain themselves.

carter-the-tomb-stone-and-a-rare-sight.blurb: Two pieces printed together in 1653 under titles that suggest a memorial rather than a treatise, running to some two hundred and twenty pages. Nothing beyond those titles is legible from the record here, and a reader should come to it expecting a monument to the dead.

carter-vindici-decimarum-of-tithes-a-ple.blurb: A plea that tithes are due by divine right, argued from the text of Scripture rather than from custom or statute. Fifty-six pages by John Carter, deacon, printed in 1640, at the moment when the maintenance of the ministry was becoming a live question in Parliament and parish alike.

greene-a-briefe-vnvailing-of-god-and-man.blurb: A short piece unfolding the glory of God and of man in numbered heads, the first of which rehearses happiness in general. Twenty-four pages printed in 1641; the title's list is cut off after that first item, so the remaining heads cannot be given here.

greene-nehemiah-s-teares-and-prayers-for.blurb: A sermon on Nehemiah's weeping and praying over a ruined city, applied to the affliction of England and to the work of repair then being attempted. Forty-six pages printed in 1644, in the manner of the sermons delivered before Parliament on its monthly days of humiliation.

greene-the-vvorlds-riddle-and-the-saints.blurb: Twenty-seven pages printed in 1641 under a title promising the world's riddle and the happiness of the saints. Nothing further about the contents can be given from the record here; the title is the whole of what is known, and it is offered as the title stands.

hickes-the-advantage-of-afflictions-a-se.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Lords, preached in January and printed in 1646, on the advantage that afflictions bring to those who suffer them. Thirty-four pages by Gaspar Hickes, a Cornish minister who sat in the Westminster Assembly, addressed to the peers in the closing stage of the first civil war.

hickes-the-glory-and-beauty-of-gods-port.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons on what the title calls God's portion, and the glory and beauty belonging to it. Forty-seven pages printed in 1644, preached on one of the monthly days of humiliation that the House kept through the war years.

hickes-the-life-and-death-of-david-a-ser.blurb: A funeral sermon for a member of the House of Commons, preached in 1645 and printed at thirty-one pages. The frame is the life and death of David, set beside the life and death of the man being buried; the title breaks off before naming him.

thorowgood-digitus-dei-nevv-discoveryes-.blurb: The sequel to Jewes in America, gathering further arguments that the tribes lost out of the world are to be found among the peoples of the New World. A hundred and seventy-four pages printed in 1652, taking its title from the finger of God and pressing the bearing of the discovery on the conversion of the Jews and the mission then under way in New England.

thorowgood-ievves-in-america-or-probabil.blurb: The argument that the native peoples of America descend from the lost tribes of Israel, with the objections removed one at a time. A hundred and eighty pages printed in 1650, written in support of the New England mission and bound up with the expectation, widely held among English divines of the period, of a national conversion of the Jews.

thorowgood-moderation-iustified-and-the-.blurb: A sermon at Westminster before the House of Commons, printed in 1644, taking the two halves of its title from Philippians 4:5, let your moderation be known unto all men, the Lord is at hand. Thirty-eight pages urging moderation on a Parliament in the middle of a war.

tozer-a-christian-amendment-delivered-in.blurb: A New Year's Day sermon preached in St Martin's church in Oxford and afterwards enlarged for the press, on the amendment of life. Ninety-four pages by Henry Tozer, fellow of Exeter College, printed in 1633; the occasion is the turn of the year, and the matter is practical throughout.

tozer-christian-wisdome-or-the-excellenc.blurb: Sermons on wisdom, briefly delivered and then expanded for the press, treating its excellency, its fame, and the right means of coming by it. A hundred and seventeen pages by Henry Tozer of Exeter College, Oxford, printed in 1639.

tozer-directions-for-a-godly-life-especi.blurb: A manual of directions for godly living, with particular attention to preparation for the Lord's table, written first for private use and then printed. Two hundred and eleven pages by Henry Tozer, in the line of English communion manuals that carried a reader through self-examination before receiving.

valentine-a-charge-against-the-jews-and-.blurb: A sermon charging both the Jews and the Christian world with refusing to come to Christ, who would have given freely to any who came. Thirty-five pages printed in 1647 by Thomas Valentine, a member of the Westminster Assembly.

valentine-christs-counsell-to-poore-and-.blurb: A sermon on Christ's counsel to the poor and naked, drawn from the message to Laodicea and its offer of gold tried in the fire and white raiment to cover nakedness. Twenty-eight pages printed in 1647 by Thomas Valentine, a member of the Westminster Assembly.

valentine-tvvo-sermons-preached-one-befo.blurb: Two sermons printed together in 1647, the first of them preached before the House of Lords on their public fast in May. Twenty-four pages in all, brief even by the measure of the printed fast sermon, by a member of the Westminster Assembly.

woodcock-ioseph-paralled-sic-by-the-pres.blurb: A sermon setting Joseph, sold into Egypt and then raised to power, beside the present Parliament in its sufferings and advancement. Thirty-five pages printed in 1646 by Francis Woodcock, a member of the Westminster Assembly, in the typological manner that the Parliamentary fast sermons made ordinary.

woodcock-lex-talionis-or-god-paying-ever.blurb: A sermon on retribution, God paying every man in his own coin, preached at St Margaret's Westminster and printed in 1646. Thirty-one pages by Francis Woodcock; St Margaret's was the parish church where the Commons heard their fast sermons, and the lex talionis of the title is the whole of the argument.

woodcock-the-two-vvitnesses-discovered-i.blurb: An exposition of the eleventh chapter of Revelation in several sermons, on the two witnesses, their prophesying, their death and their rising. A hundred and six pages printed in 1643, when the apocalyptic reading of that chapter was much in use among preachers who took the war for part of the last things.

young-englands-bane-or-the-description-o.blurb: A pamphlet against drunkenness, describing the vice, its stages and its effects, and calling it the bane of England. Fifty-four pages printed in 1617, in the moral complaint genre of Jacobean London, where the alehouse was a standing target for preachers and pamphleteers alike.

young-hopes-incovragement-pointed-at-in-.blurb: A sermon preached at St Margaret's Westminster before the House of Commons and printed in 1644, pointing at the encouragements that hope may still take. Forty-four pages by Thomas Young, a member of the Westminster Assembly and one of the five who wrote against episcopacy under the name Smectymnuus.

young-the-lords-day-or-a-succinct-narrat.blurb: A sabbatarian treatise, compiled out of the testimonies of Scripture and of the fathers and later writers to establish the Lord's day. Four hundred and fifty-nine pages printed in 1672, long after Young's own part in the Westminster Assembly and the debates on the Sabbath that ran through it.

alsted-metaphysica.blurb: Metaphysics in three books, treating being as such and its transcendental properties before descending to the classes of being. Two hundred and eighty-eight pages from Herborn in 1613, part of the encyclopaedic project by which Alsted tried to give every discipline a teachable order, and the philosophical groundwork underneath his theological writing.

alsted-synopsis-theologiae.blurb: A compend of theology in synoptic form, laying out the loci in short compass for students to hold in view at once. A hundred and twenty-six pages from Hanau in 1627, the reduced counterpart to the vast encyclopaedias for which Alsted is otherwise known.

becanus-manuale-controversiarum.blurb: A handbook of the controversies of the age by the Jesuit Martin Becanus, some nine hundred pages arranged by point of dispute rather than by head of doctrine: Scripture and its rule, the church, the papacy, justification, the sacraments. Written for use in argument, it states the Protestant position and answers it from Scripture, the fathers and the councils.

becanus-summa-theologiae-scholasticae-pa.blurb: The second part of Becanus's scholastic summa, arranged after the order of Aquinas and written for the classroom, though the controversies of his day are never far from the surface. Just under a thousand pages; the record here gives no account of which questions fall in this part beyond its place in the sequence.

cartwright-electa-thargumico-rabbinica-e.blurb: Selections from the Targums and the rabbinic commentators, set out as annotations on Exodus. Five hundred and seventy-two pages by Christopher Cartwright of York, whose Hebrew learning was employed to show what Jewish interpreters made of the text and where Christian exegesis must part from them.

cartwright-electa-thargumico-rabbinica-g.blurb: Annotations on Genesis drawn from the Targums and the rabbinic commentators, companion to Cartwright's volume on Exodus. Five hundred and forty-two pages of Hebraic learning, quoting Jewish interpretation at length and then weighing it, a method English divines of the period used for exegesis and for controversy together.

chamier-corpus-theologicum.blurb: A body of divinity in the form of theological commonplaces, printed at Geneva in 1653, long after Chamier's death at the siege of Montauban. Five hundred and ninety-seven pages; the loci here are the doctrinal substance lying behind the polemic that occupied most of his working life.

chamierus-contractus-1642.blurb: An epitome of Chamier's Panstratia Catholica, compressed into a single volume of some seventeen hundred pages. The original ran to four folios of Reformed argument against Bellarmine, covering the principles of faith, God, Christ, the church and the sacraments; this is that argument reduced to a form a working minister could carry and consult.

essenius-synopsis-controversiarum.blurb: A synopsis of the theological controversies written for students at Utrecht by a colleague of Voetius. Four hundred and ninety-four pages taking in the disputes with Rome, with the Socinians, with the Remonstrants and with the Anabaptists, each position stated and then answered in the elenctic manner of the Dutch schools.

essenius-triumphus-crucis.blurb: A defence of the satisfaction of Christ against those who denied it, six hundred pages under a title claiming the triumph of the cross. The argument is the Reformed one, that divine justice required a price and that Christ paid it, worked out at length against Socinus and the writers who followed him.

heshusius-explicatio-in-1-corinthios.blurb: A full exposition of First Corinthians by the Gnesio-Lutheran Tilemann Heshusius, printed at Jena in 1573. Seven hundred and sixty-eight pages; given the author's lifelong quarrel over the presence of Christ in the Supper, the chapters on the Lord's table are where a reader will find him most engaged.

heshusius-explicatio-in-galatas.blurb: An exposition of Galatians printed at Helmstedt in 1579, six hundred and eighty-five pages on the epistle that Lutheran commentators treated as the charter of justification by faith. Heshusius was a polemicist by temperament, and the confessional quarrels of the 1570s are carried along with the exegesis.

hyperius-de-theologo.blurb: Four books on the theologian and the right method of theological study, by the Marburg professor Andreas Hyperius. Eight hundred and forty-three pages printed at Basel in 1556, on what a student of divinity should read, in what order and to what end, one of the earliest Protestant attempts to describe a whole theological formation.

hyperius-methodus-theologiae.blurb: Hyperius's theology in three books, arranged as commonplaces on the chief heads of the Christian religion. Eight hundred and sixty-two pages; the method announced in the title is the point of the work, the ordering of doctrine so that it can be taught and retained, which was Hyperius's particular concern.

keckermann-systema-ethicae.blurb: A system of ethics in the Aristotelian frame, worked out for the classroom at Danzig and printed at London in 1607. Two hundred and ninety-four pages on the good, the virtues and the ordering of the appetites, one of the series of systemata by which Keckermann tried to give each discipline a definite shape.

keckermann-systema-ss-theologiae.blurb: Keckermann's system of theology, printed at Hanau in 1602, five hundred and twenty pages arranged by the method he applied to every art and science: definitions, divisions, and the whole so laid out that a student can hold it together. Reformed in substance, with the ordering driven throughout by the needs of teaching.

lainez-disputationes-tridentinae-vol-1-a.blurb: The first volume of the disputations Diego Laínez prepared for the Council of Trent, on the origin of episcopal jurisdiction and the primacy of the Roman pontiff. Laínez, second general of the Society of Jesus, held that bishops receive jurisdiction through the pope rather than immediately from Christ, the question that divided the council's later sessions; six hundred pages set out the case.

lainez-disputationes-tridentinae-vol-2-a.blurb: The second volume of Laínez's Tridentine disputations, gathering various questions raised in and around the council. Six hundred and sixty pages; where the first volume was given over to episcopal jurisdiction and the papal primacy, this one ranges across the other matters the council had before it.

marck-compendium-theologiae-christianae.blurb: A compendium of Christian theology, both didactic and elenctic, which served the Dutch Reformed churches as a teaching text well into the eighteenth century. Eight hundred and forty-eight pages from Amsterdam in 1716, each locus stated positively and then defended against the errors ranged against it, a form that made the book usable for instruction and for dispute at once.

marck-scripturariae-exercitationes.blurb: Exegetical exercitations on twenty-five selected passages of the Old Testament, printed at Amsterdam in 1709. Twelve hundred pages, each exercitation a sustained treatment of one difficult or contested text, philological and doctrinal together, by the Leiden professor whose dogmatic compendium was the standard Dutch textbook of the period.

martini-christiana-et-catholica-fides.blurb: An exposition of the Apostles' Creed under the title of the Christian and catholic faith, by the Bremen theologian Matthias Martini. Seven hundred and sixty-seven pages printed in 1618, the year Martini went as a delegate to the Synod of Dort, where his handling of election and covenant drew scrutiny from the stricter members.

martini-methodus-theologiae.blurb: Martini's method of theology, printed at Herborn in 1603, six hundred and twelve pages setting out the whole of divinity in the ordered form that the Herborn teachers favoured. An early work, from before the covenant emphasis of his later years brought him into controversy at Dort.

olevian-in-ad-philippenses-colossenses.blurb: Olevianus on Philippians and Colossians, two hundred and six pages printed at Geneva in 1580. The notes come out of his teaching and are analytic rather than discursive, tracing the argument of each epistle through its parts, by the theologian associated with the making of the Heidelberg Catechism.

olevian-in-ad-romanos.blurb: Notes on Romans taken from Olevianus's lectures, seven hundred and seventy-three pages printed at Geneva in 1579. The method is analytic, following the scope and argument of the epistle through its divisions; readers come to it for the covenant emphasis that marks Olevianus's account of how the benefits of Christ are conveyed to believers.

pareus-collegia-theologica.blurb: Theological colleges, that is series of disputations covering the whole of orthodox theology, from the Heidelberg professor David Pareus. Nine hundred pages in which the disputation is the working unit: a question stated, the terms distinguished, the objections answered, which is how doctrine was actually taught in the Reformed academies.

pareus-in-romanos.blurb: Pareus's commentary on Romans, fourteen hundred pages, the largest of his exegetical works and the one that got him into trouble. His remarks on the thirteenth chapter, allowing that inferior magistrates might in some case resist a tyrant, were condemned in England and the book publicly burned at Oxford. Exegesis, doctrinal loci and controversy with Rome run together throughout.

possevino-apparatus-sacer.blurb: A bibliographical apparatus for the study of Scripture, listing and describing writers on the Old and New Testaments. Over two thousand pages in the Venice printing of 1603, arranged by author, the work of a Jesuit who spent his career on the ordering and policing of Catholic learning. A reader uses it as a finding aid rather than reading it through.

possevino-bibliotheca-selecta.blurb: A guide to the ordering of studies, a thousand pages on what a Catholic should read and in what order, discipline by discipline, with judgements on which authors may be trusted and which avoided. Printed at Cologne in 1607, it is a programme of learning and a censor's manual at once, and it shows what the Counter-Reformation took a library to be for.

robert-baron-of-st-andrews-metaphysica-g.blurb: General metaphysics from the Aberdeen theologian Robert Baron, four hundred and ninety-three pages in the 1657 edition, treating being as being and the transcendental properties before any descent to particular kinds. Baron was among the Aberdeen doctors who resisted the Scottish Covenant, and his philosophical work stands behind his theological method.

robert-baron-of-st-andrews-philosophia-t.blurb: Philosophy as the handmaid of theology, three hundred and sixty-four pages on the legitimate use of reason and of the philosophical disciplines in settling theological questions. Baron writes against two parties at once: those who would banish philosophy from divinity altogether, and those who let reason sit in judgement on revelation.

sibrandus-lubbertus-commentarius-in-cate.blurb: A commentary on the Heidelberg Catechism in the form used by the Dutch churches, nine hundred pages by the Franeker professor Sibrandus Lubbertus, printed in 1618. Lubbertus was among the sharpest opponents of Arminius and Vorstius and a delegate to the Synod of Dort, and the exposition is written with those disputes in view.

sibrandus-lubbertus-de-principiis-dogmat.blurb: Seven books on the principles of Christian doctrine, that is on the sources from which doctrine is drawn and the authority by which disputes about it are settled. Six hundred and twenty-four pages printed at Hanau in 1591, an early work taking up Scripture, tradition and the church against the Roman account of each.

turrettini-de-necessaria-secessione.blurb: Disputations on the necessity of our separation from the Church of Rome, four hundred and seventy pages printed at Utrecht in 1687. The argument answers the case for reunion that Catholic controversialists were pressing on French Protestants in the years around the Revocation, holding that the corruptions of Rome are such that remaining in her communion would itself be sin.

turrettini-de-satisfactione-christi.blurb: Disputations on the satisfaction of Christ, four hundred and twenty-six pages printed at Geneva in 1666, directed against the Socinian denial that God's justice requires a satisfaction and that Christ's death supplied one. The same argument runs in compressed form through the later Institutio Theologiae Elencticae; here Turretin has room to answer Socinus point by point.

vedel-de-arcanis-arminianismi.blurb: Two books on what Vedelius calls the secrets of Arminianism, arguing that the Remonstrant positions, followed to their end, arrive at Socinianism. Two hundred and eighty-four pages in the 1631 edition, written when the exiled Remonstrants were re-establishing themselves in the Netherlands and the question was what their theology finally entailed.

vedel-rationale-theologicum.blurb: On the necessity and the true use of the principles of reason and philosophy in theological controversy, eight hundred and forty-eight pages in the 1628 edition. Vedelius holds that logic and philosophy are instruments the theologian cannot do without, while denying them any authority over revelation, a position that had to be defended on both flanks at once.

heinrich-wilhelm-bernsau-theologia-dogma.blurb: The first of two volumes of a dogmatics treated by what the title calls the scientific method, five hundred and forty-eight pages. Beyond that claim to demonstrative order, the record here gives nothing about the author or about what this volume covers; a reader should expect a school dogmatics built on definition and proof.

The second and larger volume of the same dogmatics, eight hundred and fifty-three pages, continuing the demonstrative treatment begun in the first. The record here does not divide the subject matter between the two volumes, and the title is the whole of what can honestly be reported.

burman-synopsis-theologiae-1.blurb: The first volume of Burman's synopsis of theology, with particular attention, as the title says, to the economy of God's covenants. Eight hundred pages by the Utrecht professor who was among the leading Cocceians, arranging doctrine around the successive administrations of the covenant rather than around the standard loci.

burman-synopsis-theologiae-2.blurb: The second volume of the same synopsis, seven hundred pages carrying the work through the remainder of its scheme. The federal framework announced in the title governs both halves; the record here does not divide the subject matter between them, so what falls in this volume cannot be specified.

witsius-miscellanea-sacra-1.blurb: The first volume of Witsius's miscellaneous sacred studies, in four books: on the prophets and prophecy, on the mysteries of the tabernacle, on the comparison of Aaron's priesthood with Christ's, and on the Hebrew sanhedrins. Nearly nine hundred pages of close antiquarian and exegetical work by the theologian better known for the Economy of the Covenants.

witsius-miscellanea-sacra-2.blurb: The second volume, twenty-three historical and critical-theological exercitations running to nearly a thousand pages. Each takes up a single question of biblical history, philology or church antiquity and pursues it to the sources, the same method as the first volume applied to a wider spread of subjects.

lenfant-histoire-concile-constance-1.blurb: The first volume of Lenfant's history of the Council of Constance, seven hundred pages, Amsterdam 1727. Lenfant was a Huguenot pastor at Berlin, and he tells the council's story from the Protestant side, attentive to the schism it ended, the reform it failed to accomplish, and the condemnation and burning of Jan Hus.

lenfant-histoire-concile-constance-2.blurb: The second volume, five hundred pages, Amsterdam 1714, continuing the narrative of the council along with the documentary matter Lenfant appended to his histories. It belongs with his companion volumes on the councils of Pisa and Basel, written on the same plan and out of the same Protestant reading of the conciliar age.

richer-historia-conciliorum.blurb: A history of the general councils in four books, eight hundred and fifty pages from the Cologne press. Richer was syndic of the Sorbonne and the most uncompromising of the Gallicans, and the history is written to establish that a general council holds authority over the pope, a thesis that cost him his office.

richer-historia-conciliorum-2.blurb: Books two and three of the same history, three hundred and seventy-six pages, Cologne 1681. The conciliarist argument set out at the beginning is here carried through the councils themselves, which supply the material on which Richer rested his case that the council, not the pope, is the church's highest judge.

sylvester-of-ferrara-commentaria-in-libr.blurb: The first volume of Ferrariensis's commentary on the Summa Contra Gentiles, six hundred and fifty pages. Francesco Silvestri, master general of the Dominicans, produced the commentary that has been printed alongside Aquinas's text ever since, expounding the arguments chapter by chapter and defending them against the Scotist and nominalist objections of his own day.

The third volume of the same commentary, three hundred and ninety-four pages, continuing Ferrariensis's exposition of the Contra Gentiles. The commentary is close and philosophical, following Aquinas step by step; the record here does not say which of the four books this volume covers.

journet-eglise-du-verbe-incarne-2.blurb: The second volume of Journet's theology of the Church, on her internal structure and catholic unity. Nine hundred pages of Thomist ecclesiology worked out through the causes: the first volume treated the apostolic hierarchy, and this one turns to what the Church is in herself, her soul and her body, her boundaries, and who is to be counted within them.

journet-eglise-du-verbe-incarne-3.blurb: The concluding volume of the same second part, twelve hundred pages completing Journet's treatment of the Church's internal structure and catholic unity. It belongs with the volume preceding it and does not read well alone; between them they carry the formal cause of the Church, which in Journet's scheme is the created grace that makes her one.

lessius-de-antichristo.blurb: A twin apologetic disputation on Antichrist and his forerunners, three hundred and forty-two pages by the Louvain Jesuit Leonard Lessius. The occasion is the Protestant identification of the papacy with Antichrist, and the argument runs the other way: that Antichrist is still to come, and that the marks Scripture gives him do not fit the Roman see.

lessius-de-perfectionibus-moribusque-div.blurb: Fourteen books on the divine perfections and what the title calls the divine morals, that is the attributes of God and the character of his dealing with creatures. Six hundred and twenty-nine pages by the Louvain Jesuit Leonard Lessius, written in a manner closer to contemplation than to disputation, and read outside his own communion for that reason.

luther-wa-schriften-63.blurb: The sixty-third volume of the Schriften series of the Weimar critical edition of Luther's works, six hundred and ninety-three pages. The Weimarer Ausgabe is the scholarly edition of the whole Luther corpus, printed over more than a century; what falls in this particular volume is not stated in the record here.

luther-wa-schriften-68.blurb: The sixty-eighth volume of the Schriften series of the Weimar critical edition, six hundred and ninety-three pages. The letters, the table talk and the German Bible occupy separate sequences in the edition; the contents of this volume of the Schriften are not given in the record here.

vasquez-in-primam-secundae-tomus-i.blurb: The first volume of Vázquez's commentary and disputations on the Prima Secundae of Aquinas, a thousand pages. Vázquez taught at Alcalá and was Suárez's chief rival among the Jesuit schoolmen; on the matter of this part, beatitude, human acts and the sources of moral goodness, he held that rational nature itself is the proximate ground of moral rightness.

vasquez-in-primam-secundae-tomus-ii.blurb: The second volume of the same commentary, nearly a thousand pages carrying on through the Prima Secundae, whose questions run from the passions and habits to law and grace. The record here does not divide the questions between the volumes; throughout, the disputations are long and Vázquez argues at nearly every point with Suárez and with the Dominicans.

johann-adam-scherzer-anti-bellarminus.blurb: A refutation of Bellarmine's Disputations on the Controversies, taken point by point, a thousand pages by the Leipzig Lutheran Johann Adam Scherzer. The method is the ordinary one of the confessional age: Bellarmine's argument stated, the Protestant answer given, the fathers and the schoolmen enlisted on both sides of every question.

johann-adam-scherzer-systema-theologiae.blurb: Scherzer's system of theology, nine hundred pages of Lutheran dogmatics from Leipzig in the later seventeenth century. The form is the scholastic one Lutheran orthodoxy had by then brought to a fine point: each locus defined, its parts distinguished, and the errors on either hand named and answered in turn.

durham-blessednesse-death-these-that-die.blurb: Sermons on the blessedness of those who die in the Lord, and more especially of those who die in an evil time. A hundred and seventy pages printed in 1681, long after Durham's death; the phrase about an evil time carried a particular weight for Scottish readers under the persecution that followed the Restoration, though Durham preached before it began.

durham-commentarie-book-revelation-text-.blurb: Durham's lectures on Revelation, eight hundred pages, printed in 1658, the year of his death. The text is explained, the series of the several prophecies set in order, and the whole applied to the church's condition; the long digression on scandal that grew out of these lectures has been read on its own ever since.

pearson-ansvver-dr-burges-vvord-way-post.blurb: A twenty-two page postscript answering Cornelius Burges, in defence of Pearson's tract that there was no necessity of reforming the public doctrine of the Church of England. Printed in 1660, when the terms of a church settlement were still open and the Presbyterian party was pressing for change in doctrine as well as in ceremony.

pearson-v-cl-johannis-pearsonii-s-t.blurb: Pearson's posthumous chronological works, six hundred and forty-six pages printed in 1688, after his death as bishop of Chester. The chief piece is the pair of dissertations on the series and succession of the earliest bishops of Rome, to which Pearson brought the same critical apparatus he had turned on the Ignatian epistles.

reynolds-divine-penitential-meditations-.blurb: Fourteen pages of penitential meditations and vows, given by the title as the work of Charles I in his confinement at Holmby House, printed in 1649, the year of his execution. The piece belongs with the Eikon Basilike and the devotional literature that gathered around the king's memory; the ascription to Reynolds should be treated with the caution such pieces always require.

reynolds-self-deniall-opened-applyed-ser.blurb: A sermon on self-denial preached before the Assembly of Divines on one of their private days of fasting, fifty-two pages printed in 1652. Reynolds sat in the Assembly and conformed at the Restoration, taking the see of Norwich; here he is preaching to his colleagues, which gives the sermon a different temper from those addressed to Parliament.

carter-carters-christian-common-vvealth-.blurb: A treatise on the ordering of the household, the duties of husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants, presented as a Christian commonwealth in little. Three hundred and twenty-eight pages printed in 1627, in the line of English books on domestic duties that runs from Dod and Cleaver to Gouge.

carter-prayers-prevalencie-for-israels-s.blurb: A sermon on the prevailing power of prayer for the safety of Israel, preached at St Margaret's Westminster and printed in 1643. Forty-four pages; St Margaret's was where the Commons heard their monthly fast sermons, and Israel stands here, as it does throughout that literature, for England.

coleman-gods-unusuall-answer-to-a-solemn.blurb: Coleman preaches on the question a defeat puts to a nation that has just humbled itself before God: what does it mean when a solemn fast is answered with a reverse in the field rather than a victory? The occasion is the sad success in the west of 1644, and the observations that follow are addressed to hearers tempted to read providence as a verdict on their cause.

coleman-huls-pillar-of-providence-erecte.blurb: Sixteen pages taking the deliverance of Hull as a pillar raised to providence, a standing column set up so that heaven's care for the town would not be forgotten. The conceit is architectural, and the argument is the ordinary one of thanksgiving preaching, that a particular escape is evidence of a general care.

gibson-a-sermon-of-ecclesiastical-benedi.blurb: A visitation sermon delivered at Oundle in April 1619, preached to the clergy of the district gathered as such occasions required. Its subject is ecclesiastical benediction, the blessing pronounced by a minister, and what warrant and effect the church may claim for it.

gibson-the-ruine-of-the-authors-and-fome.blurb: A sermon of 1645 on the destruction that overtakes the authors and fomenters of civil wars, delivered, as the title says, before one of the bodies that heard such preaching through the decade. The charge is aimed at causes rather than combatants, at those who begin and feed a war rather than those who fight it.

hall-digitus-testium-or-a-dreadful-alarm.blurb: An alarm addressed to the whole kingdom and particularly to the magistracy of London, the Lord Mayor and the aldermen, printed in 1651. The Latin of the title means the finger of the witnesses; past that, the piece announces itself as warning rather than argument, and the title is the whole of what it discloses in advance.

hall-heaven-ravished-or-a-glorious-prize.blurb: A sermon built on the storming of heaven, the glorious prize achieved by a heroic enterprise, language that echoes Christ's saying that the violent take the kingdom of heaven by force. What the title promises is an exhortation to importunity rather than a doctrinal treatise; the printing of 1644 runs to seventy-seven pages.

staunton-phinehas-s-zeal-in-execution-of.blurb: A fast sermon on Phinehas, whose zeal in executing judgment stayed the plague in Israel, offered here as a divine remedy for England's misery. Staunton sat in the Westminster Assembly, and the sermon presses the harder half of the fast-day case, that a nation's deliverance may require the execution of judgment and not repentance only.

staunton-rupes-israelis-the-rock-of-isra.blurb: A sermon on God as the Rock of Israel, laying out, as the title modestly has it, a little part of that rock's glory. Staunton was a member of the Westminster Assembly and president of a college at Oxford; the printed text of 1644 runs to forty pages.

westfield-eleaven-choice-sermons-as-they.blurb: Eleven sermons of Thomas Westfield, bishop of Bristol, printed in 1655 and described on the title as the work of a divine already dead. The volume is a gathering rather than a course, and the word choice carries the whole of the claim made for the selection.

westfield-englands-face-in-israels-glass.blurb: Sermons setting England's condition against Israel's, the sins, mercies and judgments of the one read in the mirror of the other. The typological habit is the common one of the 1640s pulpit, which took the national history of Scripture as a glass in which a later nation could see itself.

oviedo-treatises-faith-hope-charity.blurb: Scholastic treatment of the three theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, handled in the Jesuit manner: theological, scholastic and moral questions taken in order, with the disputed points argued at length rather than summarised. Oviedo works in the tradition of commentary on the second part of Aquinas's Summa, and the volume runs past a thousand pages.

oviedo-cursus-philosophicus.blurb: A complete Jesuit course in philosophy, running from logic through natural philosophy and the soul to metaphysics across more than two thousand seven hundred pages. Oviedo belonged to the generation of Spanish Jesuits who argued these questions hard among themselves rather than repeating Aristotle, and the disputations here are conducted at that scale.

johann-franz-buddeus-institutiones-theol.blurb: A systematic moral theology from Jena, arranging Christian ethics as a body of doctrine with its own principles rather than as an appendix to dogmatics. Budde stands where Lutheran orthodoxy meets Pietist concern for practice and the early Enlightenment's appetite for natural law, and the Institutiones bear marks of all three.

johannes-combach-metaphysicorum-libri-du.blurb: Two books of metaphysics from a Marburg Aristotelian, belonging to the genre of Protestant scholastic textbook that supplied the philosophy course standing behind Reformed theology. The division into two books is all the title discloses of its arrangement, and the work runs to six hundred and fifty pages.

david-derodon-philosophia-contracta.blurb: Philosophy in compressed form, a full course reduced to essentials by a French Reformed logician who taught at Nimes and at Geneva and who wrote as readily against the Mass as about syllogisms. The title promises brevity, and six hundred and forty pages is what brevity meant in this genre.

georg-m-ller-metaphysica.blurb: A metaphysics of some two hundred pages by a Reformed teacher, short by the standards of a genre that regularly ran to four times the length. The title indicates neither the school it follows nor the quarrels it enters.

johannes-greydanus-institutiones-metaphy.blurb: Institutes of metaphysics in the Reformed scholastic manner, a teaching text of the kind written for students who would go on to divinity. The title places it in that genre and says nothing further about its positions; the work runs to some four hundred and fifty pages.

lucas-trelcatius-opuscula-theologica-omn.blurb: The collected shorter theological works of Trelcatius, gathered into a single volume of some twelve hundred pages. The Trelcatii, father and son, taught at Leiden in the generation immediately before the Arminian crisis, and the opuscula belong to the early Dutch Reformed scholasticism of that faculty.

johannes-althusius-dicaeologicae-libri-t.blurb: Three books on right, in which Althusius attempts for law what his Politica attempted for political life: a single method covering the whole of it, Roman civil law, the law of Scripture and the customary law of the German lands brought under one set of distinctions. The organisation proceeds by division from the general to the particular, and the aim is a jurisprudence that is a science rather than a collection of cases.

aretius-theologiae-problemata.blurb: The theological system of the Bernese reformer, cast as problemata, questions posed and then resolved, and serving as his loci communes. Aretius taught at Bern and wrote commentaries on most of the New Testament; this Bern printing of 1573 gathers the doctrinal matter into one course of nearly six hundred pages.

braun-doctrina-foederum.blurb: A system of theology organised around the doctrine of the covenants, in the Cocceian manner that read redemption as a sequence of covenant administrations rather than as a set of timeless loci. Braun taught at Groningen, and the Amsterdam printing of 1688 presents the covenant doctrine and the didactic system as one work.

brenz-in-apologiam-confessionis.blurb: Brenz was the principal author of the Wurttemberg Confession, drawn up for presentation at Trent, and this is his defense of it against the Catholic reply it drew. The Tubingen printing of 1555 belongs to the exchange that followed the confession's presentation, and it is the mature controversial work of the reformer of Wurttemberg.
