calvin-commentary-on-psalms-vol-4.blurb: The fourth of five volumes, and the one in which his treatment of the law psalms falls. With it comes his answer to the objection that a religion of grace cannot also delight in commandments: the psalmist's love of the law is evidence that law, read as the rule of a covenant already established, stands in no opposition to faith. The psalms of God's reign occupy the earlier part.

calvin-commentary-on-psalms-vol-5.blurb: The last of the five volumes, closing the Psalter. Calvin worked on this exposition alongside the effort to put the Psalms into French metre for congregational singing at Geneva, and the commentary keeps that use in view, asking what a congregation is to do with each psalm. The songs of ascents and the closing psalms of praise fall in this volume.

calvin-commentary-on-isaiah-vol-1.blurb: The first of four volumes. The work began as lectures, was published from a hearer's notes, and was afterwards revised by Calvin himself. This volume covers the opening oracles against Judah and the beginning of the burdens against surrounding nations. He treats the prophets as preachers to their own generation first, and warns repeatedly against turning prophecy into a calendar. The book was dedicated to Edward VI of England, the later revision to Elizabeth.

calvin-commentary-on-isaiah-vol-2.blurb: The second of four volumes, taking in the remaining burdens against the nations and the historical chapters on Hezekiah and the Assyrian siege. What holds Calvin's attention is the political question Isaiah presses on Judah: whether a small and threatened people will rest on a promise or on a treaty with a stronger neighbour. He applies it to the churches of his own day without embarrassment.

calvin-commentary-on-isaiah-vol-3.blurb: The third of four volumes, covering the chapters of judgment and consolation that stand between the Assyrian crisis and the prophecies of return, including the polemic against idols and the naming of Cyrus as God's instrument. Calvin uses the Cyrus oracles to argue that prophecy is proof of divine foreknowledge, against readers who would place the writing after the event.

calvin-commentary-on-isaiah-vol-4.blurb: The last of the four volumes, taking up the closing chapters, among them the servant passages and Isaiah 53. Calvin argues that the servant is Christ and not merely Israel or the prophet, and reads the chapter as the plainest statement of substitution in the Old Testament. The concluding prophecies of new heavens and a restored city he understands as descriptions of the church's condition under the gospel.

calvin-commentary-on-jeremiah-and-lament.blurb: The last volume of the five that make up Calvin's lectures on Jeremiah, carrying the prophecy to its close and then running through the whole of Lamentations. These were praelectiones delivered before the ministers and students of Geneva and taken down by hearers, which accounts for their pace and their directness. Calvin's Jeremiah is a preacher to a doomed city, and the application to France is never far from view.

calvin-commentary-on-ezekiel-vol-1.blurb: The first of two volumes of lectures, covering the opening vision by the river Chebar, the prophet's commission, and the oracles of judgment on Jerusalem. Calvin is characteristically restrained about the chariot vision, refusing the elaborate schemes earlier commentators had built on it. Like his other prophetic lectures, the text was taken down by hearers as he delivered it rather than written out for the press.

calvin-commentary-on-ezekiel-vol-2.blurb: The second volume, and the end of the work. Calvin lectured on Ezekiel only as far as chapter twenty and died before going further, so the commentary stops well short of the temple vision at the close of the book. What survives here includes the chapters on false prophets, on the soul that sins bearing its own guilt, and on Israel's history retold as a history of unfaithfulness.

calvin-commentary-on-daniel-vol-1.blurb: The first of two volumes of lectures, covering the court narratives and the dream of the monarchies through chapter six. Calvin reads the four kingdoms as Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome, terminating at the coming of Christ, and refuses the reading that turns them into a chart of later European history. The dedication addresses the persecuted French Protestants, and the parallel between their case and Daniel's exile is stated without disguise.

calvin-commentary-on-daniel-vol-2.blurb: The second volume, taking up the visions from chapter seven onward: the beasts, the ram and the goat, the seventy weeks, and the long final prophecy of the kings of north and south. Calvin works through the seventy weeks arithmetically and ends them in Christ. He rejects a future earthly reign of a thousand years, and reads the promise at the close of the book as the general and final resurrection.

calvin-commentary-on-hosea.blurb: The first of five volumes of lectures on the Minor Prophets, given wholly to Hosea. Calvin takes the marriage of the opening chapters to have been shown to the prophet in vision rather than acted out, and the burden of the exposition is the covenant read as a marriage Israel has broken. As with his other prophetic lectures, the text comes from notes taken down while he spoke.

calvin-commentary-on-joel-amos-obadiah.blurb: The second of five volumes of lectures on the Minor Prophets: Joel's locusts and day of the Lord, Amos preaching against a prosperous and comfortable Israel, and the short oracle of Obadiah against Edom. Calvin is at his most pointed in Amos, where the indictment of those at ease and the rebuke of a worship that continues while justice fails are turned directly on his own hearers.

calvin-commentary-on-jonah-micah-nahum.blurb: The third of five volumes of lectures on the Minor Prophets. Calvin treats Jonah as history and reads the flight and the anger as a study of a believer's rebellion rather than as a marvel. Micah supplies the contrast between corrupt rulers and the promise attached to Bethlehem; Nahum raises the question of what it means for God to avenge, which Calvin handles without apology.

calvin-commentary-on-habakkuk-zephaniah-.blurb: The fourth of five volumes of lectures on the Minor Prophets. Habakkuk's complaint that God stays silent while the wicked prosper draws from Calvin a sustained treatment of faith holding on without sight, and of the just living by faith as Paul afterwards used the phrase. Zephaniah supplies the day of wrath, and Haggai the rebuilding of a temple by a discouraged and impoverished remnant.

calvin-commentary-on-zechariah-malachi.blurb: The last of five volumes of lectures on the Minor Prophets. Zechariah's night visions Calvin handles cautiously, taking them as encouragement to a small returned community rather than as a key to the future, though he reads the pierced one and the stricken shepherd of the later chapters as fulfilled in Christ. Malachi closes the set with the dispute over careless worship and the covenant made with Levi.

calvin-commentary-on-a-harmony-of-the-ev.blurb: The third and closing volume of Calvin's harmony of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, a work that expounds the three narratives together rather than taking each Gospel in turn. This volume brings the harmony through the last week in Jerusalem, the passion, and the resurrection. Calvin deals candidly with the places where the evangelists differ in order, arguing that they did not set out to write chronicles.

calvin-commentary-on-john-vol-1.blurb: The first of two volumes, running from the prologue through the discourses of the middle chapters to the raising of Lazarus. Calvin's preface argues that John supplies the key by which the other three Gospels are to be read, since he sets out the power and office of Christ where they narrate his acts. The exposition of chapter six carries his account of eating Christ by faith.

calvin-commentary-on-john-vol-2.blurb: The second volume, taking up the entry into Jerusalem and continuing through the farewell discourses, the prayer of chapter seventeen, the passion, and the resurrection appearances. The promise of the Comforter receives extended treatment, as does the vine, which Calvin uses to state union with Christ while refusing any mixture of the believer's substance with his.

calvin-commentary-on-acts-vol-1.blurb: The first of two volumes, covering the ascension and Pentecost, the early Jerusalem community, the trial and death of Stephen, and the mission that follows the scattering, up to the sending out of Paul. Calvin reads Acts as the record of how the church was in fact planted, and takes a steady interest in the ordering of ministry, the relief of the poor, and the discipline of a congregation.

calvin-commentary-on-acts-vol-2.blurb: The second volume, following Paul from the first journey through the council at Jerusalem, the churches of Asia and Greece, the arrest in the temple, the hearings before governors and king, and the voyage to Rome. The council of chapter fifteen occasions Calvin's account of how a synod ought to proceed; the trial scenes occasion his remarks on the Christian standing before a magistrate.

calvin-commentary-on-corinthians-vol-1.blurb: The first of two volumes, on First Corinthians: the parties in the congregation, the case of incest and its discipline, lawsuits between believers, marriage and celibacy, meat offered to idols, the covering of heads, the Supper, the spiritual gifts and their ordering, and the resurrection chapter. His treatment of the Supper here is among the fullest statements of his eucharistic position outside the Institutes.

calvin-commentary-on-corinthians-vol-2.blurb: The second volume, on Second Corinthians, where Paul defends his ministry against rivals who have gained a hearing in the congregation. Calvin follows the argument about letter and Spirit, the treasure in earthen vessels, and the ministry of reconciliation, and gives close attention to the two chapters on the collection for Jerusalem, which he reads as a rule for how churches are to relieve one another.

calvin-commentary-on-galatians-and-ephes.blurb: Two letters in one volume. On Galatians Calvin works out justification against the imposition of the law, and the confrontation at Antioch gives him occasion to ask whether an apostle may be publicly corrected. On Ephesians he turns to election in the opening chapter, to the making of one body out of Jew and Gentile, and to the household instructions, which he treats as a serious account of Christian callings.

calvin-commentary-on-philippians-colossi.blurb: Three sets of letters in one volume. Philippians brings Calvin to the hymn of chapter two and its account of Christ's self-emptying, which he expounds without surrendering the deity. Colossians occasions a polemic against additions to Christ, whether angels, ceremonies, or a false austerity. The Thessalonian letters bring him to the return of Christ and to the man of sin, whom he identifies with the papacy rather than a single future person.

calvin-commentary-on-timothy-titus-phile.blurb: The pastoral letters together with the short note to Philemon. Calvin uses them for the shape of the ministry: the qualifications of pastors and deacons, the calling and examining of men for office, the support of widows, the handling of accusations against elders. The exposition of the passage on all Scripture being breathed out by God stands here, as does his treatment of the injunctions concerning women.

calvin-commentary-on-hebrews.blurb: Calvin denies that Paul wrote this letter, on the ground of its style and its manner of citing apostolic testimony, while insisting that its authority is in no way lessened by the author being unknown. The commentary follows the argument about the priesthood after the order of Melchizedek and the sacrifice offered once for all, and takes up the warnings against apostasy without conceding that the elect may finally be lost.

calvin-commentaries-on-the-catholic-epis.blurb: Calvin's exposition of James, First and Second Peter, First John, and Jude. He wrote nothing on Second and Third John, and never commented on Revelation, so this volume completes his work on the New Testament. James on faith and works receives the treatment the controversy demanded, Calvin arguing that James speaks of the proof of faith where Paul speaks of its ground. On First John the tests of assurance occupy him.

calvin-a-treatise-on-relics.blurb: A polemical inventory of the relics venerated in the churches of Europe, written in French for lay readers: the pieces of the true cross, the bodies claimed by several cities at once, the milk of the Virgin, the several heads of John the Baptist. Calvin's method is to set the competing claims side by side and let the arithmetic do the work. The satire is dry, and the intent is pastoral rather than antiquarian.

calvin-sermons-job-hezekiah-isaiah.blurb: A large collection of sermons preached at Geneva, dominated by the long series on Job, with shorter series on the song of Hezekiah in Isaiah 38, on Isaiah 53, and on the prophecy of Christ. Calvin preached without a manuscript and these texts derive from stenographic notes taken in the congregation, so the prose is spoken rather than composed, with the repetitions and direct address of a man at work on his hearers.

duns-scotus-collationes-seu-disputatione.blurb: Short disputed questions held outside the ordinary lecture cycle, each putting one point and arguing it through: the divine attributes, the will, individuation, and the soul are among the matters that recur. The collations survive in an Oxford and a Paris group, and they are among the places where Scotus states a position more compactly than in the commentaries on the Sentences. The Wadding text is not a critical edition.

duns-scotus-de-cognitione-dei-tractatus-.blurb: A short and unfinished treatise on the knowledge of God, printed among Scotus's works in the Wadding edition. That edition also carries pieces now firmly assigned to other authors, and this one does not stand among the securely attested works, so a reader should take it as Scotist rather than as certainly Scotus. The title promises an account of what the mind may reach of God short of the beatific vision.

duns-scotus-de-primo-rerum-omnium-princi.blurb: A compact treatise in four chapters arguing from creatures to a first principle. Scotus builds it on the essential orders of dependence and eminence, denies that an infinite regress is possible among essentially ordered causes, concludes to a being first in efficiency, in finality, and in eminence, and then shows that these coincide in one infinite being. The whole is addressed to God in the second person, in the form of a prayer.

duns-scotus-dilucidissima-expositio-et-q.blurb: A running exposition of Aristotle's Physics with questions attached, printed in the Wadding edition under Scotus's name. The Physics material transmitted with his works is not secure, and this full exposition is generally judged to be by another hand. It remains a witness to how the early Scotist schools read Aristotle on motion, place, time, infinity, and the first mover.

duns-scotus-in-duos-libros-perihermenias.blurb: Eight questions on Aristotle's two books on interpretation, forming the second of the two sets of Perihermenias questions transmitted under Scotus's name. Both belong to the logical teaching of his early years, before the theology, and take up signification, the truth of propositions about the future, and the relation between spoken words, written marks, and what is in the mind.

duns-scotus-in-libros-de-anima.blurb: Material on Aristotle's books on the soul, printed in the Wadding corpus. That corpus carries more than one body of De anima teaching under Scotus's name, and not all of it is his: the questions on the soul are now accepted as authentic, while other expositions printed alongside them are not. Which of these the present volume represents cannot be settled from the title alone.

duns-scotus-in-libros-elenchorum-quaesti.blurb: Part of the course in logic Scotus gave early in his career, and accepted as his in the critical edition of the philosophical works. The Aristotelian text behind it is the Sophistical Refutations, and the subject accordingly is fallacy: how an argument can appear to conclude when it does not, and what that appearance shows about signification, equivocation, and the way words stand for things.

duns-scotus-in-librum-praedicamentorum-q.blurb: From the same early course in logic, working through Aristotle on the ten categories. Scotus asks what the categories are categories of, whether the division is complete and on what principle it is made, and how substance differs from the accidents said of it. His handling of relation and of quantity bears on positions he takes later in theology, where relation carries the weight of the Trinitarian account.

duns-scotus-in-librum-primum-posteriorum.blurb: Aristotle on demonstration, put into question form: what makes a proposition scientific, what the first principles of a science are and how they come to be known, and what it is for a science to have a subject at all. The Analytics commentaries in the Wadding edition are not among the logical works admitted as certainly Scotus's, and the ascription should be treated with caution.

duns-scotus-in-librum-primum-priorum-ana.blurb: The syllogism as such, taken question by question: the figures and the moods, the conversion of premises, and the reduction of imperfect syllogisms to the perfect. As with the questions on the Posterior Analytics, this set belongs to the part of the Wadding corpus whose ascription to Scotus is doubted, and it is better read as Scotist school material unless shown to be more.

duns-scotus-in-librum-primum-sententiaru.blurb: Book one of the commentary on Peter Lombard, the Ordinatio or Opus Oxoniense, the version Scotus revised himself and the source of most of what he is known for: that being is said univocally of God and creatures, that a formal distinction holds among the divine attributes without dividing the essence, and the argument to an actually infinite being. The later distinctions treat the Trinity. Wadding prints Lychetus's commentary alongside the text.

duns-scotus-in-librum-quartum-sententiar.blurb: Book four, the longest part of the commentary, given to the sacraments and the last things. Scotus treats sacramental causality and the sense in which words effect what they signify, transubstantiation and the manner of Christ's presence, penance and attrition, orders, and marriage, before closing with resurrection, judgment, and beatitude. The distinctions on penance and on marriage are among the most detailed canonical discussions anywhere in his work.

duns-scotus-in-librum-secundum-posterior.blurb: Aristotle's second book turns from demonstration to definition, to the knowledge of what a thing is as distinct from that it is, and to the way first principles are grasped; these questions follow him through it. The same caution applies as to the first book: the Analytics material in the Wadding edition is not securely Scotus's, though it was read as his for centuries.

duns-scotus-in-librum-secundum-priorum-a.blurb: A brief set of questions on the second book of the Prior Analytics, on what follows once the figures are established: the conversion of syllogisms, circular proof, and what can be concluded from false premises. Its brevity and its place in the Wadding corpus, whose Analytics material is of doubtful ascription, both counsel against treating it as Scotus's own work.

duns-scotus-in-librum-secundum-sententia.blurb: Book two, on creation and creatures. The third distinction carries Scotus's account of individuation, the positive entity by which a common nature is contracted to this thing and no other, later called haecceity, together with his rejection of matter, quantity, and negation as principles of individuality. The book also holds his angelology, his account of the will's freedom and its priority over intellect, and the fall.

duns-scotus-in-librum-tertium-sententiar.blurb: Book three, on the Incarnation and the virtues. Two positions here are the ones most often cited: that Christ was predestined to glory independently of Adam's sin, so that the Incarnation was not occasioned by the fall, and that the Virgin was preserved from original sin, which Scotus defends by arguing that the most perfect redemption prevents rather than repairs. Faith, hope, and charity occupy the later distinctions.

duns-scotus-in-primum-librum-perihermeni.blurb: The first of the two sets of questions on Aristotle on interpretation transmitted under Scotus's name. The matter is the proposition: what a name and a verb signify, how affirmation and negation are opposed, and the problem of the sea battle, where a statement about a future contingent appears to be true or false already and so to remove contingency from the world.

duns-scotus-in-xii-libros-metaphysicorum.blurb: A literal exposition of Aristotle's Metaphysics printed with Scotus's works. It is not by him: the exposition has long been identified as the work of Antonius Andreas, a Catalan Franciscan who had studied under Scotus and was nicknamed the little Scotus for how closely he followed him. Read as what it is, it is an early and largely faithful record of how a direct pupil understood his master's metaphysics.

duns-scotus-incipit.blurb: A single leaf of front matter carrying the author's name and nothing else. The abbreviation before the name stands for Beatus, blessed, the style used of him once his cult was confirmed. Readers looking for text should turn to the works themselves; this page is retained because it stands where it does in the volume as printed.

duns-scotus-meteorologicorum.blurb: A commentary on Aristotle's Meteorology printed among Scotus's works. Like several of the pieces of natural philosophy in the Wadding corpus, its ascription to him is not accepted, and it is generally assigned to another master of roughly the same period. The subject is the region below the heavens: exhalations, comets, winds, rain and hail, the rainbow, and the salt sea, treated as effects of the elements under celestial causes.

duns-scotus-opusculum-de243-contradictio.blurb: Not a work of Scotus but a later reconciling exercise: someone has gathered two hundred and forty three places where his writings appear to contradict one another and supplied a solution to each. Lists of this kind were a standard genre in the Scotist schools, where the consistency and the authenticity of the master's corpus were live questions. Its chief use now is as evidence of what early readers found hard in him.

duns-scotus-quaestiones-disputatae-de-re.blurb: Printed as Scotus's for centuries and now assigned to Vital du Four, a Franciscan of about the same generation. The misattribution had consequences, since these disputed questions teach universal hylomorphism, matter in every creature including the angels, a position Scotus does not hold, and older accounts of his thought that lean on this text misdescribe him.

duns-scotus-quaestiones-quodlibetales.blurb: The questions Scotus disputed as regent master at Paris, in the format where anyone present might propose the question and the master had to answer whatever was raised. The result ranges over the divine essence and attributes, relation, the Trinity, grace and merit, the will, and the Eucharist. Because they come from his last years, the Quodlibet is often read as his settled mind where it diverges from the earlier Sentences material.

duns-scotus-quaestiones-subtilissimae-su.blurb: Questions rather than a running exposition on Aristotle's Metaphysics, and a work generally accepted as Scotus's own. He argues about the subject of metaphysics and settles on being as being, works out the univocity of the concept of being, treats the transcendentals and the distinctions among them, and takes up matter, form, and individuation from the philosophical side. The later books show signs of revision and of an unfinished state.

duns-scotus-quaestiones-super-libros-ari.blurb: Admitted as authentic in the critical edition of the philosophical works, and the place to see Scotus on the soul as a philosopher rather than as a theologian. He asks whether the soul can be the subject of a science, how the senses know, what the agent and possible intellect contribute, whether the intellect knows the singular directly, and whether immortality can be demonstrated or only held on faith.

duns-scotus-reportata-parisiensia-liber-.blurb: Book one of the report of Scotus's Paris lectures on the Sentences, taken down by a hearer rather than written out by him. For this book a version examined and corrected by Scotus himself is known, which gives it a standing the other reportationes lack. Read against the Ordinatio it shows where he changed his mind and where he was simply putting the same case more briefly to a Paris audience.

Book four of the Paris report, on the sacraments and the last things, covering the same ground as book four of the Ordinatio but as heard in the lecture room. The text is a student's record, so its authority is limited; where it differs from the Ordinatio the difference may be Scotus revising or the reporter mishearing, and the printed editions do not always let a reader tell which.

Book two of the Paris report, on creation, the angels, individuation, and the will. Scotus lectured on the Sentences more than once, at Oxford and at Paris, and the same distinctions therefore exist in several states; this is the Paris state of book two as a student set it down. It is a check on the Ordinatio rather than a substitute for it.

Book three of the Paris report, on the Incarnation, the Virgin, and the virtues. The Paris lectures are where Scotus is traditionally said to have defended the preservation of the Virgin from original sin in public disputation, and the material here should be compared with the corresponding distinctions of the Ordinatio, which he revised, before conclusions are drawn about his final position.

duns-scotus-super-universalia-porphyrii-.blurb: Questions on Porphyry's Isagoge, the standard introduction to Aristotle's logic and the opening text of the medieval arts course. The subject is the five predicables, genus, species, difference, property, and accident, and behind them the question Porphyry raised and declined to answer: whether genera and species subsist in things or exist only in the understanding. The answers here bear on the common nature Scotus later works out.

duns-scotus-theoremata-subtilissima.blurb: A series of theorems set out with proofs rather than in the question form Scotus normally uses. Their authenticity has been argued over for a long time, chiefly because several of them deny that certain truths about God can be demonstrated, which is hard to reconcile with the arguments of De primo principio and the Ordinatio. Some resolve the tension by separating what metaphysics proves from what theology holds; others reject the work.

duns-scotus-tractatus-de-modis-significa.blurb: A treatise on the modes of signifying, the central text of speculative grammar, in which the ways a word signifies are correlated with the ways a thing exists and the ways the mind understands it. It is not by Scotus: it has been identified as the work of Thomas of Erfurt, though it circulated under his name for centuries and shaped how he was read. Heidegger's habilitation was written on it as Scotus's.

duns-scotus-tractatus-de-perfectione-sta.blurb: A treatise on the states of life, arguing for the comparative perfection of the religious state and, within it, of the mendicant orders, against objections raised on behalf of the secular clergy. It is not accepted as Scotus's: it belongs to the polemical literature the mendicant controversies produced and was gathered into his works by later editors.

duns-scotus-summa-theologica-vol-1.blurb: Not a work Scotus wrote but a compilation: Hieronymus de Montefortino, a Franciscan of the eighteenth century, gathered Scotist doctrine from across the corpus and set it out in the order, and even the article form, of Aquinas's Summa, so that the two can be read against each other page by page. This first of six volumes begins where Aquinas begins, with the existence and nature of God and the divine attributes.

duns-scotus-summa-theologica-vol-2.blurb: The second of six volumes of Montefortino's arrangement of Scotus in the order of Aquinas's Summa. The seams show throughout: the compiler must supply an answer where Scotus left none, and must decide which of several states of a disputed question counts as the master's mind. Anyone working from it should treat it as an eighteenth-century Scotist's report and check the citations against the Ordinatio.

duns-scotus-summa-theologica-vol-3.blurb: The third of six volumes compiled from Scotus's works and laid out in the order of Aquinas's. Because the frame is Thomist and the matter Scotist, the compilation is most instructive where the two diverge: on the univocity of being, on the formal distinction, on the priority of will to intellect, and on where moral obligation is finally grounded.

duns-scotus-summa-theologica-vol-4.blurb: The fourth of six volumes of Montefortino's compilation. Since the arrangement follows Aquinas's plan, the moral part of the Summa occupies its own long stretch of the work, and there the Scotist positions on natural law, on whether the precepts of the second table admit of dispensation, and on charity and the virtues can be set directly beside the Thomist ones.

duns-scotus-summa-theologica-vol-5.blurb: The fifth of six volumes drawn out of Scotus's writings and arranged after Aquinas. Readers come to the later volumes chiefly for the Christological and sacramental matter, where the compiler has to represent the two theses Scotus is best known for, the Incarnation willed apart from the fall, and the preservation of the Virgin from original sin, inside a frame built by a man who denied the second.

duns-scotus-summa-theologica-vol-6.blurb: The last of the six volumes of Montefortino's compilation. Aquinas's own Summa broke off unfinished and was completed by other hands from his earlier writings; this arrangement runs to the end, because its compiler was working from a corpus already complete. The completeness is the editor's rather than the author's, and the whole is best checked against the Ordinatio and the Quodlibet.

watson-autarkeia-art-divine-contentment-.blurb: An exposition of Paul's words at Philippians 4:11, that he had learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content. Watson takes the Greek term of the title, self-sufficiency, and turns it against its Stoic use: contentment is not a temper native to the mind but a lesson taught by grace. He works through the nature of contentment, the arguments that support it, and the impediments a discontented heart raises against them.

watson-beatitudes-discourse-part-christs.blurb: A long course of sermons on Matthew 5, taking the beatitudes in order and anatomising each into its nature, its evidences, and the marks by which a hearer may test whether the blessing is his own. Poverty of spirit and mourning for sin receive the fullest handling. A further discourse on Christ is bound in at the end, its title cut short in this entry.

watson-body-practical-divinity-consistin.blurb: A hundred and seventy six sermons on the Westminster Shorter Catechism, gathered and printed after Watson's death. They run from man's chief end through the doctrine of God, the fall, the covenant of grace, the person and offices of Christ, effectual calling, justification, adoption and sanctification, and end in the state of glory. Pulpit work throughout, and closer to sustained exposition than to system.

watson-christian-s-charter-shewing-privi.blurb: A treatise on the privileges that belong to a believer by title rather than by feeling, and on the security of holding them from God's grant instead of one's own performance. Watson's usual method holds: name a mercy, prove it from Scripture, then press the reader to ask what claim he actually has to it. Written as a book of comfort, though the comfort is made conditional on examination.

watson-crown-righteousness-set-forth-ser.blurb: A funeral sermon preached at St Stephen Walbrook, Watson's own London church, on 1 May 1656. The crown of the title is the one Paul says is laid up for all that love Christ's appearing. The name of the person buried is cut off the title page as it is given here, and nothing else in the entry supplies it.

watson-divine-cordial-transcendent-privi.blurb: An exposition of Romans 8:28, that all things work together for good to them that love God. Watson takes the best and the worst of a Christian's condition in turn, showing how mercies, afflictions and temptations are made to serve the believer, then examines the two marks the verse itself supplies, love to God and effectual calling. Later reprinted under the title All Things for Good.

watson-doctrine-repentance-useful-these-.blurb: A practical treatise on evangelical repentance as distinct from legal terror, working through the ingredients Watson finds in it: sight of sin, sorrow for sin, confession, shame, hatred of sin, and turning from it. He sets out the counterfeits, the motives, and the marks by which a man may know his sorrow is godly. Short, plain, and unsparing about the difference between being sorry and being changed.

watson-duty-self-denial-briefly-opened-u.blurb: A short practical treatise opening what self-denial is and pressing it as a duty laid on every Christian rather than a counsel for the few. Watson's ordinary pattern applies: the doctrine stated, the reasons given, the objections met, the application driven home. A slight thing beside his sermon courses, and evidently meant to be read at a sitting.

watson-eglogue-death-right-honorable-sir.blurb: A pastoral elegy on the death of Elizabeth's principal secretary, by Thomas Watson the Elizabethan poet and Latinist, not the Puritan preacher of the same name. Watson wrote the poem first in Latin and then put it into English himself, mourning Walsingham under a shepherd's name in the manner of classical eclogue. Court poetry, and in this collection through a shared name only.

watson-fight-faith-crowned-sermon-preach.blurb: A funeral sermon for Henry Stubbs, a nonconformist minister, taking up Paul's account of having fought a good fight and finished his course. Watson preached a number of these for ejected brethren in his later years, and the form is constant: the text opened briefly, then a character of the dead man offered as the doctrine made visible.

watson-first-sett-italian-madrigalls-eng.blurb: English texts fitted to Italian madrigals, chiefly those of Luca Marenzio, by Thomas Watson the Elizabethan poet rather than the Puritan divine. Watson says on the title page that he has not translated the original words but written to the affection of the music. The set is also where two settings by William Byrd on the sweet and merry month of May first appeared.

watson-godly-mans-picture-drawn-scriptur.blurb: A portrait of the regenerate man drawn in a series of characteristic marks, each proved from Scripture and each turned into a test: a man of knowledge, of faith, of prayer, of sincerity, a lover of the word, a weeper over other men's sins. The purpose is diagnostic rather than descriptive. Watson wants the reader to hold the picture beside himself and judge whether it is a likeness.

watson-gods-anatomy-mans-heart-sermon-pr.blurb: A sermon preached by order of the House of Commons at St Margaret's Westminster, anatomising the human heart as a surgeon would a body: its deceitfulness, its hardness, and what is found when it is laid open. The occasion was political and the auditory was Parliament, but the substance is Watson's ordinary work on indwelling sin, addressed to men used to hearing about other people's.

watson-heaven-taken-storm-holy-violence-.blurb: An exposition of Christ's saying that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and the violent take it by force. Watson applies that violence in turn to reading, hearing the word, prayer, meditation, self-examination, holy conversation and the mortifying of one's own corruptions, arguing that heaven is never come at by a sleepy religion. The most strenuous of his practical books, and the least consoling.

watson-hekatompathia-passionate-centurie.blurb: A hundred love poems by Thomas Watson the Elizabethan poet, not the divine, each of eighteen lines rather than fourteen, and each preceded by a prose headnote in which Watson names the Petrarchan, Greek or French source he is working from and explains what he has made of it. Dedicated to the Earl of Oxford, and among the earliest English sonnet sequences, unusually candid about its borrowings.

watson-holsome-catholyke-doctryne-concer.blurb: Sermons on the seven sacraments by Thomas Watson, Bishop of Lincoln under Mary I, and a Catholic work rather than a Protestant one. It sets out the received doctrine of baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, extreme unction, orders and matrimony for parish instruction, with the fullest weight on the sacrament of the altar. Watson was deprived and imprisoned after Elizabeth's accession the following year.

watson-holy-eucharist-mystery-lords-supp.blurb: A treatise on the Lord's Supper: the nature of the sacrament, the ends for which it was instituted, what the elements signify, the duty of preparation, and the examination a communicant owes himself before coming. Reformed on the question of presence, but the weight falls on preparation and on the self-scrutiny Watson thought most communicants skipped.

watson-holy-longing-saints-desire-be-chr.blurb: A single sermon at All Hallows Lombard Street on the saint's desire to depart and be with Christ, opening why a believer should wish for death and why he should nonetheless be content to wait for it. Watson reads the desire as evidence of grace rather than as weariness with life, and applies it as a test of where a man's treasure lies.

watson-jerusalems-glory-saints-safetie-e.blurb: A discourse on the safety of the church and the comfort a believer may take from it, published in 1661 as the settlement that would soon eject Watson was taking shape. The title carries most of what can be said from this entry alone; the matter is of a piece with his other consolatory writing for a church under pressure.

watson-lamentations-amyntas-death-philli.blurb: An English version of the Latin Amyntas of Thomas Watson the Elizabethan poet, whose lamentations for the dead Phillis were turned into English hexameters by Abraham Fraunce. The title page calls the rendering paraphrastic, and it is: Fraunce is experimenting with quantitative measure in English as much as translating. Not the work of the Puritan preacher of the same name.

watson-light-darkness-deliverance-procla.blurb: A short discourse promising deliverance to a discouraged church, printed in 1679. The title carries the argument: that the church's despondencies are the dark in which God's deliverance is worked rather than evidence against it. Little more can be said of the contents from the title alone.

watson-mischief-sinne-it-brings-person-l.blurb: A practical treatise on what sin does to the sinner, taking as its theme that it brings a person low: low in comfort, in credit, in conscience, in estate, and at the last in torment. Watson's method is cumulative rather than argumentative, piling instance on instance until the point is felt. Among the plainest and most alarming of his shorter works.

watson-one-thing-necessary-preached-serm.blurb: A sermon at Paul's before the Lord Mayor and aldermen of London on Christ's word to Martha, that one thing is needful and that Mary has chosen the good part. Watson presses the singularity of that claim on an auditory with a great many other things to attend to, and the application is civic as much as personal.

watson-ould-facioned-love-loue-ould-faci.blurb: An English poem printed under the initials I.T., drawing on selections from the Latin Amintae Gaudia of Thomas Watson the Elizabethan poet, which had appeared at the end of his life. It is catalogued with Watson's works on that account; the English verse is another hand's. Nothing to do with the Puritan preacher of the same name.

watson-paramuthion-word-comfort-church-g.blurb: A word of comfort for an afflicted church, the Greek title meaning consolation. Printed in 1662, the year the Act of Uniformity put Watson out of St Stephen Walbrook. What it contains beyond consolation for a people losing their ministers cannot be said from the title alone.

watson-pastors-love-expressed-loving-peo.blurb: The farewell sermon Watson preached at St Stephen Walbrook in August 1662, when the Act of Uniformity required conformity or ejection and he chose ejection. Twenty four pages of pastoral counsel and leave-taking, and one of a considerable number of such sermons by London ministers that were printed singly and then gathered together in the months that followed.

watson-plea-almes-delivered-sermon-at-sp.blurb: A Spital sermon, preached in Easter week before the mayor, aldermen and citizens at the assembly where the city's charities were customarily commended. Watson argues almsgiving as a debt owed rather than a generosity offered, answers the excuses of the unwilling, and distinguishes the giving that is charity from the giving that is display.

watson-plea-godly-is-shown-excellency-ri.blurb: A defence of the righteous man against the world's estimate of him, setting out wherein his excellency consists and answering the reproaches commonly laid on serious religion. Printed in 1672, a decade into Watson's nonconformity, so that the plea reads as much for a slandered party as for a virtue in the abstract.

watson-religion-our-true-interest-practi.blurb: Practical notes on Malachi 3:16 to 18: those that feared the Lord speaking often one to another, the book of remembrance written before him, and the day when he makes up his jewels. Watson draws from the verses a defence of religious conference among Christians, the assurance that such speech is recorded, and the difference the last day will make between him that serves God and him that serves him not.

watson-righteous-mans-vveal-vvicked-mans.blurb: Thirty two pages on the two ends set before the righteous and the wicked, printed in 1662. The title states the whole argument, and without the text in hand little can be added beyond that it belongs with Watson's other short pieces pressing the difference the two conditions make at last.

watson-saints-delight-which-is-annexed-t.blurb: A substantial volume on the believer's delight in God, to which is annexed a treatise of meditation, the fullest thing Watson wrote on that practice: what meditation is, how it differs from bare reading and from prayer, what subjects are fit for it, and what helps a wandering mind. The two parts belong together, the treatise supplying the method by which the delight of the first is to be got.

watson-sermon-preached-july-at-funeral-m.blurb: A funeral sermon for John Wells, minister of St Olave Jewry, preached on 2 July 1676. Wells was among the London ministers put out in 1662, and Watson's sermon is of the kind he preached repeatedly for that generation: the text opened briefly, then the man's life set out as the doctrine in practice.

watson-seven-sermons-on-several-select-s.blurb: Seven occasional sermons gathered and printed in 1689, after Watson's death. The subjects are not named on the title page as it is given here, and nothing indicates whether the sermons had been printed singly before. Watson's shorter pieces were often issued in this way.

watson-twoo-notable-sermons-made-thirde-.blurb: Two Lenten sermons preached before Queen Mary in 1554 by Thomas Watson, then dean of Durham and later Bishop of Lincoln, a Catholic churchman and not the Puritan of the same name. They concern the sacrament of the altar and the sacrifice of the Mass, and were printed as part of the Marian effort to restore the old doctrine by preaching as well as by statute.

watson-upright-mans-character-crown-prea.blurb: A sermon at Paul's before the Lord Mayor, drawing a character of the upright man and setting out what is promised him at the end. The method is the one Watson used at length in The Godly Man's Picture: marks named, proved from Scripture, and applied as a test rather than a compliment. Preached to the city magistracy, and pointed accordingly.

joseph-hall-ansvver-pope-vrban-inurbanit.blurb: Hall's reply to a brief of Urban VIII sent to the French king and urging him on against the Protestant interest, which Hall reads as evidence that Rome's quarrel with the reformed churches is political before it is religious. The tone is the controversial one he reserved for Rome, ironic about the pope's urbanity and unyielding about his claims. Occasional writing in the strict sense.

joseph-hall-apologeticall-letter-person-.blurb: Thirteen pages written late in Hall's life, answering a charge made against him in a conference and reported to a person of quality. What the scandalous passage was cannot be recovered from the title. Hall was by then deprived of Norwich and living at Higham, and this belongs with the small self-defences of those last years.

joseph-hall-arte-diuine-meditation-profi.blurb: A method of meditation put into Protestant hands, distinguishing extemporal meditation, occasioned by whatever the eye falls on, from deliberate meditation on a chosen subject, and giving the second a graded scale of steps running from understanding through affection to resolution and prayer. Hall takes the frame from medieval and Continental devotional writers, strips out what he judges unusable, and closes with a worked example.

joseph-hall-characters-vertues-vices-two.blurb: Two books of Theophrastan characters, the first of virtues, the second of vices: the wise man, the honest man and the valiant man on one side; the hypocrite, the busybody, the flatterer, the malcontent and the superstitious man on the other. Each is a short prose portrait built from accumulated particulars rather than from definition. Hall's preface claims Theophrastus as his model and moral use as his end.

joseph-hall-christ-mysticall-blessed-uni.blurb: A treatise on the union of Christ and his members, the mystical body taken as a real union rather than a figure of speech, with the consequences drawn out for the church, for the sacraments and for the believer's assurance. Printed with a holy rapture appended, a pathetical meditation on the love of Christ. Devotional in aim, though scholastic in its distinctions.

joseph-hall-common-apologie-church-engla.blurb: Hall's answer to the separatists, the over-just sect of the title, and specifically to the reply his earlier letter had drawn from John Robinson. The argument is the conformist one: that the remaining faults of the Church of England do not unchurch it, and that separation is a graver sin than the corruptions it flees. Written before Hall held a bishopric, and already committed to the position he defended for the rest of his life.

joseph-hall-contemplations-principall-pa.blurb: The first of eight volumes of Hall's meditations on the biblical narrative, in four books, beginning at the Creation and working forward through the earliest history. The method is fixed from the outset: retell an episode in his own prose, stay close to the human particulars of it, then turn the whole to devotional use without allegorising. Narrative divinity rather than commentary.

joseph-hall-contemplations-principal-pas.blurb: The second of the eight volumes, in four books, carrying the sequence of scriptural meditations forward from where the first left off. Hall does not comment verse by verse and does not pretend to. He selects the passages that will bear meditation, tells them with attention to what the actors would have seen and felt, and passes over the rest.

The third volume, in three books rather than the four of the two before it, continuing the same course of meditations on the passages of Old Testament history. The strength of the series lies in the narrative writing, which makes a familiar episode strange again by attending to its circumstances before any application is drawn from it.

joseph-hall-contemplations-principall-pa.blurb: The fourth volume of the series, continuing the meditations on the holy story. The entry gives no division into books, where the first three name theirs. By this point the volumes were appearing every few years and being reissued alongside one another, and the manner is entirely settled: episode, circumstance, reflection.

joseph-hall-contemplations-historie-old-.blurb: The seventh volume, in two books, and by now retitled as contemplations on the history of the Old Testament rather than on the passages of the holy story. The later volumes carry the series toward the end of that history and are longer than the early ones, and less often excerpted than the patriarchal meditations that made Hall's name as a devotional writer.

joseph-hall-contemplations-historicall-p.blurb: The eighth and last volume, in two books, closing the course of contemplations on the Old Testament that Hall had been publishing volume by volume since 1612. Contemplations on the New Testament followed as a separate undertaking. The method is unchanged to the end: the episode retold, its circumstances weighed, the reflection drawn.

joseph-hall-discouery-new-world-descript.blurb: An English rendering by John Healey of Mundus Alter et Idem, the Latin satire Hall published without his name, framed as a voyage to the great southern continent. The traveller passes through lands governed by the vices they are named for, gluttony and folly and thievery among them, each described with the deadpan particularity of real travel writing. The least devotional thing in Hall's corpus, and the one he never openly owned.

joseph-hall-episcopacie-divine-right-ass.blurb: Hall's defence of bishops as an order of divine institution rather than of human convenience, written as episcopacy came under parliamentary attack and gone over by Laud before it was printed. The argument runs from Scripture to the practice of the primitive church. It drew the reply of the five ministers writing jointly as Smectymnuus, and through that exchange, Milton's antiprelatical tracts.

joseph-hall-epistles-first-volume-contai.blurb: The first volume of Hall's letters, two decades of them, written for print rather than gathered up after the fact. They are essays in epistolary form, addressed to named correspondents but composed for a reading public, taking up cases of conscience and questions of Christian practice. The Senecan manner that earned Hall his nickname is already fixed here.

joseph-hall-epistles-third-last-volume-c.blurb: The third and last volume, two decades of letters, completing the collection begun three years earlier. Same form as before: letters addressed to particular correspondents but composed for readers, treating a case of conscience or a question of practice at essay length. A reader wanting Hall's mind on a specific difficulty is likelier to find it here than in the treatises.

joseph-hall-heauen-earth-true-peace-tran.blurb: A Christian answer to Seneca's treatise on tranquillity of mind, granting the Stoic diagnosis of what disturbs a man and denying that the Stoic remedy can reach it. Hall works through the causes of disquiet, the false peaces men make with themselves, and the grounds of a peace that rests outside the mind altogether. The book that fixed his reputation as the English Seneca.

joseph-hall-holy-obseruations-lib-also-s.blurb: A first book of short observations, aphoristic in the manner Hall had already used in his Meditations and Vows, each turning some point of Scripture or of experience in a sentence or a paragraph. Bound with them are metrical versions of a few of David's psalms, offered on the title page as a taste of the rest.

joseph-hall-holy-raptures-patheticall-me.blurb: The 1647 pairing reversed, with the pathetical meditations on the love of Christ leading and the treatise of Christ mystical following. The raptures are affective devotional writing of Hall's late manner, sustained address to Christ rather than argument about him. A reader holding the earlier volume has substantially the same matter in the other order.

joseph-hall-honor-married-clergie-mainta.blurb: A defence of clerical marriage against a Catholic controversialist writing as C.E., arguing from Scripture, from the practice of the primitive church, and from what Hall takes to be the fruits of enforced celibacy. The tone is more combative than in the devotional books, and the personal stake is plain: Hall was a married minister answering a priest who denied that such a thing could be.

joseph-hall-kings-prophecie-vveeping-ioy.blurb: A poem of 1603 on the death of Elizabeth and the accession of James, the weeping and the joy of the subtitle held together as the two solemnities of a single year. Hall was in his twenties and had already published the Virgidemiarum satires, and this verse belongs with that earlier literary career rather than with the divinity that followed.

joseph-hall-lavvfvlnes-vnlavvfvlnes-oath.blurb: Six pages of short propositions on when an oath or covenant binds the conscience and when it does not, set out as bare theses rather than argued at length. Printed in 1643, when the question of what a pressed subscription could oblige a man to was very live. The brevity is the point; it is a set of tests, not a treatise.

joseph-hall-letter-lately-sent-reverend-.blurb: A letter written from the Tower, where Hall was imprisoned with eleven other bishops after their protest at being kept from the House of Lords. Addressed to a private friend and printed, as the title says, on the friend's judgment rather than the writer's. Two 1642 printings are held in this collection; this is the longer setting at fifteen pages.

Another 1642 printing of the same letter from the Tower, set at thirteen pages rather than fifteen. Hall was among the twelve bishops imprisoned after the December 1641 protest, and the letter reports his condition to a private friend who then put it in print. The entry does not distinguish the two issues beyond their length.

joseph-hall-meditations-vowes-diuine-mor.blurb: Short meditations, each closing in a resolution, arranged in books and covering the whole of ordinary conduct, civil as well as religious. The form is Hall's own contribution to English devotional writing: an observation stated, its moral drawn in a sentence or two, then a vow made in the first person. One of his earliest books, and the manner he kept for the rest of his life.

joseph-hall-modest-confutation-slanderou.blurb: The anonymous reply to Milton's Animadversions, which had itself answered Hall's defence of the Humble Remonstrance. Authorship has never been settled: it has been given to Hall, to his son Robert, and to the two working together. Milton took it as Hall's and answered it in An Apology against a Pamphlet, which is where most readers now meet it.

joseph-hall-occasionall-meditations-ios-.blurb: Short meditations struck off from ordinary sights, each headed with its occasion, upon the sight of this or that, and moving from the thing observed to a spiritual application within a page or two. This is the extemporal meditation Hall had described in The Art of Divine Meditation, here practised at length and in quantity, and the source of much of his reputation as a devotional writer.

joseph-hall-oration-pronounced-july-at-r.blurb: Not the bishop. This is a Fourth of July oration delivered at Boston in 1800 at the town's invitation by a later Joseph Hall, and printed in the ordinary way of such addresses. It sits among the works of the English divine through a collision of names, nearly a century and a half after his death, and a reader looking for the bishop should pass it by.

joseph-hall-quo-vadis-iust-censure-trave.blurb: An argument against the fashion for continental travel among English gentlemen, addressed to the parents who paid for it as much as to the young men who went. Hall grants the case for necessary voyages and denies that a tour of Catholic Europe teaches a young man anything he could not learn at home, while exposing him to religion and manners Hall thought corrupting. Written by someone who had himself been abroad in embassy.

joseph-hall-salomons-diuine-arts-ethicke.blurb: Solomon's three books taken apart and rearranged under the heads of classical practical philosophy: ethics for the government of behaviour, politics for the government of the commonwealth, economics for the government of the household. Hall's claim is that Scripture already holds the substance of what the philosophers systematised. The book is an ordering of biblical material rather than a commentary on it.

joseph-hall-sermon-preached-at-happily-r.blurb: A sermon at the reopening of a private chapel rebuilt by the Earl of Exeter, an occasion sermon of the kind a well-placed preacher was regularly called on for. Nothing in the entry indicates the text preached from or the argument taken from it.

joseph-hall-sermon-publike-thanksgiuing-.blurb: A thanksgiving sermon preached before the King for the abating of the plague that had killed heavily through the preceding year. The occasion sets the shape such sermons take: the mortality read as judgment, its mitigation read as mercy, and both pressed on hearers likely to forget the first as soon as the second arrived.

joseph-hall-survay-that-foolish-seditiou.blurb: Hall's answer to an anonymous pamphlet arguing that the Protestation then being subscribed committed those who took it against episcopacy. He denies the reading and defends the bishops' place, in the run of controversial writing that occupied him from 1640 until his imprisonment. The abuse heaped up in the title is a fair sample of the register on both sides of that quarrel.

joseph-hall-vvorks-ioseph-hall-doctor-di.blurb: The collected folio published in Hall's lifetime, while he was Dean of Worcester and before either bishopric, gathering the meditations, the contemplations, the epistles, the characters, the devotional treatises and the sermons that had appeared separately over the previous twenty years, with a table added for the whole. Over fourteen hundred pages, and the single volume in which most of Hall's early work can be found together.

dury-a-case-of-conscience-concerning-min.blurb: A case of conscience on a question the civil wars made urgent: how far a minister may speak to matters of state, whether from the pulpit or outside it. Dury handles it in the casuist's manner, stating the scruple, weighing the arguments on either side, and resolving it. Printed in 1649, the year the king was executed, which is the political weather it answers.

dury-a-demonstration-of-the-necessity-of.blurb: An argument that the churches of Christ cannot be left in the unsettled condition the Interregnum had produced, and that some form of gospel government must be agreed and put in place among them. Characteristic of Dury's lifelong effort to find a frame of order that competing Protestant parties could accept without any of them surrendering what they held essential. Printed 1654.

dury-a-memoriall-concerning-peace-eccles.blurb: A short memorial, sixteen pages, setting out the case for ecclesiastical peace among Protestants. Dury spent decades travelling the Continent and Britain on precisely this errand, and pieces like this one were the working instruments of the negotiation, drawn up to be laid before princes, divines, and assemblies whose backing he needed. Printed 1641.

dury-a-model-of-church-government-or-the.blurb: Church polity argued from the grounds of the spiritual frame and government of the house of God. Dury is less interested in vindicating one of the competing polities than in finding the principles beneath them on which men of different parties might agree. Printed in 1647, while the Westminster Assembly’s settlement was still contested.

dury-a-motion-tending-to-the-publick-goo.blurb: A proposal for the public good of the present age and of posterity, printed with copies of certain letters. Dury worked in close concert with Samuel Hartlib, and the motion belongs to that circle's habit of advancing schemes for learning, piety, and correspondence by publishing the letters that had passed about them. Printed 1642.

dury-a-peace-maker-without-partiality-an.blurb: Offered as a gospel way to make up the breaches then dividing English religion, written by a man who made peacemaking his vocation and who insisted the work be done without partiality to any party. Printed in 1648, when the fracture between Presbyterian, Independent, and sectarian was at its widest and reconciliation looked least likely.

dury-a-petition-to-the-honourable-house-.blurb: An eight page petition to the House of Commons, with further matter annexed. Dury depended on parliamentary countenance and funds for his negotiations among the Protestant churches, and petitions of this kind were how he sought them. Printed 1642. Beyond the title page little can be said here about its particular requests.

dury-a-seasonable-discourse-written-by-m.blurb: A discourse written, as the title page says, at the earnest request of many, and briefly showing what the case before them required. Twenty seven pages, printed in 1649. The occasion is the crisis of that year in English church and state, though the surviving title gives no more of the argument than that it was thought seasonable.

dury-a-summarie-account-of-mr-iohn-dury-.blurb: Dury's own summary of his earlier and later negotiations for the procuring of Protestant agreement, rendering account of what he had attempted and what had come of it. He had by 1657 been at the work for some thirty years across England, Scotland, and the German and Scandinavian courts, and the report is both a narrative and a defence of the enterprise.

dury-a-summarie-platform-of-the-heads-of.blurb: Twelve pages sketching the heads of a body of practical divinity, proposed for the ministers of the Protestant churches. Dury's ecumenical strategy leaned on agreement in the practice of godliness where agreement in speculative divinity failed, and an outline of this sort is that strategy reduced to a table of contents. Printed 1654.

dury-a-summary-discourse-concerning-the-.blurb: On the work of ecclesiastical peace and how it may run together with the aims of those whose support Dury was seeking. The argument is the one he made everywhere, that Protestant reconciliation serves the interests of the powers asked to sponsor it, set out here at some length rather than in the brief memorial form. Printed 1641.

dury-an-epistolary-discourse-wherein-amo.blurb: A discourse in letter form which, among other particulars, takes up and briefly resolves a set of stated questions. Much of Dury's output began as correspondence and reached print in that shape, so the epistolary frame here is method rather than affectation. Printed 1644, during the sitting of the Westminster Assembly.

dury-certaine-considerations-shewing-the.blurb: An argument that the Protestant churches must maintain a standing correspondence with one another in spiritual matters. Dury treated regular communication, letters, agents, shared intelligence, as the practical substratum of any eventual union, and this short piece of 1642 makes the case for the correspondence itself rather than for a doctrinal settlement.

dury-conscience-eased-or-the-main-scrupl.blurb: Addressed to the chief scruple that had kept conscientious men from subscribing the Engagement to the Commonwealth. Dury took the side of subscription and wrote repeatedly in its defence between 1649 and 1651, arguing that fidelity to the present government did not require approving how it came to be. Printed 1651.

dury-considerations-concerning-the-prese.blurb: On whether the Engagement, the promise of fidelity to the Commonwealth as governed without king or House of Lords, could lawfully be taken. Dury argued for taking it, and the position cost him with those who held earlier oaths still binding. One of several pieces he wrote on the question in 1649 and 1650.

dury-good-counsells-for-the-peace-of-ref.blurb: A collection of counsels for the peace of the reformed churches, gathered from bishops and other divines and put into English. Dury's method was frequently to let respected authorities on several sides speak for moderation in their own words, so that the plea for peace would not rest on his credit alone. Printed 1641.

dury-gospel-communion-in-the-way-of-godl.blurb: The Protestant churches in Germany applying to the churches of Great Britain for communion in the way of godliness. Dury acted as the channel between the two, and this brief piece of 1654 carries the Continental request into English print, seeking practical fellowship rather than a negotiated confession.

dury-israels-call-to-march-out-of-babylo.blurb: A sermon preached before the House of Commons, taking Israel's departure from Babylon toward Jerusalem as the figure for what Dury thought England was called to do in religion. Fast sermons before Parliament were a public office as much as a homily, and this one puts his reforming and reconciling programme before the men who could fund it. Printed 1646.

dury-john-dury-his-petition-to-the-honou.blurb: Three pages, a petition addressed to the Commons assembled in Parliament and printed in 1641. Dury's Protestant peace negotiation ran on official countenance and money, both of which had to be asked for repeatedly. The title is very nearly all the document announces of itself.

dury-just-re-proposals-to-humble-proposa.blurb: An impartial consideration of, and answer to, a set of humble proposals then before the public. The counter-proposal was a standard form of Interregnum debate about how religion should be settled and ministers maintained, and Dury enters it here in his usual posture, weighing the other side's terms before offering his own. Printed 1650.

dury-madam-although-my-former-freedom-in.blurb: A letter to a lady, opening with an apology for the freedom of his earlier writing to her, printed as a short pamphlet of eight pages in 1645. It belongs with the companion piece of the same year in which Dury writes of his resolution to marry. What is here is a private correspondence that reached print; the title supplies the occasion and no more.

dury-madam-ever-since-i-had-a-resolution.blurb: A letter to a lady concerning his resolution to change his life by marriage, printed in 1645 in seven pages. It stands with the companion letter of the same year, and readers have generally taken the pair together as a courtship correspondence conducted in the idiom of vocation and providence rather than of romance.

dury-motives-to-induce-the-protestant-pr.blurb: Eleven pages of motives addressed to the Protestant princes, urging them to attend to the work of ecclesiastical peace among themselves. Dury's negotiations depended on secular patrons in Germany, Scandinavia, and Britain, and this is the argument he put to them: that Protestant division was a political liability as well as a scandal. Printed 1641.

dury-objections-against-the-taking-of-th.blurb: An answer to scruples of conscience raised against subscribing the Engagement to the Commonwealth. Dury defended taking it, treating the objections one by one in the casuistical style, and returned to the question in more than one pamphlet around 1650. The controversy divided men who had been allies in the war.

dury-the-copy-of-a-letter-written-to-mr-.blurb: A letter to Alexander Henderson, the Scottish minister who was the principal architect of the Covenanting settlement and a leading figure at the Westminster Assembly. Dury, himself a Scot, needed Scottish goodwill for his Protestant peace project, and correspondence with Henderson was the natural route to it. Printed 1643.

dury-the-earnest-breathings-of-forreign-.blurb: Foreign Protestant divines and others appealing to the ministers and other able Christians of these nations. Dury spent his life carrying such appeals in both directions, and here the Continental churches address England directly. Printed 1658, when the Protectorate still made English support of foreign Protestants a live prospect.

dury-the-effect-of-master-dury-s-negotia.blurb: Seven pages briefly stating what his negotiation for the uniting of Protestants in a gospel interest had actually effected. A companion in substance to the fuller account he published the same year, 1657, and written for readers who wanted the result without the history.

dury-the-interest-of-england-in-the-prot.blurb: An argument that England's own interest is bound up with the Protestant cause abroad, printed in 1659 as the Protectorate collapsed and the shape of the next government was uncertain. Dury habitually pressed the case for foreign Protestantism in terms of national advantage as well as religious duty, since the men he needed to persuade thought in those terms.

dury-the-plain-way-of-peace-and-unity-in.blurb: Thirteen pages reducing his lifelong argument to a set of maxims he supposed no party would deny, from which the way to peace and unity in religion is then drawn. Printed in 1660, the year of the Restoration, when the settlement of English religion was again open and Dury was again making the case that had occupied him for three decades.

dury-the-reformed-librarie-keeper-with-a.blurb: An argument that a library keeper is not a doorkeeper set to guard books but an agent for the advancement of learning, charged with knowing what the collection holds, making it useful to scholars, and trading in knowledge with keepers elsewhere. Dury had charge of the royal library, and writes from the desk. Issued with a supplement to his Reformed School.

dury-the-reformed-school-by-john-dury.blurb: A plan of education from the Hartlib circle, setting out how a school should be ordered, what should be taught, in what sequence, and to what end. The end is not learning for its own sake but the forming of children in piety and useful knowledge, and the scheme is meant to be executed rather than admired. Printed 1649.

dury-the-revelation-reveled-by-two-apoca.blurb: Two treatises on the Apocalypse, the first arguing how near the period of the prophesied time then stood. This is the least familiar side of Dury, who is remembered for irenic negotiation rather than prophecy, though the two went together in his circle: the expectation of an approaching end gave the labour for Protestant union its urgency. Printed 1651.

dury-two-treatises-concerning-the-matter.blurb: Two treatises on the Engagement bound together, the first by an unnamed author objecting to it, the second answering him. Printing the opposing case alongside the reply was Dury's usual practice, and here it lets a reader watch the argument over subscription to the Commonwealth conducted on both sides. Printed 1650.

wallis-a-defence-of-the-royal-society-an.blurb: A defence of the Royal Society and its Philosophical Transactions, occasioned by a quarrel with William Holder over which of them had taught a deaf man to speak. Wallis had published his method of teaching the deaf, Holder claimed the credit, and the dispute drew in the Society because its Transactions had printed Wallis. Sharp and personal, as his controversies generally were.

wallis-a-defense-of-the-christian-sabbat.blurb: An answer to Thomas Bampfield, who had argued that the seventh day, Saturday, remains the sabbath binding on Christians. Wallis defends the observance of the first day, working through the scriptural and patristic grounds for the change. The seventh day question was a live one among English dissenters, and Bampfield was among its most persistent advocates. Printed 1692.

wallis-a-discourse-of-gravity-and-gravit.blurb: A discourse on gravity and gravitation grounded on experimental observation, presented to the Royal Society. This is Wallis the mathematician and natural philosopher rather than the divine, working in the decade before Newton's Principia on the same questions of weight, descent, and the centre of gravity. Printed 1675.

wallis-a-fifth-letter-concerning-the-sac.blurb: The fifth of the series of letters Wallis wrote in the Trinitarian controversy of the early 1690s, answering a piece put out as the Arian's vindication of himself against the fourth letter. The exchange ran letter for letter with anonymous Unitarian opponents, each printing against the last. Printed 1691.

wallis-a-fourth-letter-concerning-the-sa.blurb: The fourth letter in Wallis's Trinitarian series, replying to a published answer to his first three. The controversy of the 1690s turned on whether the doctrine of three persons in one God could be stated without contradiction, and Wallis's method throughout is to press the charge of unintelligibility back on his opponents. Printed 1691.

wallis-a-proposal-about-printing-a-treat.blurb: A four page proposal soliciting support for the printing of his Treatise of Algebra, historical and practical. Books of that bulk were often financed by subscription got up in advance, and this is the advertisement for it, describing what the projected work would contain. Of interest chiefly as a document of how a mathematical book reached the press in 1683.

wallis-a-second-letter-concerning-the-ho.blurb: The second of Wallis's letters on the Trinity, written to the same correspondent as the first and occasioned by objections raised against it. Fourteen pages, printed 1691. He had begun the series with a short explanation of the doctrine for a friend, and the objections kept coming until the letters numbered eight.

wallis-a-seventh-letter-concerning-the-s.blurb: The seventh letter of the Trinitarian series, occasioned by a second letter from the writer who signed himself W. J. By this point the exchange had become a running debate conducted in print between named and anonymous parties, each answering the last piece as it appeared. Printed 1691.

wallis-a-sixth-letter-concerning-the-sac.blurb: The sixth letter, answering a book of observations published against the four letters that preceded it. Wallis was in his seventies and Savilian professor at Oxford when he took up the Trinitarian controversy, and he prosecuted it with the same persistence he had shown against Hobbes forty years earlier. Printed 1691.

wallis-a-treatise-of-angular-sections-by.blurb: Mathematics, not divinity: a treatise on the section of angles, that is, the division of an angle into equal parts and the algebraic relations that follow from it. The problem connects trigonometry with the theory of equations, and Wallis had worked on it long before it saw print in 1684.

wallis-an-answer-to-three-papers-of-mr-h.blurb: Two pages answering three papers Hobbes had published in August and September of that year. Wallis and Hobbes quarrelled in print for a quarter of a century over the squaring of the circle, the foundations of geometry, and each other's competence, and this is one of the later brief exchanges in that long war. Printed 1671.

wallis-an-eighth-letter-concerning-the-s.blurb: The last of the eight letters on the Trinity, prompted by further correspondence on the subject. Printed 1692, after which Wallis gathered the letters with his sermons on the same doctrine. Twenty two pages closing an exchange that had run for something over two years.

wallis-an-explication-and-vindication-of.blurb: The third letter of the Trinitarian series, given over to the Athanasian Creed, whose damnatory clauses and technical vocabulary were a standing target for Unitarian writers. Wallis explains the creed's terms and defends its language as saying no more than Scripture requires. The longest of the letters at seventy pages. Printed 1691.

wallis-cono-cuneus-or-the-shipwright-s-c.blurb: A geometrical study of a solid that is part cone and part wedge, which shipwrights used and which Wallis treats analytically, deriving its sections and their properties. Pure mathematics arising from a craftsman's shape, and a good example of how Wallis moved between practical geometry and the algebra of curves. Printed 1684.

wallis-due-correction-for-mr-hobbes-or-s.blurb: Wallis's reply to Hobbes's Six Lessons, delivered under the conceit that the philosopher is a schoolboy who has not said his lessons right. Behind the mockery lies a serious charge, that Hobbes did not understand the mathematics he was attacking. One of the sharpest documents in the long quarrel between them. Printed 1656.

wallis-on-the-sad-losse-of-the-truly-hon.blurb: An elegy on the death of Robert Greville, Lord Brooke, addressed to his widow. Brooke was a leading parliamentarian peer and a writer whose book on truth Wallis had answered in print the same year, 1643. Eight pages of occasional verse from a man remembered for geometry rather than poetry.

wallis-reasons-shewing-the-consistency-o.blurb: A single sheet arguing that the office of Custos Archivorum, keeper of the university archives, may lawfully be held together with a Savilian professorship. Wallis held both and was defending his own position against the objection that the two were incompatible. A small document of Oxford institutional politics, printed 1658.

wallis-the-doctrine-of-the-blessed-trini.blurb: The first of the letters that grew into Wallis's long defence of the Trinity, written to a friend and offered as a brief explanation rather than a controversy. It is the letter containing his much repeated comparison of the one cube with its length, breadth, and height, an analogy his opponents attacked and his defenders quoted for a century. Printed 1690.

wallis-the-life-of-faith-in-two-sermons-.blurb: Two university sermons preached at St Mary's, Oxford, on the life of faith. Wallis held the Savilian chair of geometry for over half a century but was ordained and had served as a scribe to the Westminster Assembly, and he preached before the university throughout. Printed 1684.

wallis-the-necessity-of-regeneration-in-.blurb: Two sermons preached before the University of Oxford on the necessity of the new birth, printed in 1682. The doctrine is standard Reformed teaching on regeneration; what a reader may find of interest is hearing it from the professor of geometry, in the pulpit rather than the lecture room.

wallis-the-resurrection-asserted-in-a-se.blurb: An Easter sermon preached before the University of Oxford in 1679, asserting the resurrection. Wallis's university sermons take a doctrine under dispute or under strain and argue it in an orderly way, and this one falls in the years when the credibility of the article was being pressed by writers he elsewhere answered at length.

wallis-theological-discourses-in-two-par.blurb: The collected theological writings, gathered in two parts, the first containing the eight letters and three sermons on the Trinity that Wallis had published separately in the early 1690s. Anyone wanting the whole Trinitarian series in one place rather than as a run of pamphlets will want this. Printed 1695.

wallis-three-sermons-concerning-the-sacr.blurb: The preached counterpart to the letters Wallis was publishing in the same controversy, three sermons stating the doctrine of the Trinity positively and at length.
