A sermon let him lay out the article on his own terms, where the letters were bound to the shape of whatever tract had last appeared against him. Printed 1691.

wallis-truth-tried-or-animadversions-on-.blurb: Animadversions on The Nature of Truth by Robert Greville, Lord Brooke, examining the peer's Platonizing account of truth and light and answering it point by point. Wallis was then a young minister, and this is his earliest substantial book, published in 1643, some years before he was made Savilian professor of geometry.

walker-a-brotherly-and-friendly-censure-.blurb: Twelve pages correcting the error of a man the author calls a dear friend and brother, the courtesy of the title being the usual form for controversy conducted within one's own party. Printed 1645. The friend is not named on the title page, and nothing further about the disputed point can be said here with confidence.

walker-a-defence-of-the-true-sence-and-m.blurb: An exegetical defence of Romans 4, verses 3, 5, and 9, the verses on Abraham's faith being counted to him for righteousness. Everything in the seventeenth century debate over justification turned on how that counting was construed, and Walker, a London minister who spent years disputing the point, argues for imputed righteousness against readings that made faith itself the thing accepted.

walker-a-modell-of-the-government-of-the.blurb: A scriptural case for the government of the church by presbyters, printed in 1646 while the Westminster Assembly's presbyterian settlement was before Parliament and contested by Independents on one side and Erastians on the other. The London divine of that name sat in the Assembly, which is the setting this short model belongs to.

walker-a-new-letter-from-london-derry-gi.blurb: A two page newsletter reporting further success obtained by the Protestant forces at Londonderry. It belongs to the very different George Walker who was joint governor of the city during the siege of 1689 and whose several accounts of it were rushed into London print while the war in Ireland was still being fought.

walker-a-sermon-being-an-incouragement-f.blurb: A sermon of encouragement to Protestants, holding out the prospect of success and exhorting them accordingly. Printed in 1689 and connected with the defence of Londonderry, where the George Walker of the siege preached to the besieged garrison. Another issue of the same sermon appeared under the title The substance of a sermon.

walker-a-sermon-preached-in-london-by-a-.blurb: A sermon preached in London and afterwards perfected by its author for the press, published anonymously in 1642 as the work of a faithful minister of Christ. The reticence of the title page was common in that year. Beyond the occasion, London in the first months of the civil war, the title tells a reader nothing of the text or the argument.

walker-a-true-account-of-the-present-sta.blurb: A report on the state of Ireland and the new establishment made there, printed in London in 1689 for readers following the war between the Jacobite and Williamite causes. It is attributed to the George Walker associated with the defence of Londonderry, though pamphlets of this kind were freely ascribed to whichever name would sell them.

walker-a-true-account-of-the-siege-of-lo.blurb: The governor's own narrative of the siege of Londonderry, written by the Church of Ireland clergyman who shared command of the city through the blockade of 1689 and published within months of its relief. It is the best known account of the siege and also the most disputed, since other survivors thought Walker had given himself too large a part.

walker-a-trve-relation-of-the-chiefe-pas.blurb: Walker's account of the chief passages between himself and Anthony Wotton, the London minister he had accused of Socinian error in the doctrine of justification. The quarrel occupied both men and their friends for years and was referred to arbitrators, and this relation, printed in 1642, is Walker's version of how it proceeded.

walker-a-vindication-of-the-true-account.blurb: A defence of his own account of the siege of Derry against the objections it had drawn. Walker's narrative was challenged almost at once by other participants who thought his share of the credit overstated and the Presbyterian contribution slighted, and this 1689 pamphlet answers them.

walker-an-exhortation-to-his-dearely-bel.blurb: An exhortation addressed to the natives of Lancashire, the county of the author's birth, printed in 1641. Lancashire retained a larger Catholic population than most English counties, and appeals from a minister to his countrymen there commonly had that circumstance in view, though the title alone does not settle what this one urges.

walker-anglo-tyrannus-or-the-idea-of-a-n.blurb: A republican tract setting the reign of Henry the Third beside a later king to argue that English monarchy since the Conquest has been a Norman tyranny imposed on a free people. The Norman yoke was a standard weapon of Commonwealth polemic. Printed 1650, and the George Walker named as author is not to be identified with the Puritan divine without further evidence.

walker-fishers-folly-unfolded-or-the-vau.blurb: An attack on the Jesuit who went by the name Fisher, John Percy, who had issued a challenge to Protestant ministers and disputed publicly with several of them in the 1620s. Walker took up the challenge and here exposes what he takes to be the vanity of it. Printed 1624, and a companion to his account of their disputation the same year.

walker-god-made-visible-in-his-workes-or.blurb: A short treatise on the external works of God, treating them first in general before descending to particulars, on the principle that the invisible God is known through what he has made. Printed 1641. It stands close in subject to the same author's much longer exposition of the creation narrative.

walker-socinianisme-in-the-fundamentall-.blurb: A long refutation, some three hundred and sixty pages, of what Walker judged to be Socinian doctrine in the article of justification, framed as an answer to a particular writing. The charge grew out of his running dispute with Anthony Wotton and his followers over whether faith is imputed for righteousness or Christ's righteousness is imputed to faith. Printed 1641.

walker-the-christian-champion-being-the-.blurb: The substance of a second discourse delivered to the soldiers besieged in Londonderry, printed in 1689. Preaching to a starving garrison under blockade is an unusual homiletic occasion, and the pamphlet preserves what the governor and clergyman told them, published in London while the outcome of the Irish war was still open.

walker-the-doctrine-of-the-sabbath-where.blurb: A treatise on the sabbath, beginning with its first institution as a weekly ordinance and the time of that institution, then working forward. Printed in 1638, when sabbath observance was among the sharpest points of division between Laudian churchmen and their Puritan opponents, and Walker writes from the Puritan side of it.

walker-the-history-of-the-creation-as-it.blurb: An extended exposition of the first two chapters of Genesis, taking the six days in order and drawing doctrine from each. Three hundred pages on two chapters gives the measure of the method, which is the ordinary Puritan practice of expounding a text clause by clause and applying it. Printed 1641.

walker-the-key-of-saving-knovvledge-open.blurb: A treatise opening from Scripture what the author calls the right way and straight passage to salvation, in the manner of the Puritan handbooks that set out the order of conversion for readers examining their own state. Printed 1641. The title supplies the design; the particular scheme of doctrine it follows is not evident from it.

walker-the-manifold-vvisedome-of-god-in-.blurb: On the diverse dispensations of grace by Jesus Christ under the Old Testament and the New, the standard Reformed question of how the covenant of grace is one while its administrations differ. Walker's title takes its phrase from Ephesians. Printed 1641, when covenant theology was the common frame of English divinity.

walker-the-protestant-s-crums-of-comfort.blurb: A devotional manual of prayers and meditations with ejaculations for daily use, in the tradition of the small pocket books of comfort that sold steadily through the century. Printed 1690, with the Protestant framing of a book issued in the years of the Williamite settlement. Attribution to a George Walker is what the title page gives.

walker-the-substance-of-a-sermon-being-a.blurb: The substance of a sermon encouraging Protestants with the prospect of success, from the defence of Londonderry in 1689. It is the same discourse issued elsewhere simply as A sermon being an incouragement for Protestants, one of the several forms in which siege pamphlets were reprinted for the London trade.

walker-the-svmme-of-a-dispvtation-betwee.blurb: The record of a disputation between Walker, pastor of St John the Evangelist in Watling Street, London, and a Jesuit opponent. Set public debates between Protestant ministers and Roman priests were a recognised genre in the 1620s, and both sides regularly printed their own account of who had prevailed. Printed 1624.

baxter-account-to-kidderminster.blurb: Baxter's explanation, in 1662, to the parish he had served for the better part of two decades of why their pulpit was now closed to him and by what authority he had been forbidden to preach in the diocese. He rehearses the terms he had offered, the refusals he met, and the grounds on which conscience would not let him conform, and takes his leave of a congregation he never ceased to count his own.

baxter-breviate-life-margaret-daughter-f.blurb: A memoir of his wife, Margaret Charlton, written soon after her death in 1681 and printed while the grief was still fresh. Baxter gives her family and upbringing, the illness and the conversion that ran together in her, her part in his ministry, and their marriage under the penal laws, and prints papers in her own hand at the end. He is candid about her fears and about his own hardness toward them.

baxter-catholick-communion-defended-agai.blurb: A defence in five parts, from 1684, of Baxter's practice of communicating with the parish churches while remaining a nonconformist. The two extremes are the strict conformist who unchurches the dissenters and the separatist who unchurches the parish assemblies; against both he argues that unnecessary division is itself a sin, and sets out what lawful communion with a faulty church requires and what it does not.

baxter-catholick-communion-doubly-defend.blurb: A short rejoinder of 1684 in the same quarrel, occasioned by a writer vindicating John Owen. Baxter restates the terms on which he holds communion with the parish churches and tries to fix the state of the question between himself and the Independents. Thirty-seven pages of controversy that presuppose the fuller argument he had made in Catholick Communion Defended.

baxter-catholick-theologie.blurb: An attempt to end the quarrel over grace and free will by showing how much of it is a war about words. Cast largely as dialogue, it works through the disputes on predestination, the extent of redemption, the operation of grace and the liberty of the will, distinguishing at each point the real difference from the verbal one, and ranging over Dominican, Jesuit, Arminian and Calvinist positions alike. Long, taxonomic, and written by a man every party had accused.

baxter-catholick-vnity-only-way-bring-us.blurb: Printed in 1660 while the church settlement was still open, an argument that the only ground on which Englishmen will ever be of one religion is the plain Christianity common to them all, held as necessary with the rest left free. Baxter presses the case against the parties on either hand and describes what a comprehending church would have to concede in order to be one.

baxter-confession-of-his-faith.blurb: Baxter's own account of his doctrine, drawn up after his Aphorismes of Justification had drawn charges of unsoundness from Reformed readers. The disputed point is the interest of repentance and sincere obedience in justification, and he states his position at length, with testimonies from others set alongside. A large and defensive book, and the fullest early statement of the scheme his critics would afterwards call Baxterianism.

baxter-dangerous-schismatick-clearly-det.blurb: A pamphlet of 1683 in the Restoration quarrel over separation from the parish churches, promising in its title the detection and confutation of a schismatic and the saving of a distracted nation from him. Who is confuted, and by which hand, the record does not settle; the piece belongs to exchanges in which Baxter stood on both the giving and the receiving side. Little more can be said from sixty-two pages and a title.

baxter-directions-to-slave-holders.blurb: A chapter of Baxter's Christian Directory of 1673, lifted out and reprinted on its own in 1785 with further matter added. The original directions were addressed to masters in the foreign plantations who held slaves, and treat those slaves as men with souls, owed instruction, rest and the prospect of liberty, with hard words for those who catch and sell them. A short pamphlet, revived more than a century later for a different argument.

baxter-full-easie-satisfaction-which-is-.blurb: A conference in which a doubter, a papist and other voices press the question of which religion is true and which is safe, and Baxter answers for a reformed Christianity resting on what all Christians confess. The dialogue form lets him meet the convert-making arguments of Rome and the objections of unbelief in the order a troubled reader actually meets them.

baxter-grand-debate-between-most-reveren.blurb: The papers of the Savoy Conference of 1661, at which bishops and Presbyterian divines were commissioned to consider the revision of the Book of Common Prayer. Printed here are the exceptions taken against the liturgy, the bishops' answers, and the rejoinders that followed. Baxter was the chief hand on the Presbyterian side, and the documents show both what the ministers would have accepted and how little of it was granted.

baxter-how-far-holinesse-is-design-chris.blurb: A brief treatise of 1671 on the place of holiness in the Christian religion, opening what holiness and what morality are and how the two stand to one another. Baxter's practical divinity turned constantly on this question, and against readers who set the moral and the evangelical at odds he argues that sanctity is the end for which the gospel was given. Twenty-five pages, stating a position rather than defending it at length.

baxter-immortality-mans-soul-nature-it-o.blurb: Two discourses of 1682 on the immortality of the human soul and the nature of spirits, one of them cast as a letter. Baxter argues against the materialism that would let the soul perish with the body, and takes up what may be said of the substance and operations of spirits, human and other. The subject held him to the end of his life.

baxter-mr-baxter-s-judgment-reasons-agai.blurb: Forty pages printed in 1684 under Baxter's name, giving reasons against communicating with the parish assemblies as the law required. His own settled judgment, argued at length that same year in Catholick Communion Defended, was for such communion where conscience allowed it. A reader should hold the two together and ask what part of his writing this collection represents and who saw it into print.

baxter-mr-baxters-rules-directions-famil.blurb: A single sheet of rules for the duties of a Christian household, showing how each member ought to behave in his place. The matter is the family divinity Baxter treats at length elsewhere, cut down here to something a family could keep by them or fix to a wall. Three pages, and to be read as an abstract rather than an argument.

baxter-notes-on-life-of-matthew-hale.blurb: Additional notes on the life and death of Sir Matthew Hale, the judge, appended to the printed life of him. Baxter had been Hale's neighbour and friend at Acton and adds what he could report at first hand of his character, his religion and his conversation. A short piece, valuable chiefly as the testimony of a nonconformist minister about a conforming lawyer he admired without reserve.

baxter-sermon-iudgement-preached-at-paul.blurb: A sermon on the day of judgment preached at Paul's before the Lord Mayor and aldermen of London and printed in 1655. The three hundred pages of the volume indicate that a good deal more was bound with the sermon itself. Baxter preaching to magistrates about the account they must one day give, which was his standing manner with men in office.

baxter-sermon-preached-at-funeral-that-f.blurb: A funeral sermon of 1680 for John Corbet, the ejected minister, printed with Corbet's own account of himself annexed. The sermon does the ordinary work of the genre; the appended papers do the rest, giving a nonconformist's reckoning of his own conscience in his own words. Forty pages, and read now more for the second part than the first.

baxter-sober-useful-reflections-treatise.blurb: Not by Baxter but against him: reflections upon his Sacrilegious Desertion of the Holy Ministry, the tract in which he had rebuked ministers who abandoned their charges rather than face the penalties of preaching. The reply takes up his argument in order and returns it. Printed in 1680, and catalogued with his works because it cannot be read apart from them.

baxter-three-treatises-tending-awaken-se.blurb: Three practical treatises bound together in 1656, aimed not at the doubting Christian but at the settled and untroubled sinner who has never thought his case dangerous. Rousing the secure was Baxter's steadiest theme in the Kidderminster years, and the volume belongs beside his Call to the Unconverted, with the same directness and the same refusal to let a reader put the question off.

baxter-two-papers-proposals-concerning-d.blurb: Twenty-four pages of proposals on discipline and ceremonies, presented to the king in 1661 by the Presbyterian divines at the Savoy Conference. They ask for the terms on which the ministers might conform: relief in the ceremonies, a working discipline in the parishes, an amended liturgy. Baxter had the chief hand in drafting them, and they record the settlement that was asked for and did not come.

baxter-two-treatises-first-death-on-i.blurb: Two treatises of 1672, the first on death from the last enemy of 1 Corinthians 15, the second on judgment from the appearing before the tribunal of Christ in 2 Corinthians 5. Both are handled in the plain doctrinal and applicatory order of the pulpit, and both belong to the vein of Baxter's writing that runs from the Saints' Everlasting Rest onward.

perkins-c-e-treatise-manner-order-predes.blurb: The English version of Perkins's Latin treatise on the manner and order of predestination and the largeness of God's grace. It defends a high account of the decree, ordering the causes of salvation and damnation, against Lutheran and free-will objections, and argues that the doctrine leaves God clear of the authorship of sin and the reprobate without excuse. Arminius wrote his examination in answer to this treatise, which is much of the reason it is still read.

perkins-case-conscience-greatest-taht-eu.blurb: The question is assurance: how a man may know whether or not he is a son of God. Perkins resolves it out of the First Epistle of John, laying down the marks by which saving grace may be discerned in someone who cannot find it by feeling, and answering in turn the objections a distressed conscience raises against every one of them. His casuistry at work on its hardest case.

perkins-christian-oeconomie-short-survey.blurb: A treatise on the ordering of a household, translated out of Perkins's Latin. It takes marriage first, the contract, the choice of a spouse and the duties of husband and wife, then parents and children, then masters and servants, resolving as it goes the cases that arise: what makes a marriage, what may dissolve one, how far obedience is owed and where it stops. Domestic ethics on the same method as his cases of conscience.

perkins-cloud-faithfull-witnesses-leadin.blurb: A commentary on the eleventh chapter of Hebrews, from lectures given at Cambridge and printed after Perkins's death. The nature of faith is opened from the definition at the head of the chapter, and the roll of witnesses is then taken example by example, each applied to the reader's own case. Six hundred pages on a single chapter, which is a fair measure of how he lectured.

perkins-combat-betvveene-christ-diuell-d.blurb: A short commentary, delivered from the pulpit, on the temptation of Christ in the wilderness. Perkins takes the three assaults in order, draws from each the devil's method and the force of Christ's answer, and turns both to the use of the tempted believer. Seventy pages, over the same ground he covers at greater length in the sermons printed as Satan's Sophistry Answered.

perkins-commentarie-exposition-fiue-firs.blurb: A commentary on the first five chapters of Galatians, taken from Perkins's Cambridge lectures and published after his death. It is doctrinal rather than philological, working verse by verse to doctrine and then to use, with the controversy with Rome over justification seldom far from the surface. The exposition breaks off at the end of the fifth chapter and was completed by another hand.

perkins-faithfull-plaine-exposition-chap.blurb: An exposition of the second chapter of Zephaniah, printed after Perkins's death from his preaching. The text is the prophet's call to gather and to seek the Lord before the day of wrath comes, and the treatment is the ordinary sermon method of doctrine and application. It stands close to the two sermons on Zephaniah printed separately as an exhortation to repentance.

perkins-first-part-cases-conscience-spec.blurb: The first book of Perkins's casuistry, on man considered simply in himself, before his callings and his dealings with other men. Three questions govern it: how a man may come to be in God's favour, how he may be certain that he is, and how, having lost the sense of it, he may recover. The method is scholastic and the intended use pastoral, for ministers resolving troubled consciences one at a time.

perkins-foure-great-lyers-striuing-who-s.blurb: A satire against the makers of almanacs, four of whom are set to contend for the silver whetstone awarded to the best liar, with a plain resolution to the countryman appended proving it unlawful to buy or use the yearly prognostications. Astrological prediction is the target throughout: not the calendar or the weather sign, but the claim to read a man's fortune and his death out of the stars.

perkins-garden-spirituall-flowers-plante.blurb: A devotional collection gathered from several hands, Richard Rogers and Richard Greenham and George Webbe among them, with Perkins's contribution the reason it is shelved under his name. It offers meditations, rules for the daily walk with God, prayers and directions for self-examination. Compilations of this kind were the ordinary devotional reading of English Protestant households, and were reprinted in varying arrangements.

perkins-godlie-learned-exposition-whole-.blurb: An exposition of the whole epistle of Jude in sixty-six sermons, preached and then printed after Perkins's death. Jude's short letter against the ungodly who creep in unawares is taken clause by clause, at better than two sermons to a verse. The method is the doctrine-and-use preaching he set out formally in his treatise on the art of prophesying.

perkins-godly-learned-exposition-comment.blurb: Perkins on the opening of the Revelation, from lectures given at Cambridge and printed after his death: the vision of Christ among the candlesticks and the letters to the seven churches. He reads the chapters as Christ's judgment of particular congregations and applies them to the English church and to the individual conscience, not as a key to unlock the prophecies that follow. The same course of lectures was printed under other titles, and the issues differ in length.

perkins-graine-musterd-seede-least-measu.blurb: Propositions on the least measure of grace that can be effectual to salvation, written for the Christian who can find in himself no more than a desire to believe. Perkins argues that a will to repent, where God has given it, is grace already begun and carries the promise with it. The pastoral counterweight to his doctrine of election, and short by design.

perkins-hepie-keia-treatise-christian-eq.blurb: A treatise on epieikeia, the equity that moderates the rigour of the law, delivered as public lectures. Perkins distinguishes public equity, which belongs to the magistrate and the judge in mitigating the letter of a law to reach its intent, from private equity, the moderation a man owes his neighbour in bearing wrongs and construing offences. The term is taken from Aristotle and put to Christian use.

perkins-how-liue-that-well-all-estates.blurb: Directions for living well in every estate and season, and particularly when the ordinary helps and comforts fail. Perkins writes for the Christian in want, in sickness, in disgrace or alone, and sets out what remains to such a person when the usual means of comfort have been taken away. Practical divinity of the plainest kind, and brief.

perkins-lectures-three-first-chapters-re.blurb: The Cambridge lectures of 1595 on the first three chapters of the Revelation, printed here in the fuller of the surviving forms. The date on the title page places it: Perkins in the lecture room, opening the vision of Christ among the candlesticks and the letters to the seven churches. This is the same course that appears elsewhere as a godly and learned exposition, and the two printings are better compared than read in succession.

perkins-m-perkins-exhortation-repentance.blurb: Two sermons preached at Sturbridge Fair, the great annual market outside Cambridge, calling that crowd to repentance out of Zephaniah. Other pieces are bound with them, the volume running well beyond the two sermons named. Perkins preaching to a general audience rather than to the university, which makes it a useful specimen of what his plain style sounded like away from the schools.

perkins-prophetica-sive-de-sacra-et-vnic.blurb: The Latin treatise on preaching that appeared in English as The Art of Prophesying. Perkins sets out the whole method: the interpretation of a text by Scripture and context, the drawing out of doctrine, the resolution of doctrine into use, and the application of the word to the several sorts of hearers, from the ignorant and unteachable to the humbled and the fallen back. It closes with memory and delivery, and prefers the plain style to the ornamented one throughout.

perkins-reformation-couetousnesse-writte.blurb: An exposition of the close of Matthew 6, from the command against laying up treasure on earth to the end of the chapter, preached against covetousness. Perkins treats the sin as a settled disorder of the heart rather than an occasional act, opens the promise about the birds and the lilies against anxious providing, and applies the whole to trade, to hoarding and to the care of the poor.

perkins-satans-sophistrie-ansuuered-our-.blurb: Sermons on the temptation of Christ, taking the devil's arguments as sophistry to be answered rather than force to be resisted. Perkins shows how each temptation is framed, what Scripture is abused in the framing, and how Christ's reply refutes it, then turns the same pattern on the suggestions a Christian meets in his own case. Further sermons are printed with them.

perkins-treatise-tending-vnto-declaratio.blurb: An early treatise on the two estates, damnation and grace, and how a man may tell which is his. It works through the causes of salvation and of damnation in order, the scheme Perkins drew as a table and expounded at length in his Golden Chain, and turns it to the diagnostic use that occupied him ever after: the marks of a work of grace begun, and the signs of a heart still unchanged.

perkins-tvvo-treatises-i-nature-practise.blurb: Two short treatises, the first on the nature and practice of repentance, the second on the combat between the flesh and the spirit. The first defines repentance as a settled turning rather than a passing sorrow and gives the practice of it; the second takes up the war described in Romans 7 and Galatians 5, and what a Christian may conclude from finding himself in that fight at all.

hammond-alien-al-theuein-brief-account-o.blurb: Nine pages answering a single suggestion made by a Roman controversialist against Hammond's own Dispatcher Dispatched, itself one stage of the long exchange begun by his book Of Schisme. The Greek of the title turns on speaking the truth. A note rather than a treatise, and unintelligible apart from the books on either side of it.

hammond-ansvver-animadversions-on-disser.blurb: A defence of Hammond's dissertations on the epistles of Ignatius against animadversions made upon them. The genuineness of the Ignatian letters was not an antiquarian matter in 1654: if the letters are what they claim, episcopacy is apostolic, and Hammond had argued so against the continental critics who rejected them. Here he answers the reply, on the text, the manuscripts, and what the epistles say about bishops.

hammond-baptizing-infants-revievved-defe.blurb: A defence of infant baptism against John Tombes, the ablest of the English antipaedobaptists, answering the last three chapters of his book. The argument runs on the covenant and its seal, the practice of the primitive church, and the disputed texts, carried through with the philological care that marks all of Hammond's controversial writing.

hammond-charis-kai-eir-n-pacifick-discou.blurb: Grace and peace, in the words of the Greek title, and the matter is God's grace and his decrees, treated pacifically and cast as a letter of full accordance with its recipient. Hammond argues for a universal redemption and a conditional decree against the higher Calvinist account, and does it as an offer of concord rather than a refutation. Printed in 1660, when such offers were being made on every side.

hammond-deuterai-phrontides-review-parap.blurb: Second thoughts, as the Greek title has it: a review of Hammond's paraphrase and annotations on the New Testament, occasioned by objections taken to the first edition. He returns to the disputed places, defends his readings of the Greek, his account of the heretics named in the epistles and his account of apostolic church order, and revises where he judged the objection just.

hammond-ektenesteron-degrees-ardency-chr.blurb: A short piece on the word at Luke 22:44, that Christ in his agony prayed more earnestly, and how degrees of ardency in his prayer may be reconciled with the fulness of habitual grace in him. A question in Christology approached, as Hammond approaches most questions, through the exact force of a Greek comparative.

hammond-last-words-reverend-pious-learne.blurb: Two prayers for the peaceful resettlement of the church, printed in 1696 as the last words of Hammond, who had died in 1660 on the eve of the Restoration. Short and devotional, and issued a generation after the events they were composed in, which is worth keeping in view when weighing what the title claims for them.

hammond-paraphrase-annotations-all-books.blurb: The New Testament with a paraphrase alongside the text and annotations beneath it, the work Hammond was best known for. The paraphrase renders the sense in expanded plain prose; the notes carry the philology, drawn largely from the Greek fathers, and carry the argument too: that much of the prophetic matter looks to the destruction of Jerusalem, that the heretics of the epistles are the Gnostics, and that the churches of the apostles were governed by bishops.

hammond-practicall-catechisme.blurb: A catechism in dialogue between catechist and scholar, built not on the usual heads of doctrine but on Christian duty: the covenant, the commandments as Christ expounds them in the Sermon on the Mount, prayer, and the sacraments. Hammond writes for the practice of religion rather than its controversies, though the book was attacked as Arminian almost at once. It was often reprinted and stands at the head of his practical work.

hammond-reply-catholick-gentlemans-answe.blurb: A reply, in the controversy over schism, to a Roman gentleman's answer to the most material parts of Hammond's Of Schisme, with further matter annexed. The question at issue is whether the Church of England departed from the catholic church or was cast out of it, and it is argued from the ancient canons, the bounds of the Roman patriarchate, and the case of the English sees at the Reformation.

hammond-resisting-lavvfull-magistrate-un.blurb: The royalist case against armed resistance, published in 1644 while the war was being fought. Hammond argues from Romans 13 that subjects may not take up arms against the lawful magistrate on any pretence of religion, and appends a study of the word krima in the second verse, which he takes to mean judgment rather than eternal damnation. Short, exegetical, and directly political.

hammond-right-honourable-lord-fairfax-co.blurb: An address to Fairfax and his council of war, printed in 1649, when the army held the king and the trial was in prospect. Twenty pages from a chaplain who had attended Charles I and could plead only in the terms left to him. The occasion gives the piece most of its interest, and the outcome is known.

hammond-scandal.blurb: A tract on the doctrine of scandal: what it is to give offence, what it is merely to take it, and how far one Christian's liberty is bound by another's weakness. The question was pressing in 1646 because both sides in the quarrel over ceremonies and the liturgy were arguing from scandal. Thirty-four pages, and mostly a careful clearing of the term before anyone reasons from it.

hammond-schisme-defence-church-england-a.blurb: Hammond's answer to the Roman charge that the Church of England stands in schism. He defines schism, distinguishes it from separation made on cause, and argues the English case historically: the early independence of the British church, the limits of the Roman patriarchate, and the regularity of what was done in the sixteenth century. The book set off a controversy that occupied him for the rest of the decade.

hammond-second-defence-learned-hugo-grot.blurb: Twenty pages defending Hugo Grotius against the charge that he had turned papist or meant to make Rome's terms. Hammond had praised him in a digression in an earlier book and had been attacked for it; here he defends the digression, and with it his own reading of Grotius on the reunion of a divided Christendom.

hammond-sinnes-vveaknesse-vvilfulnesse-a.blurb: On the difference between sins of weakness and sins of wilfulness, a distinction on which much of Hammond's moral divinity turns, since he denies that a Christian may live in the second and be safe. Appended is a paraphrastic explication of two difficult texts, the kind of exegetical note he attached to most of his practical writing.

hammond-tracts.blurb: Thirty-eight pages gathering short pieces by Hammond under the bare title of tracts, from 1645, when he was writing a great deal of occasional divinity in small compass. The record supplies no list of contents, and the volume has to be opened to know what is in it.

hammond-view-nevv-directorie-vindication.blurb: Hammond against the Directory for Public Worship, which Parliament had set in place of the Book of Common Prayer. He goes through the Directory's provisions and its preface, and defends set forms of prayer and the ancient liturgy of the English church, with its offices for baptism, marriage and burial, against the objections raised to them.

hammond-view-some-exceptions-which-have-.blurb: A defence of Lucius Cary, Viscount Falkland, whose discourse against the infallibility of the church of Rome had been answered by a Roman controversialist. Hammond takes the exceptions in order, on the rule of faith, the authority of tradition, and how faith is finally resolved. Falkland had been killed at Newbury in 1643 and could not answer for himself.

hammond-vindication-ancient-liturgie-chu.blurb: A defence of the Prayer Book, going through the several reasons alleged for altering it and answering them in turn. It appeared in 1660, when the liturgy was coming back into use and its revision was again in debate; the title repeats that of the vindication Hammond had joined to his answer against the Directory some years earlier.

hammond-works-reverend-learned-henry-ham.blurb: The fourth volume of the folio Works of Hammond, printed in 1684, given over to paraphrase and annotations on Scripture. The collected edition gathered his controversial, practical and exegetical writing after his death, and this volume carries the biblical commentary. Nearly nine hundred folio pages, and the record does not say which books of Scripture are covered here.

ley-a-case-of-conscience-concerning-the-.blurb: A case of conscience on the Lord's Supper: what is to be done when either the bread or the wine is wanting. Ley resolves it as a casuist would, from the words of institution and the practice of the church, and the answer bears on the Roman communion in one kind whether or not he presses the application. Twenty-eight pages, printed in 1641.

ley-a-comparison-of-the-parliamentary-pr.blurb: A comparison of the Protestation taken by the Commons in 1641, in defence of the true reformed Protestant religion, with the oath imposed by the canons of the year before, the so-called et cetera oath, which required swearing never to consent to alter the government of the church by archbishops, bishops, deans and archdeacons. Ley sets the two side by side to show that a man might take the one and refuse the other.

ley-a-debate-concerning-the-english-litu.blurb: A debate on the English liturgy considered both as it once stood established in the worship of the church and as it now stood abolished out of it, written in 1656, when use of the Prayer Book was proscribed and had become a live case of conscience. Ley sat in the Westminster Assembly, and writes from that side of the question.

ley-a-discourse-concerning-puritans-a-vi.blurb: A vindication of those who suffer unjustly under the name of Puritan, arguing that the word is used loosely and by way of abuse, and distinguishing the sober conforming Protestant it is commonly thrown at from anything it might properly describe. Printed in 1641, when the label was doing heavy political work. The tract appeared without a name on it and has been assigned to more than one author.

ley-a-discourse-of-disputations-chiefly-.blurb: On disputation itself, chiefly in matters of religion: when it serves, what rules ought to govern it, and what mischief follows when they are ignored, with animadversions on two printed disputations by way of instance. Ley had spent much of his life in controversy by 1658 and writes here as a practitioner about the practice.

ley-a-letter-against-the-erection-of-an-.blurb: A letter written in June 1635 to the Bishop of Chester against the erection of an altar, printed six years later when the Laudian altar policy could be attacked in the open. Ley argues that the communion table should stand table-wise in the body of the church, as the English rite intends, and not be railed altar-wise at the east end. A document of the 1630s issued as a weapon of the 1640s.

ley-a-letter-to-dr-e-hyde-in-answer-to-o.blurb: Eighteen pages answering a letter from Dr Edward Hyde, occasioned by the royalist insurrection at Salisbury in 1655. The two men were already at odds over a living that Hyde had lost and Ley now held, and the rising gave a parish quarrel a political edge. Best read with the other pieces here on the demand for a fifth part.

ley-a-moniter-of-mortalitie-in-two-sermo.blurb: Two funeral sermons of 1643 on the suddenness with which death overtakes people, the manifold and uncertain surprisals of mortality being the stated theme. The warning is pressed on the living in a year that was making the point without help from preachers. The second of the two was also issued on its own.

ley-a-monitor-of-mortality-the-second-se.blurb: The second of the two sermons issued as a monitor of mortality, printed separately. It was occasioned by the death of Mrs Harpur, described on the title page as a grave and godly matron. Funeral preaching of the usual shape: the text, the character of the deceased, then the application to those still listening.

ley-an-acquittance-or-discharge-from-dr-.blurb: Ley's answer to Dr Edward Hyde's demand for a fifth part of the revenues of the rectory of Brightwell in Berkshire. By ordinance the family of a sequestered minister was to be allowed a fifth of the living; Ley, who held the rectory, disputes the claim and prints his reckoning. A parish quarrel, and a specimen of what sequestration meant in practice for both men involved.

ley-an-after-reckoning-with-mr-saltmarsh.blurb: A further round against John Saltmarsh, appealing to the impartial and conscientious reader to judge between them. Saltmarsh was pressing for liberty of conscience and against the imposition of a presbyterian settlement; Ley, who sat in the Assembly, holds him to what he had already written and reckons up the exchange. One of several pieces that passed between the two.

ley-defensive-doubts-hopes-and-reasons-f.blurb: Reasons for refusing the oath imposed by the sixth canon of the convocation of 1640, the et cetera oath, which bound the swearer never to consent to alter the government of the church by archbishops, bishops, deans and archdeacons. Ley states his case defensively rather than aggressively: not that the government is unlawful, but that the oath as framed cannot be taken with a clear conscience. The fullest of his tracts on the question.

ley-exceptions-many-and-just-against-two.blurb: Exceptions taken against two petitions presented to Parliament, which Ley judged injurious, one of them dated in July. Printed in 1653, the year the Rump was turned out and the Nominated Parliament sat, when petitioning was one of the ways the settlement of religion was being fought over. The record does not say whose petitions they were.

ley-general-reasons-grounded-on-piety-ch.blurb: The general case behind a particular quarrel: reasons from piety, charity, justice and equity against the defalcation of a fifth part of a sequestered living. Ley argues the principle here rather than the account, and the piece belongs beside his answer to Dr Hyde's demand of the year before.

ley-light-for-smoke-or-a-cleare-and-dist.blurb: A reply to John Saltmarsh, whose Smoke in the Temple had urged forbearance among the several ways of church government and left the choice to each conscience. Ley answers clearly and distinctly, as his title promises, writing as a member of the Assembly of Divines at Westminster and pressing the case for a settled discipline against the plea for liberty.

ley-sunday-a-sabbath-or-a-preparative-di.blurb: A preparative discourse on the sabbatarian question that had been agitated in England since the Book of Sports. Ley argues that the Lord's Day is a sabbath, resting the case on the fourth commandment as moral and perpetual rather than on the appointment of the church alone, and clearing the doubts a reader would raise against it. At two hundred and forty pages, the longest of his writings gathered here.

ley-the-a-fury-of-vvarre-and-b-folly-of-.blurb: Preached and printed in 1643, on the fury of war and on the folly of the sin that serves as an incentive to it, declared and then applied by way of caution. Ley takes the war as a judgment and directs his hearers to the repentance that would end it, in the manner of the fast sermons of those years.

ley-the-nevv-quere-and-determination-upo.blurb: An answer to a new query lately published by John Saltmarsh, which Ley took to be an attempt to retard the establishing of church government while the Assembly was still at work on it. He states the query, determines it against Saltmarsh, and argues that delay in settling discipline serves only the sects. One of several exchanges between the two in the middle of the decade.

calov-scripta-philosophica.blurb: The philosophical writings, containing the Gnostologia, the Noologia and the Metaphysica Divina. The first treats the knowable as such and the general conditions of knowing, the second the intellect and the first principles it holds by habit, the third being as being and its transcendental attributes, ordered toward theology. These are school texts of Lutheran metaphysics in its later flowering, and they stand behind the doctrinal method of the Systema.

calov-socinismus-profligatus.blurb: Socinianism routed, in more than eleven hundred pages. Calov takes the Socinian denial of the Trinity, of the satisfaction made by Christ and of original sin, and answers it text by text and argument by argument, together with the underlying claim that reason is judge of what revelation may contain. The Wittenberg faculty took Socinianism for the chief solvent of Christian doctrine, and this is the arsenal built against it.

calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-as-4.blurb: The first of the twelve volumes of Calov's dogmatics, published at Wittenberg from 1655. The Systema proceeds locus by locus in the scholastic manner, stating the question, the orthodox thesis, the positions opposed to it and the arguments on either side, so that any volume serves as a reference on the loci it contains. At more than thirteen hundred pages this is the largest of the set; the record does not specify which loci it covers.

The second volume, printed with the first in 1655. Calov's method throughout is that of the Lutheran schools: each locus opened by definitions and distinctions, then the controverted points set out with the adversaries named, Socinian, Arminian, Reformed, Roman and syncretist in turn. To be read alongside the volume it appeared with. The loci treated here are not named in the record.

calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-as-v.blurb: The third volume, of 1659, and the first to follow the two that appeared together in 1655. Nearly thirteen hundred pages, which is a measure of how much room a locus takes when every objection is answered where it stands. Calov wrote as the leading opponent of Georg Calixt and the Helmstedt syncretists, and that polemic runs through the whole set. The contents of this volume are not given in the record.

The fourth volume, of 1661, after which the work paused for some years before the remaining volumes came out together in the 1670s. The apparatus is constant across the set: the state of the controversy, the thesis, the antithesis, then the arguments and the solutions to them. What loci this volume contains the record does not say.

calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-as-4.blurb: The fifth volume, one of the seven that came from the press in 1677 when Calov brought the long-delayed remainder of the work through together. By that date he had held his chair at Wittenberg for more than a quarter of a century and was the recognised head of the strict Lutheran party. The record gives no contents beyond the volume number.

The seventh volume, printed in 1677 with the rest of the later part of the work. The set runs to twelve volumes in all; the sixth is not present in this collection, so a reader working through the loci in order will find a gap here. Contents beyond the number are not recorded.

The eighth volume, from the group printed in 1677. Calov's opponents are the same throughout the work: Rome, the Reformed on the sacraments and the person of Christ, the Socinians, the Arminians, and the irenicists who would build a union on fundamental articles alone. Which loci this volume treats is not recorded here.

calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-as-v.blurb: The ninth volume, one of the shorter ones, printed in 1677. A reader coming to the Systema for the first time should know that it was made for reference rather than continuous reading: the loci are self-contained and the volumes were used as such. The contents of this one are not given in the record.

calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-as-4.blurb: The tenth volume, of 1677. Calov's dogmatics belongs to the late scholastic method of Lutheran orthodoxy, in which the substance of the Formula of Concord is expounded with the full apparatus of school philosophy that his own Scripta Philosophica had supplied. What this volume covers the record does not say.

The eleventh volume, and the shortest of those present here at under three hundred pages, printed in 1677 with the others of the later group. The record gives no account of the loci it contains, and the volume should be identified from its own title page before anything is cited from it.

calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-as-v.blurb: The twelfth and last volume, closing in 1677 a work whose first two volumes had appeared twenty-two years earlier. Systems built on this plan commonly end with the last things, though the record does not confirm what is treated here. Four hundred pages, and the end of an undertaking that occupied Calov for most of his career at Wittenberg.

calov-dissertationes-theologicae-rostoch.blurb: Theological disputations from Calov's years at Rostock, printed in 1637, eighteen years before the first volume of his dogmatic system. Disputations of this kind were argued in the schools and then published: a thesis, its distinctions, the objections raised and their solutions. Early work, useful chiefly for seeing in small the method he would afterwards apply at enormous length.

calov-biblia-novi-testamenti-illustrata-.blurb: Part of Calov's commentary on the whole Bible, here the second volume on the New Testament in its first part. The Biblia Illustrata sets out the text with Calov's exposition and, at great length, a running refutation of the annotations of Hugo Grotius, whose habit of finding a prophecy fulfilled within its own historical moment Calov judged destructive of the church's testimonies to Christ. Doctrinal commentary conducted as controversy.

calov-consideration-of-arminianism.blurb: A refutation of Arminianism running to something under five hundred pages, taking the Remonstrant account of election, grace and the freedom of the will and answering it from Scripture and from the Lutheran confessional writings. Calov's own church was not Reformed, and part of the interest of the book lies in watching the Arminian scheme opposed from a position that is neither Dort's nor the Remonstrants'.

salmeron-epistolas-pauli-tomus-1.blurb: The first of four tomes covering the Pauline and canonical epistles. Salmeron was one of Ignatius Loyola's original companions and served as a papal theologian through the sessions of Trent, and his method here is disputation rather than running gloss: a passage raises a numbered question, and the question is settled from the fathers, the schoolmen and the councils. The Protestant reading is usually stated before it is answered.

salmeron-epistolas-pauli-tomus-2.blurb: The second and shortest of the four tomes on the epistles, continuing the sequence of disputations begun in the first. Salmeron wrote these at Naples in his last years, and they were printed as part of a large collected commentary well after his death in 1585. A reader comes to them for a Jesuit exegesis worked out with the Reformation controversies in full view.

salmeron-epistolas-pauli-tomus-3.blurb: The third and largest of the four tomes on the epistles, at eight hundred pages. The form throughout is the disputatio: Salmeron breaks the text into questions, ranges the authorities on either side, and resolves. Readers who know Cornelius a Lapide will find an older and more combative kind of Jesuit commentary here, closer to the controversial theology of the Tridentine decades.

salmeron-epistolas-pauli-tomus-4.blurb: The fourth and last tome, which leaves Paul for the catholic epistles and the Apocalypse, as its title page indicates. James, Peter, John and Jude receive the same treatment as the rest of the series, numbered disputations resolved from patristic and scholastic authority, and the commentary on Revelation closes both this volume and Salmeron's work on the epistles.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-primus.blurb: The volume that opens twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts, and it opens as such works usually did, with preliminary matter on the evangelists and the standing of the gospel text. Salmeron then takes the four gospels as one continuous narrative and breaks it into numbered questions, answered from the fathers, the councils and the schoolmen.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-secundus.blurb: The second of twelve tomes and the shortest in the set, following directly on the preliminary matter of the first. Salmeron proceeds through the gospel history in order, raising the questions each episode was taken to raise in Catholic controversial theology and answering them at length from patristic and conciliar authority.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-tertius.blurb: The third of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts, continuing the exposition from the second. Salmeron's readers came to him for the questions: what a passage settles, whom it refutes, and which patristic authorities stand behind the Catholic reading. Continuous paraphrase is not what the series offers.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-quartus.blurb: The fourth of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts, and among the largest in the series at over seven hundred pages. The form is consistent throughout: a stretch of narrative, then a series of disputations on what it raises, resolved by authority rather than by philology. Salmeron is arguing with Protestant exegetes as much as expounding the text.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-quintus.blurb: The fifth of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts. Salmeron worked on this commentary at Naples in the last years of his life, and the volumes reached print only long after his death in 1585. A reader comes to any single tome for its disputations rather than for continuous exposition, since the questions rather than the verses carry the argument.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-sextus.blurb: The sixth of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts. Salmeron belonged to the first generation of the Society of Jesus, and this commentary is the fruit of his retirement rather than of a university chair; it reads as the work of a controversialist who had argued these questions in council before he wrote them down.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-septimus.blurb: The seventh of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts, and one of the slighter volumes. The method does not change across the series: numbered disputations on the difficulties of the narrative, argued from the fathers and the schoolmen by a theologian who had spent much of his working life at the Council of Trent.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-octavus.blurb: The eighth of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts. Salmeron was one of the first Jesuits, present at Trent as a papal theologian, and the controversial temper of those years runs through the exegesis. This volume belongs to the first group of eight, printed in 1602, with the remaining four following two years later.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-nonus.blurb: The ninth of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts, and one of the longer volumes in the set. Salmeron's unit is the disputation rather than the verse: a passage generates numbered questions, each answered with patristic citation and scholastic distinction, and the Reformation reading is regularly named before it is refuted.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-decimus.blurb: The tenth of twelve tomes on the gospel history and the Acts of the Apostles. Salmeron treats the four gospels as one continuous narrative and works through it in order, stopping at each difficulty to raise a formal question and settle it from the fathers and the schoolmen. This volume falls in the last quarter of the series.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-undecimus.blurb: The eleventh of twelve tomes on the gospel history and Acts, and next to last in the series. It belongs to the group of four volumes printed in 1604, after the first eight had appeared in 1602. The disputational method of the earlier tomes carries through to the end.

salmeron-evangelicam-historiam-duodecimu.blurb: The twelfth and final tome, where the commentary leaves the gospel narrative for the Acts of the Apostles named in the series title. At six hundred pages it is one of the fuller volumes, and it closes Salmeron's treatment of the historical books before the separate tomes on the epistles begin.

burges-a-case-concerning-the-buying-of-b.blurb: Burges, an assessor of the Westminster Assembly, had himself bought former episcopal property at Wells, and this tract argues that such purchases were lawful. He distinguishes the case of bishops' lands from outright sacrilege and takes up the objections of those who held that church property could not be alienated at all. Printed a year before the Restoration made the question a personal one.

burges-a-chaine-of-graces-drawne-out-at-.blurb: An exposition of the chain of virtues in the first chapter of Second Peter, where faith is to have knowledge added to it, and temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness and love in turn. Burges takes the links one at a time and presses each on the conscience, with reformation of manners rather than doctrinal controversy as the declared aim.

burges-a-new-discouery-of-personal-tithe.blurb: An argument that the tenth is owed not only from land but from the clear gains of trade, craft and profession, and that these personal tithes are due both in conscience and at law. Burges is writing for the maintenance of a preaching ministry in towns, where glebe and predial tithe brought a minister little. The case is made from scripture and from English precedent.

burges-a-sermon-preached-to-the-honourab.blurb: One of the fast sermons Burges preached to the Long Parliament, printed with the Commons' order for its publication. The monthly fast before the House became the chief pulpit of the Puritan cause in the early 1640s, and these sermons were as much political counsel as exposition: a text opened, a national sin named, and reformation urged on the men able to enact it.

burges-a-vindication-of-the-ministers-of.blurb: A ten-page defence of the Presbyterian ministers of London against charges laid on them in print. Burges was among the leading London clergy, and the year places the piece in the aftermath of the king's trial, when the city's ministers were under public attack. Short, occasional and defensive in the plain sense.

burges-an-humble-examination-of-a-printe.blurb: A reply in the pamphlet exchange over whether bishops should sit and vote in the House of Lords. The Commons had put out nine reasons against it; an answer to those reasons was printed; Burges examines that answer point by point. The argument turns on whether spiritual office is compatible with temporal jurisdiction, and it belongs to the first year of the Long Parliament's assault on the episcopate.

burges-another-sermon-preached-to-the-ho.blurb: A companion to the sermon Burges preached at the Commons' first public fast, printed separately as well as with its fellow. Stephen Marshall preached alongside him on that occasion. These were the sermons that inaugurated the long series of parliamentary fast sermons, and their appearance in print gave the Puritan ministry a standing audience beyond the House.

burges-baptismall-regeneration-of-elect-.blurb: A defence of the proposition that elect infants of believers are regenerated in baptism, which Burges takes to be the doctrine of the Church of England as its liturgy and articles state it. The book is aimed at fellow Calvinists uneasy with the prayer book's language of regeneration, and it argues that the sacrament may be held to convey what it signifies without conceding anything to Rome.

burges-no-sacrilege-nor-sin-to-alienate-.blurb: A second defence of purchasers of church lands, this time cathedral rather than episcopal property, published in the year the Restoration put every such title in question. Burges argues that alienating or buying these lands is neither sacrilege nor sin as such, and answers the charge of sacrilege on its own theological ground rather than resting on the acts of the Long Parliament.

burges-reasons-shewing-the-necessity-of-.blurb: The Presbyterian case, put at the Restoration, for reforming the public doctrine, worship, rites and ceremonies, government and discipline of the church rather than restoring them unaltered. Burges sets out reasons under each head. It belongs to the negotiations that produced the Savoy Conference and, in the end, the ejections of 1662.

burges-some-of-the-differences-and-alter.blurb: Seven pages collating the Book of Common Prayer then in use against the book actually established by law, listing the places where the printed text had drifted from the statute. The point is polemical: if the church has already tolerated alteration without authority, the Presbyterian request for revision asks nothing new.

burges-the-fire-of-the-sanctuarie-newly-.blurb: A long treatise on zeal, its nature, its counterfeits and its right use, running to more than five hundred pages. Burges works out what distinguishes true zeal from passion, faction and mere heat, a question that mattered acutely to a ministry accused of both coldness and fanaticism. Practical divinity of the sort English readers expected in the 1620s.

burges-the-first-sermon-preached-to-the-.blurb: The sermon Burges preached at the first public fast of the Long Parliament, printed at the Commons' order and issued with a substantial epistle. It opens the series of fast sermons that ran through the 1640s, and it sets the pattern: a text expounded, the nation's sins laid out, and the House told what God requires of a reforming Parliament.

burges-the-necessity-of-agreement-with-g.blurb: A sermon on agreement with God, preached before the Lords and printed in 1645. Burges was by then a fixture of the parliamentary pulpit and an assessor of the Westminster Assembly, and the sermon presses reconciliation with God as the condition of any settlement between men. Fifty-five pages, in the fast sermon manner.

burges-to-the-honourable-the-knights-cit.blurb: A single-sheet petition addressed to the Commons, of the kind printed in quantity in 1641 when the House was besieged with them. Burges's name carried weight with the parliamentary party, and the petition was the standard instrument for putting a ministerial grievance or proposal before members. One page, and no more than that.

burges-two-sermons-preached-to-the-honor.blurb: The pair of sermons Burges preached to the Commons at their public fast, gathered in one volume. The two were also issued separately, so a reader will meet them under more than one title. Together they are the opening statement of the parliamentary fast sermon, the genre through which the Puritan ministry addressed the Long Parliament for a decade.

flacius-clavis-scripturae-sacrae-1567.blurb: Two works in one volume, and the foundation of Lutheran hermeneutics. The first part is an alphabetical lexicon of scriptural words, tracing how each is used across the canon; the second is a set of treatises on how scripture is to be read, covering its tropes and figures, the causes of obscurity in the text, and the rule that scripture interprets itself. Flacius wrote it to show that the plain sense is recoverable without the church's magisterium.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-1a.blurb: The first book of the first century, opening the Ecclesiastica Historia. The apostolic age is given two books rather than one because everything after it is measured against it: the centuriators' argument is that the doctrine, worship and government of the first hundred years are recoverable from the sources and that later ages departed from them. This is the first of the two.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-1b.blurb: The second book of the first century, completing the treatment of the apostolic age that the work takes as its standard. From the second century onward each hundred years receives a single volume; here the material required two. Readers came to these books for the evidence that the primitive church knew nothing of the papacy as later centuries knew it.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-2.blurb: The second volume, on the years 100 to 200, and the slightest in the set at a hundred and fifty pages. The century left little material, and the fixed chapter headings on councils, ceremonies and government are answered thinly, which the centuriators take as evidence in itself: what later ages claim as ancient cannot be found here.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-3.blurb: The third volume, on the years 200 to 300, the century of Origen, Cyprian and the persecutions before Constantine. The standard chapters on martyrs, heresies and church government carry most of the material. Like the second century, the third is treated briefly by comparison with what follows.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-4.blurb: The fourth volume, on the years 300 to 400, and one of the largest in the work. Constantine, Nicaea, the Arian controversy and the great fourth-century bishops fall here, and the centuriators had both abundant sources and a strong interest in the period, since Rome's claims for its own antiquity rested heavily on it.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-5.blurb: The fifth volume, on the years 400 to 500: Ephesus and Chalcedon, the Pelagian and christological disputes, and the growth of the Roman see under Leo. The uniform chapters on doctrine and on councils are unusually full, and the volume is among the longest in the set.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-6.blurb: The sixth volume, on the years 500 to 600, closing with the pontificate of Gregory the Great. Protestant readers of church history have long treated this stretch as the hinge between the ancient church and the medieval one, and the centuriators' fixed chapters on ceremonies, government and the bishops of Rome are where that judgment is worked out.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-7.blurb: The seventh volume, on the years 600 to 700, the century in which Islam appeared and in which the bishops of Rome pressed the title of universal bishop. Both feature in the centuriators' account of decline. The chapters follow the same order as every other century in the work, which is the whole point of the design.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-8.blurb: The eighth volume, on the years 700 to 800: the iconoclastic controversy in the East, the rise of the Frankish alliance, and the reign of Charlemagne at the century's end. The fixed headings on ceremonies and on images gave the Magdeburg writers their opening, since the veneration of images was among the practices they wanted shown to be late.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-9.blurb: The ninth volume, on the years 800 to 900. The material is thinner than the fourth and fifth centuries afforded, but the scheme is unchanged: propagation of the church, persecutions, doctrine, heresies, ceremonies, government, councils, bishops and notable men, century by century, so that any one strand can be followed across the whole.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-10.blurb: The tenth volume of the Ecclesiastica Historia, covering the years 900 to 1000. Each century in the work is divided into the same fixed set of chapters, so a reader can compare doctrine, ceremonies, church government, councils, heresies and bishops from one hundred years to the next. Flacius and his collaborators at Magdeburg were building a case that the church had declined from its apostolic form.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-11.blurb: The eleventh volume, on the years 1000 to 1100, the century of Gregory VII and the contest over investiture. The centuriators read that pontificate as the point at which the Roman claim to temporal supremacy became explicit, and the standard chapters on church government and on the bishops of Rome carry the weight of the argument here.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-12.blurb: The twelfth volume, on the years 1100 to 1200, and one of the longest in the set at over a thousand pages. The uniform chapter scheme runs as always through doctrine, heresies, ceremonies, government, councils, persecutions and notable men. The scholastic theology then taking shape in the schools gave the Magdeburg writers a great deal to record and to object to.

magdeburg-centuriae-cent-13.blurb: The thirteenth and final volume, covering the years 1200 to 1300. The work stops here, well short of the Reformation it was written to justify, which leaves the case resting on the accumulated evidence of decline rather than on any account of Luther. The rise of the mendicant orders and the height of papal jurisdiction fall in this century.

junius-animadversiones-controversia-1.blurb: Junius on the first of Bellarmine's general controversies, De Verbo Dei, which takes up the canon of scripture, the versions, the authority of the Vulgate, the perspicuity of the text and the standing of unwritten tradition. This is the ground on which the whole Reformation dispute is decided, and Junius answers point by point in the margin of Bellarmine's own argument rather than composing a rival treatise.

junius-animadversiones-controversia-2.blurb: Junius on Bellarmine's second general controversy, which concerns Christ as head of the church. Forty-seven pages of animadversions, following the Roman text through its chapters. Junius had by this time settled at Leiden, and the campaign against Bellarmine occupied the last years of his life; the pieces appeared separately at Geneva over more than a decade.

junius-animadversiones-controversia-3.blurb: Junius on Bellarmine's third general controversy, on the Roman pontiff, and the longest of these installments. The papal claim was the point at which the Protestant case had most to answer and most to gain, and the length of the notes reflects it. Printed at Geneva in the year of Junius's death.

junius-animadversiones-controversia-4.blurb: Junius's animadversions on the fourth general controversy in Bellarmine's Disputationes de controversiis christianae fidei. Bellarmine's work was the most formidable statement of the Roman position produced in that century, and the Reformed answer to it was piecemeal by necessity; Junius took the controversies one at a time and did not live to finish.

junius-animadversiones-controversia-5.blurb: Junius on the fifth of Bellarmine's general controversies, at a hundred and twenty-six pages the fullest of the set apart from the third. The method is unchanged throughout the series: Bellarmine's chapters are followed in order and answered in short compass, with the Roman argument quoted before it is met.

junius-animadversiones-controversia-6.blurb: Junius on the sixth of Bellarmine's general controversies, published at Geneva in the year after his death. Sixty pages of notes, following the Roman text through its divisions. The Geneva press issued these pieces as they came, which is why they carry dates spread across a decade and appear under slightly varying titles.

junius-animadversiones-bellarmini-contro.blurb: Junius's notes on the seventh of the general controversies in Bellarmine's Disputationes, printed at Geneva seven years after his death. The form is animadversion rather than treatise: he follows Bellarmine chapter by chapter, quoting and answering, so the book is meant to be read alongside the Roman original rather than on its own.

junius-apocalypsis-methodica-analysis.blurb: A structural outline of Revelation rather than a commentary: Junius divides the book into its parts and their subdivisions and shows how each hangs on the last, in the analytic manner then favoured in Reformed schools. His work on the Apocalypse had a long afterlife in English Bibles, where his notes replaced the earlier annotations in later editions of the Geneva version.

junius-confutatio-argumentorum-xxii.blurb: Eleven pages refuting twenty-two arguments, taken one by one. The title gives the form and not the subject, and beyond the number and the fact that Junius was then in controversy with both Rome and the antitrinitarians, the piece announces nothing about what is being confuted.

junius-de-peccato-primo-adami.blurb: A short disputation on the first sin of Adam: what it was, how a creature made upright could commit it, and what followed from it for the race. The Reformed schools handled the question under the heading of the fall, and Junius's treatment is thesis and argument in the academic form rather than exposition of Genesis.

junius-de-politiae-mosis-observatione.blurb: On how far the Mosaic polity binds Christian commonwealths. Junius distinguishes what in Israel's law belongs to common right and natural equity, and so remains obligatory, from what was proper to that nation in that land, and so lapsed with it. The distinction became standard in Reformed political theology, and the tract is short enough to be read at a sitting.

junius-defensio-de-sancta-trinitate.blurb: A defence of the catholic doctrine of the Trinity, at length. Junius wrote in a decade when antitrinitarian arguments were circulating from Poland and Transylvania and when Reformed theologians were obliged to show that they held the ancient creeds on the ancient grounds. The case is made from scripture and from the fathers.

junius-ecclesiastici.blurb: Theses on the nature of the church and on its administrations, that is, the offices and functions through which it is governed. Junius works in the academic form of proposition and proof, and the questions are the ones a Reformed faculty would have set: what the church is, who belongs to it, and by what authority its ministers act.

junius-eirenicum-de-pace-ecclesiae.blurb: An irenic piece on the peace of the catholic church, arguing for terms on which divided Christians might hold together. Junius was known for this temper, and the tract distinguishes what must be agreed from what may be borne with. It is worth reading next to his animadversions on Bellarmine, which show where he thought the line fell.

junius-praelectiones-in-genesim.blurb: Lectures on the first three chapters of Genesis, covering the creation, the state of man before the fall and the fall itself. Junius was one of the two translators of the Latin Bible that bears his name with Tremellius, and his handling of the Hebrew shows in the exposition. Fifty pages, in the form of academic lectures.

andrewes-concio-habita-coram-serenissimo.blurb: A sermon preached in Latin before James, styled king of England, Scotland, France and Ireland and Defender of the Faith. Andrewes preached at court throughout the reign, and the Latin marks this one as addressed beyond the English congregation to the learned readers of Europe. The title gives the occasion and the audience but not the text.

andrewes-copie-sermon-preached-on-good-f.blurb: A Good Friday sermon preached before James at court while Andrewes was Dean of Westminster, printed as a separate copy. His Passion sermons work in the way his hearers came to expect: a short text taken apart word by word, each word turned until it yields, the Latin and Greek held up beside the English. The sermons were gathered later into the folio of ninety-six.

A later issue of the Good Friday sermon Andrewes preached at court during his years as Dean of Westminster, printed again in 1620, when he was Bishop of Winchester and his sermons had an established market. The title page still gives the older style, Dean of Westminster, which fixes the occasion rather than the printing.

andrewes-manuall-directions-visitation-s.blurb: A manual for visiting the sick, with meditations and prayers for use at the bedside, issued under Andrewes's name sixteen years after his death. Devotional compilations of this kind circulated freely with his name attached, and the relation of any one of them to what he actually wrote is not always clear. What the book offers is a set of forms for the dying and for those attending them.

andrewes-morall-law-expounded-that-is-lo.blurb: An exposition of the Ten Commandments in more than seven hundred pages, taken from the catechetical lectures Andrewes gave early in his career and published long after his death from hearers' notes. Each commandment is opened at length, with the duties it requires and the sins it forbids set out in the manner of English practical divinity. It is the fullest thing under his name after the sermons.

andrewes-private-devotions-right-reveren.blurb: The Preces Privatae in English. Andrewes compiled these prayers for his own use, in Greek and Latin, out of scripture, the liturgies of the ancient church and the fathers, and arranged them for the days of the week with orders for confession, intercession and thanksgiving. Almost nothing in the book is original phrasing; the art is in the selection and the fitting together. It reached print only after his death.

andrewes-sermon-preached-before-kings-ma.blurb: A Nativity sermon preached before James at Whitehall on Christmas Day, printed on its own. Andrewes preached before the king at Christmas for many years, and the sermons on the Incarnation are the ones most often read now: a single verse worked over syllable by syllable until the doctrine stands out of it.

A sermon preached before James at Hampton Court on the right and power of calling assemblies, that is, on whether the prince or the church summons synods. Andrewes preached it with the Scottish presbyterian claim in view, and the argument runs from the silver trumpets of the tenth chapter of Numbers, sounded at Moses' command to gather the congregation.

The earlier printing of Andrewes's Hampton Court sermon on the right and power of calling assemblies, from the year it was preached. The occasion was the presence at court of Scottish ministers who held that the church might convene its own assemblies without the king. Andrewes argues the contrary from the Old Testament ordering of the congregation.

andrewes-sermon-preached-before-maiestie.blurb: Preached before the king on the fifth of August, the anniversary of his deliverance from the Gowrie conspiracy, which James kept as an annual thanksgiving and Andrewes was regularly appointed to mark. The title page gives him as Bishop of Ely, the see he held from 1609. The style is his: a text divided minutely, and the king's preservation read as an instance of providence rather than flattered directly.

andrewes-seven-sermons-on-wonderfull-com.blurb: Seven sermons on the temptation of Christ in the wilderness, taken as a single combat between Christ and Satan and followed through its three assaults. These are early sermons of Andrewes, preached long before the court years, and they were printed from hearers' notes without his hand in it. This issue appeared the year after his death.

andrewes-summarie-view-government-both-o.blurb: A short defence of episcopacy, arguing that the government of the church under the gospel answers to the ordering of ministry under the law and so rests on more than custom. It came out under Andrewes's name in 1641, when the bishops were under attack in Parliament and in the press, and his authority was worth invoking on that side.
