andrewes-tvvo-sermons-preached-before-ki.blurb: Two Nativity sermons preached before James at Whitehall, one of them on Christmas Day, issued together. Andrewes's Christmas sermons are the best known part of his preaching, and the manner is unmistakable: a verse taken in pieces, each piece pressed for what it says about the Word made flesh, with the Latin and Greek always in view.

andrewes-wonderfull-combate-gods-glorie-.blurb: Seven sermons on the temptation of Christ, published in 1592 from notes taken by hearers rather than from Andrewes's own copy. He treats the wilderness as a set combat and works through Satan's three assaults in order, drawing the pastoral use as he goes. This is early work, and it predates the court manner by many years.

andrewes-xcvi-sermons-right-honorable-re.blurb: The collected sermons, gathered in folio three years after Andrewes's death by John Buckeridge and William Laud at the king's command. They are arranged by the church's year and the state's: Nativity, Lent, Passion, Resurrection, Pentecost, then the sermons for the Gowrie deliverance and the Gunpowder Treason, with others at the end. The manner throughout is minute division of a short text, heavy use of the Latin and Greek, and a preference for the words of scripture over any paraphrase of them.

white-a-commentary-upon-the-three-first-.blurb: A commentary on the first three chapters of Genesis by John White of Dorchester, the Westminster divine known as the patriarch of Dorchester, printed after his death. Five hundred pages on the creation, the garden and the fall, in the expository style of English puritan divinity: the text opened clause by clause, doctrines raised from it, and uses pressed on the reader.

white-a-rich-cabinet-with-variety-of-inv.blurb: A collection of receipts, tricks, experiments and household inventions, of the sort published as books of secrets for the amusement and use of ordinary readers. It carries the name John White, but the contents belong to that popular trade rather than to the Dorchester divine of the same name, and the attribution here should be treated with caution.

white-a-sermon-preached-at-dorchester-in.blurb: An assize sermon preached at Dorchester before the judges of the county, printed in 1648. White had been rector there for most of his life, and the assize sermon was the occasion on which a minister addressed magistrates on the duties of their office. Forty pages, from the last year of his life.

white-a-speech-of-mr-iohn-white-counsell.blurb: A speech in the Commons on episcopacy by John White the lawyer, member for Southwark, who is a different man from the Dorchester minister of the same name. He chaired the committee on scandalous ministers and was among the more determined opponents of the bishops in the Long Parliament. Eighteen pages, printed as spoken.

white-a-vvay-to-the-tree-of-life-discove.blurb: Directions for reading the scriptures with profit, in a series of rules covering what a reader should bring to the text, how to proceed through it and what to expect from it. White of Dorchester wrote it near the end of a long ministry, and it belongs to the puritan literature on the private use of the Bible rather than to academic hermeneutics.

white-arts-treasury-or-a-profitable-and-.blurb: A compendium of practical arts and ingenious devices for the curious reader, printed in 1688. The name on the title page is John White, but the book belongs to the trade in popular how-to compilations, and it cannot be the work of the Dorchester divine, who died forty years earlier.

white-davids-psalms-in-metre-agreeable-t.blurb: A metrical psalter, the psalms turned into English verse close to the Hebrew and set to the tunes then in common use, so that a congregation could sing them without learning anything new. Psalters of this kind were produced in numbers in the 1650s as rivals to Sternhold and Hopkins. The title page is all that identifies this one.

white-iohn-white-s-defence-in-the-behalf.blurb: A short self-defence, written on behalf of the author and of his commander, the Lieutenant of the Tower. This is civil war personal apologetic rather than divinity, and the John White who wrote it is not securely identified with either the Dorchester minister or the member for Southwark. Seventeen pages.

white-mr-vvhites-speech-in-parliament-on.blurb: A speech in the Commons on the seventeenth of January concerning the trial of the twelve bishops who had protested that Parliament could not act in their absence. The speaker is John White the lawyer, member for Southwark. The imprint year follows the old style, in which January falls at the end of the year rather than the beginning. Eight pages, printed while the case was live.

white-the-art-of-ringing-etc-pt-1-the-ar.blurb: The first part of a composite volume, giving rules for ringing changes on church bells. Change ringing was a serious amateur pursuit in Restoration England and generated a small technical literature of its own. The John White named on the title page is a compiler of practical handbooks, not the divine under whose name this has been filed.

white-the-art-of-ringing-etc-pt-2-artifi.blurb: The second part of the same composite volume, containing instructions for making artificial fireworks and a treatise on gardening. The pairing is ordinary for the genre, which bundled whatever practical arts would sell together. As with the first part, the author is not the Dorchester divine but a compiler of popular handbooks.

white-the-first-centvry-of-scandalous-ma.blurb: A catalogue of a hundred clergymen charged with scandal or with malignancy, that is, with royalism, drawn up from the depositions taken before the parliamentary committee on scandalous ministers. The compiler is John White the member for Southwark, who chaired that committee and was afterwards known as Century White. It is a document of the ejections rather than an argument about them.

white-the-planters-plea-or-the-grounds-o.blurb: A defence of the plantation of New England, written as the Massachusetts Bay emigration was under way and answering the objections then current: that the country was not lawfully taken, that departure was desertion, that the venture would fail. White of Dorchester was among the promoters of the settlement without ever crossing to it, and the tract belongs to the founding documents of that migration.

white-the-protestation-of-iohn-white-doc.blurb: A single leaf, a protestation which the title says White caused to be written the day before his death. He was rector of Dorchester and an assessor of the Westminster Assembly, and he died in 1648. One page, and the interest of it is the circumstance rather than the argument.

white-the-troubles-of-jerusalems-restaur.blurb: A sermon on the rebuilding of Jerusalem, read as a figure of the reformation of the church then being attempted, in the manner of the sermons preached before Parliament in those years. The difficulties Nehemiah met are set against the difficulties of the Westminster settlement: opposition from without, division within, and the slowness of a work that everyone approves in principle.

bucer-acta-colloquii-ratisbonae.blurb: The record of a colloquy at Regensburg, where Catholic and evangelical theologians met under imperial auspices to see whether the religious division of Germany could be settled by conference. Bucer was one of the evangelical collocutors, and the volume prints the articles debated together with the replies and protests they drew. A reader comes to it for the moment when reunion by negotiation was still thought possible, and for the exact points at which it failed.

bucer-an-statui-ecclesiasticorum.blurb: A short Latin case for clerical marriage, arguing that wedlock is no derogation from the standing and dignity of men in orders but agrees with their office. Bucer, a former Dominican who had married, writes as a practised controversialist against the law of celibacy, and the piece belongs with the wider evangelical campaign to have the ministry ordered by Scripture rather than by canon.

bucer-constans-defensio.blurb: A sustained defence out of Scripture of the reforming order proposed for the archbishopric of Cologne, answering the cathedral clergy and the university theologians who had denounced it. Bucer had drawn up that order at the archbishop's request, and here he takes the heads of doctrine and ceremony in turn, defending each from Scripture and from the ancient church rather than from the authority of the reformers.

bucer-de-caena-dominica.blurb: A short Strasbourg treatise on the Lord's Supper from the first years of Bucer's reforming work, written before the eucharistic quarrel between Wittenberg and Zurich had hardened into parties. Readers come to it for the terms in which he first stated the question of Christ's presence and the use of the sacrament, the question he would spend the rest of his life trying to keep from dividing the evangelical churches.

bucer-de-regno-christi.blurb: Written for Edward VI in the last months of Bucer's life at Cambridge, this is a programme for a Christian commonwealth: the marks of Christ's kingdom, the offices and discipline of the church, and then a series of laws by which a godly prince might order education, poor relief, marriage and divorce, the observance of the Lord's Day, and the reform of the courts. It is the fullest statement of what the Strasbourg reformer thought reformation should actually accomplish in a kingdom.

bucer-de-vera-ecclesiarum-reconciliation.blurb: On the true reconciliation of the churches in doctrine, ceremonies and discipline. It belongs to the long effort by which Bucer sought agreement among the evangelical parties, and where possible with those still in obedience to Rome, without giving up the substance of reform. A reader comes to it for his account of what must be held in common and what may be borne with, the distinction on which all his mediating work rested.

bucer-defensio-adversus-axioma-catholicu.blurb: A reply to the Axioma Catholicum of Robert Ceneau, bishop of Avranches, who had written against the evangelical cause in France. Bucer answers the charge that the reformers had broken with the catholic faith, arguing that the doctrine preached at Strasbourg is the doctrine of Scripture and of the ancient church, and that the innovation lies on the other side.

bucer-epistola-apologetica.blurb: Published in the name of the Strasbourg preachers, this open letter defends their ministry against the charges Erasmus had brought against the evangelicals, that their preaching bred sedition, contempt of learning and moral licence. Bucer answers point by point and sets out what the Strasbourg church actually taught and practised, which makes it one of the fullest early descriptions of that church by one of its own ministers.

bucer-gratulatio-ad-ecclesiam-anglicanam.blurb: A congratulatory address to the church in England on the restoration of religion there, written after Bucer had taken refuge in the kingdom, and directed against Stephen Gardiner, who had defended the older order and the celibacy of the clergy. It is short, occasional and combative, and shows a foreign divine assessing the English settlement while it was still being made.

bucer-in-ephesios.blurb: A commentary on Paul's letter to the Ephesians from Bucer's Strasbourg years, expounding the text clause by clause with the long doctrinal digressions that were his habit. Election, the church as Christ's body, and the ordering of household and ministry all take more room than a bare exposition would allow, and the reader sees the pattern of teaching that Strasbourg was then putting in place.

bucer-in-quatuor-evangelia.blurb: A continuous exposition of the four gospels, the revised form of a commentary Bucer had been enlarging since the 1520s. He harmonises the evangelists, treats the text section by section, and breaks off repeatedly into set discussions of doctrine and of church order, which is where most readers have gone: justification, the use of the law, discipline, and the care of souls. The bulk is considerable and the arrangement is not always easy to follow.

bucer-metaphrasis-in-romanos.blurb: A paraphrase and full exposition of Romans, and the longest sustained piece of theology Bucer wrote. Each section is first restated and then argued out, with extended treatments of justification, of election and reprobation, and of the place of the law in the Christian life; the fathers and the medieval commentators are quoted at length and often disputed. Calvin knew this book and complained about its length.

bucer-praelectiones-in-ephesios.blurb: Lectures on Ephesians delivered from the Regius chair of divinity at Cambridge near the end of Bucer's life and printed after his death. The exposition is that of a working lecturer rather than a commentator preparing a book, and it can be read against his earlier Strasbourg commentary on the same epistle for what a quarter century of controversy had changed and what it had not.

bucer-scripta-duo-adversaria-latomum.blurb: Two opposed writings printed together, Bucer's exchange with Bartholomaeus Latomus, the humanist and controversialist who had attacked the evangelical position. The form is that of the printed dispute, the adversary's piece and the reply set against each other, so a reader can follow the argument over the church, its authority and the warrant for reform without taking either man's summary of the other on trust.

ussher-ansvver-challenge-made-iesuite-ir.blurb: Ussher's reply to a challenge issued by the Jesuit William Malone, who had asked Protestants to produce the testimony of the first centuries for their doctrine. Ussher takes the disputed heads one at a time, among them tradition, the real presence, confession, purgatory, prayer for the dead, images and the invocation of saints, and sets out what the fathers and councils actually say. The learning carries the argument; this is a work of citation and collation rather than exhortation, and the marginal apparatus is as much the substance as the text.

ussher-bishop-ushers-second-prophesie-wh.blurb: A seven-page pamphlet printing a prophecy said to have been delivered by Ussher to his daughter on his sickbed, foretelling a persecution to come. It appeared long after his death and belongs to the trade in prophecies circulated under the names of dead bishops in the years of the popish plot, rather than to anything Ussher is known to have written.

ussher-body-divinitie-summe-substance-ch.blurb: A complete system of divinity in question and answer, running from Scripture and the knowledge of God through creation, fall, covenant, Christ, the church and the last things, printed under Ussher's name. He protested at the publication and said the material was a commonplace collection gathered in his youth rather than a book he had composed, and the attribution has been argued over since. It remains the fullest catechetical statement associated with him and was long used as one.

ussher-briefe-declaration-universalitie-.blurb: A short treatise on the universality of the church of Christ and the unity of the catholic faith, answering the Roman demand to know where the Protestant church was before Luther. Ussher argues that the visible church has always been, though not always in the obedience of Rome, and gathers testimonies to show a continuity of the faith professed rather than of a single see.

ussher-dailie-examination-arraignment-si.blurb: A single sheet, drawn out of sermons by the primate of Ireland, setting the sins of the day in order for self-examination. It is a devotional broadside for household or closet use, compiled by another hand from Ussher's preaching rather than written by him as a book.

ussher-geographicall-historicall-disqvis.blurb: A short piece of learned geography distinguishing the several senses the name Asia carried in ancient use: the Lydian or proconsular Asia, the region, and the later diocese. The question is not merely antiquarian, since the address of certain early letters and the standing of the churches named in them turn on which Asia is meant. It belongs with Ussher's work on the earliest episcopal records rather than with his controversial writing.

ussher-iudgement-doctor-rainoldes-touchi.blurb: Twenty pages printed in the year the English parliament took up the question of bishops. Ussher sets out the judgement of John Rainolds on the origin of episcopacy and then confirms it at greater length from antiquity, arguing that the presidency of one bishop over a college of presbyters reaches back to the apostolic age. Rainolds was a name the presbyterian side claimed, which is why Ussher wanted his opinion stated exactly.

ussher-prophecys-concerning-return-poper.blurb: A collection of prophecies about the return of popery to England, Scotland and Ireland, gathered under the names of Ussher and others and printed in the anxious years after the popish plot. The pieces are short and the attributions traditional rather than documented. The interest lies in what a London reader of the 1680s was being told to expect, not in Ussher.

ussher-reduction-episcopacie-unto-form-s.blurb: The scheme of a reduced or synodical episcopacy: bishops retained, but governing with the counsel of their presbyters in a graded series of assemblies, parochial, diocesan, provincial and national, on the pattern Ussher read out of the ancient church. It was drawn up as ground on which episcopalians and presbyterians might have settled together, was not adopted, and went on being reprinted after his death as a proposal worth reviving.

A brief statement of the plan by which Ussher would have had bishops govern with their presbyters in a graded series of assemblies, parochial, diocesan, provincial and national, drawn from what he took to be the practice of the ancient church. It was framed as ground on which episcopalians and presbyterians might meet, and was printed and reprinted through the years when a church settlement was still an open question.

ussher-right-honourable-house-peeres-now.blurb: A two-page petition to the House of Lords from the archbishop of Armagh, printed as a single item. The title states its occasion and the sheet contains little else. A reader will come to it for the wording of the request itself rather than for argument.

ussher-sermon-preached-before-commos-hou.blurb: Ussher preaching before the House of Commons at their fast in St Margaret's, Westminster, in February 1620 by the old reckoning, printed here in a later edition. The first printing appeared as the substance of what was delivered, and the two should be read together. The sermon fell in a parliament much occupied with the state of religion at home and the war in the Palatinate.

ussher-substance-that-vvhich-was-deliuer.blurb: The first printing of Ussher's sermon before the Commons at St Margaret's, Westminster, issued as the substance of what was delivered rather than as the text preached, a common form when a preacher wrote up an address afterward from notes. It was reprinted three years later under a title claiming the sermon itself. A reader comparing the two can watch a Jacobean sermon being turned into a book.

ussher-vox-hibern-rather-voyce-lord-from.blurb: A sermon preached at St Peter's, Westminster, and printed as the voice of the Lord from Ireland, delivered in the months after the Irish rising by a primate who had lost his province to it. The occasion is what the title supplies; a reader comes to it for how the rising was preached in Westminster while it was still news.

baillie-a-brief-account-of-the-indictmen.blurb: A two-page news account of the indictment, trial, conviction and execution of Robert Baillie of Jerviswood, the Scottish laird put to death at Edinburgh for alleged complicity in the plotting against Charles II. He is a different man from Robert Baillie the Glasgow divine, under whose name this sheet is filed, and the pamphlet is contemporary reporting rather than a work of divinity.

baillie-a-dissuasive-from-the-errours-of.blurb: A survey of the sects, written by one of the Scottish commissioners to the Westminster Assembly while the Assembly was sitting. Baillie sets out the tenets of the Independents, Brownists, Antinomians, Anabaptists, Familists and the rest, traces their descent from one another, and argues that the Independent way opens the door to the whole train. It is heresiography written to a purpose, and the purpose was to turn the English parliament against toleration.

baillie-a-parallel-or-briefe-comparison-.blurb: A point by point comparison of the service book with the mass book, the breviary and the Roman ceremonial, printed while the Covenanting settlement was being defended before an English audience. The method is columnar and cumulative: set the liturgy beside its supposed sources and let the correspondences carry the charge that the book was Rome brought back by degrees.

baillie-a-review-of-doctor-bramble-late-.blurb: An answer to John Bramhall, the exiled bishop of Derry, whose Fair Warning had told England what Scottish discipline would mean if it were received there. Baillie takes the charges in order, defending the government and discipline of the Church of Scotland, the authority of its assemblies and its dealings with the civil power, and returning the accusation of tyranny upon the bishops.

baillie-a-review-of-the-seditious-pamphl.blurb: A second engagement with the same pamphlet of Bramhall's, printed in Holland, which Baillie treats as seditious in intent as well as false in substance. The defence covers the discipline and courts of the Church of Scotland and the conduct of its assemblies. The two replies of that year go over much the same ground and are best read together.

baillie-a-scotch-antidote-against-the-en.blurb: A defence of the doctrine of grace as received in Scotland against what Baillie regarded as an English infection: the Arminian teaching on election, the extent of redemption, and the power of the will. The frame is national as much as theological, a Scottish churchman writing after the kingdoms had come to arms, treating error as something carried across a border.

baillie-an-historicall-vindication-of-th.blurb: A defence of the government of the Church of Scotland against the calumnies then in print in England, arguing the case historically: what the Scottish church has actually done in its assemblies, in its dealings with the crown, and in matters of discipline, as against what its accusers say it does. Written while the shape of the English settlement was still before parliament, and meant to affect it.

baillie-anabaptism-the-true-fountaine-of.blurb: The sequel to his Dissuasive, arguing that Anabaptism is the root from which Independency, Brownism, Antinomianism and Familism have all grown, and that the sects of the present day are the continental radicalism of the previous century in English dress. The genealogy is the argument, and the practical conclusion is against granting toleration to the Independents on the ground that the rest come with them.

baillie-errours-and-induration-are-the-g.blurb: A fast sermon printed with its occasion in the title, taking error and hardness of heart as both the sins of the time and the judgement upon them. Baillie preached in London as a Scottish commissioner, and the pulpit here does the work of his controversial writing: the errors are those of the sects, and the induration is the failure to suppress them.

baillie-ladensium-autokatakrisis-the-can.blurb: The Canterburians convicted out of their own mouths. Baillie assembles the printed statements of Laud and the divines who wrote with him, on ceremonies, on the altar, on the Roman church and on the powers of the crown, and argues that the sum of their avowed opinions is a design to carry the churches back toward Rome. It appeared as Scottish resistance to the prayer book was becoming open war, and the method throughout is quotation.

baillie-satan-the-leader-in-chief-to-all.blurb: A sermon on the opposition raised against the rebuilding of Zion, preached before an English audience by one of the Scottish divines then in London and printed with its occasion in the title. The text is applied directly to the present: those who obstruct the reformation of the church are doing another's work.

baillie-the-life-of-william-now-lord-arc.blurb: An examination of the career of William Laud, going through his principal actions and their consequences while he lay in the Tower and before his trial. It is not biography in any neutral sense but a case assembled against a living man, drawing on his own writings and on his dealings with Scotland, and it should be read alongside Baillie's other attacks on the Canterburian party.

baillie-the-tryal-and-process-of-high-tr.blurb: The record of the trial of Robert Baillie of Jerviswood for high treason, with the doom of forfeiture pronounced against him. Jerviswood was a Covenanting laird accused of complicity in the plotting against Charles II, and is not the Robert Baillie of Glasgow whose controversial writings this collection otherwise gathers. The document is a legal one: indictment, process and sentence.

baillie-the-unlavvfulnesse-and-danger-of.blurb: An argument that episcopacy limited by law and hedged with conditions is no more lawful than the unlimited kind, since the office itself lacks warrant, with a short reply appended to the answers then being made. It was printed in a year when moderate men on both sides were proposing a bishop bounded by his presbyters, and Baillie writes to close that door.

cawdrey-a-late-great-shipwrack-of-faith-.blurb: A sermon on apostasy, occasioned by a particular defection that Cawdrey treats as a shipwreck of faith following upon a wounded conscience. The aim is pastoral and the tone admonitory, and the case is used to warn the hearers rather than to argue a controverted point.

cawdrey-a-sober-ansvver-to-a-serious-que.blurb: A reply to a question put in print by Giles Firmin, minister at Shalford, on a point then dividing the presbyterian and congregational ministers of the eastern counties. Cawdrey answers briefly and, as his title insists, soberly. The pamphlet is one turn in a longer exchange and reads best beside the piece it answers.

cawdrey-diatribe-triplex-or-a-threefold-.blurb: Three connected exercitations, on superstition, on will worship, and on Christian liberty, written against Henry Hammond, who had used those heads to defend the ceremonies of the English church against their puritan critics. Cawdrey's concern is the regulative principle in practice: what may be added to worship, by whose authority, and where liberty ends. The exchange with Hammond ran on through several further volumes.

cawdrey-family-reformation-promoted-in-a.blurb: A sermon on Joshua 24:15 urging the reformation of households, printed together with short catechisms fitted to the capacities of different members of a family. The pairing is the point: first the argument that a nation is reformed household by household, then the actual instruments for doing it, in a form a master of a family could use at home.

cawdrey-independencie-a-great-schism-pro.blurb: An answer to John Owen's tract on schism, arguing that Owen's definition, which confined schism to divisions within a particular congregation, was framed to acquit the Independents of a charge they could not otherwise escape. Cawdrey holds that separation from the parish churches of England is schism in the older and catholic sense, and presses Owen on the fathers and on his own earlier positions. The first of Cawdrey's two books in this exchange.

cawdrey-independency-further-proved-to-b.blurb: The second round against John Owen, replying to Owen's review of his own tract on schism. The ground is unchanged, whether withdrawal from the parochial churches is separation, but the argument is now conducted largely over what each man had already written, which is the usual fate of such exchanges. Read it after the earlier book rather than on its own.

cawdrey-sabbatum-redivivum-or-the-christ.blurb: A full treatise on the sabbath, written with Herbert Palmer, defending the morality of the fourth commandment and the observance of the Lord's Day against the divines who had written for liberty in the Book of Sports controversy. It handles the institution at creation, the change of the day, and the manner of keeping it, and stands as the most detailed statement of the sabbatarian case from the Assembly's side.

cawdrey-the-account-audited-and-discount.blurb: A vindication of the threefold Diatribe on superstition, will worship and Christian liberty against Henry Hammond's answer to it, running to more than four hundred pages of point by point accounting. The metaphor of the title is carried through, Hammond's reckoning audited and found short. A reader should come to it having read the Diatribe first, since almost nothing here is stated afresh.

cawdrey-the-depths-of-satan-discovered-o.blurb: A short piece charging the Jesuits with a design against religion, offering observations upon a discovery said to have been made of their counsels. It belongs to a durable genre of the period in which every unwelcome turn in English affairs is traced to a Roman hand, and it is best read as a specimen of that genre.

cawdrey-the-good-man-a-publick-good-1-pa.blurb: A sermon on the good man as a public benefit both in what he suffers and in what he does, preached to a public auditory and printed with the occasion named in the title. The doctrine is plain and the use practical, the work of a Westminster divine preaching in a year when public men were being asked to justify themselves.

cawdrey-the-inconsistencie-of-the-indepe.blurb: A short piece arguing that the Independent way is inconsistent both with Scripture and with itself, set out in a threefold discourse. The second charge is the sharper one: Cawdrey sets the congregational writers against each other and against their own earlier positions rather than only against the presbyterian case.

cawdrey-three-sermons-viz-1-a-commission.blurb: Three sermons printed together, one on a commission for an assize granted to the saints, one on the discovering of the close hypocrite, and a third. The titles indicate the method, a doctrine stated under a figure and then applied at length, and the pieces are gathered as a volume rather than composed as one.

cawdrey-vindici-clavium-or-a-vindication.blurb: A vindication of the power of the keys into the hands of those Cawdrey held to be their rightful owners, the presbytery rather than the congregation, written against John Cotton's account of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The question is who may admit, censure and exclude, and the argument turns on whether the power Christ gave was given to the whole body of the faithful or to the elders.

cawdrey-vindiciae-vindiciarum-or-a-furth.blurb: A further round against John Cotton, the M.J.C. of the title, undertaking to show his contradictions on the power of the keys and on church government. It follows Cawdrey's earlier Vindiciae and answers what Cotton had said in reply; the method is to set passages from Cotton beside each other and let the inconsistency stand as the argument.

maynard-a-memento-to-young-and-old-or-th.blurb: Practical divinity addressed to the two ends of life, the young man to be put in remembrance and the old man to be admonished, described on the title page as the work of an eminent divine. This is John Maynard the minister rather than the parliamentary lawyer of the same name whose speeches are also gathered here. The matter is pastoral throughout: the shortness of life, the duty of early repentance, and the danger of a religion put off.

maynard-a-sermon-preached-to-the-honorab.blurb: A fast sermon before the House of Commons, printed with the day of its delivery in the title as such sermons ordinarily were. The monthly fast before parliament was a standing institution of the war years, and the sermons preached at it form a running commentary on the political and religious business then in hand.

maynard-a-shadovv-of-the-victory-of-chri.blurb: A sermon before the House of Commons taking an Old Testament deliverance as a shadow or type of the victory of Christ, and applying it to the state of the parliament's cause. Typological preaching of this kind was the ordinary idiom of the parliamentary fast, and the printed sermon carries its occasion in the title.

maynard-a-speech-spoken-by-an-honorable-.blurb: Seven pages reporting a speech in the House of Commons upon the delivery of a petition from the city. The speaker is Sir John Maynard, knight of the Bath and a Presbyterian member, not the divine of the same surname. It is parliamentary reporting from the year in which the army and the Presbyterian interest came to an open breach.

maynard-a-speech-spoken-in-the-honourabl.blurb: A speech in the Commons by Sir John Maynard, knight of the Bath, printed as spoken. Maynard was one of the Presbyterian members who resisted the army's proceedings and was imprisoned for it, and speeches like this were put into print to carry the argument outside the House to a reading public.

maynard-an-answer-to-a-printed-paper-dis.blurb: Not by Maynard but against him: an answer to a printed paper he had dispersed, itself a petition of the owners of land in the fens. The dispute is over the drainage undertaking and who was to hold the land it created. The two papers should be read together, the petition first, since this one answers it clause by clause.

maynard-england-s-champion-or-the-iust-m.blurb: A single-sheet celebration of Sir John Maynard's refusal to submit to the proceedings taken against him, printed while he was in custody. It is partisan ephemera from the quarrel between the Presbyterian members and the army, and it does little more than press the claim its title makes.

maynard-londons-liberties-or-a-learned-a.blurb: An argument of law made before the lord mayor and court of aldermen concerning the liberties and franchises of the city of London, printed in the years when those liberties were under attack in the courts. The speaker is Sir John Maynard the serjeant at law, an eminent common lawyer, not the divine. What it offers is a lawyer's case from charters and precedent.

maynard-mr-maynards-speech-before-both-h.blurb: A speech at a conference of both Houses in March 1641, made in reply to something said on the other side and printed at once, as the speeches of that spring generally were. The speaker is John Maynard the lawyer and member for Totnes, one of those managing the proceedings against the earl of Strafford, which were then at their height.

maynard-the-beauty-and-order-of-the-crea.blurb: Meditations on the six days of creation, natural and allegorical, taking the order of Genesis 1 as the frame. The natural meditations consider the works themselves and the allegorical read them for spiritual instruction, a method with a long history in Christian writing on the hexaemeron. This is John Maynard the minister, and the book is practical divinity rather than natural philosophy.

maynard-the-copy-of-a-letter-addressed-t.blurb: An eight-page pamphlet printing a letter said to have been addressed to the Jesuit rector at Brussels and found among papers taken with captured Jesuits. Documents of this kind were printed to prove a Roman design behind the king's party, and their authenticity was disputed at the time. The name attached to this record belongs to the printing rather than to the composition.

maynard-the-humble-plea-and-protest-of-s.blurb: A single sheet in which Sir John Maynard, knight of the Bath and a member of the Commons, pleads and protests against the proceedings taken against him. It belongs with the other papers he put out in the same year, when the Presbyterian members were being removed and imprisoned, and it is a document of that quarrel rather than of divinity.

maynard-the-law-of-god-ratified-by-the-g.blurb: A treatise on the harmony of the doctrine of faith with the law of God, arguing that the gospel establishes rather than dissolves the moral law. The question was live because the antinomian writers of the preceding decades had pressed the opposite, and books of this kind answer them by showing the law's continuing use for the believer. This is John Maynard the minister, and the work is doctrinal and practical rather than controversial in form.

maynard-the-picklock-of-the-old-fenne-pr.blurb: Heads of several speeches by Sir John Maynard on the fen drainage project, printed under a title that treats the undertaking as a lock to be picked. The quarrel is over the draining of the level and the lands assigned to the adventurers in return, and Maynard argues for the commoners against the undertakers.

melanchthon-commentarii-in-romanos.blurb: Melanchthon's full commentary on Romans, the fruit of repeated lecturing on the epistle and the place where his account of justification is worked out at length: righteousness imputed and not infused, faith as trust in the promise, and the forensic language of acceptance before God that would pass from here into Lutheran orthodoxy. The rhetorical method is on display throughout, the scope of the epistle stated first and the argument of each section traced before the text is expounded.

melanchthon-confessio-augustana-apologia.blurb: The confession presented to Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, drafted by Melanchthon on behalf of the evangelical estates, together with the much longer Apology he wrote to answer the Roman confutation of it. The confession's articles of doctrine and its articles on abuses are stated with deliberate restraint; the Apology drops the restraint, above all in its long article on justification, which is the fullest statement Melanchthon made of that doctrine in confessional form.

melanchthon-de-ecclesiae-autoritate.blurb: A short book on the authority of the church and on the writings of the ancients, setting out how far the fathers are to be received and on what terms. Melanchthon's answer is that the church has authority to teach but not to establish articles of faith apart from Scripture, and that the fathers are themselves witnesses who ask to be judged by the same rule. It is the standing evangelical account of tradition, argued by a man who had read the fathers closely.

melanchthon-de-officio-principum.blurb: An argument that the command of God requires princes to remove ecclesiastical abuses, written against the objection that the reform of the church is no business of the civil magistrate. Melanchthon grounds the duty in the prince's office as custodian of both tables of the law, which made the Lutheran territorial reformation defensible in conscience and not merely convenient in practice.

melanchthon-disputationes-theologicae.blurb: Theses propounded for disputation in the Wittenberg schools across some two decades, printed as a set. Academic disputation was how theology was taught and examined, and these are the propositions to be defended rather than the arguments themselves, which makes them terse and often the clearest short statements of Melanchthon's position on a given head. The span of years means the collection also registers his changes of mind.

melanchthon-enarratio-ecclesiastes.blurb: A brief exposition of Ecclesiastes, treating Solomon's book as a discourse on the government of human affairs and the limits of counsel and industry rather than as a counsel of despair. It is short and evidently meant for the lecture room, and it is characteristic of Melanchthon's way with the wisdom books, which he read for moral and political instruction as much as for doctrine.

melanchthon-ethicae-doctrinae-elementa.blurb: The elements of ethical doctrine together with an exposition of the fifth book of Aristotle's Ethics, the book on justice. Melanchthon taught moral philosophy as the exposition of natural law, distinguishing what reason can know of the divine law from what only the gospel supplies, and this is the mature form of that teaching: philosophical ethics kept within its own province and denied any part in justification.

melanchthon-explicatio-proverbiorum.blurb: An exposition of the Proverbs of Solomon, read as instruction in the ordering of life, household and commonwealth. Melanchthon valued the book as a meeting place of philosophy and Scripture, since much of what it teaches reason can also see, and the exposition is short and sententious in keeping with its subject.

melanchthon-in-danielem-prophetam.blurb: A commentary on Daniel, expounding the visions of the four monarchies as a history of empire running down to the present, with the Turkish power and the papacy found in the later prophecies. Melanchthon's chronological interests are much in evidence, and so is the sense that the last age is far advanced. The book was written for readers who took the prophecies as a guide to their own century.

melanchthon-in-ioannem-annotationes.blurb: Annotations on the Gospel of John from Melanchthon's early years of lecturing, brief notes on the text rather than a continuous commentary. They belong to the period just after the first edition of the Loci, when he was applying the same rhetorical analysis to the gospels, and they show him working out how the doctrine of faith is to be drawn from a narrative text.

melanchthon-liber-de-anima.blurb: A revised textbook on the soul, following the order of Aristotle's De Anima but filled out with a great deal of anatomy and physiology drawn from Galen and from the dissection-based work of Melanchthon's own century. The result is a natural philosophy of the human being that treats the body in detail and then argues from the soul's powers to its immortality and to the knowledge of God available to reason. Generations of Lutheran students learned psychology from it.

melanchthon-moralis-philosophiae-epitome.blurb: An epitome of moral philosophy in short compass: its subject, the natural law and its precepts, the virtues, and the relation of philosophical ethics to the gospel. Melanchthon insists that philosophy governs civil life and says nothing of the remission of sins, a division he maintained against those who wanted either to abolish philosophy from the schools or to let it teach righteousness before God.

melanchthon-scholia-in-colossenses.blurb: Scholia on Colossians, notes on the epistle in the form Melanchthon favoured for his early exegesis, and among the first of his Pauline commentaries to be printed. The letter's warnings against human traditions and elementary observances gave him occasion to state the evangelical case on works, ceremonies and Christian liberty, and much of the book's interest lies in those excursions.

twisse-discovery-jacksons-vanitie.blurb: An attack on Thomas Jackson, the Oxford divine whose commentaries on the creed were read as carrying Arminian doctrine under a show of philosophical depth. Twisse holds the perspective glass of his subtitle up to Jackson's writing and argues that what looks profound is confused, and that the confusion serves an account of grace made to depend on the will of man. The scholastic apparatus is heavy and the length considerable.

twisse-dissertatio-de-scientia-media.blurb: A disputation against middle knowledge, the Jesuit doctrine that God knows what any free creature would do in any possible circumstance, and knows it prior to any decree of his own. Twisse argues that this leaves the divine foreknowledge dependent on the creature and providence without a ground, and he pursues the doctrine through the Jesuit authors and the Arminians who had taken it up. It is the most technical thing he wrote.

twisse-doctrine-synod-of-dort-and-arles.blurb: A reply to a piece that professed to set out the doctrine of the Synod of Dort in its practical consequences, printed with Twisse's consideration of it. The method is to state the doctrine as the adversary represents it in practice and then to show where the representation departs from what was decreed, chiefly on reprobation and on whether an absolute decree makes God the author of sin.

twisse-vindiciae-gratiae.blurb: Twisse's answer to Arminius, and the largest of his Latin works: a vindication of the grace, power and providence of God against the Examen of Perkins and the Arminian account of predestination. He defends a supralapsarian order of the decrees, argues that the divine will is the first cause of all things without being the author of sin, and works through the objections in scholastic form, distinction by distinction. Heavy going, and the standard reference for his position.

twisse-briefe-catecheticall-exposition-c.blurb: Four short catechisms taken together as an exposition of Christian doctrine, from the future prolocutor of the Westminster Assembly during his years as a parish minister at Newbury. The division into four suggests a graded course, the shorter forms for children and the fuller for those further on, which was the ordinary practice in English catechizing.

twisse-christian-sabbath-defended-agains.blurb: A defence of the Christian sabbath against the antisabbatarian writers of the day, arguing the perpetual obligation of the fourth commandment and the observance of the Lord's Day as a divine institution rather than an ordinance of the church. Twisse handles the change of the day, the question of what rest requires, and the appeal to Christian liberty by which his opponents set the day loose.

twisse-discovery-d-iacksons-vanitie-pers.blurb: A book-length examination of Thomas Jackson's commentaries on the creed, which Twisse read as carrying an Arminian doctrine of grace under a show of philosophical profundity. The perspective glass of the title is the method, each passage held up until its obscurity can be seen for what it is. Jackson's account of faith, election and perseverance takes the weight of the attack, and the treatment runs to more than seven hundred pages.

twisse-doctrine-synod-dort-arles-reduced.blurb: An answer to a piece that claimed to show what the decrees of Dort amount to when reduced to practice. Twisse states the charge as his adversary made it and then considers it, the argument turning on reprobation and on whether an absolute decree leaves men without ground for exhortation, prayer, or the use of means.

twisse-doubting-conscience-resolved-answ.blurb: A reply to a question that had been put in print as a perplexing one, with Twisse undertaking to resolve it. The form is that of a case of conscience, a doubt stated and then answered by distinctions. A reader comes to it for the way an academic divine handled a practical difficulty rather than for systematic treatment.

twisse-morality-fourth-commandement-as-s.blurb: An argument that the fourth commandment binds Christians as moral law and not merely as a Jewish ordinance, delivered by way of answer to a treatise on the sabbath then in print. The occasion was the campaign against sabbath observance conducted with court support in the previous decade, and Twisse writes as one of the divines who took that campaign to be an attack on the substance of religion.

twisse-riches-gods-love-unto-vessells-me.blurb: An answer to Samuel Hoard's God's Love to Mankind, published after Twisse's death: a defence of the consistency of God's love toward the vessels of mercy with his absolute reprobation of the vessels of wrath. Hoard had argued that the Reformed decree makes God cruel and unjust, and Twisse answers through the whole length of the book, on the order of the decrees, the sufficiency of Christ's death, and the justice of condemning for a sin permitted rather than caused.

twisse-scriptures-sufficiency-determine-.blurb: An argument against the Roman controversialists that Scripture is sufficient to determine all matters of faith, and that a Christian may find in it what he must believe without recourse to an infallible living judge. The case is made in the usual order: the perspicuity of Scripture, the office of the church as witness rather than judge, and the regress that follows from making the church the ground of faith.

twisse-treatise-mr-cottons-clearing-cert.blurb: John Cotton's paper clearing certain doubts about predestination, printed together with Twisse's examination of it. The two men agreed on the substance of the Reformed doctrine and differed over how it should be stated and applied, particularly on the place of preparation and on what may be said to the unconverted. The volume prints both sides, and lets an English supralapsarian be seen reading a New England divine on their common ground.

robert-baron-of-st-andrews-philosophia-t.blurb: A treatise on philosophy as the handmaid of theology by a Scottish divine who taught divinity at Aberdeen. Its subject is the philosophical questions that keep surfacing inside theological disputation, which Baron argues should be handled soberly and in their proper subordinate place rather than either ignored by divines or allowed to set the terms. The disputed points of metaphysics and logic are taken up as divinity requires them.

palmer-the-soule-of-fasting-or-affection.blurb: A short piece on the affections proper to a day of solemn fasting and humiliation, arguing that the outward abstinence is a body without a soul unless the heart is engaged. Palmer was a member of the Westminster Assembly, and public fast days were then a fixed part of the national calendar. Nine pages.
